title: PrintChum
pitch: Your companion for print-ready photos.
about_excerpt: Your companion for print-ready photos. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP in PrintChum Inspiration Walk into almost any computer shop or small photo studio in the Philippines and ask for ID photos, and you’ll probably see the same routine. The operator opens a general-purpose photo editor, drops your photo onto a blank page, resizes it until the ruler looks about right, copies it over and over, lines everything up into rows, and prints it on short bond paper. Then comes the ruler. If that 1 × 1 photo turns out to be 0.94 inches instead, the whole sheet goes into the bin and they start again. That routine bothered me enough to build something. The first problem was accuracy. The photo might be the correct size in the file, but that doesn’t mean it will come out at the correct size on paper. Print drivers can silently scale a page to fit, turning an exact 1 × 1 into something slightly smaller. In a workflow where a few millimeters can mean reprinting an entire sheet, “close enough” isn’t good enough. The second problem was privacy. Once someone uploads a photo, it often ends up sitting in a Downloads folder on a shared computer. There’s usually no retention policy, no cleanup step, and no reason for that photo to still be there after the customer leaves. So PrintChum started with two simple rules: physical dimensions should be a contract the software keeps, and a customer’s photo shouldn’t outlive the session that needed it. Then I found this WebMCP Challenge, and a idea clicked. If the job is simply “put eight 2 × 2 photos on A4 with a 5 mm margin,” the operator shouldn’t have to click through five different panels to make that happen. They should be able to just say what they need. Why PrintChum Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Lots of moving parts: Creating print-ready photo layouts involves more than just choosing a paper size. Users may need to configure margins, spacing, photo sizes, quantities, aspect ratios, auto-rotation, nameplates, background colors, and other settings that depend on one another. WebMCP makes it possible to turn a simple natural-language request into a series of structured tool calls that handle these settings together. Keeping photos private: PrintChum is designed to keep customer portraits and ID photos inside the browser. Instead of sending sensitive images to an external MCP server, WebMCP runs directly in the user's browser tab through document.modelContext . The agent can work with layout information and call tools locally without needing access to the actual photo files. Reliable, precise layouts: Physical printing requires accurate measurements, so approximations aren't good enough. WebMCP lets the agent query PrintChum's predefined settings and use its deterministic 2D packing engine to calculate the layout instead of trying to guess coordinates or dimensions. How WebMCP Improves the User Experience Configure layouts using intent: Users don't have to work through several dropdowns, sliders, and dialogs just to create a layout. They can describe what they want in plain language, such as: "Set up 4 passport photos and 8 1x1 photos on A4 paper with a 5mm margin and a royal blue background." The agent can then configure the workspace automatically. No need to leave the editor: The browser agent works directly inside the active PrintChum editor. When a tool is called, the changes are applied to the live Zustand store, so users can immediately see the updated layout on the canvas. Clear permission boundaries: The 17 tools are separated into three permission levels: read for inspecting information and presets, write for changing the layout and styling, and execute for actions such as generating a PDF or opening the print dialog. This keeps potentially impactful actions explicit and under the user's control. What People and Agents Can Do Together WebMCP also makes some workflows much faster than they would be through the traditional UI. Build complete print packages from one request: A user could say: "Prepare an application package for my university ID with student number 2026-0481 at the bottom, 2 copies of 2x2 in, and 4 copies of 1x1 in on Letter paper." The agent can look up the available settings, configure the nameplate, add both photo sizes, and select the correct paper size in a single interaction. Optimize layouts when something doesn't fit: If a layout spills onto a second sheet, the agent can inspect the layout summary and identify what's causing the overflow. It can then suggest or apply changes such as auto-rotation or adjusted margins to try to fit everything onto one sheet. Create reusable studio templates: Print shop operators can also use natural-language commands for repetitive setup tasks. For example: "Save this current layout as our standard Rush Visa Package." This makes it easier to create and reuse custom service sets without manually repeating the same configuration. How WebMCP Was Implemented PrintChum uses WebMCP as a progressive enhancement built across four main layers: Model Context Bridge ( lib/webmcp/ ): This layer checks whether document.modelContext is available and provides safe fallbacks when it isn't. It also uses AbortController to manage the lifetime of browser-tab-bound tools and clean them up properly when they're no longer needed. Strict Zod Input Schemas ( features/editor/webmcp/input-schemas.ts ): Each of the 17 registered tools has a runtime-validated Zod schema. Tools such as configure-paper , add-photo-size , configure-nameplate , and set-background use these schemas to validate incoming arguments before they're passed into the application. The schemas are then converted to JSON Schema at the WebMCP boundary. Shared Single Source of Truth ( features/editor/webmcp/handlers.ts ): The handlers take the validated tool arguments and pass them into the existing Zustand actions and PrintChum's calculateLayout() engine. This means AI-driven changes use the same layout calculations and PDF export pipeline as changes made manually through the UI. React Lifecycle Integration ( components/editor/webmcp-registration.tsx ): A React client component registers the WebMCP tools when the editor loads and removes the registration when the editor is unmounted. This keeps the tool lifecycle tied directly to the editor instead of leaving registrations active after the workspace is gone. title: Openings — Agent Native Job Discovery
pitch: A workspace where you and an in-browser AI agent work the same job board resolving official career portals, extracting real openings, and scoring them against your resume, all via WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
A workspace where you and an in-browser AI agent work the same job board resolving official career portals, extracting real openings, and scoring them against your resume, all via WebMCP tools.

 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Openings — Agent-Native Job Discovery 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Job hunting is a two-surface problem. Aggregators like Naukri and Indeed are great at telling you which companies are hiring — but they surface only a fraction of each company's roles and bury the link to the company's own careers page, where the complete, current list actually lives. Bridging those two surfaces — take a company name, find its official portal, extract every matching role, repeat, twenty times over — is exactly the repetitive, multi-step web work a human dreads and an agent is good at. 

 We wanted to see what happens when an AI agent and a human work the same job board, live, on the same page — not a chatbot bolted on the side, but an agent driving the app's real functions. That's the promise of WebMCP , and job discovery turned out to be a perfect fit. 

 What it does 

 Openings is an agent-native job-discovery workspace. You start from a Naukri search or just name a few companies, and Openings: 

 
 Resolves each company's official career portal — skipping aggregators, going straight to the source (e.g. stripe.com/jobs , ramp.com/careers ). 
 Extracts the real, current openings from that portal via a server-side crawl and structured extraction. 
 Scores every role 0–100 against your resume , with honest strengths, gaps, and tailored bullet rewrites that reframe your real experience — never fabricated. 
 Keeps everything on one shared board with a live activity feed . 
 

 The key idea: nothing is "agent-only" or "human-only." Every WebMCP tool is a thin wrapper over the same store action a UI button calls, so the human and the agent drive identical code and see one shared state . Paste companies and click Import, or ask the agent to do it — the outcome is the same. The agent handles the breadth (opening twenty portals in seconds); the human keeps the judgment (shortlisting, accepting resume edits). 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS — a split-screen workspace (pipeline board on the left, resume canvas + activity feed on the right). 
 State: a framework-agnostic observable store ( src/store.ts ) shared by both the UI and the agent, persisted to the browser's localStorage . 
 WebMCP: five tools registered on document.modelContext.registerTool(...) — import_from_naukri , discover_company_jobs , add_job_to_board , match_with_resume , list_board_jobs . Each is a thin wrapper over a store action, and registration no-ops gracefully when WebMCP is absent, so the app still works as an ordinary web app. 
 Serverless: Netlify Functions handle portal resolution, career-page crawling, structured extraction, and resume scoring — so no API key ever touches the browser, and the SPA and functions share one origin (which WebMCP requires). 
 AI: a pluggable provider facade — Mistral ( mistral-small-latest , default) or Google Gemini ( gemini-3.6-flash ) — behind one generateJson contract, swappable with a single env var. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 JS-only career SPAs that can't be crawled. We added a knowledge-based fallback that returns the model's best-known roles, clearly flagged unverified in the activity feed so the user is never misled. 
 Structured-output reliability. Gemini's JSON mode could stall, so we built a circuit breaker : structured output is throttled independently, and if it trips, the helper falls back to plain-text JSON and skips the slow path on later calls. 
 Bounded latency. SDK retries are capped and every attempt is timed out, so a request never hangs for minutes during a live demo. 
 One-origin constraint. WebMCP requires the SPA and its functions on the same origin — we run everything through netlify dev locally so the tools connect exactly as they do in production. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A genuinely shared human–agent surface : one code path, one board, no "demo-only" wiring. 
 Going past aggregators to the official source for every role, with a direct link on every card. 
 Honest resume scoring with truthful bullet rewrites — sharpening real experience, never inventing it. 
 A backend that stays resilient even on free API tiers, so the demo doesn't fall over. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how you architect an app: the moment your UI actions and your agent tools are the same functions , "agentic" stops being a bolt-on and becomes the natural shape of the code. The hard part isn't exposing tools — it's designing a store clean enough that a button and an agent can safely share it. 

 What's next for Openings — Agent Native Job Discovery 

 
 More ATS adapters (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby) for deeper, verified extraction. 
 Application tracking and status stages on the board. 
 Multi-resume profiles and per-role tailoring. 
 Swappable persistence (Netlify Blobs) so a board can sync across devices.

title: LabSpace Atlas
pitch: Tell LabSpace Atlas what you need. It shapes the room, knows where everything lives, and guides you from question to ready workspace—while every important decision remains yours.
about_excerpt: Tell LabSpace Atlas what you need. It shapes the room, knows where everything lives, and guides you from question to ready workspace—while every important decision remains yours. Like Comment Story Updates LabSpace Atlas connects synchronized 2D and 3D planning with inventory and exact-location evidence. Improved UI for Layout Editor and Inspector WebMCP UI Pop-up / Judges Mission and Use Cases Suggestions WebMCP UI Pop-up / Evidence Tracker with export WebMCP UI Pop-up / Tools UI Facility Viewer (For Research Institutions and University usage) Spatial Index Update With Agent Progress Tracker Confirmation Window for Human Approval / Reviewed Mode Process Tracker in Action / Go With The Experiment Step-by-Step Process Tracker Records Holder The New Universal Inventory Studio Storage Workspace - Assigning Items Location Couldn't Be Easier New Assets Detailed Viewer Spatial Index Update With Agent Placement Tracking Inspiration I am a biologist and researcher, not a programmer. LabSpace began with a familiar laboratory question: “Where is it?” The answer might be in a spreadsheet, on a label, or in the memory of the person who last used it. A floor plan tells me where a cabinet stands; an inventory list tells me a reagent exists. Neither necessarily helps me find the right drawer and get ready to work. I started LabSpace to bring those pieces together. For this challenge, I wanted to go further: could I describe what I need to a browser agent, watch it work with my actual laboratory, and still make the decisions myself? That became LabSpace Atlas. What it does Atlas is where I can plan a room, keep track of its contents, and find what I need for work. The three tasks in the video are just the tip of the iceberg. I chose them to tell one short story, not to limit what you can try. Once you have connected the browser agent, please make it your own. Open the Inspector's Tools tab and explore all 24 tools: plan an annex, inspect nested storage, check a room for placement problems, or validate a move before approving it. Change the requests, combine the tools, and bring a question from your own lab. The same checks and approval controls still apply. Here is the short journey I chose for the video: Build a place to work. I ask for a 38-square-metre researcher office, R-003, with three desks and matching chairs, doors and windows in specific positions, a locker, and basic safety equipment. After I enable Fast Draft, one request takes it through building, furnishing, and checking the layout. I can then inspect and edit the room in 2D and 3D. Record new stock. I ask it to add alpha-glucosidase and lipase, with quantities and expiry dates. Atlas prepares both entries together and waits for me to approve them inside the app. I have not specified a shelf, so it leaves storage unassigned. Later, I can add a photograph from my computer or an image URL, and place the record on a named shelf or drawer in the Storage workspace. Find the materials, then the workspace. I give the agent my DPPH checklist: reagent, pipette holder, 100 and 200 microlitre tips, and a microplate reader. It looks for those records, points out anything missing or uncertain, and recommends a work surface. I also ask about chloroform separately to show what happens when an item has no recorded match. That check does not add chloroform, methanol, or any other solvent to my checklist. Before the collection starts, I see the items and final workbench in Atlas's Review collection dialog. After I approve, I can move through the locations with Next and Previous, see supported drawers or doors open, and finish at the chosen bench. The guide stays below the scene, leaving the location details in view. I confirm each step myself. Following the guide does not deduct stock or approve the experiment. Why WebMCP fits this problem “Put this on the bench” sounds simple until there are several benches, different heights, and equipment already in the way. The agent needs to know which object I mean and whether the placement makes sense. The same is true when I ask for something inside a particular drawer. The 24 WebMCP tools give the browser agent those details: record IDs, dimensions, storage paths, stock information, and the results of the app's checks. It works with the same room and records that I see on screen. I can describe a task without knowing every menu or field. The browser agent interprets my request, and Atlas carries out the supported actions and checks. If the host supports voice, I can speak the request there too. There is no second chatbot inside Atlas. I also wanted to decide how much freedom to give it. Every session starts in Reviewed mode. I can switch on Fast Draft for a validated new blank room and its complete first blueprint, but that choice lasts only for the session. Inventory changes, moves, resizes, and changes to existing rooms still need review; a failed check cannot silently pass. The agent cannot enable Fast Draft or approve its own proposals. What existed before, and what I added for this challenge I brought an existing project to this challenge: LabSpace AI . It already had the synchronized 2D/3D editor, inventory and storage, a Spatial Index, placement checks, and local saving. I am not claiming that foundation as new challenge work. For the challenge, I added the WebMCP tools and the workflows around them: room and annex planning, inventory and layout proposals, Reviewed and Fast Draft modes, checklist assessment, and a collection guide with approval and exportable evidence. Getting that to work also meant revisiting the cameras, storage views, assets, and tests. A tool call succeeding was not enough if I still could not understand its result on screen. The repository's annotated pre-webmcp-2026-08-27 tag and dated implementation notes preserve that boundary. How we built it I came up with LabSpace from problems I encountered as a researcher and shaped its development into LabSpace Atlas. I defined the laboratory workflows, supplied reference photographs and equipment requirements, and directed the product design and AI-assisted development. I tested the application myself, set priorities for fixes, and kept revising layouts, cameras, and equipment models when they did not make sense in a real lab. I also planned, recorded, and edited the demonstration video. GPT-5.6 helped me turn those observations into requirements, and Codex helped implement, debug, test, and document the application. I repeatedly tested the results myself and pushed back when an arrangement, camera view, or equipment model did not make sense as a researcher. Hilal helped with end-to-end regression testing and debugging, including checking how natural-language requests worked through WebMCP. Eman helped review the designs and created reference diagrams to guide our work with GPT-5.6 Sol. She also checked for inconsistencies as the designs developed. The application uses React and TypeScript, React Konva for 2D planning, and Three.js/React Three Fiber for 3D. Detailed assets use optimized Blender-authored GLBs. Node and Express serve the Render-hosted app; SQLite supports local development, while each public visitor's workspace persists in that browser's IndexedDB. Under the hood, document.modelContext.registerTool registers each tool with an input schema and an execution handler. The handlers call the same search, planning, validation, and staging functions used by the app. I can inspect the calls and my decisions in the Inspector, or export them to review later. Atlas has no embedded language model and requires no application API key. Tool results are shared with the browser agent the user connects; that host's privacy policies and usage limits still apply. Challenges I ran into Getting the right record was only half the problem. Early camera views could leave it hidden behind a wall or another object. I refined the viewpoints around actual storage faces, with closer, slightly elevated framing and temporary wall cutaways. Trust also needed more than a confirmation sentence in chat. Inventory and collection approvals became visible product dialogs, with cancellation and recorded decisions. The collection guide was reorganized so it no longer competed with the evidence panel. Even connection setup mattered. Tools being registered on the page did not mean a new conversation had discovered them. Atlas now separates “connect once” from the shorter task prompts and makes that first step explicit. Accomplishments I am proud of The moment that matters to me is when the answer leaves the chat and appears in the room: the office is there, the inventory entry is saved after my approval, or the drawer I was looking for opens in front of me. There are 115 searchable assets that can be viewed from all sides, along with storage maps, item photographs, and reversible editing. title: Ghosted
pitch: A tracker that admits when someone's gone silent — on a job application or an unpaid invoice — and gives your agent real tools to do something about it.
about_excerpt: A tracker that admits when someone's gone silent — on a job application or an unpaid invoice — and gives your agent real tools to do something about it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We started this project somewhere else entirely — a manual leads board, then a subscription-cancellation demo — before realizing the actual differentiator was never going to be what task an app does. In 2026, almost any "paste something in, get a useful result" idea already exists as a free tool somewhere. What's structurally different about WebMCP is that your own agent — not a company's closed AI — acts live on a page you're both looking at, with real, verifiable consequences. That reframing sent us looking for a task where a live, shared, mutable record is the whole point, and where the friction is something an agent can genuinely remove rather than just reformat. Job hunting fit immediately: 53% ghosting, ~40 applications per interview, and existing trackers (Teal, Huntr) are well-built but entirely passive — you re-enter every application by hand and check staleness yourself. None of them can be handed to an agent. What it does Ghosted is a two-tab tracker — Job Applications and Freelance Invoices — exposing eighteen WebMCP tools total, because being ignored by an employer and being ignored by a client on an invoice are the same mechanic wearing a different name. Job applications (9 tools): log_application , get_application / list_applications / search_applications , update_status (applied → interviewing → offer / rejected / ghosted / withdrawn), flag_stale_applications (mark every application silent for 21+ days as ghosted in one call), get_followup_reminders , get_pipeline_summary (response rate, ghost rate, average response time), get_leverage_opportunities (cross-references live applications worth notifying once one reaches offer stage). Freelance invoices (8 tools, mirroring the same shape): log_invoice , get_invoice , list_invoices , search_invoices , update_invoice_status , flag_stale_invoices , get_invoice_followup_reminders , get_payment_summary . A human can do everything by hand too, but the point is watching an agent do the tedious parts (bulk staleness checks, cross-referencing an offer against a dozen other processes) in one call, live, on the same page: a card briefly highlights when its status just changed. The eighteenth tool, get_daily_digest , spans both trackers in one call — every stale item, every follow-up worth sending, any offer worth leveraging — rendered as a "Today" panel above the tabs. How we built it Single static HTML/CSS/JS file, no backend, no build step, localStorage for persistence, WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext . Colors follow a CVD-validated dark palette rather than hand-picked hex values, including a proper ordinal-ramp funnel chart for pipeline stage counts. Every tool was tested in a headless Node harness (mocked document.modelContext and localStorage ) before being verified live in a real browser. Challenges we ran into Three real bugs surfaced during testing: a pause action with no way back to "active" in an earlier iteration; a "leverage opportunities" tool that initially recommended notifying companies that had already gone dark for 45+ days; and, when the invoices tab was added, a "Reset demo" handler that replaced the entire saved-state object instead of just its own slice — which would have silently wiped every invoice. All three were caught by actually running the tools end-to-end, not by reasoning about the code in the abstract. Accomplishments we're proud of Getting to a concept that's differentiated by mechanism , not by chasing an ever-shrinking list of "nobody's built this exact task" ideas — after real competitive research (Rocket Money, Bobby, Monarch, MessyData, Teal, Huntr, and a direct GitHub search for other WebMCP entries), the honest answer was to lean into what the mechanism itself offers — an outside agent operating live, transparently, on shared state — and prove it generalizes by pointing it at a second real, quantified problem (freelance payment ghosting) with the same shape. What we learned That "no one else does this" is close to impossible to find for simple utility apps in 2026 — the right question is whether the mechanism (agent + human sharing live, mutable, verifiable state) does something a closed, single-shot AI feature structurally cannot. What's next Tracking interview dates directly to catch scheduling conflicts, letting a browser-extension style capture job postings or invoices straight from the page an agent is already reading, and recognizing recurring clients from a pasted bank or PayPal statement. title: Squirrel Board
pitch: Capture ideas with your agent. Decide what deserves to become work.
about_excerpt: Capture ideas with your agent. Decide what deserves to become work. Like Comment Story Updates Squirrel Board is a shared ideas backlog where AI agents can preserve and retrieve ideas that emerge during conversation, while humans retain explicit authority over priority and commitment. Inspiration Some of the best ideas appear while we are trying to do something else. That happens especially often in sustained conversations with AI. A side observation turns into a useful connection, a research question, a possible article, or the seed of a future project. Chat history is a poor backlog, but stopping to copy and organize every idea breaks the conversation. Chasing every idea immediately is worse. We wanted a collaboration pattern that protects both curiosity and focus: Capture first. Triage later. Do not turn every squirrel into a project. Squirrel Board gives the human and agent one inspectable place to preserve emerging ideas without confusing interesting with committed . What it does Squirrel Board is a public demonstration backlog with a normal human-facing web interface and four WebMCP tools. An agent can: capture a new idea with a title, why it might matter, and optional context; list the current backlog, optionally filtered by status; inspect one idea and its current fields; and propose a change to an idea's status, next action, or notes. A proposal does not silently modify the idea. It appears in a pending-review area where the human can approve or reject it. Approval updates the idea and writes the decision and reason to a visible decision log. Humans can also select Triage on any idea card to set its status, next action, and notes directly. That human-authored change requires a reason and enters the same decision log; managing the backlog never depends on first asking an agent to propose the desired action. The human remains responsible for deciding what becomes active work. How we built it Squirrel Board is built with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Cloudflare-compatible server output, and D1-compatible SQLite persistence. The top-level page registers four JavaScript WebMCP tools: capture_idea list_ideas get_idea propose_update Tool inputs are narrow, side effects are explicit, and results include enough information for the agent and human to verify what happened. Human actions and WebMCP tools reuse the same application routes and persistent data. The app contains no AI model or internal chat interface. The visiting agent is already the intelligence; the site supplies structured actions, shared durable state, and human review. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Without Squirrel Board, ideas born in AI conversations tend to suffer one of two fates: They remain buried in chat history and disappear. They derail the current work because preserving them becomes an immediate project. Squirrel Board separates capture from commitment. The agent can preserve the idea at the moment it appears, then help the human retrieve and revisit it later. The human can inspect every item, see its provenance, directly triage it, and explicitly accept or reject proposed changes. That combination supports curiosity without surrendering focus or authority. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP is fundamental to the experience rather than an alternate control surface added for the contest. The useful moment often occurs inside an AI conversation: the agent recognizes that an idea is worth preserving before the human wants to interrupt the current task. With WebMCP, the agent can capture that idea directly into the live page's structured backlog instead of guessing its way through visual controls or asking the human to copy text manually. Both participants then work with the same visible state: The agent contributes attention, structure, retrieval, and suggestions. The human contributes ideas, judgment, timing, priority, and authority. The result is not “AI manages projects for the human.” It is a durable collaboration boundary: the agent can help ideas survive; the human decides which ideas get a life. Challenges we ran into The most important design challenge was not technical. It was deciding what the agent should not be allowed to do silently. We deliberately separated propose_update from authoritative changes. That kept the product's collaboration model honest and made human approval visible rather than ceremonial. We also treated real WebMCP interoperability as the first feasibility gate. Before broad implementation, we proved the complete path in ChatGPT's in-app browser: the agent called capture_idea , the record persisted, and the human saw it appear on the board. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is the primary interaction mechanism, not a decorative contest feature. The complete capture, retrieve, propose, approve, direct human-triage, and decision-log loop works on the public deployment. The application preserves an explicit boundary between agent contribution and human authority. The public demo deliberately omits deletion from its UI and WebMCP: without authentication or record ownership, either would allow any visitor to erase shared data. A secret-protected operator command provides exact-ID and QA-prefix cleanup outside the public collaboration surface. The product has a clear real-world audience and workflow despite the deliberately playful squirrel metaphor. We resisted building authentication, embeddings, semantic search, notifications, teams, integrations, research analytics, or a rodent economy. What we learned Formal prompts are useful when the target is known. Conversation is often where the target is discovered. Squirrel Board grew out of noticing that collaborative conversations produce valuable side ideas through micro-feedback, correction, connection, and synthesis. Those ideas need somewhere to go that is durable but does not imply immediate commitment. We also learned that a good human-agent product can be defined as much by authority boundaries as by capabilities. The question is not merely “What can the agent do?” It is “What should remain a proposal until the human decides?” Hands-on testing also exposed an alternate-write-path defect: the human forms enforced text limits while the initial agent routes did not. Harmonizing server-side validation across both paths reinforced a practical lesson from the product itself: a constraint in one interface is not yet a system constraint. What's next for Squirrel Board Squirrel Board is a focused MVP for a broader class of lightweight tools designed around deliberate human-AI collaboration, from idea capture through planning and execution. Possible next directions include private workspaces, search and filtering, richer relationships between ideas, exports, and research instrumentation for studying how ideas emerge and evolve during sustained collaboration. Those are intentionally not part of the hackathon build. First, we capture the squirrels. Then we decide which ones deserve projects. title: AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun! — Our First Mission Together
pitch: Escape a lab together with AI through WebMCP, powered by Gua—my game UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity.
about_excerpt: Escape a lab together with AI through WebMCP, powered by Gua—my game UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Title image play scene image Inspiration WebMCP is usually discussed as a way for AI agents to interact with websites. I wanted to explore what would happen if that interaction extended into a game running in the browser: could a human and an AI enter the same game world, take on different roles, and complete a mission together? I have been developing Gua , a UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity. Gua was created to make game UI tests easier to build. Its structured, reliable actions also provide a foundation for AI agents to interact with games. This project originally started as a sample game for demonstrating what Gua could do. For the WebMCP Challenge, however, I wanted to explore a more playful idea: what if a human and an AI could share the same game and work toward a common goal? That idea became AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun!—a cooperative escape game in which a human player and an AI agent work together to escape from a laboratory. WebMCP exposes the game’s capabilities to the AI through the browser, while Gua connects those actions to the running game. What it does This is not a game where the AI only gives you hints. The human controls the field operative, while the AI observes authorized semantic and spatial state and operates designated control systems. They share one running game, but they have different information and abilities. By working together and taking actions in the game, you solve its puzzles and escape from the laboratory. To start playing, open the game in a WebMCP-enabled browser and tell your AI agent: Let's play this game together using WebMCP: https://link1345.github.io/gua-sample-actiongame/ The AI agent can then access the actions exposed by the game and join you in the escape. The AI does not rely on screenshots or visual guesswork. Through WebMCP and Gua, it can understand selected semantic information exposed by the game, such as the player’s position, distances to obstacles, the state of doors and hazards, and designated UI elements. The AI uses this structured information to assess the current situation, choose an appropriate action, and coordinate with the human player. The game controls exactly which information and actions are available to the AI, allowing it to participate as a game-world agent without exposing the entire internal state. How we built it I have been developing Gua, a UI testing and automation library for Godot and Unity inspired by Playwright's design principles. For this project, I extended Gua so that semantic game UI actions—such as pressing buttons and entering text—can be exposed through WebMCP and invoked by an AI agent. The game itself is built with Godot and exported as a regular web game. When it runs in the browser, WebMCP exposes the available actions to the AI agent, while Gua translates each requested action into an operation inside the running game engine. This architecture allows a human player and an AI agent to interact with the same game without rebuilding it as a conventional web application. Gua and its native Godot and Unity automation support existed before the challenge. During the submission period, I added the reusable WebMCP adapter, the Godot Web bridge, player-facing observation boundaries, browser validation, and this cooperative reference game. Challenges we ran into Before this project, Gua was designed primarily for automating native game builds. Adding WebMCP support was not simply a matter of exposing the existing testing API in a browser. A UI testing client may need detailed information about the entire interface. An AI agent playing a game, however, should receive only the state and actions intentionally made available to it. I therefore needed to support a new browser-facing interface while keeping the agent-facing surface limited and explicit. The solution came from Gua's existing architecture. Its core automation logic was already separated from its external interfaces, so I could add WebMCP as a new adapter and reuse the same semantic UI operations. The adapter exposes only the intended game actions and translates them into existing Gua operations, without spreading browser-specific code throughout the core library. As a result, the existing native automation behavior remained largely unchanged. This project became a practical test of Gua's architecture and showed that it could support a new AI-agent use case without requiring a major rewrite. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that this project produced more than a one-off WebMCP game integration. I added a reusable WebMCP path to Gua, allowing a Godot web game to expose selected semantic state and actions to an AI agent without rebuilding the game as a conventional HTML application or hard-coding every browser tool into the game itself. AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun! demonstrates that architecture in a real cooperative experience. The human and AI share the same running game, but each has different information and abilities. The AI is not limited to offering advice from outside the game: it can observe authorized game state, operate designated systems, and coordinate directly with the player. I am especially proud of the deliberately narrow agent-facing surface. WebGL controls are not automatically exposed as browsable DOM elements, and Gua reveals only the semantic state and actions permitted by the game. Human-only controls can remain outside the agent-facing projection, while agent-specific actions do not need to appear in the visible interface. Raw input is disabled by default, further reducing unintended interaction paths. This is not a complete security sandbox, but it provides game developers with a practical capability boundary for AI participation. The result is both a playable human–AI cooperative game and a reusable foundation for exploring other agent-native experiences in game engines. What we learned Implementing WebMCP taught me that connecting an AI agent to a game involves more than simply registering browser tools. The more important challenge is designing the boundary between the game and the agent: deciding which game states the agent needs, which actions it should be allowed to perform, and how those actions should be described clearly. I also learned that Gua's semantic UI automation model maps naturally to WebMCP. Operations originally designed for automated testing—such as pressing a named button or entering text into a specific field—can also become structured tools that an AI agent can understand and invoke. This changed how I think about Gua. It is not limited to running UI tests; it can also act as an interaction layer connecting human players, AI agents, and games. Finally, adding this capability without a major rewrite demonstrated the practical value of keeping the automation core separate from game-engine and browser integrations. Building the game also showed how a growing game can expose more actions and world objects than an agent needs at one moment. To keep the interaction focused, I extended Gua so agents can narrow the available actions to their current situation and look only at nearby world objects. This demo has a small action set, but its AI can now focus on the doors, hazards, and mission areas around the field operator. Because these capabilities live in Gua’s reusable interaction layer, the same approach can scale to larger Godot and Unity games without redesigning their WebMCP integration. What's next for AI Lovey-Dovey Kyun-Kyun! This project is already available as an open-source Godot sample for Gua. Rather than developing it into a commercial title, I will maintain it as a small, reproducible reference implementation of a human–AI cooperative game built with WebMCP and Gua. Gua supports both Godot and Unity. This sample demonstrates the Godot Web integration, while the reusable semantic model provides a foundation for future WebMCP-enabled experiences across supported engines. title: HALCYON — a rescue for two crew: you and your agent
pitch: You're the last awake crew member. Your agent is the ship computer. A WebMCP co-op puzzle game that neither human nor agent can finish alone.
about_excerpt: You're the last awake crew member. Your agent is the ship computer. A WebMCP co-op puzzle game that neither human nor agent can finish alone. Like 1 Comment Story Updates landing page first step Inspiration Every famous ship computer is a villain. HAL locks the pod bay doors. We wanted the opposite: a ship computer you trust with your life — because it's your own agent. When OpenAI framed the WebMCP Challenge as "an app that becomes meaningfully better when people and their agents can use it together," we took it literally: HALCYON is a game that is not merely better together — it is impossible alone . What it does You are the last awake crew member of the ISV Halcyon , drifting after a micrometeorite storm. Your agent — ChatGPT or Codex in a WebMCP browser — becomes the ship computer through tools the page registers with document.modelContext . Six chapters take the ship from dark hull to jump-home, and each one is built on a different WebMCP capability: Contact — tool discovery: you throw the breaker, the agent must catch the boot handshake inside the surge window. Manifest — read-only tools: the agent knows what broke; only you can see which hatches still open. Power — JSON-schema inputs + structured errors: the agent routes amps against hidden minimums, self-correcting from machine-readable brownout errors, while you re-seat the physical fuses. Antenna — dynamic registration: you align the dish by ear ; lock-on registers new comms tools into the live page. Two-Man Rule — human confirmation as a mechanic: the agent times the arm from telemetry; you hold both vent handles at once. WebMCP's sensitive-action philosophy, playable. Burn — orchestration: an interleaved launch checklist, then a flight-recorder replay of everything your crew did together. How we built it The game about a human-agent crew was built by a human-agent crew . Claude helped create the original design spec and implementation plan. Keelen's autonomous development loop, powered by OpenAI Codex, implemented much of that plan through CI-gated pull requests on self-hosted runners. We then used Codex and ChatGPT directly to finish the remaining work, diagnose live-play issues, and complete the recorded Chrome/WebMCP playthrough. The final app uses no frontend framework or backend and has zero runtime dependencies: TypeScript + Vite, SVG scenes, synthesized WebAudio, and a typed WebMCP registry with validation, rate limits, and coaching errors. Challenges The hard problem is asymmetry integrity : an agent can read the DOM, so "human-only" information cannot be text. We split the channels — audio pitch and motion for the human, tool-returned data (never rendered) for the agent — and gated hard state changes inside tool execute functions with no UI equivalent. What we learned Tool design is level design. A good inputSchema is a puzzle boundary; a good structured error is a hint system; readOnlyHint is dramatic irony. And an error message written for an agent ("give life_support at least 18A and route again") is the best tutorial text we have ever shipped. What's next A shared starmap: every crew that completes the rescue lights a beacon all players can see. More ships, more capability chapters as WebMCP grows. I collaborated with Claude, ChatGPT, and Keelen’s autonomous agent loop to turn the design into a working WebMCP game. I playtested every chapter as the human crew member, identified UX and sequencing problems, guided fixes through CI, and completed the production deployment and demo. Regulatory intelligence for humans and AI agents, powered by WebMCP: search, retrieve, and compare Singapore/MAS requirements through one shared interface.

 Story

 Inspiration 

 I built RegVista because regulatory research is still surprisingly manual. You search for a document, open a few PDFs, work out which version is current, and then repeat the process when you need to compare requirements. I wanted to explore what changes when the regulatory website itself can be used by an AI agent. 

 What it does 

 RegVista MAS SG is a small regulatory-intelligence MVP focused on Singapore/MAS material relevant to digital payment token services. You can search the registry, open individual records, see their metadata and official MAS sources, and compare two records side by side. The same capabilities are exposed to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 The app is intentionally lightweight: HTML, JavaScript and a small curated regulatory dataset, with three WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_regulations 
 get_regulation 
 compare_regulations 
 

 The tools are registered directly in the browser using the WebMCP Imperative API. 

 The key workflow is simple: 

 search → identify the right records → retrieve or compare them 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was working with an emerging browser standard while keeping the experience useful for a normal human user. I also wanted to avoid making the project look like an AI chatbot bolted onto a regulatory database. The agent should be able to use the same underlying capabilities as the human. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I got the full flow working end to end: a live regulatory registry, a deployed public site, and three working WebMCP tools that an agent can discover and use. I am also particularly proud of the fact that the project remains simple enough to understand end to end while demonstrating a practical use case for the emerging agent-native web. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP makes the boundary between a website and an AI agent more blurry. Instead of asking an agent to figure out how to navigate a UI, the site can tell the agent exactly what it can do. That feels particularly useful for structured domains like regulatory research. 

 What's next for RegVista MAS SG 

 This MVP is intentionally narrow. The natural next steps would be expanding the regulatory registry, supporting more jurisdictions and regulatory domains, improving document-level retrieval, and enabling richer agent-assisted research workflows. The broader idea is RegVista as an agent-accessible regulatory intelligence layer, with MAS Singapore as the starting point.

title: OpenWebOS
pitch: OpenWebOS uses WebMCP to let agents discover website capabilities, collaborate with humans, execute real actions, and create together—safely and transparently.\n
about_excerpt:
OpenWebOS uses WebMCP to let agents discover website capabilities, collaborate with humans, execute real actions, and create together—safely and transparently.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web was designed for humans to click, read, search, and fill out forms. AI agents can increasingly understand web content, but understanding a website is not the same as being able to work with it. 

 We were inspired by a simple question: 

 What if websites weren't just pages that agents could read, but environments where agents could actually work alongside us? 

 OpenWebOS explores that future. Instead of replacing the human with an autonomous agent, we wanted to create a shared space where humans express goals, agents discover capabilities, tools perform actions, and humans remain in control. 

 WebMCP gave us the opportunity to turn that idea into a working experience. 

 

 What it does 

 OpenWebOS is an agentic web workspace powered by WebMCP. 

 A user starts with a natural-language goal—for example: 

 
 "Create a sustainable 3-day weekend plan for two people under $500." 
 

 The agent then discovers the capabilities exposed by the website and uses WebMCP tools to: 

 
 Search available options 
 Retrieve details 
 Compare and rank choices 
 Calculate budgets 
 Propose decisions to the user 
 Create and update shared artifacts 
 Organize results on a collaborative canvas 
 Save and export the final result 
 

 The important difference is that the agent isn't simply reading the page or generating a response. 

 It can interact with the website through structured capabilities. 

 OpenWebOS also provides an Agent View, allowing users to see the tools available to agents, and a Safety Center that makes permissions, approvals, and tool activity transparent. 

 The result is a new interaction model: 

 Human intent → Agent discovery → WebMCP tools → Shared state → Human + Agent creation 

 

 How we built it 

 We built OpenWebOS as a modern web application with a WebMCP-first architecture. 

 The frontend provides the shared workspace, agent activity stream, tool registry, collaboration canvas, approval dialogs, and Agent View. 

 At the core is a dedicated WebMCP tool layer. Website capabilities are exposed as structured tools with defined schemas, validation, permissions, and execution handlers. 

 Our architecture is: 

 Human → OpenWebOS UI → Agent Orchestrator → WebMCP → Website Tools → Shared Workspace 

 We created tools for searching, comparing, ranking, calculating, creating artifacts, updating the workspace, saving state, summarizing, and exporting. 

 Gemini provides the intelligence for understanding user goals, selecting appropriate agent roles, generating artifacts, and explaining decisions. 

 We also created deterministic demo data so the core experience remains reproducible without depending on external services. 

 For safety, every tool is classified by capability and risk. Read operations can execute directly, while actions that modify shared state can require explicit human approval. 

 The application is designed to run in a WebMCP-enabled environment such as ChatGPT's in-app browser or a compatible Chrome environment. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was designing around a technology that represents a new interaction model rather than simply integrating another API. 

 We had to think about two different users at the same time: 

 Humans need clarity and control.
Agents need structured capabilities and predictable schemas. 

 That led us to separate the Human View from the Agent View and make the WebMCP tool registry a first-class part of the product. 

 Another challenge was deciding how much autonomy to give agents. An agent that can modify a workspace without permission can be convenient, but it can also create unexpected behavior. We therefore introduced explicit tool classifications, validation, activity logs, and human approval for consequential actions. 

 We also had to design graceful fallbacks because WebMCP availability depends on the browser environment. The application remains usable when WebMCP isn't available while clearly communicating when full agent interaction is enabled. 

 Finally, we had to make the technology understandable visually. Instead of hiding WebMCP behind the scenes, we made tool discovery and execution visible so a judge can immediately see what is happening. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that OpenWebOS doesn't treat WebMCP as a checkbox. 

 WebMCP is the foundation of the experience. 

 We built a working tool registry that turns website capabilities into structured actions that agents can discover and use. 

 We're particularly proud of the shared collaboration model. The agent doesn't simply return a wall of text. It can contribute structured artifacts to the same workspace the human is using. 

 We're also proud of the transparency layer: 

 
 Visible WebMCP capabilities 
 Agent activity history 
 Tool schemas 
 Permission boundaries 
 Human approval 
 Shared agent/human state 
 Audit-style execution logs 
 

 Most importantly, OpenWebOS demonstrates a different vision for the web: 

 The agent doesn't leave the website to perform work somewhere else. The website itself becomes part of the agent's working environment. 

 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building for agents is fundamentally different from building only for humans. 

 A good human interface communicates through visual hierarchy, buttons, menus, and natural interaction. 

 A good agent interface needs something different: 

 clear capabilities, structured inputs, predictable outputs, explicit permissions, and reliable state. 

 WebMCP made us think about websites as programmable environments rather than static destinations. 

 We also learned that human control becomes more important as agents become more capable. The goal isn't necessarily maximum autonomy. 

 The better goal is: 

 the right amount of autonomy, with the right amount of transparency. 

 This led us to design OpenWebOS around collaboration rather than replacement. 

 

 What's next for OpenWebOS 

 OpenWebOS is currently a prototype exploring what an agent-native web could look like. We see several directions for the future. 

 First, we want to expand the tool ecosystem so websites can expose richer capabilities—not only search and content tools, but workflows, transactions, creation tools, and domain-specific actions. 

 Second, we want to enable cross-site agent collaboration , where an agent can discover capabilities across multiple WebMCP-enabled websites and compose them into a single workflow. 

 Third, we want to build a richer permission system where users can define exactly what agents are allowed to do automatically and what requires approval. 

 We're also interested in persistent agent workspaces, reusable tools, agent-to-agent collaboration, provenance tracking, and standardized trust signals. 

 Our long-term vision is simple: 

 A web where humans describe what they want, agents discover what the web can do, websites provide the capabilities, and humans and agents create together. 

 OpenWebOS is our first step toward that future.

title: Playable Arena
pitch: Turn benchmark results into checks for your next agent run. Your agent tests the playable outputs; you judge what scores cannot.
about_excerpt: Turn benchmark results into checks for your next agent run. Your agent tests the playable outputs; you judge what scores cannot. Like 2 Comment Story Updates The benchmark already ran. Your product question didn't. WebMCP lets the agent continue from the published evidence. The benchmark has 22 detailed checks. The agent highlights the seven that matter for building a replayable strategy game. The agent opens four shortlisted games and completes the same level in each one using WebMCP. The games are shown without names or scores. The person plays the shortlist and chooses by feel and taste. The result becomes a concrete harness plan for the next run: what to preserve, which checks to add, and what to review with a human. The benchmark already ran. Your product question didn't. Playable Arena is a benchmark you can keep evaluating after the leaderboard is published. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench answer a valuable but fixed question: under the same tasks, checks, and agent setup, which system performed best? A developer choosing an agent for a real product asks a different question: which failure modes matter for my workflow, which output qualities feel right, and what should my agent test next? Arena preserves both kinds of evidence. Fixed checks measure whether each result meets the requirements. Playable outputs preserve qualities a score cannot settle: clarity, responsiveness, taste, and fit for a particular audience. WebMCP lets the AI agent in your browser continue that evaluation inside the same Arena page. It reads detailed evidence, updates the comparison you can see, and tests the same scenario across shortlisted outputs. You then compare them anonymously and make the subjective choice. Arena turns the fixed benchmark, live verification, and your decision into acceptance checks for the next agent run. The published score never changes. In the recorded demo, the agent reduces 22 published checks to seven relevant criteria, then completes the same six-move, three-push level in all four shortlisted builds. The result is not another leaderboard. It is a concrete plan for what the next run should preserve, test, and improve. The current release proves this pattern with five standardized browser-game tasks and 70 playable benchmark outputs . Today those outputs are produced by coding-agent configurations. The recorded demo uses Codex. Arena supports both WebMCP surfaces: document.modelContext in ChatGPT/Codex in-app browsers and navigator.modelContext in Chrome. The shared evaluation loop Read the evidence. The agent uses WebMCP to select the published checks that matter for the person's goal and updates the comparison they can see. Test the playable outputs. The agent opens the shortlist and completes the same level in each game. Agent Play verifies facts the table alone cannot: whether state is readable, actions are accepted, out-of-date actions are rejected, and a complete run works. Return the decision to the person. Arena presents the builds anonymously. The person plays them and chooses in the UI; only then are identities and published scores revealed. Improve the next run. Arena combines the fixed benchmark, live verification, and human choice into review stages and acceptance checks for the next agent run. Arena does not claim that one model or agent setup is universally best, and it never changes the published benchmark score. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP can automate a workflow end to end. Arena uses it to automate the parts of evaluation that should be automated: reading evidence, replaying scenarios, and gathering results, while keeping subjective judgment with the person. The agent and person work on the same live page. Tool calls update the visible filters, selected builds, game state, and anonymous review. The available tools change with context: benchmark tools appear on the benchmark, comparison tools on a task, game actions only for a compatible active build, and the result tool only after the person chooses. Arena never exposes a tool that lets the agent make the subjective choice or reveal identities early. Without WebMCP, the person would have to read a large result table, open builds one by one, manually repeat scenarios, copy observations into another chat, and reconstruct the comparison. With Arena, the agent handles breadth, interpretation, and repeatable checks while the person contributes the judgment automation cannot supply. The public benchmark stays fixed. What changes is how a developer can use it: what to preserve, what to borrow, which reviews to run, and what must pass next. How it works Arena registers tools for the current page with modelContext.registerTool(...) . When the person moves to another page, the old tools are removed and the relevant ones appear. Generated games run in isolated frames. A small arena.game.v1 agreement lets Arena expose only the actions owned by the current task. Each action carries a revision number, so an out-of-date action is rejected without changing the game. Anonymous review provides no tool that can choose or reveal on the person's behalf. Production runs on Cloudflare Workers. D1 stores anonymous review choices, while a separate Artifact Worker serves the playable builds from another origin. What existed before the challenge Before August 25, Arena was a private playable benchmark. It could give coding-agent configurations the same brief, score their results with fixed checks, keep the games playable, and let a person compare two results anonymously. It had no WebMCP tools, no way for an agent to inspect the detailed evidence or play the builds, and no path from a person's choice to checks for the next run. What I built during the challenge I built the missing end-to-end flow: Added page-specific WebMCP tools so the agent can read evidence and update the comparison visible to the person Added Agent Play so it can read live game state and repeat the same scenario across very different builds Rejected out-of-date actions without changing the game Connected agent-selected shortlists to a human-only anonymous choice and reveal Turned the fixed results, live verification, and human choice into review stages and acceptance checks for the next run Rebuilt the public Benchmark, task, comparison, evidence, navigation, and mobile experiences Separated the public product from private briefs, raw runs, credentials, and production history Added automated leak checks and deployed the UI, playable builds, and anonymous choice storage on Cloudflare I also expanded the working testbed from 3 tasks, 39 builds, and 13 agent configurations to 5 tasks, 70 builds, and 15 configurations . Adding LUMEN YARD and SHOAL meant more than adding two game cards. Each task needed one shared brief, fair checks for every build, independent runs across multiple agent configurations, playable published results, and a shared set of named actions so an agent could repeat the same scenario across implementations that shared no code. The new tasks expose differences in strategy, recovery, board readability, and action feedback that a top-line score alone cannot explain. I also added Antigravity + Gemini 3.8 Flash and fx + GPT-5.6 Sol configurations. HACKATHON.md records the plain-language before/after boundary and dated commit evidence. Try it Open Playable Arena in a WebMCP-capable in-app browser. No Arena account or MCP server URL is required. Ask your agent: Using this benchmark, what should I pay extra attention to when using Codex to build a replayable strategy game? Read the detailed checks, play the relevant candidates, and prepare an anonymous review. Do not choose for me. When the anonymous review opens, play the candidates and make the choice in Arena. The agent cannot make that choice for you. A trip-planning board where you and your AI agent edit the same live itinerary together no guessing, just real WebMCP tools.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Trip planning is one of those tasks that's part research, part taste. An AI agent is great at the research part searching activities, checking budgets but most agents have to guess their way through a website's buttons and forms to actually act on anything. WebMCP changes that: a site can just tell the agent exactly what it's allowed to do. We wanted to build something where that difference is immediately visible, not just theoretical 

 What it does 

 CoPlan is a shared trip-planning board. You can edit it by hand add activities, adjust costs, change the destination and an AI agent can edit the exact same board through real WebMCP tools (add_activity, search_activities, set_trip_details, and more). Whether a person or an agent makes a change, it lands on the same live itinerary, instantly. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. The backend is a set of simple API routes backed by in-memory state. On the frontend, we register WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(), and every tool's execute() calls the same API routes the human-facing UI uses one source of truth, no separate "agent path."

title: DayShift
pitch: When your day breaks, repair the plan — agents propose, DayShift verifies, and humans decide.
about_excerpt: When your day breaks, repair the plan — agents propose, DayShift verifies, and humans decide. Like Comment Story Updates What it does DayShift treats a disrupted day like a system that needs recovery, not a blank calendar that needs planning. When reality changes — for example a 50-minute bus delay — a WebMCP-aware agent can read the exact schedule, read non-negotiable constraints, simulate candidate recoveries, and stage a valid proposal. DayShift's deterministic constraint engine independently checks the proposal. The human then sees the trade-offs in the same web UI and is the only actor that can approve the change. Only after that approval can the agent commit it. Why WebMCP is essential The core experience depends on a shared semantic control surface. The agent does not infer calendar blocks from pixels or hunt for drag-and-drop controls. DayShift exposes schedule state and recovery operations directly as WebMCP tools, while the human sees and controls the same underlying state. The visible UI deliberately cannot stage or commit a recovery; removing WebMCP therefore breaks the complete recovery loop instead of merely making it slower. Better user experience The user can describe what broke in natural language and keep their decision authority. DayShift shows exactly what will move, which preference is sacrificed, and whether every hard constraint still passes. Staging is visibly different from committing, so there is no hidden mutation. What humans and agents can do together now The agent can explore the repair space quickly; DayShift enforces invariant truth deterministically; the human makes the final trade-off decision. Those three forms of authority stay separate while operating on the same live web application. WebMCP implementation DayShift registers six imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_day_state , get_constraints , report_disruption , simulate_recovery , stage_recovery , and commit_recovery . Read-only tools are annotated with readOnlyHint . Mutation tools use revision binding and deterministic re-validation. Human approval is deliberately absent from the tool surface, and commit_recovery fails closed unless the current proposal was approved in the UI. Invalid or duplicate schedule changes fail closed as well. Architecture principle Agent = proposal authority. DayShift = validity authority. Human = decision authority. title: disaster-safety-web-mcp
pitch: A WebMCP tool server for flood emergencies. Official JP/US/EU hazard feeds, first-principles flood modeling, and flood-aware evacuation routing — mapped, provenance-tagged, and agent-callable.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP tool server for flood emergencies. Official JP/US/EU hazard feeds, first-principles flood modeling, and flood-aware evacuation routing — mapped, provenance-tagged, and agent-callable. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Traditionally, AI agents have struggled during disasters to provide guidance that simultaneously ensures safety and accommodates individual needs. By leveraging WebMCP, an AI agent can dynamically access accurate, real-time disaster information and mapping data while understanding a person’s specific circumstances. Whether someone needs directions to a designated shelter, nearby high ground, or a destination compatible with mobility and transportation constraints, Untitled makes personalized evacuation guidance possible. We were inspired by the opportunity to move beyond one-size-fits-all evacuation orders and deliver practical, potentially life-saving support for each individual. ## What it does Untitled is an AI-powered disaster safety assistant that turns live geographic and emergency data into personalized evacuation guidance. Through WebMCP, the assistant can: Resolve natural-language place names while detecting ambiguous locations. Display flood forecasts and inundation zones on an interactive map. Find official evacuation shelters and classify them as clear, at risk, or unknown. Retrieve active alerts from authoritative agencies. Calculate walking or driving evacuation routes that avoid known flood hazards. Present map information as accessible text for screen readers and environments without WebGL. Rather than simply naming the nearest shelter, Untitled considers whether that shelter and the route leading to it are actually safe. ## How we built it We built Untitled as a TypeScript application running on Bun, with a MapLibre GL JS frontend and a Hono-based backend. The browser registers disaster-response capabilities directly through WebMCP, allowing an AI agent to discover and invoke tools such as geocoding, flood forecasting, shelter search, official-alert retrieval, map control, and evacuation routing. The backend integrates data from sources including the Japan Meteorological Agency, Japan’s Geospatial Information Authority, the US National Weather Service, MeteoAlarm, OpenStreetMap, Open-Meteo, and Copernicus services. Flood- aware routes are calculated using road-network data and dynamic hazard exclusions. We also developed hydrological modeling components for rainfall runoff, terrain-based inundation, river capacity, and flood-risk estimation. Every result carries provenance so the system can distinguish live observations, planning scenarios, cached information, and test fixtures. ## Challenges we ran into The greatest challenge was preventing the system from appearing more certain than its data justified. Disaster information can be delayed, incomplete, ambiguous, or temporarily unavailable, so we designed the application to report uncertainty explicitly instead of silently substituting a potentially misleading answer. Combining datasets was also difficult because each provider uses different geographic resolutions, update schedules, risk scales, and coverage boundaries. Flood forecasting introduced additional complications: some climate datasets are rate-limited, while Copernicus retrievals can take hours and must be managed as resumable jobs rather than ordinary requests. Mapping presented another subtle challenge. Data being present in application state does not necessarily mean it is visible on the rendered map. We therefore test the features that MapLibre actually draws after camera movement has completed. Finally, accessibility required us to create a synchronized text representation of every visual map feature so the experience would remain useful to people using screen readers or devices without WebGL. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Untitled provides an end-to-end workflow—from a natural-language request to hazard analysis, shelter evaluation, and a flood-aware evacuation route—through tools an AI agent can discover directly in the browser. We are especially proud of the system’s safety boundaries. Official alerts are preserved as attributed source material, ambiguous locations are not silently guessed, unavailable forecasts are not presented as “no danger,” and developer-only controls are completely excluded from the normal user experience. We also built a browser verification suite with 44 checks against the real application. It validates tool registration and invocation, error handling, accessibility, production-mode isolation, and what the map actually renders—not merely what the application intended to display. For Japan’s experimental flood-risk forecast, we achieved 98.5% exact level agreement in evaluated reference areas while documenting the more difficult flood-extent limitations honestly. That distinction reflects a principle that guided the entire project: in disaster response, trustworthy uncertainty is more valuable than impressive but misleading confidence. ## What we learned We learned that connecting an AI agent to live data is only the beginning. Useful disaster guidance requires provenance, freshness checks, spatial reasoning, uncertainty handling, and clear separation between observed hazards and planning scenarios. We also learned that “nearest” rarely means “safest.” A shelter may be close but located inside a hazard zone, and a destination may be safe while the route to it crosses floodwater. Most importantly, we learned that safety systems must test observable outcomes. A successful API response does not prove that a person can see the hazard, understand the warning, or follow the proposed route. Reliability has to be evaluated across the entire experience. ## What’s next for Untitled Next, we want to expand coverage to additional countries and disaster types, including wildfires, earthquakes, landslides, tsunamis, and extreme heat. We also plan to improve personalization for mobility needs, language preferences, family and pet evacuation, vehicle availability, medical requirements, and shelter accessibility. Offline and low-bandwidth support will make the assistant more resilient when communications infrastructure is damaged.
