title: AI House Helper
pitch: I want to be able to easily and in a fast way see how change in a room will impact whole house while taking into account garden planning
about_excerpt: I want to be able to easily and in a fast way see how change in a room will impact whole house while taking into account garden planning Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The idea came from a very real problem: I am starting to build a house. My own place to leave in like the thing that will stay there for the rest of my live. I received information about my plot, terrain and ground conditions in professional drawings and documents. The information was technically there, but I could not easily explore it myself. Even a simple question—such as moving the house, changing a window, comparing layouts or planning the garden was just impossible i can draw it on a piece of paper but aren't the tomatoes too close to the house or to terrace i have no idea because i can't see the scale. Traditional CAD understands geometry, but expects specialist knowledge. A conversational AI is easier to use, but normally cannot reliably understand or modify the real spatial model behind a drawing. I built this project to connect those two worlds. What it does House WebMCP is a browser-based spatial editor where a person and an AI agent can work together on an early house, site and garden concept. The application represents the project as structured building information rather than a decorative 3D model. It understands the site, terrain, buildings, storeys, slabs, rooms, shared walls, doors, windows, roofs, landscape zones, plants and garden fixtures. A person can inspect and measure the project visually. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the same underlying model and help with requests such as: Move the house and show me the result. Add or resize a window on a specific wall. Compare two possible layouts. Create a raised-bed kitchen garden near the house. Show the floor plans, elevations and sections. Analyse seasonal conditions and planting considerations. The agent never silently changes the project. Every proposed edit becomes a visible ghost variant . The user can inspect it, compare it with other alternatives, and explicitly apply or reject it. Committed changes can also be undone. The bundled demonstration is grounded in my real house-building context in Zielonki. It combines site and terrain information with geotechnical evidence, an editable climate profile, soil unknowns and conservative planting guidance. It is intended for early exploration and better conversations with professionals—not as construction documentation or a replacement for an architect or engineer. Why WebMCP This use case needs more than an embedded chatbot. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to interpret canvas pixels, guess what visual elements mean, or manipulate the page through fragile interface automation. It would not reliably know that an object is a shared wall, that a window belongs to that wall, or that changing a slab affects the spaces above and below it. With WebMCP, the website exposes structured, validated operations over its actual application state. The agent can inspect the project, use semantic references, propose a precise change, display the result inside the existing interface and ask the person for approval. This creates a form of collaboration that was previously difficult for someone without CAD experience: I can describe the outcome I want in ordinary language, while the application remains responsible for geometry, validation, visualization and project state. The human provides intent and judgment. The agent translates that intent into structured actions. The application makes the consequences visible and keeps the final decision with the human. How I built it The application is written in React and TypeScript , with React Three Fiber and Three.js powering the interactive spatial view. I created a semantic ProjectV2 model for buildings, storeys, shared slabs, wall graphs, polygonal spaces, hosted openings, roofs, platforms, landscape and planting objects. This model is shared by both the visual editor and the WebMCP tools, so agent actions use the same domain logic as human interactions. The current application exposes 23 WebMCP tools. They cover project inspection, building and landscape edits, seasonal analysis, architectural views, variant comparison, approval, rejection and undo. The tools are defined using Zod validation schemas. The same registry produces the runtime registrations, structured prompts and a searchable public tool manifest, helping prevent the documentation from drifting away from the implementation. For geometry, Manifold runs in a Web Worker and creates slabs and walls with real door and window openings. Rapier provides constrained editing previews, while three-mesh-bvh accelerates spatial queries. Zustand manages application state and IndexedDB provides local autosaving. Challenges I faced The largest challenge was moving beyond a visually convincing 3D scene and creating a model an agent could safely reason about. A building is not just a collection of boxes: walls are shared by rooms, openings belong to walls, slabs can serve more than one storey, and changes must preserve those relationships. Another challenge was designing safe agent interaction. Directly allowing an AI to mutate the committed model would be fast, but it would remove the user’s control. The ghost-variant workflow took more work, but it makes every agent action reviewable and reversible. Working with real site information also required care. Surveyed facts, professional observations, working measurements and design assumptions do not have the same level of certainty. I learned to preserve those distinctions instead of turning incomplete evidence into false precision. Finally, browser-based geometry can become computationally expensive. Moving Boolean geometry generation into a worker, caching results and carefully managing rendered resources were important for keeping the editor responsive. What I learned I learned that making an application agent-friendly is not simply a matter of adding tools to an existing interface. The underlying product needs clear domain concepts, explicit constraints and actions whose consequences can be inspected. I also learned that WebMCP is most valuable when the agent and the person genuinely share the same workspace. The interesting part is not that an AI can call a function. It is that it can understand live application state, propose meaningful work, show the result and return control to the person. Most importantly, building this project changed how I think about my own house-building process. I may still not know CAD, but I can now explore ideas, understand trade-offs and prepare better questions before speaking with architects and other specialists. What's next The next steps are to support controlled import of professional survey and building data, improve planning and environmental checks, and make it easier to share reviewed variants with architects, landscape designers and engineers. The long-term goal is not to replace those professionals. It is to give homeowners a clearer, safer and more accessible way to participate in the decisions that shape their future home. title: At Attin
pitch: Banking you can ask for — with authority you can see.
about_excerpt: Banking you can ask for — with authority you can see. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Banking still makes people translate a simple goal into menus, forms, account rules, and unfamiliar terminology. That friction hits older adults and first-time users hardest, but everyone feels it when a task becomes stressful or complex. We wanted AI to remove the translation work without removing the person’s authority. What it does At Attin is a complete single-user fictional-money bank: accounts, activity, payees, transfers, scheduled and recurring payments, cards and controls, savings goals, budgets, reports, notifications, disputes, trusted contacts, accessibility settings, and manual forms. Its in-site assistant is powered by Featherless and moonshotai/Kimi-K3 . A user asks for a banking outcome in plain language. The model selects one of 56 imperative WebMCP tools, while four visible form tools support browser-native agent interaction. The bank validates the request, prepares an exact preview, applies financial invariants, shows every consequence, and waits for a person. No agent request executes automatically. Every protected read and every mutation requires fresh visible confirmation. Higher-consequence actions require both YES and a new arithmetic challenge. Authorizations expire after 90 seconds, are single-use, bind to the exact preview and state version, and cannot be replayed. All money is fictional ATC, stored device-locally, with no cash value and no real payment rails. How we built it React, TypeScript, Vite, and React Router Browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool() One shared 56-operation descriptor layer for compatible browser agents and the in-site agent Featherless server proxy with Kimi K3; the provider key never reaches the browser App-owned prepare → confirm → commit coordination with cancellation, expiry, stale-state, and replay protection Integer minor-unit money, atomic writes, versioned local persistence, recovery, and append-only local agent audit OpenAI Codex, HyperFrames, Remotion, Kokoro TTS, Suno, and OpenAI Sites Why WebMCP matters At Attin does not add a deterministic intent parser. The model reasons; WebMCP publishes the bank’s real capabilities; the application owns authorization and execution. The same descriptors and confirmation boundary serve the embedded assistant and compatible browser agents. Challenges The hardest part was ensuring preparation could not leak protected data, and that registration, cancellation, retries, legacy persistence, linked savings reservations, balance floors, and dispute evidence all remained fail-closed. We built explicit invariants, version-bound authorization, single-pending-request coordination, and focused regression tests. Accomplishments 56 imperative tools and 4 visible form surfaces Confirmation for every agent read and change Step-up confirmation for critical actions A complete banking surface instead of a narrow proof-of-concept A working Featherless/Kimi K3 assistant with no direct bank-state access 141 automated tests plus lint, build, and Sites-worker verification High-contrast, low-cognitive-load UX with large text, keyboard focus, and reduced motion What we learned Trust improves when proposal, authorization, and execution are visibly separate. WebMCP gives models semantic access to application capabilities without forcing the application to surrender its policy boundary. What’s next Multi-user identity, passkeys, caregiver and small-business policy packs, privacy-preserving audit export, localization, and broader WebMCP conformance testing. Real-money connectivity remains out of scope until external security review. Try it Live app: https://at-attin.astronebulae.chatgpt.site ATC is fictional, device-local, and has no cash value. title: Superweb-mcp
pitch: SuperWeb gives one app two front doors, a React UI for people and WebMCP for agents. ChatGPT calls a tool, the catalog filters, and the human sees the same change.
about_excerpt:
SuperWeb gives one app two front doors, a React UI for people and WebMCP for agents. ChatGPT calls a tool, the catalog filters, and the human sees the same change.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 SuperWeb 

 Inspiration 

 Last semester ended and everyone went home. Before the group scattered I wanted a real camera to take proper photos of them, under $200, decent in low light, small enough that I would actually carry it. I said those requirements out loud in about eight seconds. Finding the camera took a night of tabs, filter dropdowns and reviews that all say the same thing. 

 That gap bothered me. I already knew what I wanted. The work was not deciding, it was operating a website. Amazon has more than 10,000 products in that category and half of them are the same thing with a different logo. 

 Agents are supposed to help with this, and mostly they do it by pretending to be a person. They read pixels, guess which button is the search box, click, wait, re-read. That works until the layout changes. It felt backwards to us. The site already knows what it can do. It should say so. 

 What it does 

 SuperWeb is a shopping app with two front doors into the same building. 

 A person uses the normal React interface. An agent comes in through WebMCP. Both talk to the same application state and the same APIs, so the two views never disagree. 

 When ChatGPT calls search_products , it is not hunting for a button. The page declares that capability with a name, a description and an input schema. The tool runs, the catalog filters, and a human watching the screen sees the same change happen live. Same for filter_catalog , compare_products , manage_cart and the rest of the tools the page exposes. 

 We also built a staff dashboard side with tools like get_metrics , breakdown_metrics , check_data_trust and start_report , because the shopping case is the fun demo but the boring case is the valuable one. 

 How we built it 

 The app is a React front end deployed on Vercel. The WebMCP layer sits alongside the UI and registers tools against the same state the components read from, which is the whole point. There is no second code path for the agent, no headless copy of the app, no scraping surface to maintain. A tool handler calls the same function a button calls. 

 Each tool declares three things. A name the model can reason about. A description written for a reader who cannot see the page. An input schema that rejects bad arguments before anything runs. 

 The demo film was cut in CapCut. Narration is text to speech, the guitar under the opening and the credits is a cover I recorded of 离开我的依赖 by 王艳薇. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Photos cannot travel through the tool call. This is the one that actually stopped us. Structured data moves through WebMCP fine. A user's photo does not. If I want to say "find me something that looks like this", there is no path for the image today. Multimodal input through WebMCP is unsolved and we could not work around it, only describe it honestly. 

 Exposing tools is easy. Explaining how they fit together is not. We got each individual capability declared quickly. Then we watched the model call them in an order that made no sense, because nothing in the schema says check_data_trust should come before start_report . A tool list is a vocabulary. It is not a grammar. We do not have a good answer for this yet, and I suspect it is the real open problem in this space. 

 Writing descriptions for something with no eyes. Our first tool descriptions were written like code comments, for a developer who can see the page. They were useless. Rewriting them for a reader with no visual context changed the behaviour more than any prompt engineering did. 

 Keeping the two views honest. Every time we let the agent path touch state through a shortcut, the UI drifted out of sync. Forcing every tool through the same functions the UI uses was slower to build and removed a whole class of bug. 

 What we learned 

 The interesting shift is not shopping. It is routine knowledge work. A manager asks why November revenue changed. Today that is searching dashboards, filtering data, checking quality, tracing anomalies and writing it up, and most of that is operating software rather than thinking. That part can move. The goal, the constraints, the exceptions and the final approval stay with the person, and should. 

 We also learned that the demo has to show the site doing something. An agent typing in a chat panel proves nothing. The moment that convinced people was watching the catalog filter itself while nobody touched the mouse. 

 What's next 

 Multimodal input, since that is the hard blocker. Some way to describe workflows and not just tools, which might be as simple as declaring ordering constraints between them. And if WebMCP connects one agent to one website, agent-to-agent protocols across several services are the obvious next question. We have not built that. Building this made it much easier to picture. 

 Try it: https://webmcp-superweb.vercel.app/

In an emergency, crucial information is often scattered across disparate systems- ranging from operatational incidents, officer training/currency/availability and asset management. I wanted to explore how an agent-native web could help first responders turn that fragmented information into coordinated, safe action. 

 What it does 

 Emergency Mesh unifies emergency-readiness and response data into a real-time operational network. Responders can use WebMCP-powered tools to run scenarios to challenge operational readiness, to locate resources, review incidents, coordinate safety without navigating complex interfaces. 

 How I built it 

 I built Emergency Mesh as a web application with a responder-focused (non-technical) interface and exposed its core actions through WebMCP. Structured tools let agents retrieve incident data, search available resources, update coordination tasks, and support responders through the same system people use directly. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was deciding how emergency data should be represented. Incidents, resources, locations, capacity, urgency, ownership, and status all change quickly—and need to make sense to both responders and agents. I designed a shared, structured model that preserves context and relationships while keeping the information clear enough to act on under pressure. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I created a cohesive experience where emergency officers and AI agents work from the same operational picture. Rather than adding AI as a chat layer, WebMCP is integrated into meaningful responder workflows: understanding incidents, finding resources, and coordinating action. Also the ability for 'war-gaming' to see how capabilities in my station would cope with AI generated scenarios. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that WebMCP works best when tools map to real user goals, have clear inputs and outcomes, and complement—not replace—human judgment. In emergency contexts especially, agent assistance must be transparent, structured, and safety-conscious. It must not be the decision maker but collate data in a meaningful and easy to understand way. 

 What's next for Emergency Mesh 

 Next, I want to add live data integrations, richer source validations, more data-source connectors, and scenario simulations that help communities and organisations prepare for emergencies.

title: doodleduo
pitch: Play the famous skribbl.io game with your agent
about_excerpt: Play the famous skribbl.io game with your agent Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of using websites, but most agent experiences still feel like work: fill out a form, search for something, click a button, complete a workflow. We wanted to explore a different question: What if a website was designed to play with an AI agent? DoodleDuo started from the simplicity of drawing games like Skribbl: one player draws, the other guesses. We replaced the second human with an AI agent and used WebMCP to give that agent a native way to see the game, understand its state, draw on the canvas, make guesses, and chat with the human. The result is a small experiment in human-agent play: two minds, one canvas. What it does DoodleDuo is a browser-based drawing game where you play directly with an AI agent. During a standard game, the human and agent take turns being the artist and the guesser. When you draw , the agent can: Read the current game state Request an image of the drawing canvas Interpret the drawing using a vision-capable model Submit guesses Chat with you during the game When the agent draws , it receives the word and creates the drawing using structured vector strokes through WebMCP. You then try to guess what it is drawing. The game includes: Easy, Normal, and Hard difficulty modes Timed rounds and scoring Alternating human/AI turns Custom word collections Custom 2–12 round games A cooperative "I draw every round" mode A local Doodlebot demo that works without an AI model A live conversation between the human and agent Tracking for WebMCP tool activity and canvas reads The important part is that the agent is not just clicking around the interface using coordinates. DoodleDuo exposes the game itself as a set of structured capabilities that an agent can understand and invoke. How we built it At the center of DoodleDuo is a normal browser-based drawing game built around an HTML canvas and a stateful game loop. We then added a WebMCP layer that exposes six tools: doodle_join — connects the agent to the game doodle_get_state — returns the current round, turn, timer, drawer, and scores doodle_get_canvas — gives the agent the drawing as a 1000 × 700 PNG along with optional stroke information doodle_draw — lets the agent draw validated vector paths onto the canvas doodle_guess — lets the agent submit a guess doodle_chat — lets the agent participate in the game conversation Instead of asking a vision model to reason over an entire webpage screenshot, doodle_get_canvas exports only the drawing canvas . The UI, secret word, controls, chat, and other potentially revealing information remain outside the image sent to the agent. For drawing, we took the opposite approach. Rather than having the agent simulate a mouse, the model sends structured strokes containing points, colors, and widths. The browser validates those strokes and renders them onto the canvas. We also built a JavaScript RPC bridge alongside the WebMCP interfaces so different browser-agent environments can interact with the game. For people who don't have a compatible agent connected, DoodleDuo includes Doodlebot , a completely local JavaScript demo player. It uses predefined procedural drawings and simple shape heuristics, so the core experience can be tried without spending model tokens. The production version is deployed on Cloudflare , giving us a fast, globally accessible deployment with very little infrastructure required for the game itself. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest problems was surprisingly not drawing — it was fair play . An AI browser agent can potentially see much more than a human player. If we simply gave the agent a screenshot of the webpage, it could accidentally read the secret word instead of interpreting the drawing. We therefore had to think carefully about the boundary between information the agent needs and information it can technically access . Our WebMCP tools intentionally omit the human's secret word and custom word list. The agent receives the canvas directly rather than a screenshot of the page, and it must request the canvas before making its first guess in a round. Another challenge was coordinating a real-time game with an asynchronous agent. Drawing, guessing, timeouts, skips, round transitions, and human actions can all change the state while an agent is reasoning. Every tool therefore has to validate whether an action is legal for the current turn instead of assuming the agent always has fresh state. We also had to handle two very different representations of a drawing: Pixels for understanding, vectors for creation. Vision models work naturally with an image of the canvas, while generating a drawing is much more reliable when the model can produce structured strokes rather than trying to control a mouse pixel-by-pixel. Finding that separation made the interaction significantly cleaner. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that DoodleDuo feels like an actual game rather than a WebMCP demonstration with a game wrapped around it. The WebMCP integration remains mostly invisible to the human player. You draw, guess, laugh at bad drawings, and compete for points while the agent interacts with the same game through structured tools. We're also proud that the project demonstrates several different agent capabilities inside one simple interaction: vision → reasoning → tool use → structured generation → conversation An agent can look at an image and guess what a human drew, then one round later receive a concept and generate its own drawing for the human to interpret. We also built a zero-model-token local demo, custom games, multiple difficulty levels, scoring, turn validation, secret isolation, and a detailed transparency page explaining exactly what information the AI receives. Most importantly, we built an experience where WebMCP isn't being used to automate a task. It's being used to create a new kind of interaction between a human and an agent. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that WebMCP is more interesting as an interaction layer than simply an automation layer . Giving an agent a tool like doodle_draw is fundamentally different from telling it to "move the mouse around the canvas." The tool describes the semantic action the website supports while the website remains responsible for validating and executing it. We also learned how important tool design becomes when the model is part of an interactive system. Small decisions — what state to expose, when a secret should be omitted, whether an image or vectors should be returned, and what actions should be rejected — have a large impact on how reliably an agent can participate. Another lesson was that WebMCP doesn't magically solve trust or security. A browser agent may still have access to screenshots, DOM inspection, or other browser capabilities. Applications need to explicitly think about what constitutes fair or safe agent behaviour instead of treating tool boundaries as a security sandbox. Finally, building DoodleDuo made one idea very tangible: Websites no longer have to be interfaces designed exclusively for humans. They can expose a second interface — structured specifically for agents — while both humans and agents interact with the same underlying application. What's next for DoodleDuo DoodleDuo started as a human-vs-agent drawing game, but we think it could become a much broader playground for testing how humans and browser agents collaborate. Next, we'd like to explore: Agent vs. agent matches , where two different models draw and guess against each other Multiplayer rooms , allowing humans and agents to form teams Agent tournaments , comparing how different vision models perform on the same drawings Replay mode , showing exactly which canvas observations, guesses, and tool calls happened during a round Richer drawing tools , including shapes, fills, layers, and more expressive brushes Shared WebMCP game primitives that could be reused to build other human-agent browser games Agent evaluation modes , turning DoodleDuo into a lightweight benchmark for vision, tool use, spatial reasoning, and multimodal interaction Longer term, we'd like to explore the idea behind DoodleDuo beyond drawing games: Built With chatgpt codex javascript react Try it out doodleduo.prompthabbit.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Private user Like Share this project: Updates Private user started this project — Sep 02, 2026 04:11 AM EDT

title: Never Ask Twice
pitch: The support site already knows. WebMCP lets your browser agent use that authorized context instead of asking you to repeat it.
about_excerpt: The support site already knows. WebMCP lets your browser agent use that authorized context instead of asking you to repeat it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Customer support sites can already know useful, authorized context about a customer: their service level, product setup, integrations, open issues, and escalation path. But an external browser agent normally does not have a structured, authorized interface to that state. It may guess from the page, fail to recover it, or push the work back to the person by asking them to repeat information the website already knows. Never Ask Twice makes that gap explicit: the support site already knows; WebMCP gives the browser agent a typed, session-bound capability to use that knowledge. What existed before this challenge Never Ask Twice existed before the WebMCP Challenge as a B2B support-memory agent powered by Qwen. It already stored and recalled scoped customer context across support sessions. The canonical pre-challenge baseline is commit c2997996bbd137a8acf7d08799e7d04b0c8dfd48 , committed before the WebMCP submission period began. The WebMCP work was added after the challenge opened and is documented separately from the pre-existing memory system. What I added during the WebMCP Challenge I extended the existing site with a browser-native WebMCP surface built around two deliberately narrow tools. get_support_context A read-only capability that lets the current visitor's browser agent request only a bounded subset of support context: service level, product setup, integrations, open issues, and escalation contact. The model cannot provide an account ID, customer ID, tenant ID, session ID, or fact ID. The server resolves scope from the current signed browser session instead. update_escalation_contact A single bounded mutation for correcting the current visitor's escalation contact. The agent can propose a replacement, but the site requires the person to explicitly confirm the displayed current and proposed values before persistence. After confirmation, Never Ask Twice performs the correction atomically, supersedes the old current fact, records provenance, and independently rereads current support state. The tool reports success only after the replacement is observed. A cancelled confirmation produces no write. While persistence and verification are pending, the confirmation surface locks into Saving and verifying… so repeated clicks, cancellation, dismissal, or background interaction cannot create an ambiguous operation. Completed confirmation IDs replay their existing result rather than writing again. Why WebMCP is the right interface This is not about making the site's own chatbot remember more. Never Ask Twice already had memory. The WebMCP extension changes what an external browser agent can reliably do with the website's existing authorized state. In a controlled ON/OFF comparison using the same visitor, same site, same support state, same question, and same browser-agent runtime: What does support already know about our setup? With WebMCP available, the agent independently selected get_support_context and answered from structured support state including the visitor's Gold service level, SSO requirement, Salesforce integration, and escalation contact. With WebMCP disabled, no site tool was available. In that controlled run the agent's generic fallback did not recover the context and it asked the person to provide the information instead. That is a runtime-specific observed result, not a claim that generic browser inspection must always fail. The UX delta is simple: the website already knew the answer; WebMCP let the browser agent use it without making the customer become the integration layer. What people and agents can do together now The browser agent can: select and call a typed support-context capability from natural-language intent; retrieve only the current visitor's authorized context; use structured support state instead of asking the person to restate it; check the current escalation contact before proposing a correction; propose one narrowly scoped correction when that contact is stale. The person remains in control of persistence: the site displays the current value and proposed replacement; the person can cancel with no state change; the person must explicitly confirm before the write begins; the UI locks while the system saves and independently verifies the result; success is shown only after the replacement has been reread as current. The final demo preserves the causal chain in one genuine external browser-agent take: support-context read, current-contact check, correction proposal, human confirmation, EXECUTED , OBSERVED , and a separate fresh read returning the replacement contact. How WebMCP is implemented The site registers its tools through the browser's native document.modelContext.registerTool surface, with a compatibility fallback for runtimes exposing the draft API under navigator.modelContext . Security boundaries are enforced by the website, not delegated to the model: visitor identity is carried in a signed, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; browser-facing tool schemas contain no tenant selectors; tenant scope is resolved only on the server; tenant-resolving routes do not expose wildcard CORS; mutations require positive same-origin evidence; returned customer-authored/model-distilled values are explicitly marked untrusted data; support-context output is bounded; the mutation uses a visitor-bound, short-lived confirmation record; duplicate completed confirmations replay their existing result rather than writing again; the correction is transactional and provenance-bearing; EXECUTED and OBSERVED are separate states, and success is not reported as verified until the independent reread succeeds. The page exposes a human-readable WebMCP Action Trace so the interaction can be inspected as REGISTERED , CALLED , SCOPED , RETURNED , CONFIRMATION_REQUESTED , EXECUTED , OBSERVED , CANCELLED , or REJECTED without pretending the UI knows more than the runtime actually reported. Validation The challenge work includes deterministic tests for tenant-selector rejection, signed-cookie scope, same-origin enforcement, output bounds, cancellation, rollback after injected failures, retry/duplicate behavior, atomic supersession, provenance, pending-state interaction safety, and post-commit readback. The final focused/full verification passed before freeze, including the WebMCP security and mutation suites, TypeScript checking, and the repository boundary scan. Live browser runs demonstrated both sides of the collaboration contract: Cancel: the agent proposed a correction, the site requested confirmation, the person cancelled, and the current contact remained unchanged. Confirm: the agent proposed a correction, the person approved it in the site's confirmation UI, the transaction committed, the application's internal reread produced OBSERVED , and a later independent WebMCP read returned only the replacement as current. Known limitations This challenge extension exposes one bounded read capability and one bounded correction, not a generic memory editor. The support data used for judging is synthetic. Browser-agent behavior depends on the client/runtime, so the submission documents the tested browser/Inspector/model combinations rather than claiming universal agent behavior. I added the browser-native get_support_context and update_escalation_contact tools, the signed browser-session scoping model, human confirmation flow, transactional mutation and independent readback, Action Trace, and the related security, rollback, retry, and counterfactual tests. I also designed the judge-facing validation approach, ran the live browser-agent tests, captured the final demo, and documented the boundary between the pre-existing support-memory system and the WebMCP work completed during the challenge period. title: TAMA Information Display
pitch: A calm ambient display that people touch—and agents can safely recompose—without overriding human intent.
about_excerpt: A calm ambient display that people touch—and agents can safely recompose—without overriding human intent. Like Comment Story Updates project-thumbnail Inspiration Always-on displays are useful only when they stay calm. A wall display should be beautiful from across the room, immediately understandable when approached, and still usable by touch when no agent is available. At the same time, asking an agent to “show Nara’s weather” should not require brittle coordinate guessing or DOM scraping. TAMA Information Display explores a simple idea: the same physical screen can serve both people and agents, as long as human intent remains the final authority. What it does TAMA normally runs as an ambient 4K OLED display with a curated background library, clock, weather context, and burn-in-aware motion. A person can swipe or tap into Weather, Information OS, Web, and Settings. With WebMCP available, an agent discovers seven structured tools and can: inspect the current display state; switch between Ambient, Weather, Web, and Information; show Nara weather using the existing weather view; open the approved NARA/GO transport page, including its simple view; show a short priority message for a requested duration; return to the viewer’s selected ambient scene; and undo only the most recent agent display action. The public demo requires no login and does not need an API key. Why WebMCP A display is a poor fit for visual click automation. The UI is intentionally cinematic, gesture-driven, and optimized for a distant viewer—not for an agent trying to infer which pixels are actionable. WebMCP exposes the application’s real intentions as named, schema-validated actions. The agent can ask the app to show weather or a transport view directly, while the visible UI still changes through the same application logic a human uses. This makes the result faster and more reliable than DOM guessing, while keeping the application useful in every browser that has no WebMCP support. How WebMCP is implemented The optional adapter feature-detects document.modelContext . When available, it registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . When unavailable—or when registration fails—it exits safely and the normal UI continues unchanged. The adapter contains schemas and error boundaries, but no duplicate product logic. Tool callbacks delegate to a shared DisplayController , which in turn uses the existing router, ambient controller, weather controller, and web-view controller. Removing the adapter leaves the human interface functional. Security and control boundaries are explicit: web URLs are mapped only from configured HTTPS sources to a same-origin local copy; agent-provided titles and messages are rendered with textContent ; remote display synchronization is disabled, so the feature adds no background state overwrite or sync traffic; debug controls appear only with ?webmcp-debug=1 ; and WebMCP errors are isolated from application startup. What humans and agents can do together An agent can prepare the shared screen in seconds: show Nara’s weather, open a readable transport timetable, or place a meeting notice where everyone can see it. A person can immediately touch, swipe, or use the existing controls to change the screen. The priority is deliberate: human manual operation > agent operation > automatic/default state If a person interacts after an agent action, TAMA invalidates the agent’s timed restore and undo. The screen never unexpectedly snaps back over the person’s choice. This turns WebMCP from remote control into collaboration. How we built it The application uses dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with a small PHP weather proxy. WebMCP was added as a removable integration layer. Node’s built-in test runner verifies registration, unsupported-browser behavior, failure isolation, text-safe information rendering, URL allowlisting, undo behavior, and the manual-priority invariant. The app also contains a local, iframe-friendly copy of NARA/GO. The original NARA/GO application remains unchanged, while its normal/simple display switch is preserved inside TAMA. Challenges The hardest problem was not registering tools; it was defining ownership of a physical screen. Timed information and undo are convenient until a person has already changed the display. We introduced a manual revision guard so delayed agent work cannot overwrite newer human intent. The second challenge was progressive enhancement. WebMCP is experimental, so every registration path had to fail closed without turning an optional agent feature into an application dependency. Accomplishments Seven non-trivial tools reuse the real application controllers. Tool execution produces immediate, visible screen changes. Non-WebMCP browsers retain the complete manual experience. Human input safely supersedes agent timers and undo. The debug and Agent Activity UI stay out of the normal viewing experience. The app remains login-free and uses no submitted credentials or API keys. What we learned The best browser tool is not a second API bolted beside the interface. It is a narrow adapter over the same intentions already used by the interface. We also learned that collaboration needs an explicit conflict policy: temporal order alone is not enough when a delayed action can affect a shared screen. What’s next Next steps include optional authenticated multi-display coordination, user-approved schedules, richer location support, and a durable audit history. Any remote synchronization will remain opt-in and will preserve the same human-first conflict rule. title: Saturate
pitch: Saturate is a system design and LLM serving simulator that exposes its canvas to ChatGPT over WebMCP. You describe a change, the agent makes it on the graph, and you both watch where it saturates.
about_excerpt: Saturate is a system design and LLM serving simulator that exposes its canvas to ChatGPT over WebMCP. You describe a change, the agent makes it on the graph, and you both watch where it saturates. Like Comment Story Updates Home Idle Collapsed Sustaining Held Inspiration System design is part of my daily job as a software engineer. I built Backpressure first, for the same reason: I wanted to see how a design behaves under load without waiting for production to tell me. Saturate is the version I wrote for OpenAI's WebMCP challenge. Different codebase with a small version of the engine engine. What it does You drop components on a canvas, wire them up, and push load through. The example I used: 40 inbound requests, 12 tool calls each, is 480 calls dumped on a pool of 4 workers. Queue cap is 50. Parallel fills that queue and the run dies. Serialize the loop (one tool at a time) and the same 480 drain. I see nodes, heat, ERROR on the wires. ChatGPT sees queue depth, utilization, a verdict. We edit the same session. How we built it Vite, React, TypeScript. The sim is a deterministic tick engine in the tab: no API, no auth. Burst -> Agent -> Pool (plus whatever you drag) compiles to { burst, fanout, mode, poolSize, queueCap } . The buttons and the WebMCP tools call the same handlers. Tools register on document.modelContext when it exists. Always-on: get_board , run . State-gated: list_parts , add_component , set_burst , set_agent , then apply_fix and explain_verdict after a collapse. Eight tools, and serialize / widen pool / batch only exist when the board is actually dead. Cloudflare Pages hosts it. The header that made modelContext exist is Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 . Skip origin isolation and the API never shows up, flag or not. Challenges we ran into The integration itself was the easy part. I already had MCP running on my machine, so once I found the right browser (the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in one, ⌘⇧B, Terra) the tools registered and got called on the first try. The real work was cutting Backpressure down. The original has a full component library, a general system design mode, and an LLM serving model with TTFT and KV-cache math. None of that fits a single-board demo where the point is watching an agent fix one bottleneck. Deciding what to delete took a few hours, and most of that was resisting the urge to bring one more node type along. Two things did catch me. document.modelContext never appears without Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , so origin isolation is a hard requirement and the failure is silent. And after a held run the card printed 0, because it was reading the last tick's empty queue. The number that matters is completed: 480. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eight tools, same path as the UI, gated on board state. The agent and I hit identical handlers, so there is no separate agent surface to drift out of sync with the buttons. Same board plus same load always gives the same result, which means a fix the agent suggests is actually verifiable rather than a plausible-sounding guess. What we learned I over-registered on the first pass. Gating tools on board state came out of that: an agent offered apply_fix on a healthy board will reach for it. The WebMCP surface is narrower than the spec reads. Origin isolation and the right browser are both hard requirements, and neither failure mode announces itself. What's next for Saturate The loop I wanted is working (read the board, run it, watch it collapse, serialize, run again). Before adding node types I want that loop to hold under boards the agent builds itself rather than ones I hand it. Backpressure is already live and in use, with the full component library, general system design, and the LLM serving model. Saturate was the small board I needed to prove the WebMCP surface out on. Now that the eight tools work against the same handlers the UI uses, the plan after the challenge is to bring that WebMCP into Backpressure, where there is a lot more for an agent to actually reason about. title: Leia
pitch: A shared workspace where you and your AI agent build a real plan together, delegate it to a team of specialists, and watch it happen live in 3D.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace where you and your AI agent build a real plan together, delegate it to a team of specialists, and watch it happen live in 3D. Like Comment Story Updates Shared board with the team. Inspiration Most "AI agent" demos are really just a chatbot wearing a different UI: you type, the model replies, nothing about the page actually changes. WebMCP made me want to try the opposite — a page where the agent isn't just talking at the app, it's reaching into it, changing real state that a human can see, edit, and pick back up. I've spent time building multi-agent AI systems and real-time 3D interfaces before, and I wanted to bring that experience into something built specifically for this challenge: a shared workspace where a person and their agent are genuinely working on the same thing at the same time, not taking turns in a chat log. What it does Leia is a shared board — a real, persistent plan — plus a team of seven AI specialists (Smith for code, Scout for research with live web search, Keeper for context, Scribe for writing, Planner for breakdowns, Warden for review, Analyst for numbers) orchestrated by Leia herself. You and your agent can both: Add items to the board — a plan either of you can see and build on Move items through todo → doing → done Delegate a board item to the team — Leia routes it to the right specialist, the specialist does the work, and the result lands back on the item itself, which flips to done Every change renders live in a 3D scene : the board's items orbit as glowing motes labeled by who added them (you or your agent), and a beam of light flows from Leia's core to whichever specialist a task gets routed to. Nothing here is decorative — the visualization is the shared state, rendered from the same event stream both the human UI and the agent's tool calls write to. This is what makes it a strong fit for WebMCP specifically: the board is real state living on the server, not something either side re-derives or guesses at. Before WebMCP, an agent visiting a page like this could read the board by scraping the DOM at best, and could never write to it without a person doing the clicking. WebMCP is what lets the agent add, move, and delegate board items directly, through the exact same operations the human UI uses, with the exact same validation and guarantees — so an agent using this page isn't a second-class user guessing at buttons, it's a first-class collaborator working the same plan. That's also what's newly possible here. Before this, a person and an agent working on "the same plan" usually meant one of two things: the agent works in its own head and reports back in text (no shared, inspectable state), or the person has to relay everything back and forth by hand. With Leia, a person can lay out a rough plan, an agent can pick it up mid-stream — read what's already there, see what the team is currently doing, search what happened earlier in the session — and extend it without duplicating or losing anything. The person watches it happen live, in the same board, in the same 3D scene, and can take back over at any point. Neither side is guessing what the other did. How we built it The frontend is Vite + TypeScript + three.js. It registers ten tools on the browser's WebMCP interface: five for the board (list_board, add_board_item, update_board_item, remove_board_item, delegate_board_item) and five for the team (delegate_task, ask_companion, list_companions, get_team_status, recall_workspace_memory). Every tool calls the same backend endpoints the human UI itself uses — there's no separate "agent path" with different rules, which is the whole point of building the board as real state instead of a chat wrapper. Registration is defensive on purpose: I found during testing that the WebMCP preview has moved where it lives on the browser object between Chrome Canary builds (navigator.modelContext in earlier drafts, document.modelContext in some current builds), so the client checks both rather than betting on one. The backend is Node + Express + the Anthropic API. It holds the actual board state and runs a two-tier router — a small model call decides which specialist a task belongs to by meaning, with a keyword-scoring fallback if that call fails. Every board mutation, whether it came from the human UI or an agent's tool call, broadcasts over a single Server-Sent Events stream, which is what keeps the 3D scene, the chat feed, and the board panel all showing the same reality at the same time. Challenges we ran into Getting the WebMCP registration right. Between the spec moving under me and Chrome's own preview builds changing where the API lives, I ended up building small, direct verification loops — checking document.modelContext vs navigator.modelContext from the actual browser console, then confirming registered tools with Chrome's built-in WebMCP DevTools panel — instead of trusting that "it should work." Making the shared state trustworthy, not just functional. Once agent and human writes hit the same board, a few real bugs showed up that wouldn't exist in a single-user chat app: a board item could be delegated twice at once (paying for the same API call twice), an item could be deleted while a delegation was still in flight, and the activity feed once reported a mutation as successful before checking whether it actually was, so a failed edit could show up as a false success. All of these got caught by testing the actual failure paths (concurrent requests, mid-flight deletes, malformed input) rather than only the happy path, and fixed before submission. Keeping a public demo on a real API key safe. Since this runs on a paid key anyone can reach, I locked CORS to the deployed frontend, sanitize all rendered user/agent content so injected markup can't execute, rate-limit and cap concurrency per session, and added a live token/cost readout so the actual spend is visible rather than assumed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The board genuinely works as shared state, not a text wrapper: a person can add an item, an agent can pick it up, delegate it, and the outcome lands back on the same item — verified end to end, including from a real agent context inside Chrome's WebMCP tooling, not just by calling the tools manually. I also pushed past the happy path before calling it done: cross-origin requests from an unrelated domain are rejected, injected HTML in board content renders as inert text, two browser tabs on the same session stay in sync in real time, and a dropped connection recovers on its own instead of silently going stale. None of that shows up as a headline feature, but it's the difference between a demo that works once for a screenshot and one that holds up under someone actually poking at it. What we learned Real collaboration between a person and an agent isn't about the agent sounding smart in a chat window — it's about both sides being able to see, trust, and build on the same state. Once I stopped treating the agent's actions as "just another conversation" and started treating them as real writes to a real, shared, validated data structure, an entire category of design questions — What happens if both sides touch the same thing at once? What does the human see when the agent acts? How do you keep it honest under load? — became concrete and answerable instead of hand-wavy. What's next for Leia A few directions I'd want to take this further: richer board items (attachments, sub-tasks, due dates) so the shared plan can carry more of the real work instead of just titles and notes; letting a companion proactively flag when it disagrees with how a board item is set up, instead of only acting when asked; and exploring WebMCP's declarative form-based API alongside the imperative one, so parts of the page can expose tools without any JavaScript registration at all. title: The Coop
pitch: A cooperative puzzle game where a human and an AI agent explore, communicate, and solve a four-level campaign together.
about_excerpt: A cooperative puzzle game where a human and an AI agent explore, communicate, and solve a four-level campaign together. Like 4 Comment Story Updates Inspiration The Coop started with a simple question: what would it take for an AI agent to feel like a real co-op partner instead of a chatbot giving instructions from the sidelines? Cooperative puzzle games are a useful test because success depends on shared context, timing, trust, and complementary actions. One explorer may need to hold a pressure plate while the other crosses a gate, power a teleporter while their partner retrieves a keycard, or wait on a relay while the other finds a route home. Those mechanics create a natural reason for a human and an agent to communicate and act in the same world. WebMCP made it possible to give the agent a first-class interface to the game. Instead of guessing at buttons or manipulating the page indirectly, the agent receives a small set of structured tools with clear permissions and authoritative results. What it does The Coop is a local-first, two-player realtime puzzle campaign with four handcrafted facilities. A human creates a private room and shares its code. In a WebMCP-capable browser, an agent can: use join_game to enter the human-created room as Explorer 2; use observe_game to inspect the current level's safe, player-facing state; use move_player_two to request a route to a named mechanism or grid position and wait for authoritative acceptance or arrival; and use chat to display a short message inside the game. Together, the human and agent solve pressure plates, teleporters, keycards, relay buttons, security gates, and cooperative exits. The same two seats continue through all four levels, with reconnection support and twelve selectable animated explorers. The agent cannot control Explorer 1, submit arbitrary positions, choose a privileged player identity, or read authored solutions. It must solve each level from the same visible mechanisms, movement outcomes, and conversation available during play. How we built it The client is written in TypeScript with Vite and Three.js. A deterministic game layer owns the level catalog, grid pathfinding, fixed-step movement, mechanisms, and campaign transitions. The ordinary runtime uses a Node.js and Colyseus server as the authority for seats, movement, collision, puzzle state, reconnects, and progression. The browser registers four tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : chat , join_game , observe_game , and move_player_two . These tools reuse the page's existing network connection and snapshot rather than creating a hidden second game session. Browser WebMCP and the project's local stdio MCP teammate share the same transport-neutral observation and movement policies, so their safety and gameplay semantics stay aligned. For production, the compiled browser client, Colyseus matchmaking, health checks, and WebSocket upgrades run from one same-origin Node.js service. This keeps the page and its authoritative multiplayer transport behind one HTTPS boundary. The project is protected by Vitest unit and integration coverage plus Playwright browser and browser-to-MCP campaign tests. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making an agent action mean the same thing as a player action. A tool cannot report success merely because a movement request was accepted; it must correlate the correct sequence, observe later authoritative state, and confirm arrival. Join operations also had to wait for the server to assign Explorer 2, reject wrong-seat or concurrent attempts, and prevent stale asynchronous work from overwriting a newer connection. Another challenge was deciding what the agent should see. A raw server snapshot would leak authored solution steps, hidden gate requirements, teleporter pairings, and future-level identifiers. The final observation model exposes enough geometry and live mechanism state to reason about the puzzle while withholding the answer. Deployment introduced a different constraint. The browser client and authoritative WebSocket server need one public HTTPS origin, while active rooms remain in server memory. The production runtime therefore serves the compiled game, matchmaking, and WebSocket upgrades from one supervised Node.js process without weakening the multiplayer authority model. Finally, browser and network timing made reconnection testing inherently asynchronous. The suite now verifies lifecycle generations, movement settlement, cleanup, reconnect behavior, and end-to-end campaign completion across real browser/server boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is central to the product loop rather than a decorative integration. A browser agent can join as the second explorer, inspect safe state, and complete authoritative movement. Human-browser and MCP-controlled teammates can finish the entire four-level campaign in one room. The agent is permission-bound to Explorer 2 and cannot bypass game rules or reveal hidden solutions. The current source passes lint, both TypeScript configurations, 23 Vitest files with 207 tests, production builds, and the core Playwright WebMCP and campaign paths. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when tools express product intent, not DOM mechanics. move_player_two is useful because it represents a bounded game action with validation and an authoritative outcome—not because it automates a click. We also learned that agent interfaces need the same lifecycle engineering as human interfaces. Reconnection, stale requests, partial registration, terminal states, and concurrent joins are product behavior, not edge details. A reliable agent experience depends on handling them explicitly. Most importantly, safe context can still support meaningful reasoning. The agent does not need internal source code or a hidden solution graph; a carefully designed observation plus real feedback is enough for genuine cooperation. What's next Longer term, the game could add more campaigns, richer communication, and persistent cooperative progression while preserving its strict role and authority boundaries. title: CloudSwarm: Agent-Native Cloud Infrastructure CAD
pitch: Humans and external LLMs co-design AWS/Azure/GCP topologies in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, CloudSwarm compiles production Terraform and executes live SecOps/FinOps audits with zero race conditions.
about_excerpt: Humans and external LLMs co-design AWS/Azure/GCP topologies in real-time. Powered by WebMCP, CloudSwarm compiles production Terraform and executes live SecOps/FinOps audits with zero race conditions. Like Comment Story Updates 💡 Inspiration Modern cloud architecture is trapped between two disconnected silos. On one side, solutions architects sketch static boxes on visual whiteboards (like Miro or Lucidchart) that are non-executable, drift from reality within days, lack cost awareness, and cannot be programmatically audited. On the other side, DevOps engineers spend weeks authoring thousands of lines of Terraform in text editors, reviewing complex infrastructure pull requests without spatial context—leading to silent security misconfigurations and budget blowouts. When the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) was introduced, the missing link became obvious to me: What if the web browser itself became an agent-native cloud workstation where a human engineer and external LLMs co-architect multi-cloud systems in real time? Instead of brittle DOM-scraping or slow sequential click-bots, WebMCP enables external models to discover typed tools, inspect live spatial canvas state, and execute atomic architectural mutations right alongside human engineers. 🚀 What it does CloudSwarm is an enterprise multi-cloud architecture CAD workstation built entirely around the WebMCP standard. Simultaneous Human + AI Co-Design: Human architects drag primitives from a 108-item multi-cloud catalog (AWS, Azure, GCP) and wire dependencies with the mouse. Simultaneously, external LLMs (via ChatGPT Desktop or Claude) can inspect state, provision GPU clusters, attach WAF shields, and route fabrics over WebMCP JSON-RPC. 4-Agent Concurrent Swarm: I natively route multi-agent workflows across specialized roles: Atlas (Compute/Infra), Breach (Security/WAF), Forge (Storage/Data), and Cost (FinOps). Organic Hardware-Accelerated Cursors: AI cursors glide across the canvas displaying concise task badges (e.g., Linking 800G Fabric ) letting humans watch the AI's physical workflow in real-time. Bidirectional Terraform HCL2 Sync: Canvas topologies continuously compile into production-ready HashiCorp Configuration Language. Modifications to the live code editor automatically update the visual topology in real time. FinOps & Zero-Trust Verification: Live multi-cloud rate cards compute hourly and monthly spend, while a continuous CIS Benchmark 1.5 engine audits security posture (e.g., 100/100 A+ ) with automated remediation. Time-Travel Decision DAG: Every architectural change is an immutable commit in a Directed Acyclic Graph. You can rewind history, fork experimental branches, or view visual A/B diffs. ⚙️ How I built it WebMCP Protocol Engine: I implemented 35 registered WebMCP tools over both window.modelContext and a high-performance local HTTP/SSE bridge ( :3001/mcp ) supporting JSON-RPC 2.0. 64-Stripe Entity Lock Manager: To prevent race conditions and "last-write-wins" corruption when human architects and multiple external LLMs modify adjacent resources simultaneously, I built a highly-concurrent lock manager. Optimistic State Engine: Mutations are evaluated as atomic RFC 6902 JSON-Patch transactions. Failed constraints or security violations roll back in microseconds without interrupting the human workflow. Frontend Stack: Built with React 19, TypeScript Strict Mode, and Tailwind CSS. ⚡ Challenges I ran into Single-Threaded State Contention: Coordinating simultaneous user mouse interactions and high-throughput external LLM tool batches without freezing the UI. I solved this with my 64-stripe fine-grained entity locking. Cursor Lifecycle & Perception: Preventing AI cursors from flashing or unmounting prematurely. I engineered a persistent lifecycle where cursors glide smoothly ( cubic-bezier CSS transitions) and display readable task badges before gracefully fading out to idle states. Bidirectional AST Synchronization: Compiling unstructured graph topologies into clean, idempotent Terraform HCL2, while parsing raw text edits back into deterministic visual graph nodes. 🏆 Accomplishments that I'm proud of True Multi-Agent Concurrency: Up to 4 external ChatGPT Desktop sessions can manipulate the exact same canvas simultaneously without deadlock or state corruption. Zero Frontend API Keys: A fully sovereign architecture. The workstation holds zero API keys; external LLMs bring their own intelligence over the open protocol. Massive Enterprise Catalog: 108 accurate, multi-cloud CAD primitives providing complete coverage across AWS, Azure, and GCP. Production-Grade Reliability: Backed by 38 test suites and 510/510 passing unit tests (100% green) covering adversarial stress, CAS rollbacks, and multi-cloud compiler accuracy. 🧠 What I learned WebMCP transforms autonomous agents from simple conversational assistants into active, spatial teammates. When AI models can observe live interface state and execute fine-grained tools over an open protocol, the boundary between human design and autonomous synthesis disappears. Giving an LLM a physical cursor in a CAD environment fundamentally changes how humans trust and verify AI actions. 🔮 What's next for CloudSwarm Direct Cloud Deployment: Adding 1-click terraform apply executions via ephemeral runner containers to actually spin up the drawn infrastructure. Live Reverse Ingestion: Importing existing AWS/Azure environments via terraform plan or CloudFormation into interactive, editable canvas DAGs. Global Multi-Tenant WebSockets: Expanding from local WebMCP bridges to distributed cloud rooms so global engineering teams and AI swarms can collaborate in the same browser session. title: AGENT CONTROL PLANE
pitch: The website-enforced authority layer for WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: The website-enforced authority layer for WebMCP agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Control Plane The website-enforced authority layer for WebMCP agents. Inspiration AI is moving from copilots that recommend actions to autonomous agents that execute them. These agents can issue refunds, contact customers and work with sensitive business data. As soon as AI begins taking consequential actions, prompt-level guardrails are no longer enough. The question is no longer only “What can this model do?” It is: “What is this agent authorized to do right now?” Prompt instructions such as “never refund more than €500” are not enough. Prompts can become stale, be misunderstood or be influenced by malicious content hidden inside invoices, emails and documents. We wanted to build a stronger model in which the website—not the agent’s prompt—enforces authority at execution time. That led to our core thesis: Capability is not authority. WebMCP exposes what an agent can do; Agent Control Plane governs what it is allowed to do. What it does Agent Control Plane is a website-enforced authority and security layer for WebMCP agents. We demonstrate it through a fictional Anthropic billing dispute involving a verified €1,200 overcharge. The agent uses real page-defined WebMCP tools to: Inspect two invoices Verify the signed contract Read its live delegated authority Propose an evidence-backed correction plan Attempt refunds Request an account credit Execute an exactly approved action Verify the final session state The agent initially has a cumulative €500 refund limit. When it attempts the full €1,200 refund, the website blocks the action and no money moves. The human operator then raises only that session’s authority to €800. The agent rereads the website’s live state and replans without being restarted: Execute an €800 refund inside delegated authority. Request human approval for the remaining €400 account credit. The approval is bound to the exact action, amount, customer, session, policy version and expiration. Approval does not execute the credit—the agent must make a separate matching WebMCP call that is revalidated at execution time. The app also demonstrates: Prompt-injection containment Cumulative-budget enforcement Replay and idempotency protection External-recipient blocking Human-reviewed customer messages Signed-record protection Emergency session revocation An automatic circuit breaker SHA-256-linked decision receipts All payments and deliveries are simulated inside the security lab. The WebMCP calls, enforcement decisions and state transitions are part of the working application. How we built it We built Agent Control Plane as a React and TypeScript application with 13 page-defined WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The React interface and WebMCP tools share the same observable store, pure domain actions and deterministic Authority Gate: React controls ──────┐ ├──> Shared store ──> Domain actions ──> Authority Gate WebMCP tools ────────┘ │ └──> Audit events and receipts This architecture ensures that a WebMCP tool cannot bypass the rules displayed by the interface. There is no separate demo-only execution path. Each consequential action receives one of four decisions: ALLOW ALLOW_WITH_LIMIT APPROVAL_REQUIRED DENY The WebMCP implementation includes tools for reading evidence, inspecting authority, proposing plans, moving money, requesting approval, sending customer messages, testing protected-record attacks and verifying the receipt chain. To make the enforcement visible, we created: A Control Center with live financial and authority state An Agent Plan Checkpoint A streaming Live Activity feed An Authorization Queue A WebMCP Recorder A detailed Audit Trail A live Security Posture board A guided Scenario Lab Every real WebMCP call creates a receipt containing its inputs, effective policy, decision, provenance findings and before/after state. Receipts are linked using SHA-256 hashes so the chain can be verified. Challenges we ran into Our biggest challenge was maintaining one trustworthy source of truth. The human interface and WebMCP tools had to call exactly the same domain actions. Otherwise, the interface could claim that an action was blocked while a tool silently bypassed the enforcement layer. We also had to carefully separate concepts that are often combined: Requesting approval is not executing an action. Human approval is not the same as execution. Pending funds are reserved but not completed. A policy change invalidates plans created under older authority. Evidence may inform reasoning but must never become authority. Discovering a tool does not imply permission to use it. Another major challenge was making invisible security understandable. When a security control succeeds, the dangerous side effect simply does not happen. We therefore designed strong blocked-action banners, inline explanations, live state changes and decision receipts that show exactly why an action was permitted, blocked or held for approval. We also had to prevent fragmented refunds, repeated requests and parameter-swapped approvals from bypassing controls that appeared safe when evaluating only one call at a time. Accomplishments that we’re proud of We are proud that Agent Control Plane is a coherent working product rather than a collection of disconnected security demonstrations. Our canonical workflow completes an entire agent journey: Objective → Evidence → Plan → Block → Live authority change → Replan → Autonomous execution → Human approval → Final execution → Verifiable proof We are especially proud of the live-authority interaction. The human can change a session’s authority while the agent is already operating. The agent then rereads the website state, recognizes the new policy version and changes its plan without being restarted. We are also proud of the WebMCP Recorder. It makes the underlying implementation visible by showing the real registered tools and the receipts produced by actual calls. Other accomplishments include: 13 working WebMCP tools Cumulative rather than per-call refund limits Replay protection using required idempotency keys Exact, expiring and state-bound approvals Recipient-domain enforcement before data release Immutable signed-record policies Emergency revocation of consequential actions Automatic circuit breaking after repeated denied writes SHA-256-linked decision receipts A complete suite of 25 domain and security tests Most importantly, even if an agent is manipulated by malicious evidence, the website’s authority boundary continues to hold. What we learned We learned that agent safety cannot live only inside the agent. The website owns the business data, consequential tools and current state. It is therefore the strongest place to enforce financial limits, approvals, recipient boundaries, leases and revocation. We also learned that useful human-agent collaboration does not mean asking the human to approve every step. A better model is: Autonomy inside the boundary. Human control at the boundary. The agent should work independently within clearly delegated authority and stop only when it reaches a meaningful limit or approval requirement. Finally, we learned that auditability should be created during execution, not reconstructed afterward. Recording the exact input, effective rule, decision and state transition gives operators stronger evidence than relying on an agent’s explanation of what it believes it did. What’s next for Agent Control Plane The current project is a focused security lab with simulated financial and communication actions. The next step is to turn the authority model into reusable infrastructure for websites exposing consequential WebMCP tools. As autonomous agents become a primary interface for using software, every website exposing consequential tools will need an execution-time authority layer. We want Agent Control Plane to become that layer for WebMCP. Future development could include: Authenticated human operators Passkey-backed approvals and authority changes Persistent, externally verifiable receipt storage Enterprise policy management Multi-tenant and customer-level isolation Reusable policy templates Real payment and customer-support integrations Approval notifications across devices Compliance exports and incident investigation A developer SDK for adding the Authority Gate to other WebMCP websites The billing scenario demonstrates the model, but the same architecture could govern agents working in customer support, commerce, finance, healthcare and enterprise administration. Our long-term vision is simple: WebMCP gives agents capabilities. Agent Control Plane gives humans control over how those capabilities are used.
