title: Meabs
pitch: When architects meet agents and WebMCP, who will break first
about_excerpt: When architects meet agents and WebMCP, who will break first Like Comment Story Updates Multi-Region Simulation Event Driven Reference Architectures Inspiration As an architect, I spend a lot of my time working with pictures. We use architecture diagrams to explain how systems work, how they connect and how we think they will behave. I wanted to bring those pictures to life and avoid my designs breaking things and getting people paged in the middle of the night :-) I wanted to be able to model a change and get an idea of what it might do to the design. What happens if the load increases? What if I lose a component or a zone? If I change something to recover, what impact does that have somewhere else? Having an agent working alongside me makes that much quicker to explore. The agent can stress the architecture, break things, inspect what happened and try to recover it. I can change the constraints or try a different idea and see how it responds. What it does Resilience Forge turns an architecture diagram into something I can experiment with. I can configure a scenario, change the workload and run deterministic simulations to see how the architecture responds. I can introduce failures such as losing a component or a zone, watch the impact on the architecture and metrics, and test different ways of recovering. An AI agent can work on the same scenario through WebMCP. It can inspect the architecture and metrics, run stress tests, introduce failures and make changes to try to recover the system. The agent and I work against the same state. If I change a constraint or make a decision in the UI while the agent is working, it sees that change and has to respect it. This means I can work with the agent rather than handing the whole simulation over to it. Resilience Forge also includes a flight recorder that shows the WebMCP calls as they happen, so I can see what the agent is doing and how those actions affect the simulation. For this project I've used deterministic simulations, so I can run the same scenario repeatedly and get consistent results. The idea could go much further by bringing in real telemetry, service limits, costs and other infrastructure data to create more realistic simulations. How we built it I used Codex to help with the coding and my knowledge of creating pictures as an architect :-) For hosting I am using the ChatGPT Sites capability The simulation and WebMCP tools work against the same application state. Every WebMCP mutation works against a version of that shared state. If I change the architecture while the agent is working, its old write is rejected as STALE_STATE rather than silently overwriting my change. The agent then has to read the current state and decide what to do next. Constraints such as pinned decisions are enforced in the application itself, not left to the prompt, and the Flight Data Recorder shows human and WebMCP actions against the same timelines. The WebMCP tools are domain operations rather than UI controls. The agent can inspect the architecture, run stress tests, inject failures, change scaling or traffic behaviour and apply remediations without having to work out how to click around the page. The same domain logic is used whether the change comes from me or from WebMCP. This was important because I didn't want the agent operating against a separate version of the architecture from the one I could see and change in the UI. Challenges we ran into The main one for me was keeping the state between the agent and the user aware of each other, as both parties can make changes and we need to make sure that the application is aware of those. Both can make changes while a simulation is running, so the application needs to keep them in sync. If I make a decision or add a constraint in the UI, the agent needs to know about it and respect it when deciding what to do next. Accomplishments that we're proud of Created my first ever YouTube video, and it has spurred me on to do more, I may be terrible at it for now but I will improve :-) What we learned WebMCP will change how agents and users interact with websites. When I'm designing user journeys, I now need to think about the agent journey as well as the human journey. WebMCP makes that much easier because the agent can interact with capabilities exposed by the application rather than having to pull information from the DOM and work out how to operate a UI designed for a human or have information locked away so that agents can't access it. What's next for Meabs I'm working on an agent that can read infrastructure source code such as Terraform and CDK and then model that infrastructure in Resilience Forge. I'd also like to integrate with vendors' MCP servers to bring in real-time information such as service limits. From there, I want to explore bringing in real telemetry and cost data so the simulations can move closer to the architectures I'm actually working with. This also builds on some of my other work around PEAR (Public Engagement AI-Readiness) and the Agent Observatory, where I've been exploring how we design applications for agents and how we observe what those agents are doing. Resilience Forge gave me a chance to put some of those ideas into a working application rather than leaving them as architecture diagrams or slide decks :-) Built With next.js/vinext react-19 tailwind-css three.js typescript vite Try it out github.com resilience-forge.gman72.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Garry Meaburn Like Share this project: Updates Garry Meaburn started this project — Sep 02, 2026 05:13 PM EDT

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Didaction space
pitch: didaction space is a agent-enabled alternative jupyter frontend- enabling you to learn deeper
about_excerpt: didaction space is a agent-enabled alternative jupyter frontend- enabling you to learn deeper Like Comment Story Updates 1 Launch window Regular notebook Microscopes Inspiration LLMs have been a game changer for how we learn something new now. Autodidacts can satiate their curiosity to infinite bounds, ask however many question we would like within our token budgets. But it can also be very tiring when an LLM blurts out lot of text, and UIs are trapped inside boxes. For difficult concepts, I often find myself slowing down and trying to see things step by step, or illustrate visually wishing lesser friction between what in my head and what I can put down on something external- the monitor or on paper. This is an attempt to bring that to jupyter notebooks which are versatile in learning. For each cell, this is an attempt to slow things down and understand things step by step with some visualization, and play around with a segment of code deeper. What it does didaction space is agent-enabled Jupyter-kernel frontend centered on ability to do deep dive into each small snippet of code called a“cell”. An agent creates a “microscope” to create rich interactive walkthrough about the cell's contents through WebMCP. It provides the following primitives for agents: code examples with annotations animated graphics canvas to illustrate concepts executable playgrounds to spawn quick tests It can run in your browser completely locally executing Jupyter kernels in browser, or through self-hosted docker instances of kernels executing on your local platform. With server mode, you can also have multiple collaborators with one driver and remaining following the session. WebMCP allows you to bring your own agent and leverage your context/memory about knowledge, learning preferences, and technical interests. Conventional hosted segmented LLM wrapper tools have to learn that, and have to trust them with your data too. How we built it Most of the heavy lifting was done by Codex with hackathon skills and TDD skills. I gave it the architectural decisions, feedback and guidance. Frontend Jupyter's ecosystem has kernels for various languages, and documented protocol for interaction between frontend and backend. Instead of using Jupyter's existing frontend, we chose to use egui, a Rust based immediate mode GUI rendering to the frontend canvas. This was a decision due to familiarity with that ecosystem. The WebMCP calls hook through this Rust based frontend providing much richer client-side interactivity. "Backend" A rust based gateway handles communication with "backend". For local only mode, our "backend" leveraged JupyterLite's kernel implementation for in-browser kernels, through the gateway. For docker based server backend, the gateway is a sidecar to the language specific jupyter kernel streaming updates to all clients, and controlling who is the driver for the session & is allowed to send actions to jupyter server. Jupyter's architecture helped a lot, with common gateway code implemented to interact between frontend & backend . Challenges we ran into Things that were complex to keep in scope of hackathon: Using WebAuthn authentication, but that is currently not supported in Codex browser WebRTC to talk between collaborators directly, and server WebMCP design decisions: WebMCP design applied to jupyter model- idempotic actions, such as insert relative to cell-id rather than specifying index WebMCP orchestration with different collaborators - viewing is allowed by agents, but not active operations- controlled by central server For a complex multi-mcp invocation, WebMCP description should be given enough information to pick up context from it Local pyodide packages and constraints Accomplishments that we're proud of A fixed visualization API would be difficult to maintain. So we used an arbitrary AssemblyScript to provide more flexibility with a smaller host interface. So microscope graphics are dispatched as compiled wasm artifacts compiled using a inbrowser compiler. What we learned The important capability is not more agent control. It is shared access to the application’s concepts and state. For notebooks, agents should understand cells, execution, annotations, walkthroughs, Playgrounds, graphics, and notebook state—not reconstruct them from screenshots. For effective use, a SKILLS.md is still important and a mechanism to discover this would be a great addition to WebMCP. What's next for didaction space Microscopes are a first step toward software that can explain itself with an agent. We want to make walkthroughs richer by combining: code, narration, animation, graphics, experiments, domain-specific tools. The same approach could support mathematics, robotics, simulations, engineering, and scientific computing. The long-term goal is to reduce the distance between using a technical tool and learning how it works. title: Bizgrid
pitch: Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for African sellers. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart without scraping the UI
about_excerpt: Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for African sellers. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart without scraping the UI Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Starting an online business in Africa is still harder than it should be. Many small businesses rely on social media because building an e-commerce website requires technical skills, time, and money. Existing platforms often expect merchants to understand themes, hosting, product management, and website design before they can even make their first sale. We asked a simple question: What if building an online store was as easy as describing your business to an AI? That idea became Bizgrid, this an AI-powered commerce platform that lets anyone create, customise, and launch a professional online store through natural conversation. What it does Bizgrid is an AI commerce platform for sellers and SME's. With WebMCP, any agent can search products across every live store on Bizgrid and add to the correct merchant’s cart ,without scraping the UI. Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Bizgrid is an AI-first commerce platform for African sellers: dozens of independent merchants each run their own storefront, with their own catalog, inventory, prices, and Paystack checkout, all hosted on one platform. That shape many sellers, one marketplace is exactly where WebMCP shines, because commerce is fundamentally structured data. Stores, products, prices, stock levels, variant options, and carts all have well-defined schemas. WebMCP's tool model lets us expose that structure directly, instead of forcing an agent to reverse-engineer it. Before WebMCP, an agent trying to shop on Bizgrid would have to scrape HTML fragile, slow, and blind to the rules that matter. It wouldn't reliably know whether a product is in stock, how many units can be purchased, what currency the merchant prices in, or which variant options are required. It certainly couldn't know that a "cart" on Bizgrid is scoped to a specific merchant, and that putting an item in the wrong cart means paying the wrong seller. Those are business-critical rules, not UI details. With WebMCP, we encode them once, as typed tool contracts: every tool response carries a store_slug, every add_to_cart validates stock, purchase limits, and variant options against the merchant's real data before writing. The agent can no longer guess wrong about who gets the money the platform itself enforces correctness. There's also a natural symmetry in our product story: Bizgrid merchants already run their shops with an AI assistant on WhatsApp. WebMCP completes the loop on the buyer side. Merchants sell through an agent; now buyers shop through an agent, too with Bizgrid as the structured layer that connects them. How it creates a better user experience Imagine a shopper in Lagos who wants a vitamin C serum under ₦20,000. The old way: they'd discover Bizgrid stores one at a time, open each storefront in a new tab, search each shop's catalog separately, compare prices by hand, and repeat the whole ritual for every product. The new way: they open ChatGPT (or any WebMCP-capable browser) on the Bizgrid homepage and say one sentence: "Find me a vitamin C serum under ₦20,000." The agent calls search_products with budget_max, gets back structured results from every published store at once — name, store, price, currency, stock status, and a direct product link and presents a ranked comparison. The shopper says "add the one from GlowSkin to my cart," and the agent calls add_to_cart with the correct store_slug, where the platform validates stock and variants and writes to that merchant's cart. The shopper then clicks one checkout link and pays normally with Paystack. What makes this a better experience, not just a different one: the human stays in the familiar, trusted flow the same storefront cart and checkout they already know while everything upstream (search, comparison, decision fatigue) becomes conversational. And because tools are typed, the agent quotes real prices in the right currency, never hallucinates a product, and never sends a shopper to a checkout that doesn't contain what they asked for. Discovery becomes instant; trust stays human. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before The genuinely new capability here is platform-wide shopping with a human-held checkout. Before WebMCP, an agent could only operate inside one website at a time, scraping one storefront's HTML. Cross-store comparison meant running one agent per tab, and adding to a cart meant custom per-merchant integrations that no small African seller could afford. There was no way for an agent to say "search all of Bizgrid" the marketplace existed in the URL structure, not in any machine-readable interface. WebMCP collapses that. A single tool layer registered on the platform homepage exposes every published store, every product, and every cart as first-class, callable operations. One agent can search across merchants, compare, negotiate the shopper's preferences, and fill the correct seller's cart then hand the same browser cart to a human for the final, money-moving step. That handoff is the heart of it: a division of labor that didn't exist before. The agent does what machines are good at exhaustive search, structured comparison, remembering constraints, enforcing rules. The human does what humans insist on reviewing, confirming, and paying with the checkout they trust. Agent discovers and carts; human reviews and pays. That collaboration was impossible with scraping, and it's exactly the human-agent partnership WebMCP exists to enable. How we implemented WebMCP We extended Bizgrid's Next.js frontend with a WebMCP tool layer, all client-side, no agent-specific integrations: Registration: src/lib/webmcp/bootstrap.ts polls for document.modelContext (up to 120 animation frames, so registration works even if the WebMCP runtime initializes after page load), registers all tools through registerTool, dispatches a toolchange event so agents re-discover them, dedupes via a single bootstrap promise (protecting against React Strict Mode double-invocations), and cleans up on pagehide. An app-wide provider (src/components/webmcp/platform-webmcp-provider.tsx) plus an instrumentation hook register the tools on every page, early. The seven tools (src/lib/webmcp/platform-tools.ts) — list_stores, list_catalog, get_store_info, search_products, get_product, add_to_cart, get_cart — each with a JSON Schema inputSchema, descriptions written to guide agent tool selection (e.g., "prefer search_products when the shopper has a specific query"), and readOnlyHint annotations so agents can reason about side effects. Data layer — tools call Bizgrid's existing catalog APIs (store listing, full catalog with pagination, search with budget filters, per-product lookup), so agents get live, real prices and stock, never static HTML. Shared cart, shared checkout — add_to_cart writes to the same per-store localStorage cart keys the storefronts already use (src/lib/webmcp/platform-cart.ts), with validation of stock, purchase limits, and variant options (src/lib/webmcp/shared.ts). Every response includes cart_url and checkout_url, so the human opens the exact checkout the agent filled. Agents and humans share one cart and one trusted Paystack flow nothing is simulated or sandboxed. No server changes required because everything is structured client-side on top of existing APIs, the entire WebMCP surface ships with the normal frontend bundle, live at https://www.bizgrid.shop today.  Inspiration

pitch: An agent-native production ops dashboard built with WebMCP allowing AI agents to monitor telemetry, execute Kubernetes replica autos-caling, and perform synthetic web tests in real time.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native production ops dashboard built with WebMCP allowing AI agents to monitor telemetry, execute Kubernetes replica autos-caling, and perform synthetic web tests in real time.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 OpsDesk Dahboard: Real-Time Incident - CPU 94% CRITICAL, p99 Letency 1420Oms DEGRADED, api service needs scaling 1-3 replicas

 OpsDesk Dahboard: Real-Time Incident - CPU 94% CRITICAL, p99 Letency 1420Oms DEGRADED, api service needs scaling 1-3 replicas

 OpsDesk Dahboard: Real-Time Incident - CPU 94% CRITICAL, p99 Letency 1420Oms DEGRADED, api service needs scaling 1-3 replicas 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 During high-severity incident responses, engineers often spend critical minutes toggling between multiple monitoring dashboards, terminal windows, and cloud control panels. We wanted to build a web application designed specifically for the agent-native era—a unified workspace where human operators and AI agents collaborate seamlessly during system outages to diagnose latency spikes, inspect telemetry, and execute infrastructure remediation natively. 

 What it does: 

 OpsDesk WebMCP is an agent-native DevOps management workspace that exposes client-side operations directly to AI agents using the WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext ). Key functionalities include: 

 
 Cluster Health Inspection ( get_cluster_metrics ): Enables agents to fetch live CPU usage, memory footprint, p99 latency, and error rates for targeted microservices. 
 Dynamic Infrastructure Autoscaling ( scale_service_replicas ): Allows agents to scale pod replica counts up or down to mitigate degraded service performance, updating the visual dashboard UI in real-time. 
 Synthetic Availability Testing ( run_synthetic_web_test ): Triggers browser automation benchmarks to check UI accessibility and endpoint response times. 
 

 How we built it: 

 
 Frontend & UI: Built using React and Tailwind CSS to render real-time service health, status indicators, and active pod replica counters. 
 WebMCP Integration: Integrated @modelcontextprotocol/sdk on the client side, exposing native tool signatures directly via document.modelContext.registerTool . 
 Agent Interoperability: Designed structured JSON input schemas and return payloads compatible with ChatGPT's in-app browser and WebMCP-enabled environments. 
 

 Challenges we ran into: 

 
 Client-Side Tool Synchronization: Ensuring state changes executed by an agent tool call (e.g., scaling replicas) triggered immediate visual UI updates in the React component hierarchy without requiring page refreshes. 
 Schema Precision: Crafting clear, deterministic tool descriptions and JSON schemas so LLMs select the correct diagnostic or action tool under varied prompting scenarios. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of: 

 
 Successfully implemented a functional browser-native WebMCP interface that allows an AI agent to execute end-to-end incident triage and infrastructure mitigation. 
 Created a clean visual bridge where human engineers can monitor automated agent actions live on screen. 
 

 What we learned: 

 
 How WebMCP transforms static web applications into interactive, agentic workspaces by standardizing client-side tool discovery. 
 Best practices for structuring agent inputs and fallback handling for robust client-side execution. 
 

 What's next for OpsDesk WebMCP 

 
 Adding multi-cluster support for cross-region failovers. 
 Expanding tool execution security with human-in-the-loop confirmation prompts prior to executing high-impact scaling or rollback operations.

title: Patchwork
pitch: A browser-native React workspace where people and Codex safely build, preview, recover, and export together.
about_excerpt: A browser-native React workspace where people and Codex safely build, preview, recover, and export together. Like Comment Story Updates Patchwork keeps files, code, preview, diagnostics, checkpoints, and activity in one browser workspace. Atomic multi-file WebMCP edit: one checkpoint, one revision, and the Roamly preview updated. The page becomes the tool: Patchwork exposes ten WebMCP operations while the human keeps the files, preview, and recovery controls in view. Inspiration Most AI coding tools bring the project into the agent's interface. We wanted to explore the inverse: what if the application itself could offer a precise, safe collaboration surface to the agent the user already has? Web development is a strong test case because the human needs visual context while the agent needs structured access to files, diagnostics, and mutations. Clicking through a file tree is possible, but it is slow and ambiguous. Patchwork keeps the project, preview, and recovery controls visible while WebMCP gives Codex operations with explicit schemas and outcomes. What it does Patchwork provides a browser-based workspace for small React projects. A user can load one of three deterministic starters, select and edit text files, inspect a live preview and available diagnostics, create or restore checkpoints, reset the current demo, and export the project as a ZIP. When the page is opened in a compatible ChatGPT browser, Codex can discover Patchwork's Site Tools. It can read workspace context and explicit files, apply a validated multi-file change, move or delete one explicit file, inspect preview diagnostics, manage checkpoints, and prepare an export. UI actions and agent tools call the same workspace services, so both participants see the same revision and result. Patchwork remains usable as a human-only application when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it The host application uses React, strict TypeScript, and Vite. Sandpack provides the editor/preview runtime, IndexedDB stores local workspace state, and JSZip prepares local exports. The workspace domain normalizes relative POSIX paths, allowlists text formats, enforces per-file, per-batch, and total-workspace limits, and stages complete mutations before commit. An optional expected revision prevents silent stale overwrites. Every committed content mutation creates a checkpoint first and increments the workspace revision once. WebMCP is registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool() in the top-level host document after workspace services are ready. The Sandpack iframe does not register tools. An injected Playwright adapter captures those production registrations and invokes the real handlers for deterministic tests; it is not a second tool implementation. How WebMCP is used Patchwork exposes these stable tools: get_workspace_context list_files read_files write_files move_file delete_file inspect_preview create_checkpoint restore_checkpoint prepare_project_export Read tools return bounded, structured state without changing files, checkpoints, activity, persistence, or revision. Mutations validate the entire request before committing, create recovery checkpoints, and return stable receipts with revision and changed paths. Errors are structured and repairable, including stale revision, invalid path, collision, unsupported extension, and size-limit cases. Why WebMCP is load-bearing Without WebMCP, the agent would need to guess the application's state and manipulate files through pixels, focus, and keystrokes. That makes multi-file changes, concurrency, recovery, and verification fragile. With WebMCP, the page provides explicit schemas for reading selected files, applying one atomic batch, checking the observed revision, inspecting available diagnostics, and restoring a known snapshot. This is not a shortcut around the product UI: it is the collaboration layer that lets the person and agent operate the same live application with shared state and clear effects. Challenges The hardest design problem was making Site Tools useful without turning Patchwork into a remote shell. We constrained the workspace to small text projects, made paths and payloads narrowly valid, and separated export preparation from the user-triggered download. Another challenge was integrating an iframe-based preview while respecting current ChatGPT Site Tools limitations. Registration belongs to the top-level document, so the host owns the WebMCP boundary and receives only supported preview status and diagnostics from Sandpack. Patchwork does not claim visual understanding when it only has compiler or runtime signals. Finally, UI actions and agent calls had to stay consistent. We avoided parallel implementations by routing both through the same domain and persistence services. Accomplishments A browser-native collaboration model with no embedded chatbot or API key. A shared service layer for human and WebMCP operations. Atomic, revision-aware multi-file mutations with automatic recovery snapshots. Deterministic demo starters and reset behavior. Graceful human operation when Site Tools are unavailable. A production-handler test adapter that does not duplicate business logic. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a web product already has clear domain operations. The best tools are not generic clicks; they expose meaningful application actions with narrow inputs, honest side effects, and enough result data to verify the outcome. We also learned that local-first architecture is a useful fit for agent collaboration. It reduces setup and data movement, but it still needs explicit limits, persistence validation, concurrency control, and recovery. Finally, preview diagnostics and visual review are different evidence and should never be conflated. What's next After the challenge build is frozen, potential follow-ups include a small public-GitHub import with strict limits, a human-readable diff view, and a read-only share format. These are not part of the submitted MVP unless independently implemented and verified before the deadline. title: CommentIntelligence
pitch: An AI agent that converts YouTube video's comment section into a evidence-backed map of what the audience wants, exposed entirely as WebMCP tools an agent can call directly in the browser.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent that converts YouTube video's comment section into a evidence-backed map of what the audience wants, exposed entirely as WebMCP tools an agent can call directly in the browser.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Running in Codex using WebMCPs 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Running in Codex using WebMCPs 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I was inspired to create a solution that can be used by both the creator and the marketing teams to find the audience insights. 

 What it does 

 It converts comments into meaningful insights that the creators can use to discover the audience's demands and plan their content accordingly. Also, can be used by marketing teams to find the right content creator that matches their vibes and audience. 

 How we built it 

 A React + TypeScript frontend and a Node/Express backend, wired together as a single pipeline: pull YouTube comments, classify each one with an LLM, cluster them into named themes, score demand with a transparent formula, and detect content gaps. The app's real capabilities — get comments, classify, cluster, rank, find gaps — are registered client-side as WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(), so an agent visiting the live site can discover and chain them itself. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 LLM provider reliability was the biggest fight — we hit rate limits on Groq, a fully deprecated model, a reasoning model silently burning its token budget on blocks, and NVIDIA NIM models getting decommissioned mid-build (410 errors, twice). We debugged our way through each with better logging, batch/concurrency tuning, and provider fallbacks. We also mid-flight realized WebMCP tools are registered client-side in the browser, not as a separate backend MCP server — a real architecture correction partway through the build. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A demand-scoring formula that's fully transparent — every score comes with a plain-English "why," not a black box. Real audience data driving every screen, not mocked examples: 222 real comments, 11 genuine themes, real unanswered questions in the audience's own words. And getting actual multi-step WebMCP tool-chaining working live in the browser, not just a single flat API call dressed up as a "tool." 

 What we learned 

 That building for agents is a different discipline than building for humans — the temptation is always to wrap everything into one big convenient function, but the whole point of WebMCP is resisting that and exposing the real steps so an agent can reason about which ones it actually needs. We also relearned, the hard way, that AI provider infrastructure changes constantly and silently — plan for models disappearing mid-project, not just for rate limits. 

 What's next for CommentIntelligence 

 Channel-wide analysis across a creator's last several videos to surface patterns, not just one-video insights. Trend detection by re-analyzing over time to see which requests are growing. Expanding the same pipeline beyond YouTube — podcast reviews, App Store reviews, product feedback — since the underlying problem (turn scattered audience text into ranked demand) isn't platform-specific.

title: MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab
pitch: Your approval changes what the agent can do.
about_excerpt: Your approval changes what the agent can do. Like Comment Story Updates APPLY ABSENT — The agent can inspect and propose, but no mutating tool exists before player approval. APPLY ADDED — Visible player approval creates one single-use tool bound to the exact reviewed plan. EXACT APPLY → UNDO ADDED — Apply removes itself after one use and exact undo takes its place. MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab Your approval changes what the agent can do. Live app: https://second-player-lab.asterai.chatgpt.site/ Source and MIT license: https://github.com/mcpilotandmore/mcpilot-adaptive-play-lab at v1.0.0 Demo video: https://youtu.be/etHmptvGNvc (119 seconds) What we built Most accessibility menus ask players to solve the problem before they can use the solution. A player leaves the action, guesses which settings might help, and changes several controls. MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab turns that guesswork into one short, reversible experiment. The player completes a 20-second fixed course. A browser agent reads device-local measurements such as accuracy, collisions, pauses, movement balance, and response time. It proposes the smallest supported change while explaining what it intends to preserve. The player reviews the exact values and approves or declines them. If approved, the agent applies only that reviewed plan. The player repeats the same course and answers a simple question: better, about the same, worse, or skip. The app then reports every available change, calls out regressions, and keeps an exact undo available. The agent never plays, approves, or answers the experience check-in for the person. An optional OpenAI Realtime voice guide can explain that division of labor out loud. The player explicitly starts the microphone, sees live captions, and can ask what the current step means. The guide receives only a bounded summary of visible page state, has no tools, and cannot change the lab; it automatically disconnects after two minutes. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The information needed for this interaction exists inside the open game page: the completed trial, current settings, selected needs, supported adjustment limits, proposal state, player approval, and undo snapshot. An assistant looking at screenshots would have to infer that state and hope it remained current. WebMCP lets the page expose those facts as small, structured tools tied to the live session. More importantly, it lets the page change which tools exist as the player makes decisions. Before approval, the agent can inspect the game, read the trial measurements, discover supported adaptations, and propose a plan—but there is no apply tool. When the player clicks Approve exact plan , apply_approved_tune registers for that proposal. It accepts only the approved ID and values; after use, it disappears and exact undo becomes available. The same rule protects the result. After the second trial, compare_play_trials remains unavailable until the player answers or explicitly skips the on-screen check-in. There is no WebMCP tool for submitting that answer. This is not a webpage with a permanent automation API attached. The player's visible choices determine what the agent is technically capable of doing next. How it creates a better experience Instead of trying eight settings blindly, the player gets one explainable proposal from the completed trial. Nothing changes silently. The values stay visible, the second run uses the same course, and the saved snapshot can restore every setting. The app also refuses to turn a flattering number into a success story. A higher score is not enough if collisions, response time, or the player's own experience became worse. Better can support an objectively strong result but cannot create one. About the same prevents a clear-improvement verdict. Worse vetoes success. Skip allows an objective comparison but not a player-benefit claim. Post-video live validation This final played pair was completed after the published 1:59 demo and is documented in the repository; the video demonstrates the permission-gated workflow, not these exact trial IDs or this exact outcome. The same player tested One-hand-left controls and reduced motion through In-app browser WebMCP: inspect, read signals, propose, visible approval, exact apply, then exact undo. , while preserving The player still steers, collects signals, and avoids visible hazards on the same timed course. . Baseline: trial-ebaf831f-a54c-4359-99a8-69253269ad4f Adapted trial: trial-b6cf2c66-4577-4153-bc9d-d07eb733c6ae Player check-in: Worse for me Score: 1750 → 1750 (0) Accuracy: 100% → 100% (0 pt) Collision rate: 0/10s → 0/10s (0/10s) Median collect time: 2307 ms → 2970 ms (+663 ms) Verdict: needs another iteration Player observation: The player selected Worse for me through the visible player check-in after the adapted trial. Accuracy: 100% to 100% (0 pt). The run did not produce enough qualifying gains to clear the product's success policy, so the page calls for another iteration. What people and agents can now do together The agent reads several measurements, checks supported ranges, constructs a valid configuration, keeps both trials tied to the same course and approved plan, and presents every tradeoff. The person keeps the decisions only they can make: playing the game, approving a change, and reporting how the result felt. That division is the point. A recommendation-only assistant has no page-defined, session-bound way to inspect, apply, verify, and undo this experiment. A fully autonomous agent should not grant itself permission or decide whether a change helped someone. With WebMCP, neither side impersonates the other. This is designed to reduce the guesswork involved in trying an alternative control or presentation setup. For game developers, it demonstrates a reusable permission pattern whose deterministic game state stays local. Optional voice is a separate explanation layer: microphone audio and a bounded page-state summary go to OpenAI only while the player is connected. How we implemented WebMCP MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, and the imperative WebMCP API. Six base tools handle inspection, signal reading, adaptation discovery, proposal creation, clearly labeled sample data, and preset export. Apply, compare, and undo register only when application state permits them. A server-only OpenAI Realtime WebRTC route powers the optional captioned guide with no tools and no access to game mutations. Strict schemas reject extra properties, and application code checks every supported range again. IDs and saved settings keep both runs connected, while the UI and WebMCP tools pass through the same validation rules. The exact application source is commit cb7f19545b1c22bb32003435a5655459ea2945c9 , deployed as Sites version 21. Its deterministic behavior is covered by 101 product tests. Gameplay telemetry, settings, approvals, and comparisons remain device-local; there is no account system, backend MCP server, or database. Optional voice streams microphone audio and a bounded page-state summary only while connected, and the standard API key remains server-side. The result is a working human-agent loop built around a simple rule: the agent can help the game listen, but the player remains in control. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Overturn
pitch: Analyze, recommend, and convert any website to WebMCP—in one shot.
about_excerpt: Analyze, recommend, and convert any website to WebMCP—in one shot. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web was built for people clicking. Some sites later gained APIs; many accumulated PDFs, hidden rules, multi-page forms, phone-only support, and offline handoffs. Browser agents can read those pages, but they still have to guess at the interface and often stall at the one consequential step that matters. WebMCP changes that by letting a website expose an explicit, typed contract for agents. The remaining adoption problem is substantial: a site owner still has to inspect an existing workflow, decide what should be a read, what should become an editable proposal, and what must wait for a human, then implement and verify the resulting tools. We built Overturn to make that retrofit process a product. For the end-to-end proof, we chose one of the hardest common workflows: appealing a health-plan prior-authorization denial. In Medicare Advantage in 2024, plans processed nearly 53 million prior-authorization requests. Only 11.5% of denied requests were appealed, even though 80.7% of appeals were partially or fully overturned ( KFF ). The fictional Larkspur Health Plan portal in our demo starts where many real workflows still start: a PDF letter, a six-page form, rules that are referenced but not exposed, and a fax or mailing address. What it does Overturn Retrofit takes a public URL and: Scans up to eight same-origin pages for forms, tables, detail pages, documents, offline submission instructions, cited policies, phone-only support, iframes, sign-in requirements, and WebMCP headers. Produces a 0–100 agent-readiness score and evidence-backed findings grouped as blockers, gaps, and notes. Recommends a typed WebMCP tool inventory. Reads are marked read-only, writes become on-page proposals, and consequential actions are explicitly human-gated. Generates a starter document.modelContext.registerTool() module and a Markdown implementation report. Exposes its own WebMCP meta-tools— analyze_site , get_readiness_report , list_recommended_tools , and get_generated_code —so a developer’s agent can drive the retrofit itself. The analyzer does not pretend it can infer and safely wire every site’s private business logic. It generates the tool layer and concrete fixes; a developer or coding agent connects app-specific handlers. To prove that the plan is actionable, we ran Retrofit against the fictional legacy portal, implemented its recommendations, and shipped the complete before-and-after experience on the same live site. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This project depends on WebMCP rather than merely adding it as a feature. On the Retrofit page, an agent can run the audit, inspect the findings, list the proposed tools, and retrieve the generated code through four page-native tools. On the rebuilt appeals portal, 14 tools expose the actual workflow: member context, denials, deadlines, policy criteria, drafting, evidence completeness, review type, submission, status, and external review. The tool surface is state-scoped. Drafting tools appear only in the appeal workspace; after filing, they disappear and status tools take their place. Every agent call is visible in the Activity panel, and every proposed write is rendered on the page for the person to inspect or edit. Without WebMCP, an automation agent must inspect the DOM, open PDFs, infer what fields mean, and eventually stops at the fax instruction. With WebMCP, the site itself tells the agent what it may read, what it may propose, and where the person must take over. How it creates a better user experience For a site owner, Overturn replaces a blank page with an actionable plan: what blocks agents today, which tools to expose, how to describe and scope them, which actions need confirmation, and the code to start from. For a person using the retrofitted site, the agent handles the repetitive work—reading the denial, matching records to five policy criteria, drafting one evidence-backed argument per criterion, checking completeness, and calculating deadlines. The person keeps the decisions that are actually theirs: choose records, edit the language, select standard or expedited review, and sign. The work never disappears into a chat window. Drafts are on the page, labelled and editable. Tool calls are logged. The person sees exactly what changed and remains in control. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before: an agent can read a denial letter and locate the appeal form, but the workflow is unstructured and ends at a fax or mailing address. It cannot reliably know the plan’s five criteria, prove that the evidence is complete, or safely file the appeal. After: in one sitting and on one shared page, the agent reads the structured denial and criteria, opens the appeal, drafts five arguments tied to named records, and re-checks completeness as the member attaches evidence and edits the draft. The agent can request submission, but it cannot file. It returns pending_confirmation , the site renders a Sign & submit card, and only the member’s click creates a case number and starts the decision clock. That read → proposal → human commit pattern can extend beyond appeals to any claim-shaped dispute or regulated legacy workflow. How we built it Application: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, and Vercel. Analyzer: deterministic server-side heuristics using Cheerio. Crawling is SSRF-guarded: HTTP(S) only, private network ranges refused, and redirects, response size, page count, and time are capped. WebMCP layer: document.modelContext.registerTool() with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback, one AbortController per tool, duplicate-safe registration, readOnlyHint annotations, concise descriptions, and bounded outputs. Safety: reads are free; writes render as proposals; submit_appeal and request_external_review return pending_confirmation . The server rejects submission without the human-click marker using 403 human_confirmation_required . State and judge access: each visitor receives an isolated localStorage sandbox. There is no login or database. A replay demonstrates the same flow for browsers without site-tools access. Verification: a comprehensive Puppeteer smoke suite exercises route scoping, the full appeal flow, generated code, analyzer guards, human-gated submission, and the post-filing tool transition. We also tested the deployed tools in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and WebMCP-enabled Chrome. Build workflow: we used Claude Code on an NVIDIA DGX Spark for research, implementation, debugging, testing, deployment, and the reproducible FFmpeg/edge-tts video pipeline. The submitted application does not depend on an LLM at runtime. Challenges we ran into Designing real human confirmation. WebMCP does not currently provide a tool-level confirmation primitive. We created an application protocol instead: an agent can propose a consequential action, the page renders a confirmation card, and a server-side gate accepts only the person’s click. Keeping tools synchronized with application state. The useful tool set changes as the member moves from denial to draft to filed case. We built one registry that derives tools from both the route and appeal status, unregisters stale tools, and remains stable under React Strict Mode and hot reloads. Analyzing arbitrary URLs safely. A URL analyzer can easily become an SSRF proxy or an unbounded crawler. We had to reject private addresses and tightly cap redirects, bytes, pages, and request time while still returning a useful partial report when some pages fail. Drawing an honest conversion boundary. Static HTML can reveal affordances, but it cannot reveal every private API or JavaScript-only state transition. Generated handlers therefore make app-specific wiring explicit instead of hiding it behind a false “one-click” claim. Accomplishments we are proud of Shipped the analyzer, legacy portal, agent-native portal, and readiness record as one coherent live product. Turned the legacy portal’s 40/100 audit—two blockers, two gaps, and nine recommended tools—into a working portal with 14 domain tools plus four Retrofit meta-tools. Made the agent’s work visible and editable while enforcing consequential consent on the server, not in a prompt. Built a complete, reproducible before-and-after demo and an automated verification suite during the hackathon window. What we learned Structured reads alone do not complete workflows. Agents also need typed proposals, deterministic validation, explicit commit paths, and post-action status. Human control works best as product architecture, not as a prompt instruction. Tool names, descriptions, scope, and lifecycle are part of the user experience. A generated scaffold is valuable only when it clearly shows what has been inferred and what a developer still needs to connect. What’s next Add authenticated repository and CMS integrations so a developer’s agent can open a reviewed implem

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: WebMCP Studio
pitch: WebMCP Studio turns existing websites into agent-ready experiences by discovering actions, generating structured WebMCP tools, and letting AI agents safely interact with live web apps.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Studio turns existing websites into agent-ready experiences by discovering actions, generating structured WebMCP tools, and letting AI agents safely interact with live web apps. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We were inspired by the upcoming availability of WebMCP tools and noticed that many production websites still do not expose agent-native capabilities. WebMCP Studio helps developers detect useful capabilities from existing websites, then compose them into reusable workflows. This can reduce agent tool calls and make agentic workflows easier to understand and maintain. What it does WebMCP Studio discovers native WebMCP tools and infers potential tools from a website’s semantic DOM, forms, and visible actions. Developers can review the evidence, drag actions into a workflow, generate a higher-level tool such as buy_best_product, and test it on a controlled page. The hosted Studio provides a simple judge path. An optional Chrome MV3 extension supports advanced discovery and execution on eligible live pages. How we built it We built the project in TypeScript with a dependency-light browser architecture: A discovery engine scans semantic HTML, forms, controls, Shadow DOM, and same-origin frames. A capability graph stores discovered tools, schemas, locators, evidence, confidence, and effects. A structured workflow interpreter composes primitive actions using validated JSON bindings. A hosted Studio provides the visual discovery and drag-and-drop workflow builder. A versioned postMessage bridge connects Studio to controlled commerce and travel target pages. Generated tools are registered through the browser’s document.modelContext API when WebMCP is available. External URLs remain potential-only in the hosted flow; the extension handles approved live-page instrumentation. The demo workflow searches products, filters by price, views details, and adds the selected product to a cart. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP ecosystem is still evolving. Browser support, Permissions Policy, secure-context requirements, and agent-provider capabilities vary, so successfully registering a tool on a page does not automatically prove that ChatGPT can discover and invoke it. We also had to distinguish native tools from inferred suggestions. Inferred tools may be useful, but they need evidence, confidence, schema validation, stable locators, and human review before execution. Dynamic websites introduced additional challenges, including SPA updates, Shadow DOM, iframes, weak accessibility semantics, stale elements, and potentially unsafe actions. We addressed these with bounded discovery, structured validation, explicit activation, session checks, and clear native-versus-preview states. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an end-to-end workflow from: Discover → Compose → Generate → Inject → Test We are especially proud that the product remains honest about capability status: Native WebMCP tools are clearly separated from inferred tools. Unsupported browsers receive an explicit preview path instead of a simulated native claim. Generated workflows produce structured traces and visible page effects. The project includes unit tests, Playwright end-to-end tests, deterministic target fixtures, and an optional browser extension. What we learned We learned that making websites useful to agents requires more than finding buttons or API requests. A reliable tool also needs a meaningful name, typed input schema, evidence, permissions, stable locators, and understandable failure behavior. We also learned that page-level WebMCP registration and agent-level WebMCP consumption are separate compatibility problems. Finally, structured workflows make agent behavior more reusable and auditable than repeatedly asking an agent to perform low-level website actions. What's next for WebMCP Studio Next, we want to validate the complete native ChatGPT/browser connection in a supported environment. We also plan to improve inference accuracy, add more site-specific adapters, support more dynamic and authenticated workflows, and make generated projects easier to reuse across websites and sessions. title: Bookhand
pitch: Without WebMCP, Bookhand is an EPUB reader. With WebMCP, agents turn books into living study environments: finding context and building cited explanations, lessons and even fixing broken formatting.
about_excerpt: Without WebMCP, Bookhand is an EPUB reader. With WebMCP, agents turn books into living study environments: finding context and building cited explanations, lessons and even fixing broken formatting. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Using AI agents as helpers with technical books is awesome, but what if we could bring the agents into the book reader? What happens if the ebook reader itself tells the agent what it can do through native browser semantics? Not scraping the DOM or clicking around like a blind monkey in Playwright, but genuine, typed WebMCP capabilities ( document.modelContext ). The agent spends its intelligence on actual teaching and assistance instead of reverse-engineering the browser. But once you got an AI agent with direct access to your app, all kinds fo doors open. For example, legacy ebooks look like crap. In most technical public-domain EPUBs, every single mathematical variable ($x, y, dy/dx$) is a mess, You can't search it, you can't select it, and in dark mode it turns invisible. Instead of waiting 10 years for publishers to fix it, why not let an agent act like a coding harness, read the raw chapter XHTML, and rewrite it into native MathML? Bookhand gives agents tools to do this What it does A real reader first (100% local-first): No login, no cloud, no tracking. Your books, annotations, study boards, and search index live in your browser. If your Wi-Fi dies or you turn off AI, it’s still a fast, ~gorgeous~ mediocre EPUB reader. 21 Native WebMCP Capabilities: When opened in a compatible browser (like Chromium with WebMCP or ChatGPT Desktop), Bookhand exposes 21 distinct tools directly to the model: navigation, search, styling, passage focus, study cards, and document remastering. The Book Fact-Checks the Agent: If an agent tries to save a highlight, quote, or study block, Bookhand resolves the exact CFI range, takes a SHA-256 text fingerprint, and compares the quote. If the agent hallucinates even a single word or references the wrong book, the write is rejected and nothing touches storage. . A small thing to keep agents from hallucinating quotes. Surgical Document Remastering (The Coding Harness for Books): The agent doesn't just slap a CSS theme on top of broken markup. It can read the raw EPUB's XHTML, and use edit_section to apply atomic search-and-replace patches—transcompiling blurry formula images into native, scalable MathML. Study surface: The agent can use tools to highlight passages, take notes, write small lessons, or even small quizes that get stored for future reference. It can become a nice personalized AI tutor. How I built it React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. No backend. Reader Engine: Upstream foliate-js pinned to a commit. Storage & Search: Official @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm running in a dedicated Web Worker on opfs-sahpool . Lexical search uses SQLite’s native FTS5 with BM25 ranking Agent Surface: document.modelContext WebMCP, duh. With handlers independently validating their input and returning structured success and failure content. Security & Containment: Hardened Content Security Policy (CSP) and regex sanitizers strip scripts, event handlers, and remote tracking url() calls from untrusted EPUBs. Untrusted book content is isolated before reaching the agent. Deployment: Cloudflare Workers. Challenges I ran into WebMCP in a test browser: Getting a real document.modelContext under Playwright required the exact feature flag ( --enable-features=WebMCPTesting ) on a secure origin and doesn't act exactly like something like ChatGPTs in-app browser. Quote verification normalization: Finding the exact boundary for quote comparison (Unicode NFC, normalizing CRLF to LF, collapsing whitespace runs, and trimming) while keeping case, punctuation, and math symbols strictly significant. Tbh, gpt Sol probably went overboard with this, but hey. The Invisible Calculus Bug: In Calculus Made Easy , formulas were black-on-transparent PNGs. In dark mode, all the math completely vanished. Fixing this cleanly required transcompiling equations into real MathML instead of relying on fragile CSS inversion hacks. It was at this point I started thinking "what if I could just tell the agent to fix the crazy underlying Epub file instead of fighting it with css?" Android Iframe Text Inflation: Chrome on Android silently inflates text inside iframes without a viewport tag, which threw off Foliate's multi-column pagination math. Finnicky stuff. Still clunky on Android at the moment. Accomplishments I'm proud of The Tutor: I've been using AI agents to help me really understand technical books for a while and it is pretty awesome. Being able to pull frontier model intelligence right into the reader app makes lot of sense to me. The Coding-Harness Remaster: Giving the model a genuine Read and Edit tool for XHTML, letting it transcompile broken legacy books into native MathML, and actually semantic HTML feels like the future. Genuinely Local-First: SQLite WASM over OPFS with zero accounts, zero telemetry, and zero servers. No subscription. No ads. And free, as in free beer and libre. What I learned Ebook readers are a big big rabbit hole. LLM models can play a big role in this space. Let models cook . Read and edit can go a very long way for an agent to fix an EPUB. What's next Embodied tutor presentation: Anchored plain-text explanations beside transient source cues. First-class study lessons: Titled, organized, easy to follow lessons flows. Local embeddings: Implement vector search for even better agentic results Smooth things out : Spark joy and all that.
