title: Post-Purchase Resolution
pitch: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant.
about_excerpt: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant. Like Comment Story Updates Post-Purchase Resolution Shopping agents know how to buy. What happens when something goes wrong? Post-Purchase Resolution is an agent-native post-purchase support experience built with WebMCP + Shopify . Instead of forcing a customer to search for an order number, navigate support menus, or explain the same problem several times, the customer can simply describe what went wrong in natural language. The agent can then discover the website's structured WebMCP capabilities, find the correct purchase, read authoritative Shopify state, and prepare the next step. But there is one deliberate boundary: The agent can help. It cannot silently become the customer or the merchant. The customer keeps customer authority. The merchant keeps merchant authority. Shopify remains the external source of truth. 🎥 Demo Watch the full demo In the demo, a customer reports that a Portable 4K Action Camera — $149 arrived damaged and would not turn on. The customer never provides an order number. From that natural-language request, the agent discovers the site's WebMCP tools, finds the correct authenticated purchase, reads its return eligibility, and prepares a resolution. Then: Agent prepares → Customer commits → Merchant decides → Shopify records the truth. 💡 Inspiration AI shopping experiences are becoming increasingly capable before checkout. Agents can search. They can compare. They can recommend. They can help people buy. But commerce does not end at checkout. Products arrive damaged. The wrong variant is delivered. Shipments arrive late. Customers need exchanges, returns, replacements, or refunds. And that part of the experience is still dominated by: order numbers support menus forms ticket queues policy pages repeated explanations disconnected customer and merchant workflows That led us to a simple question: If the web is becoming agentic, what should happen when the purchase itself goes wrong? We did not want to build another chatbot floating on top of an ecommerce site. We wanted the website itself to expose meaningful, structured capabilities that an agent could understand and use safely. That is where WebMCP became the core of the product rather than an add-on. ✨ What it does Post-Purchase Resolution lets a customer describe a purchase problem naturally. For example: “The action camera I bought recently arrived damaged and won't turn on. Can you find the purchase and tell me what I can do? Don't submit anything.” The customer does not need to know the order number. The agent discovers the site's available WebMCP tools and can use: find_order get_order prepare_resolution The experience then separates responsibility between three actors. 🤖 Agent The agent can: understand the customer's intent locate the relevant purchase read authoritative order information inspect return eligibility prepare the appropriate resolution The agent cannot commit the commerce action through WebMCP. 👤 Customer The authenticated customer decides whether to actually request the return. That action occurs under the customer's own Shopify Customer Account authority. 🏪 Merchant The merchant receives the pending request in a separate decision desk. Only the merchant can approve it. 🟢 Shopify Shopify records the authoritative lifecycle of the return. The website does not invent its own version of commerce state. 🔥 Why WebMCP matters Without structured site capabilities, an agent often has to reason from presentation: inspect UI interpret text locate controls infer what a button means navigate DOM state hope the page still looks the same Post-Purchase Resolution instead exposes explicit business capabilities. Customer intent ↓ ChatGPT / Codex ↓ WebMCP Site Tools ↓ find_order get_order prepare_resolution ↓ Authoritative Shopify data This means the agent does not need to guess that a certain button or piece of text represents an order lookup. The site tells the agent exactly what capability exists. And just as importantly, it tells the agent what capability does not exist. 🔐 The capability boundary This became one of the most important design decisions in the project. The WebMCP surface intentionally contains: ✓ find_order ✓ get_order ✓ prepare_resolution It intentionally does not contain: ✕ request_return ✕ approve_return ✕ refund That is not an unfinished feature. It is the authority model. The agent can find, read, and prepare. The customer commits. The merchant decides. This allowed us to design the experience around collaboration instead of maximum agent autonomy. More agent capability is not always better. The right capability at the right boundary is better. 🛍️ A real end-to-end scenario One of our clean validation runs used a fresh Shopify purchase that was never hardcoded into the application. The application discovered the purchase automatically. The customer then followed the complete flow. Fresh purchase ↓ Agent discovers purchase ↓ Agent prepares resolution ↓ Customer explicitly requests return ↓ Shopify Return = REQUESTED ↓ Merchant reviews request ↓ Merchant approves ↓ Same Shopify Return = OPEN The critical part is that the same external Shopify Return object is preserved throughout the lifecycle. The application is not maintaining a parallel pretend state. Shopify is the system of record. 🧪 Real Shopify proof We verified the architecture against a Shopify development store using test payments and real Shopify Order/Return objects . A clean flow demonstrated: Step Result Fresh order discovered without hardcoding ✅ Customer-scoped purchase ✅ Agent mutation tool exposed No Customer requested return ✅ Shopify Return created REQUESTED Merchant reviewed same Return ✅ Merchant approved ✅ Same Shopify Return updated OPEN Duplicate Return created No Refund automatically performed No This distinction matters. The agent did not manufacture a UI result. The state transition existed independently in Shopify. 🗣️ Natural-language WebMCP verification We also tested the WebMCP experience through ChatGPT/Codex Site Tools. The user described a damaged purchase without giving an order number. The agent discovered and used: find_order get_order prepare_resolution It found the correct purchase and prepared the resolution. Nothing was submitted. An independent Shopify check confirmed: Return created by agent: NO Refund created by agent: NO Approval event: NO We then repeated the experience using a spoken request in a new chat with no previous order context . The observed flow was: Spoken request ↓ ChatGPT agent turn ↓ Website Site Tools enumerated ↓ find_order ↓ get_order ↓ Correct purchase found The spoken request asked only to find the purchase and explain the available option. The agent did exactly that. It did not stage a resolution unnecessarily. That gave us an interesting proof of intent-sensitive tool selection. 🏗️ How we built it The product is built around four distinct layers. ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Customer / ChatGPT / Codex │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ WebMCP │ ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ Post-Purchase Resolution │ │ Vercel-hosted application │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ Customer Account Admin API API │ │ │ ▼ ▼ Customer action Merchant action │ │ └────────┬─────────┘ ▼ Shopify External source of truth WebMCP The site registers structured tools through the browser's model context. The final tool surface is deliberately small: find_order get_order prepare_resolution Shopify Customer Account API The authenticated customer flow uses Shopify Customer Account authentication. This keeps order discovery scoped to the currently authenticated customer's purchases. The customer action uses customer authority. Shopify Admin API Merchant approval uses a separate server-side Admin authority. The Admin credential is never exposed to the browser or agent. Vercel The public application and server-side API routes are deployed on Vercel. Secrets remain on the server boundary. 🔑 Authentication and authority Customer authentication uses OAuth/OIDC with PKCE. The customer session is used to query purchases belonging to that authenticated customer. The architecture does not permit arbitrary customer order enumeration from the customer flow. The merchant side uses a separate operator access control in the current implementation. That merchant access layer is intentionally distinct from customer authentication. Current limitation: The merchant decision desk uses an operator credential rather than full merchant OAuth/identity. We document this explicitly rather than presenting it as something it is not. 🛡️ Security by capability design Security was not treated as a final checklist item. It influenced the WebMCP architecture itself. Important boundaries include: customer-scoped order retrieval no arbitrary order lookup from authenticated customer flow S

title: LiquidHR Agent Workspace
pitch: A state-aware HR workspace where a browser agent uses WebMCP to prepare grounded development conversations while the manager retains the final decision.
about_excerpt: A state-aware HR workspace where a browser agent uses WebMCP to prepare grounded development conversations while the manager retains the final decision. Like Comment 1 Story Updates 1 Inspiration I am a product manager, not a software engineer, and I am building an HR application called LiquidHR using AI-assisted development with Codex (luna model only). I was preparing to explore a traditional MCP server for LiquidHR when the WebMCP Challenge appeared. I decided to change direction and spend a day answering a different question: What happens if the web application itself can teach an AI agent what it is allowed to do? LiquidHR Agent Workspace is the result. What it does The project demonstrates a people manager and a browser agent preparing the same employee development conversation together. The application initially exposes three WebMCP capabilities: find an employee within the manager's scope retrieve that employee's development context prepare a grounded development-conversation draft The manager can ask, in natural language, for a development conversation to be prepared for Sophie. The agent uses the capabilities exposed by the LiquidHR website to find Sophie, retrieve her current goals, open actions and skill-development signals, and create three grounded discussion topics. The manager sees that exact same draft in the human interface. This is not a chatbot creating a separate copy of HR data. The human interface and the agent operate on the same application state. State-aware WebMCP capabilities One of the ideas I especially wanted to explore was whether the capability surface itself could follow the workflow. Initially, the application exposes three tools. Once a valid conversation draft exists for the currently selected employee, LiquidHR dynamically exposes a fourth WebMCP capability: add_follow_up_action The agent can then add a bounded follow-up action to the existing draft. When the manager finally reviews and saves the conversation, that temporary capability disappears again. The capability lifecycle is therefore: 3 → 4 → 3 The application's state determines what the agent can do next. Human judgment remains human Final save is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP capability. The agent can retrieve context, organize information, prepare the draft and add a follow-up action, but the manager must perform the final Review & save action in the human interface. That creates a deliberate human-confirmation boundary around the judgment-bearing transition. The agent doesn't bypass the application. The application teaches the agent how to use it safely. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, a general-purpose assistant often has to work through a second interface, copied data, brittle browser interaction or a separately designed API. WebMCP lets the web application expose a structured capability contract directly to the browser agent. The tool names, descriptions, input schemas, annotations, authorization rules and lifecycle are defined by the application itself. That means the agent does not have to guess which buttons to click or infer hidden application state. It receives capabilities that reflect what the application can safely do at that moment. Shared application architecture The human UI and the WebMCP callbacks use the same: workspace facade → actor and manager-scope policy → domain service → shared draft state → synthetic repository Employee lookup is restricted to the fictional manager's authorized scope. Direct employee context access is validated again before information is returned. The project also contains an out-of-scope synthetic employee for authorization testing. All company, employee and activity data is fictional. Implementation The project uses the imperative WebMCP API through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The application uses object JSON Schemas, tool descriptions, annotations, structured results and lifecycle-managed registrations. The first three capabilities remain available for the workspace lifecycle. The fourth capability is dynamically registered only when a valid matching draft exists and is removed after the draft is discarded or saved. The application is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript and deployed publicly on Vercel. No production HR backend, real employee data or external AI API is embedded in the challenge application. What I proved The live end-to-end flow demonstrates: real WebMCP capability discovery and execution natural-language interaction with application-defined tools scoped employee access grounded development context shared state between human and agent dynamic state-aware capabilities a visible activity trail a deliberate human confirmation boundary The complete natural-language flow was also tested against the public application using ChatGPT's browser with a WebMCP-capable runtime. Potential impact Managers frequently spend time gathering goals, open actions and development signals before a useful conversation can even begin. An agent can remove much of that repetitive retrieval and preparation without taking over the manager's judgment. The same pattern can extend far beyond HR: applications can expose safe, contextual capabilities to agents while retaining their own business rules, permissions, workflow state and human approval boundaries. Human judgment. Agent speed. One shared HR workspace.## Inspiration Built With chatgpt next.js react typescript vercel vitest webmcp Try it out liquidhr-agent-workspace.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived, designed, built, tested, deployed and documented LiquidHR Agent Workspace as a solo project. As a product manager rather than a software engineer, I defined the product concept, WebMCP workflow, authorization boundaries, shared human-agent state and human confirmation model, and used AI-assisted development with Codex to turn those specifications into the working application. I also performed the end-to-end WebMCP testing, prepared the public demo, and created the challenge submission. title: Attune
pitch: Design physical products with your browser agent, find who can make it
about_excerpt: Design physical products with your browser agent, find who can make it Like Comment Story Updates Attune Design Attune Let the design find its maker. Inspiration I came into this challenge from a UX/UI and product design background. At first I kept asking: what can an agent do on a website? While building Attune, a better question took over: What should the person and the agent do together? A person may be better at looking at a design, moving something by eye, and deciding what feels right. An agent can help with exact values, repeated edits, relationships, checks, and multi-step work. The useful part is when both work on the same object , without the person having to explain that object again and again. That became Attune. What Attune does Attune is a shared workspace for designing physical products . The person gets the visual canvas. The browser agent gets WebMCP tools. Both work on the same underlying design. If I already selected something, I should not need to describe which part I mean. If the design already knows a measurement, the agent should not guess it from the screen. If I change something myself, the agent should continue from the new state. The goal is not “AI, finish the whole design for me.” It is closer to: I decide → the agent helps → I adjust → Attune checks → we continue. Why WebMCP here? A 2D engineering sketch is more than pixels. It contains entities, dimensions, constraints, groups, solver state, versions, and relationships between parts. A small edit can also affect what happens later. Without a structured interface, an agent has to reconstruct too much of that from the visible UI. With WebMCP, Attune can give the agent direct actions over the same design state the person is using. That lets the agent answer four useful questions: What am I working on? What can I change here? What would this change affect? What can happen next? Attune also does not expose one giant toolbox on every page. Design tools appear while editing. Manufacturing tools appear later. Buyer and Maker actions stay separate. Important commercial actions still require human confirmation. Chrome WebMCP WebMCP tools Not every tool is active at once. The current page, project state, and the person's access decide what is exposed. Surface Tool What it does / why it is exposed Dashboard inspect_projects Reads accessible projects and their current stage. Dashboard create_project Creates a blank or template project when allowed. Dashboard open_project Opens an accessible project on the right surface. Dashboard inspect_notifications Reads recent activity so the agent can find what needs attention. Dashboard open_notification Opens one notification and navigates to its authorized project surface. Design inspect_context Reads the current selection, IDs, versions, nearby geometry, constraints, solver state, and unseen human changes. Design forecast_change Previews what one proposed design action would do before anything is committed. Design modify_geometry Creates or changes real sketch geometry, including parametric recipes, radius edits, transforms, node moves, trims, deletes, and groups. Design constrain_geometry Adds or removes dimensions and engineering relationships such as tangency. Design check_design Checks solver and validation state after an edit. Manufacturing find_makers Compares the current design with Maker capability so the design itself can be used to ask who can make it. Workspace navigate_workspace Moves between valid Attune surfaces without using navigation to grant new authority. Manufacturing manage_manufacturing_request Configures, submits, quotes, requests changes, and accepts work when the operation is valid for the current role and state. Commerce inspect_commerce_pipeline Reads the request → quote → acceptance → Shopify Draft Order chain without customer contact details. Commerce prepare_customer_checkout Retrieves a verified checkout handoff only after confirmation and only when checkout is available. Workspace manage_account Exposes account/setup operations that make sense from the current workspace state. Settings inspect_account_setup Checks Buyer setup and connected Maker stores without returning private contact data. Settings start_shopify_connection Starts Shopify OAuth while the merchant still approves permissions themselves. Settings select_shopify_location Selects a real active Shopify location for the connected Maker. Settings inspect_shopify_orders Reads recent Draft Orders and their Attune version bindings without customer PII or checkout URLs. Settings open_shopify_admin Opens a previously inspected Draft Order in the Maker's Shopify Admin. Settings open_maker_workspace Opens Maker profile, incoming requests, or accepted jobs. Judge review inspect_review_flow Explains the seeded review path and why later stages are locked or available. Judge review open_review_control_center Opens the judge control center without changing workflow state. Judge review reset_judge_workspace Resets only the seeded judge workspace after explicit confirmation. The important part is not the number of tools. The tools follow the work. Co-creation, not autopilot Building the design side taught me that precise design is not really a one-prompt problem. Even a simple request can depend on what should stay fixed when something else moves. Recent Autodesk research on AI CAD editing points to the same problem: current models are improving, but matching the designer's exact intent is still difficult. That helped clarify the roles: The person provides intent and judgement. The agent helps interpret and carry out the request. The application owns the exact result. Attune works with real 2D geometry and constraints rather than treating the canvas as only a picture. Autodesk Research - AI CAD editing Why manufacturing? Manufacturing made this interaction more meaningful because a design action can have consequences outside the screen. Moving one feature can affect a constraint. It can affect whether a Maker can make the part. A later design edit can also make an older quote belong to the wrong version. So I started thinking about WebMCP actions as steps on a path: see the work → understand the change → check the result → know what can happen next The model can help understand what I want. It should not invent whether something is actually manufacturable. The design becomes the query Once the design is ready, another problem appears: Who can make this? Today that often becomes another translation step: “CNC shop”, “aluminium fabrication”, “laser cutting”. But the design already contains more useful information than those words: geometry, dimensions, material, quantity, and requirements. The longer-term idea behind Attune is: Let the design itself become the query. The person can then add what matters: prefer somebody nearby, need it quickly, preserve these mounting points, or show a specialist if nobody local fits. And Makers are not always sellers. A shop that machines one part may buy finishing, electronics, packaging, or another process from somebody else. Today's Maker can be tomorrow's customer. That is why I see the future as a network of Makers, with local opportunity and global reach, rather than only a one-way marketplace. From design to a real order I did not want the demo to end at a fake Buy button. Attune keeps an exact saved version attached to the manufacturing request. The Maker reviews that version. The quote belongs to that version. The Buyer accepts that version. If the design changes later, the old quote should not quietly become approval for something different. The challenge path is: Design → Buyer Request → Maker Review → Buyer Order → Maker Job / Shopify Shopify Draft Orders How I built it Attune uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, CanvasKit/Skia, Maker.js, PlaneGCS, Liveblocks, Yjs, Neon/PostgreSQL, Shopify, Cloudflare R2, Kumo, and WebMCP . The human interface and the WebMCP path use the same underlying design and workflow rules. They are not two separate versions of the product. Challenges I ran into This was more ambitious than I understood at the start. I was learning CAD-style interaction, geometric constraints, realtime collaboration, WebMCP, permissions, Shopify, and backend state at the same time. The 2D sketch workspace was the hardest part. Drawing geometry that looks right is much easier than building interaction where selections, dimensions, constraints, and later edits still mean what the person intended. I also learned how to work better with coding agents. Long runs could sometimes carry an older architectural assumption forward after the product had changed. I moved toward smaller tasks, checking the current code, running tests, and committing between milestones. Limited agent usage made that discipline even more important.  Inspiration 

 Most WebMCP demos automate forms or SaaS workflows. We wanted to show something more interactive. 

 Beat The Agent is a social-deduction game where humans try to identify hidden AI players, while AI players try to blend in and survive. 

 What it does 

 Aymen is the human player. Echo is a separate player controlled by an external WebMCP agent. 

 Through 7 WebMCP tools, Echo can read the game state, follow the discussion, use its power, send messages, vote, and continue across rounds. 

 The game has three phases:

title: Tabby: Collaborative Expense Splitting powered by WebMCP
pitch: Splitting group bills is messy. Tabby exposes its interface to agents through WebMCP, letting agents handle the tedious parts while humans and agents work together on the same live state.
about_excerpt: Splitting group bills is messy. Tabby exposes its interface to agents through WebMCP, letting agents handle the tedious parts while humans and agents work together on the same live state. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Splitting a restaurant bill is a nightmare. Five friends can sit around one table with different diets, different arrival times, shared dishes, tax, tip, and a receipt nobody can quite remember. The app can give you checkboxes for all of it, but eventually someone is doing mental bookkeeping at 11 PM just to answer a simple question: who actually owes what? And when the perfect split is too much work, people take the easy way out: split it evenly. Tabby started from a simple idea: what if you could tell the app what happened in the same way you'd tell a friend? That's where WebMCP became interesting. Instead of building another chat interface around an expense database, we wanted an agent that could actually work inside the expense app, alongside the person using it. What it does Tabby is a complete shared expense app: groups, receipts, itemised bills, multiple currencies, balances, settle-up, and an audit trail. You can use it entirely with a mouse. Nothing about the app requires an agent. When an agent is present, WebMCP lets it work with the same interface and the same live state. Give it a receipt. Tell it that Ravi is vegetarian, Meera arrived late, or that someone remembered something after the split. The agent can reason about those facts, propose changes, and navigate the page to show you what it means. The model handles perception and reasoning. The page handles the money. This division is deliberate. A model is good at understanding a messy receipt or a sentence like "Ravi didn't eat the prawns." The application is better at calculating exactly how much everyone owes. Tabby never asks the model to calculate a per-person monetary amount. Most importantly, the agent never silently takes control. Changes that matter are staged as proposals with a visible diff and require the human to accept them. Why WebMCP is the right primitive We could have built an agent directly into Tabby. But that would make the agent another feature of Tabby, tied to our UI, backend, and product architecture. WebMCP lets us do something more powerful: Tabby remains a normal expense app, while any compatible agent can become a participant in it. The same Tabby interface can be used normally by a person, or augmented by an agent when the task benefits from it. The agent gets access to Tabby's existing capabilities and live state without requiring a separate agent-specific workflow. This also means the human stays in control. The agent can reason, propose, and act through the application's existing operations, while Tabby remains responsible for state, validation, and money. WebMCP turns an existing web application into something an agent can participate in, rather than requiring every application to build its own agent. How we built it The central architectural decision was simple: There is one app, one state, and one set of operations. A button in the UI and a WebMCP tool call the same underlying store action. There is no separate agent backend and no special code path built only for AI. WebMCP exposes those existing operations to an agent. We deliberately split responsibilities: The model perceives and reasons. It can read a receipt photo, understand natural-language constraints, and reason about who ate what. The page computes. Tabby performs every allocation deterministically using integer minor units and largest-remainder arithmetic. The human decides. Every consequential write becomes a proposal with a visible diff before anything is committed. This means assign_items can say who ate which items , but it cannot tell Tabby how many rupees each person owes. The page calculates that. The same principle extends to settlement. Tabby computes the minimum-transfer plan rather than asking a language model to do the arithmetic. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with a navigator.modelContext fallback for client compatibility. Registration is also tied to application state, so the page only exposes tools that are actually usable at that moment. For consequential actions, Tabby uses a propose → diff → accept flow. The commit operation can wait for a human to confirm in an in-page sheet. The agent cannot bypass that interaction. What became possible For humans, Tabby replaces tedious checkbox-by-checkbox bookkeeping with natural collaboration. You can say: "Ravi's vegetarian and doesn't drink. Meera arrived after the starters. Split tax and service based on what people actually ate." The agent can turn that context into a proposed item-level split. If the user remembers something later, they can simply edit the bill directly and ask the agent to incorporate the correction. For agents, Tabby provides something more useful than a database API: a live application they can reason about. The agent can read receipts, inspect expenses and balances, navigate to the relevant part of the page, propose changes, see human edits, and amend its own pending proposal. This creates a workflow that was difficult to achieve before: The human provides judgment and memory. The agent handles context and reasoning. The application handles state and computation. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn't registering tools. It was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do . Money is a particularly unforgiving domain. A language model can be excellent at understanding "Ravi didn't eat the prawns" and still be the wrong component to calculate 17% of a ₹4,381.27 bill. So we designed the tool surface around that distinction. We also had to make the WebMCP surface reflect the actual state of the application. Tools appear and disappear as capabilities become available. A receipt-reading tool shouldn't exist when there is no receipt to read. A commit operation shouldn't exist when there is no draft to commit. We also had to handle the reality of an evolving WebMCP implementation. Clients currently differ in API support, iframe discovery, and image content handling, so Tabby uses feature detection and keeps its registration at the top level. Accomplishments we're proud of We built a real expense application, not an agent demo wearing an expense-app costume. Every feature works without an agent. We made the agent share the application's state rather than mirror it. Human edits are immediately part of what the agent can reason about. We made arithmetic impossible for the model to get wrong. Money is represented as integer minor units throughout the system. Largest-remainder allocation guarantees that every split sums exactly to the original amount. We made human approval a system property, not a prompt instruction. Consequential operations follow a propose → diff → accept flow. The agent cannot simply decide to move money. We tested the actual WebMCP boundary. 61 unit tests cover money, splitting, settlement, and parsing. 73 Playwright tests exercise the WebMCP surface, including dynamic registration, human cancellation, two-browser collaboration, hand edits beneath open drafts, amendment chains, and malformed input. What we learned The interesting question isn't: "What can an agent do?" It's: "What should the agent do, and what should the application do?" WebMCP made that boundary surprisingly clear. Models are good at ambiguity, context, perception, and language. Applications are good at state, arithmetic, validation, permissions, and consequences. The best experience isn't necessarily an agent replacing the interface. In many cases, it's an agent that can join the interface without taking it away from you. What's next for Tabby The next step is making that collaboration more configurable. We want per-group agent permissions, so you could let an agent read your ledger without giving it permission to propose changes. We want receipt processing that explicitly surfaces uncertainty instead of guessing when a line cannot be read. And we want to extend the same model beyond expense splitting. Wherever an application already has a rich interface but the task contains too much context for a human to manage comfortably, an agent should be able to join the workflow without becoming the owner of it. Tabby started with a restaurant bill. The bigger idea is giving agents a place inside the interfaces people already use. I love participating in hackathons and have an exemplary track record. If our skills compliment each other, lets team up! title: Relocates.io
pitch: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't.
about_excerpt: Where can all of us live? A map that answers it for a whole household — and negotiates when it can't. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We had one weekend of viewings, in a city none of us had lived in, and a spreadsheet. The question was simple and nothing could answer it: where can all four of us actually live? Property sites filter by price and bedroom count. But nobody is unhappy about a bedroom count. They're unhappy because the school run takes forty minutes, and because that got decided once, in a hurry, from three timezones away, and then paid for every morning for three years. So we guessed. Everybody guesses. It's a constraint satisfaction problem and it deserved a solver, so we wrote one. Every requirement becomes a comparison over a 250-metre grid of the real city: real schools from Google Places with their real ratings, real gyms, real parks, and real terrain, so a hill costs the minutes it actually costs. Where everyone's requirements overlap, a volume lights up over the photorealistic map. Then it goes to zero. Six honest requirements from four people usually don't fit in one city. Every tool we'd used treats that as a dead end. Empty list, try removing a filter. But "nowhere works" is genuinely useful information, as long as you also say which two requirements are fighting and how much one has to give. So the page tests dropping each requirement, then every pair, then sweeps the blocking thresholds to find the smallest concession that reopens the map. It draws both options at once, in the colours of the two people involved. That's the point where WebMCP stopped being a technology choice. The solver can tell you bending one limit reopens more ground than bending the other. It can't tell you that one of those limits is a bad knee and the other is a fourteen-year-old walking to school by herself. It can't know that the cheaper concession is the harder one to live with. Somebody has to say "hers is cheaper, but hers is the medical one" — and a slider is never going to say that. But it doesn't work from a server either. The agent offers two futures, the page draws both over the real city, and the person picks by looking at them. What's being compared is a shape on a map, not a number in a response. The state and the solver have to sit where the person's eyes already are. The loop runs both ways too, which is the part we didn't expect to matter as much as it does. People don't wait their turn. They drag a threshold while the agent is still talking, delete something, accept an option on their own. Those edits are real and they aren't the agent's. So the page logs who changed what and hands the agent everything a human did since its last turn. What it does Relocates.io finds the part of a city where everyone in a household gets what they need at the same time, draws it on a photorealistic 3D map, and when that region doesn't exist, tells you exactly which requirements collide and how far one has to move. You can describe your household to an agent or build it by hand. Both drive the same state. Pick a city. It builds a 250 m grid and loads the terrain. Add people, then their requirements. Not filters — requirements that belong to someone, each carrying their own reason in their own words. "She walks alone, it's her independence." "It's his knee, not a preference." That sentence matters later. Watch where they overlap. The intersection is contoured and extruded over the real buildings. The area in km² is the number on screen. When it hits zero, you get options, not an error. The page finds what's blocking, works out the smallest movement that reopens the map, and draws both candidate futures at once with the area each one buys. You choose. Click one and it resolves. Both numbers were already on screen — what the agent adds is which concession is cheaper, which is easier, and why those aren't the same. Then check a real listing. Paste an address, get pass or fail on every requirement with the margin, plus the nearest spots that would have worked. Or search homes restricted to inside the feasible region, so it can't return somewhere that fails one of your family. The 3D isn't decoration. If you can't fly out for a third viewing, the two things you most need to see are what a street looks like and how steep it is, and a flat map shows neither. Walking times run through Tobler's hiking function over real elevation, so a kilometre uphill costs about 40% more than a flat one. The hill you can see is the hill that makes the school walk eleven minutes instead of seven. Same dataset drives the picture and the arithmetic. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Google Maps Platform, WebMCP. About 4,600 lines. No server, no database, no API routes. Browser tab ├── Grid 250 m lattice over the search area ├── Layers one Float32Array per question — walk time, commute, grade ├── Solver masks · marching squares · diagnosis · relaxation sweep ├── Map3D photorealistic tiles + pooled extruded volumes ├── WebMCP 18 tools on document.modelContext └── Cache IndexedDB — a city is learned once Everything runs in the browser through the Maps JS SDK and caches locally. Nothing about the household leaves the page. That started as a constraint and turned out to be the reason the whole thing works: an agent can reach into live state and get an answer in the same tick. Places and Elevation are real. Commute times are modelled from distance and mode rather than routed, and we say so on screen. We skipped the Routes API on purpose. Real routed commutes meant thousands of billed matrix elements per origin and several seconds of latency on every threshold change, which would have killed the thing that makes the sweep feel like an instrument. Two functions carry the project. diagnose.ts answers why there's nowhere to live. With a dozen requirements over a few thousand cells there's no need to be clever, so it tests every leave-one-out combination, then every pair if none of those work. Exhaustive and exact. frontier.ts answers how far a requirement has to bend, sweeping its threshold across the grid for the smallest movement that opens any cell, then the area gained at every step after. It returns a curve, not a point, so the agent can describe what a concession costs. Both measure off the grid. Neither estimates. That's the whole technical claim, so it lives in the code rather than in a paragraph. The map uses Map3DElement with regions as extruded Polygon3DElement volumes and drawsOccludedSegments on, so buildings never hide the answer. Those are DOM nodes, not batched geometry, so they're pooled at startup and mutated in place. Three things about the tools mattered more than the rest. Descriptions say when to call something, not just what it does: "call this whenever the area is 0, before telling the user anything." Every requirement carries a required rationale field. And get_state returns humanChanges , so the agent finds out what a person did while it wasn't looking. Challenges we ran into deck.gl doesn't work over photorealistic tiles. The obvious stack was a dead end. Overlays float above the terrain instead of sitting on it. We dropped deck.gl for native Polygon3DElement , which Google renders against the same terrain as the tiles. Found it with a throwaway HTML file before writing any real code, which saved a day. Google has no ratings for schools. Gyms, parks and supermarkets all return them. Secondary schools returned zero out of eight. Our "4★ or better" filter emptied the pool, so every school requirement became permanently unsatisfiable and the map went permanently blank. Saying "nowhere qualifies" would have been a lie with a straight face, so the filter now drops itself, says so in a banner, and reports the caveat to the agent. Nobody agrees where WebMCP lives. Drafts disagree on navigator.modelContext versus document.modelContext . We built against navigator , and an agent looking at the live page told us exactly what that produces: "exposes WebMCP capability, but currently provides no WebMCP tools." It now checks document first, awaits each registration, and tears down with AbortSignal . Photorealistic tiles take no style array. No saturation: -100 , so the grey-out when there's no answer had to be a CSS filter on the container. It greys the regions too, but during a conflict there are no regions to keep coloured, so that worked out. The numbers sit in an unfiltered layer above. Cutting things. Routes API, air quality, saved sessions, multi-city. All had to go to keep one sequence working reliably: requirements, conflict, two futures, a choice. Accomplishments that we're proud of The empty state is the product. Treating "nowhere works" as the interesting case is the idea everything is built around, and it held up against real data from a real city. Every number is real. Every km² and every minute comes off the grid. The agent is told never to state a figure it didn't get from a tool, and the tools are shaped so it never nee
video_title: Relocates.io
video_transcript_excerpt: Finding a place for a family usually means juggling dozens of open tabs, trying to guess where everyone's daily life actually intersects. Relocates.io solves this geometrically. We input a family of four relocating to San Francisco. David commuting to Google, Sarah, Leah, and 8-year-old Tom. The agent parses the household and registers the profiles directly into client state. Now we define their daily mobility constraints. David needs transit within 30 minutes. Leah needs a 15-minute walk to high school. Tom needs 10 minutes to primary school, plus a nearby gym and park. The browser intersects these travel boundaries on device, 29.38 square kilometers across five candidate zones. Now the hard constraint. Sarah has an injured knee. Any pedestrian incline over a 6% grade is physically out of the question. That medical requirement is treated as non-negotiable, factoring San Francisco's elevation profiles into the pedestrian routes. >> The viable terrain immediately collapses by more than half down to 13.44 square kilometers. Hills eliminate most of the city. Instead of negotiating back and forth in chat, I open the drawer and adjust the sliders myself, granting Tom 17 minutes and tightening the park to six. Web MCP immediately detects my manual edits and synchronizes the agent state. The polygon updates dynamically to 11.88 square kilometers, highlighting five qualifying neighborhoods, including the Presidio. We drop straight into 3D terrain to verify street inclines before signing a lease. Compromise isn't an argument anymore. It's just geometry.

title: ShopMate — Agent-Native Shopping with WebMCP
pitch: An agent-native e-commerce experience where AI agents discover products, compare options, check stock, and manage carts through browser-native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native e-commerce experience where AI agents discover products, compare options, check stock, and manage carts through browser-native WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration## Inspiration 

 Traditional e-commerce websites are designed primarily for humans. Users have to search through pages, apply filters, compare products, check availability, and manually manage their carts. 

 We wanted to explore a different model: 

 What if an AI agent could interact with an e-commerce website through structured, browser-native tools instead of relying on brittle UI automation? 

 That question led us to build ShopMate , an agent-native shopping experience powered by WebMCP. 

 What we built 

 ShopMate exposes the core capabilities of an e-commerce application as WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . 

 The application currently exposes 10 tools : 

 
 search_products 
 filter_products 
 get_product_details 
 compare_products 
 check_stock 
 calculate_cart_total 
 add_to_cart 
 remove_from_cart 
 update_cart 
 build_bundle 
 

 Read-only operations can be performed autonomously, while state-changing operations require human approval. 

 This creates a human-in-the-loop shopping experience where an agent can perform useful work while the user remains in control of consequential actions. 

 For example, an agent can: 

 
 Search for laptops. 
 Filter them by price, brand, category, or stock. 
 Retrieve detailed specifications. 
 Compare multiple products. 
 Check inventory. 
 Ask the user for approval. 
 Add the selected product to the cart. 
 Calculate the resulting cart total. 
 

 How we built it 

 ShopMate was built with: 

 
 Next.js 16 
 React 19 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 React Context for application state 
 Browser-native WebMCP APIs through document.modelContext 
 

 A major part of the implementation was making WebMCP registration reliable inside React's rendering lifecycle. 

 We designed the registration system to be idempotent so that React re-renders and Strict Mode do not create duplicate tool registrations. 

 We also added a diagnostics and activity system so that WebMCP availability, registered tools, tool changes, and agent activity can be observed directly inside the application. 

 Challenges 

 One of our biggest challenges was that WebMCP registration interacts with the React lifecycle in ways that are easy to get wrong. 

 Our initial browser implementation encountered a Maximum update depth exceeded error. The underlying problem was not duplicate WebMCP registration itself, but the interaction between registration, diagnostics state updates, effects, and event listeners. 

 We investigated the lifecycle, added dedicated React lifecycle tests, and fixed the ownership of the WebMCP toolchange listener. We also eliminated a race involving the approval state reference. 

 Another interesting issue was the browser-generated toolchange event during initial registration. Since the browser emits a tool-change event for each registered tool, registering 10 tools produced unnecessary activity-panel noise. We kept the listener but suppressed those expected initialization events and retained logging for genuine post-registration tool changes. 

 What we learned 

 This project taught us that making an application "agent-compatible" is more than exposing a list of functions. 

 The tools need: 

 
 Clear schemas and descriptions. 
 Predictable inputs and outputs. 
 Safe boundaries around state-changing actions. 
 Idempotent registration. 
 Correct lifecycle management. 
 Human approval for consequential actions. 
 Observability so developers can understand what the agent is doing. 
 

 We also learned how important it is to test both the tool layer and the actual React/browser lifecycle. Our standalone WebMCP tests passed while the real browser initially exposed a lifecycle issue, which led us to add dedicated React and Strict Mode tests. 

 Final result 

 ShopMate now exposes all 10 intended WebMCP tools, supports human approval for cart mutations, and has automated tests covering registration, discovery, execution, approval, diagnostics, Strict Mode behavior, and listener lifecycle. 

 The project demonstrates how existing web applications can evolve from interfaces that humans click into interfaces that AI agents can understand and operate through structured browser-native capabilities .

title: WebMCP TDA
pitch: A browser-local topology workbench where people shape point clouds and images while agents compute and explain persistent homology through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser-local topology workbench where people shape point clouds and images while agents compute and explain persistent homology through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Persistent homology can reveal connected components, loops, and voids in point clouds and images, but most tools assume that the user already knows the right library, data format, and filtration parameters. An AI agent can help with those choices, but a normal website gives the agent only buttons and text to interpret. I built WebMCP TDA to give the person and the agent the same computational workspace. The person can manipulate the data visually. The agent can call typed topology tools directly. Both see the same inputs and results in the page. What it does The human workbench accepts 2D and 3D point clouds as well as images. A person can drag points, enter exact coordinates, choose a Vietoris-Rips, Alpha, or Cech complex, and play the filtration. For images, the page shows the original, grayscale, and binary-mask stages before computing cubical persistence. Results include feature counts, essential classes, H1 loops, runtime, a persistence diagram, and structured JSON. The point-cloud preview, filtration geometry, and persistence-diagram playhead move together. The page exposes four WebMCP tools: tda_get_capabilities describes supported complexes, parameters, limits, and image inputs. tda_compute_simplicial_persistence computes persistence for an agent-supplied 2D or 3D point cloud. tda_compute_cubical_persistence analyzes the current image, a bundled photograph, or an agent-supplied scalar grid. tda_get_latest_result reads the result currently shared by the person and agent. An agent call updates the visible workbench. This matters because the person can inspect what the agent submitted instead of trusting a hidden computation. Why WebMCP fits this use case A point cloud may contain hundreds of coordinates, and a persistence result may contain many intervals. Asking an agent to operate the visual interface would be slow and error prone. WebMCP gives the agent a bounded schema for the real computation while leaving the visual controls available to the person. The collaboration also works in both directions. A person can upload an image and ask the agent to analyze the current image. An agent can generate a point cloud, compute its persistence, and leave the exact coordinates and result visible for the person to edit or rerun. Without WebMCP, that workflow requires copying arrays between a notebook, a chat, and a visualization tool. How I built it The app registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a closed JSON schema, safety annotations, runtime validation, and an AbortSignal . Tool calls and human actions use the same runtime and workspace state. Computation runs locally through an MIT-licensed WebAssembly package in a Web Worker. The interface uses TypeScript, Vite, React, Plotly.js, PlayCanvas, and the companion tda-viz-react library. Cloudflare Pages hosts the static production build. The browser enforces limits on point count, coordinate magnitude, image dimensions, filtration scale, result count, and worst-case simplex count. Cancellation terminates the active worker so an expensive request cannot leave later computations stuck behind it. Challenges The hardest part was keeping the mathematical and visual states consistent. Rips, Cech, and Alpha complexes use different filtration conventions, so the displayed cover radius cannot be treated as the raw filtration value in every case. I also had to keep the point-cloud projection fixed while a filtration plays, preserve the axis origin while points move, and fit persistence-diagram ranges to each result without rescaling during playback. WebMCP is still an evolving browser API. I tested registration, cleanup, schemas, execution, cancellation, and malformed inputs separately instead of treating tool discovery as proof that everything worked. What I learned I learned how much better an agent interaction becomes when the website exposes a small domain API rather than asking the model to infer actions from layout. I also learned that shared state needs to be visible. A correct tool response is not enough when the person cannot inspect the input that produced it. What is next The next useful addition is a seeded point-cloud generator with named shapes, sample count, noise, and dimension. It would make agent-generated experiments reproducible without sending large coordinate arrays. I would also add accessible data tables for persistence pairs and continue profiling the large visualization bundles. title: WebMCP Retrofit Studio
pitch: Turn an owner-authorized legacy website workflow into narrow, reviewable WebMCP tools, with finalization kept outside the site-tool surface.
about_excerpt: Turn an owner-authorized legacy website workflow into narrow, reviewable WebMCP tools, with finalization kept outside the site-tool surface. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Retrofit Studio explores a practical bridge between websites built for people and agents that need explicit, dependable capabilities. It demonstrates the idea on a bundled synthetic booking fixture: the owner authorizes an inert scan, reviews the observed goals and evidence, approves a narrow tool set, inspects the generated contract, validates the behavior, and downloads a clean-room evidence and code package. It does not crawl arbitrary third-party sites, request credentials, deploy code, or create a real booking. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Many useful websites expose their workflows only through buttons, forms, and page text. An agent must repeatedly infer those controls, and that inference becomes especially risky around state-changing actions. WebMCP gives the site owner a structured contract for the actions they intentionally expose. Retrofit Studio makes that contract visible and reviewable before it reaches an agent. The synthetic booking example registers exactly three top-level imperative tools: search_services , get_availability , and stage_booking . Search and availability are marked read-only. Draft staging is explicitly state-changing, returns the visible postcondition booking_draft_updated , and creates only a reversible local draft. finalize_booking is deliberately absent from the WebMCP inventory; the visible interface contains the separate final-confirmation control. How it creates a better user experience The five-step flow makes the evidence, approval state, and finalization boundary inspectable: Scan owned fixture inertly parses a bundled synthetic snapshot after an ownership authorization check. It makes no external request and retains observations and hashes instead of raw form content. Candidate capabilities shows the evidence behind every proposed tool, the excluded final action, assumptions, unknowns, risks, counterarguments, confidence, and recommendation. Preview generated retrofit shows the exact hashed three-tool allowlist and the shared contract that will be registered. Validate generated tools activates the reviewed tool group only after the version is locked, executes eight deterministic checks, and provides an ordinary booking form. A successful stage_booking call updates every visible draft field for inspection before confirmation through the UI. Export retrofit package creates a deterministic clean-room bundle containing generated registration code, a manifest, and an evidence record. Downloading the bundle does not deploy or publish anything. If WebMCP is unavailable, the ordinary visible booking interface still works. The app does not pretend that a local deterministic check proves live agent discovery. A separate public-client receipt records discovery, execution, visible-state verification, and registration cleanup against the deployed build. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can search the known synthetic service catalog, retrieve only known availability, and stage an exact reversible draft through structured inputs. The visible interface displays the postcondition, service, date, and time; finalization is not exposed as a WebMCP site tool. The website owner can also inspect why each capability was proposed and export the reviewed implementation evidence. Before this contract, the agent would need to infer the same workflow from presentation-layer controls on each visit. The demonstrated collaboration replaces that repeated inference with an explicit tool inventory while preserving the person's existing visual context and approval boundary. How WebMCP was implemented The app is a React, TypeScript, and Vite client with no backend or API key. On the Validate screen it feature-detects the top-level document.modelContext and registers the three imperative tools with registerTool . The approval view and runtime registration use the same frozen contract objects, which prevents the displayed contract from drifting from the executed one. Every schema rejects undeclared properties. Inputs are validated again inside each handler. Tool outputs identify their synthetic source, and annotations distinguish read-only operations from draft staging while marking returned page-derived content as untrusted. Registration cleanup and supplied client execution-cancellation signals are separate; leaving Validate removes the tool group. The deterministic suite verifies the exact inventory, annotations, strict schemas, invalid input rejection, unavailable-slot rejection, cancellation, visible draft postcondition, and absence of finalization. The app also includes an Accuracy, Evidence, and Honest Feedback framework. Six selectable review modes route to centralized versioned prompts while preserving nine required sections: facts, assumptions, unknowns, confidence, evidence, risks, counterarguments, recommendation with tradeoffs, and what would change the recommendation. Related work Existing tools such as keak-ai/webmcp-core and Latch generate or auto-register WebMCP tools from a live site, and webmcpify adds an approval and browser-verification loop. Retrofit Studio narrows the problem instead: an inert scan of an owner-controlled fixture, a hash-bound approval chain that fails closed on any change, deterministic checks on the registered contracts, and a finalization action deliberately kept outside the agent surface. Judging-criteria fit WebMCP Leverage: three non-trivial imperative tools, explicit annotations, strict schemas, lifecycle cleanup, visible postconditions, and a deliberate finalization boundary outside the WebMCP tool surface. Execution: Scan, review, preview, validation, visible draft staging, and deterministic export form one guarded product flow rather than an isolated API example. The live URL and public-client WebMCP behavior have been independently read back for the tested application revision. Potential Impact: website owners and product teams with useful legacy workflows but no agent contract. The prototype shows a bounded retrofit path; it does not claim universal compatibility or production readiness. Creativity and Ambition: retrofit generation treated as an evidence and governance problem, not only a code-generation problem: source fingerprints, approval hashes, stale-artifact invalidation, truth-contract review modes, deterministic validation, and a clean-room export boundary. pitch: An agent-native negotiation room using in-browser WebMCP and deterministic simulation to keep external AI proposals strictly within human-set governance boundaries. Fully verified via automated QA.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native negotiation room using in-browser WebMCP and deterministic simulation to keep external AI proposals strictly within human-set governance boundaries. Fully verified via automated QA.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most autonomous agent workflows break down in high-stakes negotiations: either LLMs hallucinate deal terms and run unconstrained, or rigid automation strips away strategic adaptability. We wanted to invert this dynamic. What if an AI agent never invents the rules of the deal? 

 We envisioned an agent-native environment where human principals set strategic intent, deterministic calculation engines enforce mathematical reality, and external AI agents reason strictly within machine-enforced governance boundaries—discovering and executing tools natively inside the browser via WebMCP (document.modelContext). 

 What it does 

 Nexus Deal Room is a closed-loop negotiation and decision platform that bridges in-browser agent actuation with mathematical governance across four core pillars:Constraint Kitchen: Translates natural human intent (e.g., "Speed > Margin") into mathematical priority weights ($w_i$) and binds an immutable Agent Governance Authority Matrix.Deterministic Decision Twin: A zero-hallucination WASM truth engine that calculates feasibility scores (0–100), simulates trade-offs, and instantly halts non-negotiable hard-floor breaches (e.g., payment windows > 45 days, liability coverage < 1.5x).Agentic Strategist: Uses Gemini models to reason over deterministic twin projections, formulating compliant counteroffers strictly within predefined concession bands.In-Browser WebMCP Negotiation Room: Exposes client-side tools directly onto window.document.modelContext (with dual JSON-RPC FastMCP parity). External agents discover tools, simulate terms, and manipulate negotiation state across an interactive 6-node DAG without brittle DOM scraping or vision overhead.Automated WebMCP QA Suite: A continuous testing harness that acts as a synthetic, adversarial counterparty. Headless runners (Playwright) query document.modelContext directly to execute fuzzing, prompt injections, and boundary bypass attacks in CI.Wire-Agent Evolution: A sandboxed UI loop allowing agents to stage Tailwind UX improvements dynamically while hard immutability guards block any tampering with commercial variables. 

 How we built it 

 In-Browser WebMCP Engine: Polyfilled document.modelContext in TypeScript to establish a standard client-side Model Context Protocol transport layer, bridging DOM state directly to the client tools. 

 Frontend & Visual DAG: Built with React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and @xyflow/react to orchestrate and render real-time state machine transitions across 6 reactive nodes. 

 Backend & Tool Gateway: Python (FastAPI + FastMCP), Pydantic schemas, and SQLAlchemy with SQLite acting as the immutable audit log and System of Record for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests. 

 Agent Intelligence: Gemini API orchestrated via Google Cloud Vertex AI and Secret Manager. 

 Automated QA & CI/CD: Playwright-based headless WebMCP runner executing automated fuzzing and red-teaming scenarios; multi-stage Docker container deployed to Google Cloud Run via Terraform and GitHub Actions using Workload Identity Federation (WIF). 

 Challenges we ran into
Polyfilling WebMCP in the DOM: Establishing standard tool registration on document.modelContext that could synchronize bidirectionally with Zustand stores in real time without causing race conditions or client-side UI freezes. 

 Deterministic Boundary Interception: Designing structured error-handling payloads so that when an agent attempts a violation (e.g., proposing $95k against a strict $100k floor), the tool returns actionable boundary telemetry rather than throwing unhandled exceptions that trap the LLM in repetitive loops. 

 Separating Presentation from Commercial State: Granting the Wire-Agent DOM mutation access to refine Tailwind CSS styling while engineering strict immutability guards (returning 403 Forbidden) whenever a payload touched underlying pricing, liability, or agreement terms. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
Zero-Escape Governance: Proving under exhaustive testing that agents cannot bypass human sign-off (execute_contract deterministically halts and blocks unauthorized execution) or mutate protected financial thresholds. 

 Native In-Browser Agent Interaction: Achieving full tool discovery and execution via document.modelContext, eliminating vision model latency, token overhead, and brittle CSS selectors. 

 Automated WebMCP End-to-End QA: Shipping an automated headless CI test harness that directly talks to the in-browser MCP layer to continuously test boundary resilience and prompt-injection defense. 

 Production-Ready Delivery: Achieving 100% test suite completion with zero-credential, keyless CI/CD deployment running live on Google Cloud Run.

 Deterministic Boundary Interception: Designing structured error-handling payloads so that when an agent attempts a violation (e.g., proposing $95k against a strict $100k floor), the tool returns actionable boundary telemetry rather than throwing unhandled exceptions that trap the LLM in repetitive loops. 

 Separating Presentation from Commercial State: Granting the Wire-Agent DOM mutation access to refine Tailwind CSS styling while engineering strict immutability guards (returning 403 Forbidden) whenever a payload touched underlying pricing, liability, or agreement terms. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Zero-Escape Governance: Proving under exhaustive testing that agents cannot bypass human sign-off (execute_contract deterministically halts and blocks unauthorized execution) or mutate protected financial thresholds. 

 Native In-Browser Agent Interaction: Achieving full tool discovery and execution via document.modelContext, eliminating vision model latency, token overhead, and brittle CSS selectors. 

 Automated WebMCP End-to-End QA: Shipping an automated headless CI test harness that directly talks to the in-browser MCP layer to continuously test boundary resilience and prompt-injection defense. 

 Production-Ready Delivery: Achieving 100% test suite completion with zero-credential, keyless CI/CD deployment running live on Google Cloud Run. 

 What we learned 

 Generative reasoning must be decoupled from mathematical evaluation: LLMs excel at creative strategic trade-offs and natural negotiation phrasing, but numeric thresholds, risk assessments, and financial calculations must be handled deterministically. 

 UI-as-Schema changes the agent landscape: When an application exposes its DOM and capabilities as structured, discoverable schemas via WebMCP, agents become faster, cheaper to run, and fundamentally more reliable. 

 Prompt engineering is not security: Real trust in autonomous agentic workflows requires hard client- and protocol-level boundaries that intercept and reject invalid mutations before state is altered. 

 What's next for Nexus Deal Room: Agent-Native Decision Environment 

 Multi-Agent Arenas: Supporting multi-party, concurrent negotiations where multiple external buyer and seller AI agents interact within the same WebMCP governance room. 

 Universal WebMCP Browser Extension: Packaging the runtime as a Chrome Extension that injects document.modelContext and deterministic governance layers over third-party enterprise procurement platforms (Coupa, SAP Ariba, Salesforce).

title: Ordering an Endotoxin Assay from My Lab Notebook
pitch: Allowing agents to order and interpret the results of a routine biochemical assay.
about_excerpt: Allowing agents to order and interpret the results of a routine biochemical assay. Like Comment Story Updates "Notebook paired". This means a session exists between the lab notebook and chatGPT browser ClearSignal. The price from the website is quickly found and quoted via webMCP `quote_endotoxin_tests`. The lab notebook can receive status updates. Order ID available for confirmation. Results page shows actionable data and the standard curve. All in the lab notebook. Inspiration Life sciences labs sell services to other labs. One of those services is the endotoxin detection assay. An assay is a test. Endotoxin is a molecule from bacteria that can cause fevers in humans and other animals. Labs producing a product like a vaccine or a protein want to ensure their product is free of endotoxin. Detecting endotoxin is a routine, well-known biochemical assay that uses horseshoe crab blood or a protein from horseshoe crab blood. The problem is that this simple test is encumbered with difficulty. 1) A researcher who wishes an endotoxin test must search online for a provider. 2) The researcher "reaches out" through a site request form or by email or by phone calling another human. 3) The researcher and provider discuss terms: how many samples, how often, customization, etc. 4) The providers gets back in a few days with a quote. 5) The researcher agrees to the quote, signs it, sends it back. 6) The researcher prepares the samples and mails them 7) Samples are received and processed, usually 3-5 business days. 8) Provider sends email saying samples have arrived and are being processed. 9) Results are sent, usually by email, in a pdf. Fancy provider labs have the researchers create an account and sign in to download a pdf. 10) Researcher combs through 5-8 pages of lot numbers and temperature settings to find the 3 or 5 datapoints that are actionable, i.e. "Endotoxin < 0.05 EU/mL". I want to condense the above steps to one step: A researcher uses their lab notebook to order an endotoxin test. And then I want every lab in the world to join us. Every lab selling their specialized assay order-able, update-able and interpretable with webMCP-enabled sites. This is the Federated Cloud Laboratory Network. Materials Needed 1) chatGPT desktop with browser and webMCP enabled. 2) Obsidian, https://obsidian.md/ 3) Obisidian plugin, "ClearSignal Lab Assistant", https://github.com/har1eyk/clearsignal-lab-assistant 4) Lab notebook page for testing (any markdown file will do!) 5) ClearSignal access, https://clearsignal-gray.vercel.app/ 1) user: endo@toxin.com 2) pass: horseshoe What it does A researcher keeps a lab notebook in a markdown file. A markdown viewer like Obsidian is used. Obsidian can use plugins for beyond-markdown functionality. I created a plugin that allows a researcher to call for an endotoxin assay test from their lab notebook using three backticks. After the backticks, "clearsignal" is typed and a researcher can request: Order an endotoxin assay on two samples if the price is less than <$500. The sample IDs are: "ID-0001 and ID-0002". Then, the plugin begins a session with chatGPT's browser and the ClearSignal site. The webMCP-enabled site can easily find the endotoxin-per-sample-cost and report it. The quote is provided to the lab researcher in their notebook! Additionally, the researcher can also ask questions in their original prompt like: Can I send in plasmid samples? (Plasmids are circular pieces of DNA purified from bacteria.) The webMCP-enabled site answers it directly from the FAQ. No hunting and clicking for the page and the question. Save those tokens with webMCP. Lastly, the researcher's samples are loaded and the price is visible. The final "submit" creates the order. Order information is transmitted to the lab notebook. Status updates are also provided. In this demo version, status updates occur every few seconds. In real testing conditions, the status updates occur every few days. I like that when the testing is "complete", that endotoxin concentration and standard curve data is sent to the lab notebook so the researcher can take actionable next steps. Table 1: Time Savings with WebMCP-enabled ClearSignal Site With WebMCP Without WebMCP Calls quote_endotoxin_tests with two sample IDs Has to navigate forms, locate fields, type IDs, submit, and inspect the rendered result Receives exact fields such as unit_price: 375 and total: 750 Extracts prices from page text and infers which numbers represent unit price and total Automatically returns structured events to the Obsidian note Require a separate copy/paste or integration workflow How we built it 1) Building landing page. Paper and ChatGPT desktop 2) Build backend (postgres, Supabase) 3) Create login page 1) successful via chatGPT sites 2) successful via localhost 4) Create user dashboard or login landing page 5) Create order page, make it webMCP enabled 1) Human successfully order via chatGPT site? 2) Human successfully order via localhost? 3) Bot successfully order via chatGPT site? 1. Logged in (success) 2. Not Logged in (success) 4) Bot successfully order via localhost? 1) Logged in (can't get chatgpt plugin to use webmcp; uses navigation.) 2) Not Logged in 6) Build Obsidian plugin 7) Publish website (Vercel) 8) Use Obsidian plugin chatbot to order via published clearsignal site 1) get status updates from backend 2) Upon status update "Complete", Obsidian plugin connection automatically closes. 9) Generate supabase cronjob to process all the order sequences steps for demo purposes. Real testing takes days/weeks. 10) Next Steps: Use Benchling plugin to order via published clearsignal site Challenges we ran into Lots of hard parts here. Some we overcame, some we patched, and some we're leaving for later. Overcame 1) How do we get markdown to chat with a website? Answer: The Obsidian plugin routes with chatGPT desktop session which connects to the webMCP-enabled site. 2) How do we get so much sci-knowledge into webMCP? Even a simple test like the endotoxin assay can have dozens of questions from researchers, e.g. Do samples need to be aqueous? Do you perform dilution series? What about inhibition? Answer: this one was easier to solve than expected. Having a FAQ list and then loading the questions and answers into get_endotoxin_faqs was a nice, quick way to help find answers. I imagine an entire page of FAQs with every question a researcher has every asked easily navigable with webMCP. 3) How do we show a quote, order updates and results? Answer: we instantiate a session between Obsidian plugin and chatGPT desktop. Quotes, results and updates are added to the lab notebook. Patch 1) Chrome chatGPT extension with sites-enabled still did not invoke some of webMCP items on ClearSignal. For isntance, sometimes I would ask "What is the cost per sample?" and the extension would show a pointer and click around until it found a price. Lots of troubleshooting later, I realized that chatGPT desktop web interface behaves different than Chrome websites with chatGPT extension enabled. So, I continued to use chatGPT desktop. Future Work 1) The site still relies on chatGPT desktop. Can we make an Obsidian Plugin chatGPT API and bypass chatGPT desktop? Still, how do we sign off on the ordering step. 2) Right now the order status come in a few seconds after each other, e.g. "in_preparation", "in_testing", etc. These updates typically occur every couple of days. How do I keep a Obsidian-plugin-chatGPT session going that long? I probably can't. I need to build out the plugin to do periodic polling probably via REST API or webhook. 3) I would love to see this in popular Lab notebook like Benchling and Notion. Custom plugin for each? Chrome extension? 4) What would it take to let every biotech lab sell and describe their assays to researchers and their agents so that they can be ordered from a lab notebook? Accomplishments that we're proud of Two that I'm proud of: 1) Quotes, ordering, questions, updates and results are all incorporated into the lab notebook. Having all these timestamped updates and results in one place with a collapsible menu is so fun! 2) Using webMCP on a science site as a way to quickly arrive at answers like cost and sample criteria will save days of back-and-forth clarification and negotiation. What we learned 1) The FAQ lives on. 2) All scientists should be keeping a lab notebook in mardown. 3) Obsidian is a fabulous markdown viewer. 4) There are important webMCP differences between chatGPT desktop browser and Chrome chatGPT extension. What's next for Endotoxin Let's help all researchers order all assays via their lab notebooks!
