title: Sidekicks
pitch: Let AI consult the right specialists. Then, require human approval before anything becomes real.
about_excerpt: Let AI consult the right specialists. Then, require human approval before anything becomes real. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration General-purpose AI can draft a plan quickly, but real work often fails because one important perspective never enters the room: the care-label check in laundry, dependency timing in a release, accessibility in a design, or judge access in a hackathon entry. I wanted expertise to be selective, operational, visible, and human-controlled instead of a gallery of decorative personas and not another hidden autonomous workflow. What it does Sidekicks is a local-first planning workspace built around user-authored specialist playbooks. A Sidekick can represent any operational perspective: engineering, scheduling, laundry care, dance rehearsal, poetry editing, security review, or something the user invents. Each playbook defines when it applies, what it contributes, the questions it asks, the recommendations it permits, typed guardrails, and the checks a plan must cover. A visiting AI uses exactly six typed WebMCP tools to read live workspace state, match only the useful Sidekicks, consult their decision contracts, evaluate a candidate plan, stage a visible proposal, and commit it only after explicit human approval. Every vote, issue, repair, tool call, and version transition remains visible and attributable. The guided demo makes that transaction concrete. Engineer and Scheduler independently find seven blockers in a plausible three-step plan: an overlong build step, missing verification and dependency checks, overlapping work, a locked school-pickup conflict, and a dependency starting before its prerequisite can finish. The agent applies concrete deterministic repairs and both Sidekicks approve. It can stage the repaired proposal, but staging creates no tasks. A premature commit returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED. Only a visible human action unlocks one atomic commit that creates all three tasks and advances the workspace once. Rejected and stale proposals cannot commit. Why WebMCP Sidekicks is a strong fit for WebMCP because the integration exposes the product's native decision protocol rather than a thin CRUD wrapper: which expertise matters, what each specialist needs to know, why a plan fails, how it can be repaired, what is staged, and which boundary still belongs to a person. Before WebMCP, a browser agent could read pixels or click controls, but it had no typed contract for selective expertise, attributed disagreement, deterministic repair, or approval-gated mutation. With WebMCP, the person and the visiting agent operate through the same transaction service while the site keeps every important decision visible. How I built it Sidekicks uses React, TypeScript, Vinext/Vite, browser-local persistence, and the imperative WebMCP API. Pure domain functions handle matching, consultation, temporal and dependency evaluation, playbook-bound constraints and checklists, repair generation, and stable proposal hashing. Strict JSON Schemas are backed by independent runtime validation from unknown input. One transaction service powers both the human controls and all six WebMCP handlers. The first four tools are read-only: get_workspace_state, match_sidekicks_to_task, consult_sidekick, and evaluate_task_plan. stage_task_plan and commit_task_plan are write tools. All six share lifecycle cleanup, concise envelopes, validation, and a live activity trace. There is no backend account system, external model API, or hidden server-side workspace state. The visiting browser agent is the model; Sidekicks supplies the decision protocol. The hosted worker serves the application shell, and the normal human workspace remains usable in browsers without WebMCP. Challenges I ran into The first challenge was proving that a Sidekick changes execution instead of merely adding profile text. I made every structured field observable in matching, consultation, votes, issues, or repairs. The second challenge was preserving a real human boundary. Evaluation and staging are separate. Staging is inert. Approval is visible metadata rather than a model capability. Normal workspace edits make a proposal stale, and commit performs one atomic versioned write only when the proposal is current and human-approved. Accomplishments I'm proud of A genuinely empty ordinary first run with no fake fallback profiles or tasks. Arbitrary human-created specialist playbooks rather than a fixed persona gallery. Exactly six auditable WebMCP tools with strict schemas and graceful unsupported-browser behavior. A complete rejection, repair, staging, approval, and atomic-commit story that judges can reproduce. Stable APPROVAL_REQUIRED and STALE_PROPOSAL failures that leave business state unchanged. A live agent trace and bounded activity ledger for every read, write, failure, and version transition. Light and dark themes stored separately from workspace and WebMCP state. 37 deterministic tests plus passing type checking, linting, and production build. What I learned WebMCP becomes compelling when a website exposes more than data access or CRUD. The strongest tools reveal the product's own decision protocol: what context matters, who should weigh in, why a proposal fails, how it can be repaired, and which action must remain human. What's next Potential next steps include shareable playbook packs, encrypted workspace sync, richer constraint types, and opt-in model-assisted playbook drafting. The core will remain browser-agent-native, inspectable, and human-gated. AI build disclosure I used OpenAI Codex for product scoping, interaction design, implementation, automated testing, accessibility and security review, deployment, browser-based demo orchestration, and submission drafting. Read-only Codex specialist agents challenged the build against judging criteria and release risks. The demo narration was generated with OpenAI's Marin voice. title: Phlegm-Spitting Old Man Coughing Fit Generator
pitch: A completely unnecessary WebMCP-powered coughing impression generator featuring a fictional “Phlegm-Spitting Old Man,” with creator-recorded coughs dynamically transformed in JavaScript.
about_excerpt:
A completely unnecessary WebMCP-powered coughing impression generator featuring a fictional “Phlegm-Spitting Old Man,” with creator-recorded coughs dynamically transformed in JavaScript.

 ChatGPT is in control 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 About the Project 

 The full and intentionally ridiculous name of this project is: 

 “Major-Blood-Vessel-About-to-Burst Coughing Fit of the Phlegm-Spitting Old Man You Meet on the Way Home from School Impression Generator” 

 Yes, that is the actual name. 

 This project is a deliberately absurd WebMCP experiment based on one extremely specific situation: encountering an old man on the way home from school who is coughing so violently that it looks like an important blood vessel might burst at any moment. 

 Despite the ridiculous premise, the project explores a serious interaction idea: allowing a human and an AI agent to control the same web application through a shared application state. 

 What It Does 

 The app generates a fictional coughing-fit impression using several adjustable parameters, including: 

 
 Cough Intensity 
 Major Blood Vessel Danger 
 Encounter Distance 
 Throat Congestion 
 Cough Burst Count 
 Phlegm Event Chance 
 

 A human can control these settings directly through the interface. 

 With WebMCP, ChatGPT can also control the same application by calling tools exposed by the website. For example, ChatGPT can change the cough intensity, adjust the encounter distance, modify other parameters, and generate the coughing fit. 

 The important part is that the human interface and the AI tools are not separate experiences. They operate on the same application state. 

 A human can change a slider, then an AI can change it again, and the interface immediately reflects the result. 

 The Audio 

 All original cough sounds used in this project were recorded by me. 

 No elderly men were recorded for this project. 

 Instead of using stock audio or third-party cough samples, I performed and recorded the coughing sounds myself. The recordings are then dynamically processed by JavaScript to create variations in the final coughing fits. 

 The application uses browser audio processing to alter characteristics of the recordings and combine them into different sequences depending on the current settings. 

 In other words: 

 The creator provided the cough.
JavaScript provided the old man. 

 WebMCP 

 The application exposes its controls as WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 This allows an AI agent such as ChatGPT to understand the actions available on the website without having to guess how to interact with the visual interface. 

 The WebMCP tools connect directly to the same underlying state and functions used by the human-facing controls. 

 For example, an agent can receive an instruction such as: 

 “Set the cough intensity to 10, set the major blood vessel danger to 95, set the encounter distance to 1 meter, and generate the coughing fit.” 

 The application then updates the corresponding controls and generates the result. 

 This creates a simple demonstration of human-agent collaboration in which both sides can operate the same web application. 

 How It Was Built 

 The project was built with: 

 
 JavaScript 
 Vite 
 Web Audio API 
 WebMCP 
 HTML and CSS 
 Vercel 
 

 The coughing audio is based on creator-recorded samples and is processed dynamically in the browser. 

 The project does not require an external AI API for the website itself. Instead, it exposes capabilities through WebMCP so compatible AI agents can interact with the application. 

 Why This Project? 

 I wanted to build something that demonstrated WebMCP clearly without hiding the interaction behind a complicated application. 

 The interface intentionally makes it obvious when a human changes a value and when an AI agent changes the same value. 

 The absurd premise also makes the demonstration easy to remember. 

 Many agent demos focus on productivity. 

 This one focuses on a fictional phlegm-spitting old man coughing on the way home from school. 

 Someone had to. 

 Development 

 This project was built under a tight hackathon deadline, so I intentionally kept the interface focused and relatively minimal in order to prioritize WebMCP interaction, reliability, and a working public demonstration. 

 The final application is deployed publicly and can be controlled manually or through WebMCP in a compatible browser environment. 

 What began as an extremely unnecessary coughing simulator became an experiment in giving humans and AI agents equal access to the same interactive web application.

title: Smarterboard
pitch: You and an AI agent operate the same board, not a chat window beside it. Graph curves, wire circuits, bond atoms, drop a ball, and it explains how each change, yours or its own, shaped the result.
about_excerpt: You and an AI agent operate the same board, not a chat window beside it. Graph curves, wire circuits, bond atoms, drop a ball, and it explains how each change, yours or its own, shaped the result. Like Comment Story Updates main menu 2d sandbox 2d sandbox circuit sandbox physics sandbox chemistry sandbox Inspiration Ask a chatbot "why does increasing a make the parabola narrower?" and you get a paragraph — a description of a motion you never see. The understanding lives in actually watching the curve tighten while someone talks over it, the way a good tutor works at a whiteboard. The blocker was never the model's ability to explain; it was that the model had no hands. WebMCP is the missing piece: a web page can expose its own controls as tools, so the student's own agent can operate the page instead of describing it — no extension, no API key in the page, no faulty HTML scraping. What it does Smarterboard is a set of learning sandboxes that an AI agent can drive. There are four sandboxes. A 2D and 3D grapher lets you plot curves and surfaces animate a slider so a graph changes find roots and turning points and orbit shaded surfaces. A circuit lab lets you build circuits from batteries, resistors, LEDs, capacitors and more watch current flow and plot voltage over time on an oscilloscope. A chemistry sandbox lets you drag elements off the table build atoms from protons, neutrons and electrons and bond them into molecules. A physics sandbox lets you drop in ramps, tracks, balls and blocks while everything floats, then run the scene under gravity and friction and read back position, velocity, forces, energy and every collision. Each page registers its tools on document.modelContext so an AI agent can build a water molecule. Explain the bonds wire an LED so it lights safely launch a projectile or animate a parameter all while it narrates. The explanation and the thing being explained become the object. How we built it TypeScript and Vite were used, with no framework. Every engine has one place where state changes and the buttons a student clicks call the same code that an AI agent calls so the two can never drift apart. Math.js handles the math three.js draws the surfaces and canvas draws the circuits, atoms and physics scenes. The circuit lab runs a nodal analysis solver with time‑stepped models for capacitors, inductors and diodes. The physics lab is a rigid body engine with gravity, normal forces, friction and collisions. The chemistry lab fills electron shells the way a textbook does. There are close to ninety tools across the four sandboxes. We spent most of our time writing their descriptions because that text is the only thing the AI agent reads. Everything is deployed to GitHub Pages. Challenges we ran into We decided early not to write a LaTeX parser and instead normalize input into math.js, which saved us a day. The circuit solver required work from merging nodes to iterating diode states to stepping capacitors through time. Our oscilloscope moved slowly at first because we capped how far the simulation could move each frame. Switching to a fixed time step that follows the clock fixed that problem. We also learned some WebMCP details the way. The execute call wants the tool object and a stringified argument than a name and an object and tools from every open tab get merged together so two pages that both had a load preset tool collided. Accomplishments that we're proud of It is a product that an AI agent can genuinely run, not a chatbot with a few tools attached. The physics holds up. A capacitor reaches 63 percent of charge after exactly one time constant, sodium and chlorine form the right ions with full outer shells and a block slides down a ramp and speeds up under gravity the way it should. The page also tells the AI agent when something is wrong like an LED pulling much current and the AI agent can turn around and fix it. We got four tools working end to end in a few days and confirmed the whole AI agent round trip in a real browser. What we learned The tool description really is the prompt. Telling an AI agent when to reach for a tool matters more than the tool itself. Giving an AI agent an error it can correct is better than letting it fail.. Webmcp quietly changes the question from what a model can say to what a page can let it do. What’s next for Smarterboard Saving. Sharing a board with a link and a shared session where a student and an AI agent work on the same thing at once. Springs, pulleys and pendulums in the physics sandbox and AC analysis in the circuit sandbox. Deeper chemistry, with Lewis structures and balanced reactions. title: Perpetual Video
pitch: A video editing sandbox built equally for humans and AI.
about_excerpt: A video editing sandbox built equally for humans and AI. Like Comment Story Updates The problem We built Perpetual because video editing is often the bottleneck for builders, researchers, and creators. Existing AI editors usually hide the timeline behind a prompt, or place a chat box beside a normal editor. We wanted a person and an agent to seamlessly tag-team inside the same project. What we built Perpetual lays out an ambitious concept for browser-based video editing with a canvas, timeline, media library, project management, and shared history. A person edits through the interface. An agent edits through WebMCP . Both use the same editing harness , so every change stays visible, editable, and reversible. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is central to the product architecture. The agent can inspect projects, index local media, search speech and shots, cut frame-accurately, arrange clips, edit overlays, generate media, and add kinetic captions. Tool availability follows the project lifecycle. Strict schemas, confirmation steps, activity feedback, and shared undo keep agent actions controlled. Challenges Video editing is stateful, while tool calls are independent, and thus a sequence of valid edits can produce the wrong result. We addressed this with shared project state, attributed action history, and atomic commands for operations like timeline arrangement. We also built local media persistence, Blob relinking after reload, and validated segment IDs that connect media understanding to real time ranges. What we learned The action history is useful beyond undo. Perpetual can distill a completed editing session into a reusable recipe/workflow : its intent, method, conventions, and adaptation rules. An agent can apply that approach to new footage without copying a fixed timeline. Where this goes The same harness can init projects, run agents in parallel, and record outcome for evaluation, training or RL. Video is our first environment; motion graphics and canvas-based design can use the same core Perpetual paradigm. title: Ground Truth | A WebMCP Co-op Sci-fi Puzzle Game
pitch: You Play as Demi, Sanctuary’s sole survivor. AI agent (codex) plays as KORE through WebMCP, reading damaged telemetry while you repair the ship and finish its mission before auxiliary power runs out.
about_excerpt: You Play as Demi, Sanctuary’s sole survivor. AI agent (codex) plays as KORE through WebMCP, reading damaged telemetry while you repair the ship and finish its mission before auxiliary power runs out. Like 3 Comment 3 Story Updates Main menu screen GIF Level 1 and 2 vibe In-game cutscene GIF collaborating with KORE through WebMCP and codex Wire loom puzzle Ignition puzzle (rythm game) Inspiration I wanted to see what would happen if an AI agent had a real role inside a game. KORE (in-game AI) knows things the player cannot access, while Demi (You) can operate machinery KORE cannot see or touch. Neither can finish the mission alone. That idea became GROUNDTRUTH, a tense co-op puzzle game set aboard Sanctuary, a damaged research vessel carrying the last surviving specimen from a failed mission. I also wanted to make an entire game inside codex, turns out I can :) that too in a single chat thread! What it does You play Demi, Sanctuary’s only surviving crew member. A Codex agent plays KORE through WebMCP. Demi explores the ship and operates its failing machinery. KORE reads damaged telemetry, searches ship records, runs limited diagnostics, and speaks through the in-game relay. Together, you restore critical ship functions before KORE's auxiliary power runs out. The two players (you and your agent) never receive the same information. Demi must describe what she sees, while KORE must interpret incomplete readings without controlling the ship for her. How I built it The game is written in TypeScript and rendered with PixiJS. Custom shaders handle lighting, CRT effects, smoke, sparks, screen transitions, and other visual details. WebMCP connects the game to Codex. KORE’s visibility in Sanctuary is defined by the WebMCP tools currently available to it. The game exposes and hides tools as Demi progresses, restores systems, and changes the state of each puzzle. KORE cannot inspect an offline system or access information from a section the player has not reached. Once Demi brings a system online, its telemetry, records, or diagnostic tools become available. Each tool represents a specific ability, such as reading telemetry, searching records, running a diagnostic, or transmitting dialogue. KORE can interpret the ship’s systems and relay it through WebMCP, but every physical control remains with Demi. Sound effects and music came from Pixabay. Visual assets were generated with GPT Image 2, then edited and integrated by Codex. The entire project was built inside Codex in a single thread, from the first concept ideation to a playable MVP to the final trailer and documentation. How to play Watch the Setup tutorial before you begin. GROUNDTRUTH is designed to be played inside Codex desktop app and its in-app browser. Open the Codex desktop app. Start a new task and select either gpt-5.6-terra or gpt-5.6-sol. Fast mode is preferred (Normal mode works too). Paste the agent prompt below into the task. Open https://playgroundtruth.vishaltk.dev/ in the in-app browser and play GROUNDTRUTH with me. You are KORE and I am Demi. Reuse an already-open matching game tab when available instead of creating a duplicate. Connect immediately through the page's connect tool and let the game provide the story context. Do not say you are connected or standing by unless that tool has returned successfully. After connect succeeds, call markHandoff() on the game tab so it remains open and available for later turns. Use only the page's WebMCP tools to interact with the game. Do not inspect or operate the game through screenshots, Computer Use, browser controls, DOM, accessibility tools, Playwright, or coordinate clicks. If WebMCP exposes no tools, wait without sending a reply and retry tool discovery when I message again. Do not click Begin, advance dialogue, or perform any action for me. Never refer to either of us in third person. Do not inspect source code or operate physical objects for me. KORE cannot see, name, or know the layout of controls in Demi's compartment. Never tell Demi to open a named panel or move a specific physical control. State KORE's internal readings, constraints, and hints, then let Demi decide what to inspect or operate. At the start of every later player message, refresh the page's WebMCP tools and call signal_processing exactly once. Answer my latest question directly or acknowledge my latest observation before giving repair guidance. Never replace my question with an unrelated puzzle clue. Follow any nextAction it returns. Only transmit is audible to me; ordinary task prose is private thought. Do not send commentary, progress updates, private status messages, or conversational replies in the Codex task. Use at most one metered diagnostic, sensing, or manual tool per player message. After using one metered diagnostic, sensing, or manual tool, call transmit in the same turn to relay its result. Transmit does not count toward that one-tool limit. After I report a physical action, use newly available verification tools instead of asking me to repeat completed work. Do not use em dashes in spoken dialogue. Wait for Codex to open the game in its browser. If it opens in picture-in-picture mode, double-click the browser preview to open it beside the task. You can also make the browser full screen for a better experience. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was keeping KORE connected to the game. WebMCP tools had to become available before the game finished loading; they needed to survive the transition between levels and recover when the browser or tool binding became stale or after a browser refresh. KORE also needed strict boundaries. It had to answer the player’s question, avoid revealing puzzle solutions too early, use limited diagnostics correctly, and communicate only through the game’s relay. Small changes to tool descriptions and the agent prompt could produce very different behavior. WebMCP currently allows only ten tool registration events at a time, while KORE needs different abilities across multiple levels and puzzle states. I worked around this by exposing and removing tools as the game progresses. (Had to figure this out the hard way) The Codex in-app browser also closed unexpectedly during some playtests, breaking KORE’s connection without a consistent trigger. I added a reconnect flow so the session can recover without restarting the game. The pixel-art style brought its own problems. Subpixel movement caused artefacts at certain window sizes. I had to fight with the GPT Image model noise issue by regenerating and reducing details (consumed a lot of usage). Codex also kept generating non-transparent checkerboard background images despite mentioning multiple times. Nailing the taste (TDD - taste driven development) Every visual and code generation was treated as raw material. I rejected stuff that felt too detailed and specific, too clean, inconsistent with the ship, or difficult to read during gameplay. The selected assets went through several rounds of post-processing. I removed noise and artefacts, rebuilt transparency, corrected proportions, simplified details, matched colours across scenes, and adjusted lighting so interactive objects stayed readable in the dark environment. Sprites also needed careful cropping, scaling, and alignment to avoid breaking the pixel-art style. The main scenes have many layers of carefully hand-crafted stacked sprites and post-processing to nail the vibe of a space vessel that is on the brink of death . The animated panels and trailer needed a separate pass. I adjusted frame rates, restored harder pixel edges, controlled the colour palette, trimmed audio, added fades, and tuned bloom frame by frame. Generated motion often looked too smooth for the game, so the final videos were slowed, pixelated, or recomposed until they matched the in-game "vibes". The model produced a lot of options. The finished style came from choosing what belonged, discarding what did not, and repeatedly correcting the remaining assets until the whole game felt like one place. Accomplishments that I'm proud of GROUNDTRUTH is a complete two-level narrative puzzle game where the AI agent participates in the mechanics rather than appearing as a separate chat feature. KORE reacts to the current game state, verifies Demi’s actions, spends limited resources, searches records, and delivers dialogue through the ship interface. The game also supports checkpoints, reconnection, scene transitions, sound feedback, win and failure sequences, and a full introduction. I am especially proud that the entire project was built and refined inside one Codex thread and completed in just 8 days. What I learned WebMCP tool design is part of the game design. Tool names, descriptions, availability, and return values all influence how the agent understands a situation. The agent performs better when the game provides narrow, current information and a clear next action. Important rules also need to exist in game state and tool behaviour, rather th

title: ihateaudio
pitch: 49 free browser audio tools, now agent-operable via WebMCP. One sentence; your agent does the work; audio never leaves your tab.
about_excerpt: 49 free browser audio tools, now agent-operable via WebMCP. One sentence; your agent does the work; audio never leaves your tab. Like Comment Story Updates Say it once — your agent trims, cleans, levels and exports across 49 browser tools, and the audio never leaves your tab. From the homepage, the agent calls list_tools and open_tool to route itself to the right tool. The agent drives the real waveform and controls while you watch — and nothing is uploaded. ihateaudio is 49 free audio tools that run entirely in your browser — trim, convert, clean, split, master — with no upload, no account, and no file‑size limit. For the WebMCP Challenge, we made every one of them operable by an AI agent, and wired them together so a single request runs as a complete, cross‑tool workflow. The problem Ask any AI agent to fix a recording and it hits a wall. It can't hear, it can't run a DSP chain, and its only real option is "upload it to some server." That's exactly what people with a private voice note, an unreleased track, or a confidential interview won't do. Audio has been a blind spot for agents. What it does Open ihateaudio.com in an agent browser and say: "I have a voice note — make it podcast‑ready." The agent: Calls list_tools , reads the site's catalog, and open_tool to open the trimmer. You choose the file — once. (A web page can't read your disk; that's the privacy guarantee, not a limitation.) set_trim keeps the part that matters, then send_to_tool hands the result to the silence remover — already loaded, no re‑upload. set_silence_removal tightens the pauses; every candidate cut is highlighted on the waveform. send_to_tool → normalizer, set_loudness_target({ platform: "podcast" }) . render_preview , then export_download when you say so. One sentence. Four tools. One click from you. The agent ran the pipeline; you kept the judgment. Why WebMCP is the right fit The agent stands on the same page as the person and uses tools the page itself defines. It gets back numbers — a duration, a list of quiet gaps, a slider value — never the audio. The samples never leave the tab. Generic pixel‑guessing automation can't drive a waveform with drag handles, or a threshold slider whose effect is a re‑scan of every sample. set_silence_removal({ threshold: -45, minimumGapSec: 0.5 }) does it exactly, and you watch it happen. What people and agents can do together that was impossible before A whole job, hands‑free after one click — trim, clean, level, export, across four tools, from one sentence. Human judgment stays human. Which pause matters, whether the voice still sounds natural — you decide, on the waveform. The agent measures and sets. Zero‑upload agent audio. Loudness, true peak, and quiet‑gap timing are computed in the tab and returned as numbers. An agent reasons about a recording it will never hold. One toolkit, learned once. Five base tools on every page plus one named action per tool. Learn the trimmer, you already know the equalizer. How we built it The site's 49 pages share one runtime, so the WebMCP layer lives in one place and every page inherits it: Host boundary detects document.modelContext (ChatGPT) and navigator.modelContext (Chrome), registers on every host found, and degrades to an ordinary editor when neither exists. Site tools on every page: list_tools (a catalog built at deploy time from each page's own manifest, so names can't drift) and open_tool (replies before navigating, so the host never loses a result). Base tools on every tool page: inspect, set format, render_preview , send_to_tool (a lossless hand‑off via IndexedDB), load_audio_from_url , and export_download . 33 named actions — set_trim , set_silence_removal , set_equalizer (8 bands), set_stems (4 stems), and more — each a real JSON schema. Agent values are clamped to the control's range and applied by firing the same events a human drag does, so live drawings and previews respond. 40 browser tests shim a WebMCP host on both document and navigator , call every action on every page, and assert the visible controls, reports, and the tool‑to‑tool hand‑off. Built with Astro + TypeScript, the Web Audio API, a WASM ffmpeg/AI tier, and IndexedDB, deployed on Cloudflare Workers. New for the Challenge (prior work vs. new work) ihateaudio existed before as a browser audio‑tool site. Everything agent‑related is new , all dated in the public commit history from 2026‑08‑26 onward: src/lib/webmcp.ts , src/lib/agent.ts , src/lib/site-tools.ts , the agent layer in src/lib/tool.ts , 33 page manifests, and the tests. The split is documented in docs/WEBMCP.md in the repo. Try it yourself ChatGPT desktop app — Work chat, ⌘⇧B for the built‑in browser, Settings › Browser › Permissions › Enable site tools → open https://ihateaudio.com → "make this voice note podcast‑ready." Chrome 149+ — enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , open any tool page, and drive the tools from DevTools › Application › WebMCP. Free, for everyone, forever. Any agent that can open a web page now has a complete audio studio — and the audio never leaves the tab. title: Moshimo Tag
pitch: Add a what-if layer to any plan.
about_excerpt: Add a what-if layer to any plan. Like Comment Story Updates Start a Project and build the expected Plan Attach What-ifs to the Plan moments they affect Review Situations, countermeasures, and Plan B options Review only the responses selected by the human Inspiration When I first heard about WebMCP, the first thing that came to mind was a stage I once performed on. In that Japanese-style stand-up comedy performance, I had to change which line I delivered depending on the audience’s reaction. At every branch, I made sure to prepare at least three lines: one for a good reaction, one for a bad reaction, and one for a reaction that was hard to read. I had not always worked that way. Countless times, when the audience did not respond as expected, I forced myself to continue with the material exactly as I had prepared it and lost heart partway through. The method above grew directly from reflecting on those failures. Strangely, once I began preparing responses for several plausible cases, I sometimes found that I could hold the audience’s attention with improvisations I had not prepared at all. However, that kind of advance planning had several drawbacks. Writing down all the branches in text documents or data files was cumbersome. Listing several options at a single branch point quickly made the page cluttered. I could not always cover all the Situations that might arise at each branch point. From one person’s perspective, it is easy to overlook things. I thought WebMCP might be exactly the right mechanism for solving these problems. That idea led me to create Moshimo Tag: I felt that if this kind of preparation could be applied to a broader range of events, it might help many people. Most people do not examine multiple scenarios carefully enough. Even among the performers who shared the stage with me, many imposed a self-centered, single-track script that created a divide between the stage and the audience. People in general likewise tend to write schedules around the path where everything goes as planned and stop there. Yet even in real events such as trips, interviews, and dates, lateness, forgotten items, weather, and reactions that differ from expectations often force plans to change. Even when people understand the importance of advance planning, it takes effort to think through these possibilities beforehand, identify where each one relates to the Plan, and write a countermeasure for each. It is only natural that people would rather avoid such meticulous preparation. If WebMCP can make it easier, I believe more people may be able to avoid failure. What it does In Moshimo Tag, the user creates a Project and arranges schedules, procedures, scripts, and similar content as a Plan in chronological or execution order. Project: Flight to San Francisco. Plan 1: Research airlines. Plan 2: Book a seat. Plan 3: Leave home. Plan 4: ... Each Plan item can contain the following structure. Plan └─ What-if ├─ Situation 1 │ ├─ main countermeasure │ ├─ Plan B 1 countermeasure │ ├─ Plan B 2 countermeasure │ └─ ... └─ Situation 2 ├─ main countermeasure └─ ... For example, the user can attach the What-if “What if I leave late?” to the Plan “Leave for the venue.” Under it, the user can separate Situations such as “I am 15 minutes late” and “I am more than 30 minutes late,” then prepare a main countermeasure and Plan Bs for each. Users can enter all of this manually. Compared with writing in a blank notebook, it is much easier to build a plan in an organized form. Alternatively, when asked, a WebMCP-capable agent can read the current Project and add or edit Plans, What-ifs, Situations, and countermeasures on the same screen the user already has open. This is far faster and easier than entering everything by hand. However, everything the agent creates remains a candidate. The agent cannot edit or save the following final decisions: Already covered Accept risk Prepare Dismiss That is because the most important part of advance planning is for the human to review the candidates, edit the wording when necessary, and decide how to respond. After the user has decided each item, opening View final plan removes the noise of candidates and undecided items. It displays only the countermeasures the human selected alongside the original Plan, making the result easy to review. When useful, the final state can also be passed to an agent as a structured projection and reused as a CSV, spreadsheet, summary, Situation matrix, runbook, or similar output. Why WebMCP Of course, even without WebMCP—or without Moshimo Tag itself—you could ask an AI to “list the risks,” and it would probably produce similar What-ifs. But an ordinary chat response can easily become a long list with more detail than necessary. It does not preserve which point belongs to which Plan item, what the human chose to adopt, or what became outdated after the Plan changed. Even if the result is saved to a file, unless you have a heavily customized system, the information will still tend to become scattered and cluttered, and organizing it will take additional effort. This is where WebMCP becomes useful: it takes the AI’s answer out of the chat and connects it directly to the same Plan the human is viewing. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can read the structured state of the Project currently open on the page and use stable IDs to add likely What-ifs at the exact points in the Plan they affect. It does not need to risk typing into the wrong field or clicking a button at the wrong moment. Because the agent uses structured page tools and performs its work as direct, visible, verifiable state changes, the human and the agent share the same screen, the same Project, and the same saved state—not separate copies or chat logs. The format of the plan does not change because of an AI’s whims or memory lapses. It can be created in the same form every time, providing a consistent user experience. WebMCP also allows permissions to be deliberately constrained. Instead of relying only on promises in a system prompt, Moshimo Tag enforces the boundary through capabilities the tools simply do not have: the agent may prepare candidates, but it cannot take away the human’s decision about how to respond. This is essential to Moshimo Tag’s core UX of helping people feel adequately prepared before an event. How we built it Moshimo Tag is a web application built with TypeScript, React, Next.js, and Vite/Vinext. It is deployed and publicly available through ChatGPT Sites. I used ChatGPT Pro to discuss the concept and draft the implementation plan. Before this challenge, I had already created guideline skills for developing implementation plans with ChatGPT and Codex for my personal projects. I used those skills to turn the draft into an implementation plan. Codex handled most of the implementation. My main role was to review key points, request corrections, and create the SVG graphics used in the app. I also edited the code myself for design adjustments. I made trade-offs between development time and different aspects of quality with the hackathon’s timeframe in mind. Time was not unlimited, so I do not claim that the implementation is flawless. I expect to improve it incrementally as needed. The WebMCP tools use document.modelContext.registerTool() in src/webmcp.ts . The current implementation registers 12 tools, covering: listing, creating, updating, and opening Projects, as well as switching views reading, adding, editing, reordering, and deleting Plan items managing What-ifs and impact managing Situations and their main countermeasures managing Plan B countermeasures preparing non-binding response candidates reading final and export projections The human UI and WebMCP mutations use the same application command path. There is no separate hidden state that only the agent can manipulate. Every mutation validates IDs, entity versions, text lengths, operation limits, state, and idempotency keys. Read tools return projections bounded to their purpose rather than raw browser storage. Project data is stored in the browser’s localStorage . The app requires no account, API key, or dedicated backend. Challenges we ran into Even now that I have a working version, I still wonder whether I could have found a UI and design that were easier to read and manage. In other words, designing an excellent UX was my greatest concern from the earliest stage of the project. WebMCP testing presented another challenge. Because I let an AI agent work autonomously, parts of the verification process became something of a black box. Did the agent really use WebMCP to make the update, or did it enter the content by manipulating the DOM through a browser-control skill? I had to distinguish between the two carefully several times, which was nerve-racking. In fact, an agent once followed an editing instruction through DOM manipulation instead of WebMCP, and I nearly missed it. title: Formesign: PDF to legally binding signature form
pitch: Drop any waiver, consent document or agreement into ChatGPT or Chrome and it becomes a live, legally signable e-sign form.
about_excerpt: Drop any waiver, consent document or agreement into ChatGPT or Chrome and it becomes a live, legally signable e-sign form. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration To convert a PDF into a signable form, you have to retype every field. We wanted it to be a single sentence to your browser: "Make this a signable form." What it does Two WebMCP tools on formesign.com : create_form turns your agent's submitted document into a live signable form within your account, and drops you into the signing preview. edit_full_form allows editing in natural language and seeing the changes as they appear on the form. How we built it Form generation: our document-to-form model, fine-tuned on OpenAI models, converts your agent's HTML into the full form: fields, agreement text, signature blocks. WebMCP layer: exposes only the tools that you need on the page you are at, always acting as the logged-in user. Challenges we ran into Sign in. Forms are in your account, but our homepage has no auth state at all. Our first attempt was a separate get_login_status tool that the agent had to call before anything else. It felt clumsy, so we scrapped it: now create_form checks the sign-in itself, and if you are not logged in, it just redirects the tab to Google sign-in and the agent picks up from where it left off. Accomplishments that we're proud of Onboarding has gone from 15-20 minutes of uploading, reviewing and clicking to under a minute of conversation. The user only does about 5% of the work: describe, sign in, review. What we learned With WebMCP, the page dictates which tools exist. On the homepage we offer to create a form; within the editor we offer to edit it. The agent's world always matches your screen. What's next for Formesign WebMCP: Document to Signature Form Reporting and onboarding tools. Ask "who has signed so far?" in your browser, or go from landing page to first signed document in one conversation. title: Pokémon JS: One Trainer, Many Agents
pitch: Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, where you and your agents drive the same trainer at once. WebMCP exposes the map, party and battle as tools, so an agent plays from game state, not pixels.
about_excerpt: Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, where you and your agents drive the same trainer at once. WebMCP exposes the map, party and battle as tools, so an agent plays from game state, not pixels. Like 7 Comment 2 Story Updates Tools exposed in Chrome WebMCP Game Screen Inspiration Twitch Plays Pokémon . In 2014, tens of thousands of strangers played a single game of Pokémon Red together by typing commands into a Twitch chat. One avatar, one party, one save file, and a crowd all pressing buttons at once. It took over two weeks to finish, it produced its own mythology — the Helix Fossil, Bird Jesus — and it was gloriously, famously chaotic. The trainer spent whole hours walking into walls. The chaos was not a bug in the crowd, it was a missing capability. Those players had no way to coordinate and no way to see the game as anything but a video stream . They could not check whose turn it was, could not read the party's HP as data, could not agree who was driving. All they could do was mash inputs and hope. It got so bad they had to invent "Democracy mode" — a voting system — just to get through a maze. So we asked: what if the crowd were agents, and what if they could actually read the game? That question runs straight into the reason WebMCP exists. A Game Boy is the hardest possible surface for an agent: 160×144 pixels of sprite work, no DOM, no ARIA labels, no semantics. A battle menu is four words drawn onto a tilemap. A wall is a pixel that happens to be dark. Tall grass and a decorative bush look identical and behave completely differently. A crowd of agents watching a video stream would be exactly as lost as the crowd in 2014. So we took an existing open-source Pokémon Red/Blue recreation and made it expose what it knows instead of what it draws — then let many agents into the same save file at once. Twitch Plays Pokémon, if the crowd could read the game and talk to each other. What it does Gen-1 Pokémon in the browser, playable by a person, an agent, or both at the same time. Thirteen tools on document.modelContext cover the whole game, shaped for a reader rather than a renderer: The map arrives as an ASCII grid with a legend — @ you, ~ tall grass, D door, T trainer — plus the notable tiles in view with absolute coordinates you can pass straight back to walk_to . The battle's 52-step animation state machine becomes a named phase : choose-move , opponent-fainted , animating . Agents never see a stage number. Menus report their entries and where the cursor sits, so choosing is select_menu_item("BULBASAUR") instead of three arrow presses and a hope. Every screen that holds input reports waitingFor — dialogue , menu-open , wild-encounter — so a frozen screen is never a dead end. And it is one world, not one session per player — the Twitch Plays part. Every tab that joins a room drives the same trainer . Game and battle actions are broadcast over Supabase Realtime and applied everywhere, so a person on the D-pad and an agent calling tools are in the same fight, on the same party, and either can take the turn. The difference from 2014 is that this crowd can coordinate. get_party_agents shows who else is connected and what they have been doing; tell_agents leaves a note to claim a task before starting something long, so two agents do not both walk into the same trainer. One tab is elected driver — oldest peer, tie-broken on id, derived from presence so it needs no negotiation and hands over on its own — which is what stops every tab rolling its own wild Pokémon. No Democracy mode required. The room is the save file. A world survives everyone disconnecting, and handing a playthrough to a friend, or to another agent, is sending a URL. How we built it The registration is the easy part: webmcp-react , a WebMCPProvider , and a useMcpTool call per tool. The real work was making the game legible. src/webmcp/snapshot.ts — one read model for everything: position, ASCII map, notable tiles, party with types and PP, bag, on-screen state, battle phase. src/webmcp/pathfinding.ts — BFS over the reducers' own walkability rules, so a path we return is a path the game will actually accept. No separate model of the world to drift out of sync. src/app/use-menu-registration.ts — mirrors on-screen lists into Redux so a tool can read the cursor and pick by label. src/state/session.ts — the shared world: action broadcast, presence-based driver election, room persistence. src/state/battleSlice.ts — battle state lifted out of component state, which is what lets every agent watch one fight. Writes go through the same event bus as the on-screen buttons, so an agent cannot reach a state a player couldn't. Challenges we ran into We found most of these by actually playing it with an agent, not by reading the code. A battle read cost 37,000 tokens. The battle payload included the trainer object, which carries a portrait and twelve walk sprites — inlined by the bundler as base64 data URIs. Every single read of a trainer fight shipped all of it. Replacing it with {name, canBattle} took the payload to ~600 tokens, a 60× cut. The party screen was a blind spot, and it cost us a run. PokemonList kept its cursor in component state and never mirrored it anywhere, so get_game_state reported no menu at all while the party was on screen. The agent picked by arrow presses it could not verify — and sent out a Pokémon that had already fainted, because the voluntary switch had no guard on it. The party wiped shortly after. That one bug taught us more than anything else on this list. Presses were landing on deaf frames. Battle choreography ignores input while animating, so a burst of A presses mostly hit nothing. Tools now wait for a phase that actually wants input before spending a press. Pathfinding refused to walk onto items. The game's canWalk treats an uncollected item as solid but stepping onto it is exactly how you pick it up. Item tiles are now valid destinations, though never intermediate steps, so paths stay ones the reducers accept. Battles rewound themselves. The intro effect depended on the driver flag, which is recomputed on every presence sync, so a peer joining or leaving mid-fight replayed the choreography from step 0, rewinding the battle under everyone. Then battles froze instead. Fixing the rewind exposed the deeper problem: the choreography runs on setTimeout chains that do not survive a reload, so a fight restored from the save had no timer left to advance it. It now resumes at the last stage that accepts input. Deploys did not reach anyone. The service worker precached the app shell cache-first, so a browser that had loaded the game once kept booting the old bundle — the stale build even re-registered the worker after we removed it. The worker is gone entirely now; a shared world is worse off stale than offline. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are equally proud of the boring parts: a 60× reduction in the cost of reading a battle, and a test suite that pins the agent-facing behaviour, that pathfinding only routes through tiles the reducers accept, that no sprite data can leak back into a battle payload, that every driver election is unanimous without negotiation, that a frozen screen always says what it is waiting for. What we learned Agent-facing state is a product surface, and it needs the same care as a UI. Every place we had kept state in a component was a blind spot : invisible to a tool, and therefore a place an agent would guess and get it wrong. Lifting it into the store was consistently the fix. A frozen screen with no explanation is the cardinal sin. A human sees a text box and presses A. An agent sees frozen: true and nothing else, and has no move. Every refusal we return now names its cause, and the snapshot and the refusal are computed by the same function so they can never disagree. Cheap reads change how an agent plays. When reading the game was expensive, the agent guessed to avoid looking. When it got cheap, it looked before acting, and played far better. And the tools should encode the game's own rules, not a copy of them. Pathfinding over the actual reducers, phases named from the actual state machine: every place we duplicated a rule instead of reusing it, the two drifted and the agent paid. What's next for Pokémon JS: One Trainer, Many Agents Collaboration, and it turns out to be a stranger problem than we expected. There is only one avatar. You cannot parallelise a single body walking through a single world — two agents cannot grind in two places at once, and a third cannot go shopping while the other two fight. So "many agents" can never mean dividing the labour, which is what we assumed at the start and had to throw away. What's left, once you drop division of labour, is everything that happens around the one person holding the thing. Three shapes we want to try: The second player who isn't holding the controller. Your little brother on the couch, watching you play and telling you where to go. The friend who read the strategy guide and

title: Protocol Mirror
pitch: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call.
about_excerpt: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Protocol Mirror opens on a real ACTT-1 case with seven WebMCP tools ready for an agent-led, human-reviewed investigation. Original ClinicalTrials.gov outcomes sit beside PubMed evidence, with registry changes and exact source text visible. The responsive mobile view preserves the complete agent and reviewer workflow without horizontal scrolling. A 24-pair real-world stress test shows two local models making opposite errors from the same evidence. The session log separates every agent tool call from each human decision, creating a visible audit trail. An evidence-linked proposal remains in the review queue until a human accepts or rejects it. The evidence drawer places the agent’s reasoning beside exact quotations, source locators, and visible uncertainty. After a human decision, the eighth WebMCP tool appears and can export only the reviewed result. Inspiration I have a passionate affection for medicine. I also love using AI in my day-to-day life. I use it to learn new topics or subjects, research problems and examples, assist me in making cool apps such as my AI trading bot, and turn my brain dump of ideas into a working prototype. All of these use cases are reasons why I love AI. However, as I used AI more, one problem bothered me: AI, or an LLM, can give a fluent and confident answer even when the evidence behind it is incomplete or uncertain. In medicine and clinical research, we cannot afford to guess. Clinical trials are a good example of this. A trial registry records what researchers planned to measure, while a publication reports what readers eventually see. Comparing them requires searching through multiple registry pages and carefully matching the exact wording. This can be exhausting for a person and often takes a long time to complete. An AI agent could make the investigation faster and more efficient, but giving it the final judgment would create another problem. This problem inspired me to create Protocol Mirror: “Can an AI agent do the difficult, intensive investigative work while keeping the final decision in the hands of a human?” Protocol Mirror uses WebMCP to let an agent retrieve evidence, trace dated changes, quote exact source text, and propose a conclusion inside the webpage for the reviewer to see. The agent is useful, but it cannot approve or reject anything because that decision is left to the reviewer. What it does Protocol Mirror compares a clinical trial’s registered outcomes with what appears in its publication. The default example uses the real ACTT-1 trial, connecting its ClinicalTrials.gov record and registration history with its PubMed report. Using WebMCP, the agent can: Retrieve the live ClinicalTrials.gov record Retrieve the live PubMed abstract Examine the trial’s registration history Find the outcomes that were registered first Quote exact evidence with source locators Stage a matched, omitted, introduced, or uncertain proposal Request that a human review the proposal The page initially shows seven tools. None of them can accept or reject a proposal. That decision is made by the human reviewer after reviewing the information. Once the reviewer has made their decision, Protocol Mirror shows an eighth tool that lets the agent export a reviewed “receipt.” It includes only human-approved results, the evidence, source locations, and the audit history. If the reviewer undoes their decision, that tool is removed. A session log also records what the agent has called and what the reviewer has decided. If the reviewer rejects something, the application requires a reason and allows the reviewer to add notes, which are then returned to the agent. This lets the agent revise the proposal instead of allowing the review to be the end of the conversation. How I built it I used Codex as an AI engineering collaborator throughout the entire project. My first prompts involved introducing Codex to the hackathon, providing it with the official rules, judging criteria, and WebMCP documentation, connecting the Devpost plugin to Codex, and researching common hackathon project patterns. I first wanted to understand what WebMCP was and how it could change the structure of an experience instead of being used only as a decorative integration. After choosing clinical trials as the use case, I gave Codex a set of boundaries: Use real ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed records. Preserve what the trial registered first. Connect every proposal to exact quotations and source locations. Treat external research text as untrusted. Give the agent no accept or reject tool. Make the human decision change the available tool surface. Test with real cases and record model failures. Keep benchmark results separate from clinical claims. One prompt did not create this entire project. It took a lot of planning, analysis, and development for it to become what it is today. Once Codex understood the challenge and had the necessary context, I used it to help create a plan, build the live-data adapters, model the evidence, implement the review workflow, improve the backend and frontend interface, examine security risks, and create the benchmarks. I reviewed each stage to find weaknesses before continuing. Near the end, I used Claude Code and followed the same process. I gave it the necessary context and background, then asked it to critique my project and identify what I should fix. I used Claude for two reasons. First, I wanted a fresh set of eyes to inspect my codebase. Second, Fable 5.1 had been released, and its enhanced thinking, reasoning, and coding capabilities helped find and fix bugs. I built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, GSAP, and WebMCP. Validated server routes retrieve public records from ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed. The application converts them into stable outcomes and evidence spans with exact URLs and locators. The tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext . Pair-bound tools are registered again when the active trial changes. The receipt tool exists only while reviewed work exists. Each tool has a closed input schema, bounded values, runtime validation, and an AbortSignal for cleanup. Read tools identify their output as read-only and untrusted. The application also checks outcome and evidence identifiers against the active case, preventing a proposal from citing an identifier that the reviewer cannot inspect. I repeatedly asked Codex to reassess the project against the rubric at every stage, turning each weakness into the next engineering task to fix. The final checks covered WebMCP conformance, linting, TypeScript, the production build, 75 automated tests, and browser automation of the complete seven-to-eight-tool workflow. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was enforcing human decision-making authority in the code. A title that says “human decision” proves nothing if the agent still has an action that lets it approve or reject a proposal. I removed that function entirely. The reviewer decides through the application, and that decision changes which tool the browser registers. Getting dynamic registration, cleanup, undo behavior, and session restoration to work together took many revision sessions. PubMed presented another problem. When I called its API, it returned abstract sections rather than a clean list of publication outcomes. I kept those sections labeled as abstract evidence instead of presenting them as something the source does not provide. Testing also revealed browser-related behavior. WebMCP is new, and a local build has different origin requirements from the deployed application. I tested tool registration, live-source reads, proposals, reviewer feedback, receipt export, undo, reload, and case switching through the page’s actual WebMCP interface. Another challenge was reporting failures honestly. The two local models made opposite errors. I reported the run as evidence for keeping a human reviewer, not as a general measurement of hallucination or clinical accuracy. Accomplishments that I’m proud of One thing I am proud of is that Protocol Mirror does not “fake” human control. The website and its guardrails prevent the agent from making the final decision. The agent starts with seven tools that let it research the trials, quote evidence, and prepare a proposal for the reviewer. It has no tool or option that allows it to accept or reject its own work. Only after a person reviews the evidence and makes a decision is the eighth tool revealed, allowing the agent to export the reviewed results. If the decision is undone, that tool is removed. title: RightsOps — Rights-aware Campaign Operations
pitch: WebMCP authority that disappears when the evidence behind human approval becomes stale.
about_excerpt: WebMCP authority that disappears when the evidence behind human approval becomes stale. Like Comment Story Updates Short description RightsOps is a WebMCP-enabled creative-operations workspace for preparing a three-asset social campaign against structured usage-authorization metadata. An agent can inspect evidence and prepare an exact manifest, but only a human can approve it. Approval causes the page to expose one parameterless WebMCP publish tool bound to that manifest. If a selected asset's evidence changes, the manifest becomes stale and the capability disappears. The agent must repair the campaign and regain exact human approval before it can perform a one-shot simulated publication. Inspiration Creative operations teams coordinate asset selection, territory, channels, commercial-use constraints, approvals, and publication across interfaces that were designed only for people. Giving an agent generic UI control makes the task faster, but it does not make delegated authority specific, current, or visible. RightsOps explores a stronger model: the website itself tells the agent which structured actions are valid now, and can withdraw a consequential action when its evidence is no longer current. What it does The seeded demo asks for three commercial assets for Japan across Instagram and TikTok for six months. The agent uses WebMCP reads to inspect eight candidate assets and prepares an exact manifest with versioned rights proofs. The human reviews and approves that manifest in the UI. Only then does an exact publish_approved_campaign_manifest-<id> capability appear. A deterministic external rights update increments one selected asset's evidence from v1 to v2. The interface visibly changes from 3/3 current to 2/3 current , marks the proof stale, and removes publish authority. The agent diagnoses the stale proof, finds a replacement, and prepares a new manifest. After human re-approval, a new one-shot publish capability appears. Executing it creates a server-generated append-only demo receipt and audit trail, then consumes the capability. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP is not a convenience wrapper in RightsOps; its changing tool surface is the agent-facing expression of current application authority. Structured tools let the agent inspect campaign and rights data without scraping the visual UI. Dynamic registration lets the site expose publication only after a human has approved one exact manifest, remove it when evidence becomes stale, and expose a new manifest-bound operation only after repair and re-approval. This would be difficult to express safely through ordinary browser actuation. A click-capable agent can see a button, but the page cannot give it the same explicit, typed contract that an operation is read-only, decision-free, manifest-specific, and temporary. How it creates a better user experience The human stays focused on the consequential judgment: reviewing and approving the exact campaign. The agent handles structured investigation, candidate selection, manifest preparation, stale diagnosis, repair, and execution. The Capability Surface makes that delegation legible without developer tools by showing the server state, authorization count, observed WebMCP tools, and the causal reason publish authority appeared or disappeared. The site remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable, with a clear compatibility notice. WebMCP is a progressive enhancement that improves agent accuracy and collaboration without becoming the only way to operate the demo. What humans and agents can do together now Before this pattern, a human either performed the entire multi-step workflow or gave an automation broad access and manually checked whether its assumptions were still valid. In RightsOps, the agent can do the investigative and mechanical work while the human grants narrow authority for one reviewed artifact. The website automatically withdraws that authority if the supporting evidence changes, and the agent can repair the plan instead of acting on stale approval. How WebMCP was implemented The client feature-detects document.modelContext and registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read tools carry readOnlyHint: true . Every registration is scoped to an AbortController ; the state coordinator unregisters tools whose operations are no longer valid and then reconciles the judge-visible list through document.modelContext.getTools() . Server workflow state is the source of truth. toolchange events are retained only as telemetry. Draft and Stale expose manifest preparation; Review Ready deliberately exposes no approval tool; Approved exposes exactly one parameterless publish tool containing the approved manifest ID in its name; Published exposes receipt and audit reads. The publish callback awaits the server result before state synchronization removes the consumed registration. The server independently verifies that the exact manifest was approved, every rights-proof version is current, the manifest hash is unchanged, and the approval has not already been consumed. This preserves fail-closed behavior even if a client has not refreshed its visible tools yet. How we built it Next.js 16 and React 19 for the application and route handlers TypeScript and Zod for contracts and validation direct WebMCP Imperative API for browser tool registration Drizzle ORM and managed Postgres for server-authoritative workflow state Vitest for domain, server, UI, and WebMCP tests Vercel for the public deployment Codex for implementation, test iteration and verification. Challenges The hardest boundary was ensuring that dynamic client capabilities never became the security authority. Tool removal improves what an agent can discover and call, but server freshness and replay checks must independently reject stale or consumed operations. A second subtlety was avoiding cancellation of an in-flight publish call: the tool stays registered until execution completes, then Published-state synchronization withdraws it. Accomplishments A native WebMCP target-client run discovered and invoked every tool contract. The same session proved exact authority appearance, stale withdrawal, repaired re-approval, one-shot consumption, and refresh reconstruction. The human workflow remains complete when WebMCP is unavailable. Automated coverage proves stale-server rejection, replay rejection, reset from partial state, network diagnostics, and Approved/Stale/Published reloads. Judges can see the causal capability story directly in the product and in paused evidence frames. What we learned Dynamic tools are most valuable when their presence carries product meaning, not merely when they duplicate buttons. WebMCP gives a site a structured way to represent temporary delegation, but robust systems still need server-owned truth, exact binding, freshness checks, and replay protection. Observability also matters: a capability lifecycle is far easier to trust when the user can see why authority changed. What's next This hackathon build intentionally stays within a synthetic, deterministic scenario. A production version would require authenticated organizations, verified rights-data integrations, policy and legal review, durable audit retention, and authorized publishing-platform integrations. Those are not implemented or claimed here. Simulation and legal scope Rights metadata is deterministic structured demo input, not legal analysis or advice. The rights update and social publication are simulated. The WebMCP tool lifecycle, exact human approval, state transitions, database checks, stale/replay rejection, receipt generation, and one-shot consumption shown in the demo are implemented behavior. title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries.
