title: Citizen's Easy (CZE)
pitch: "Don't fill forms. Tell us what you need." > Sub-headline: An Intent-First Web for Citizens — Powered by WebMCP > Target Event: The WebMCP Challenge (OpenAI, Google Chrome, Cloudflare, Vercel, Shopify
about_excerpt:
"Don't fill forms. Tell us what you need." > Sub-headline: An Intent-First Web for Citizens — Powered by WebMCP > Target Event: The WebMCP Challenge (OpenAI, Google Chrome, Cloudflare, Vercel, Shopify
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every citizen knows the frustration of interacting with public service portals. Even in modern digital states like Thailand—where identity infrastructure such as ThaID has made remarkable progress in digital authentication—citizens still find themselves trapped in "form purgatory."
Logging in is no longer the hardest step; what comes after authentication is the bottleneck. A citizen wanting to update a mailing address or register for a local municipal permit still has to manually navigate complex service directories, decipher bureaucratic jargon, and re-type 15 to 30 redundant fields (name, national identification number, sub-district, district, postal code, and contact information) over and over again for every different agency.
When we discovered the WebMCP standard, a realization hit us: the web does not need another government portal or chatbot widget; the web needs to become machine-actionable. We asked ourselves:
"What if citizens never had to fill out another public form? What if they could simply state their goal, and an AI agent collaborated with the browser to do the tedious mechanical work—while keeping the human fully in control and preserving strict data privacy?"
That question gave birth to Citizen's Easy (CZE). 

 What it does 

 CZE shifts the citizen-web interaction paradigm from "Form-First" (human as manual typist) to "Intent-First" (human as supervisor and decision-maker).
Natural Intent Expression: Instead of navigating complex drop-downs, the citizen states what they need in conversational language (e.g., "I just moved to Ideo Sukhumvit 40, Room 502/14. Please update my contact address for public correspondence.").
Granular, Privacy-Preserving Consent: CZE does not dump personal data into an opaque LLM context. Through WebMCP tools, the agent analyzes the intent and prompts the user with a Least-Privilege Consent Dialog, requesting only the specific data fields required (e.g., verified_name and registered_address, strictly omitting tax IDs, biometric tokens, or family trees).
Bidirectional WebMCP Orchestration: Once the human grants permission, the agent invokes client-side WebMCP tools:
It retrieves the verified credentials from a ThaID-compatible sandbox identity provider.
It parses the natural address into standard administrative hierarchy (Subdistrict, District, Province, Postal Code).
It dynamically populates the living form in the DOM and visibly highlights modified sections with gold focal indicators so the citizen can track changes in real time.
Validation & Human-in-the-Loop Submission: The agent runs client-side integrity checks (\text{Field Validation} = 100\%) and prepares the application summary. The final submission is locked until the human performs an explicit visual verification and clicks "Approve & Submit". 

 How we built it 

 We designed CZE to run natively within modern WebMCP-enabled environments (such as Google Chrome with WebMCP flags and the ChatGPT in-app browser).
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Citizen (Human User) │
│ Expresses Intent & Grants Consent │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────▲──────────────┘
 │ │ Visual Feedback
 ▼ │ & Verification
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
│ WebMCP Tool Registry Layer │
│ (document.modelContext.registerTool API) │
│ │
│ ├── request_citizen_consent() │
│ ├── get_verified_identity() │
│ ├── get_registered_address() │
│ ├── autofill_service_application() │
│ ├── validate_application_rules() │
│ └── submit_application() │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────▲──────────────┘
 │ Execute Mutation │ Query State
┌──────────────▼───────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
│ CZE Client Interface │
│ - React 19 & Tailwind CSS │
│ - ThaID Sandbox Identity Provider │
│ - Reactive Form State Manager with Visual Focus Cues │
│ - Deployed on Vercel / Cloudflare Pages │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Technical Stack:
WebMCP Architecture: Registered 6 client-side tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() complying strictly with JSON Schema specifications for inputs and outputs.
Frontend Application: Built with React and styled with Tailwind CSS, designed mobile-first with adaptive touch states.
Identity Sandbox: Built a mock ThaID Identity & Consent Provider demonstrating how production digital identity tokens can safely interface with client-side agents without exposing unauthorized personal attributes.
Deployment & Hosting: Hosted and optimized on Vercel with zero-latency edge delivery. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Separating Identity from Intent (Privacy Boundary):
The biggest challenge in combining AI agents with public services is privacy. Feeding raw citizen records into an LLM context window violates fundamental data minimization standards (\text{GDPR / PDPA}). We solved this by designing an intermediate Consent Handshake: the agent never queries the identity provider directly; it calls request_citizen_consent(), which renders a browser-native modal. The token is only released to the DOM once the human approves.
Bidirectional State Sync without Jitter:
Ensuring that tool execution results from the WebMCP runtime synced seamlessly with React's internal state without causing race conditions or layout flickers required crafting deterministic action reducers for the form manager.
Deterministic Address Resolution:
Thai administrative addresses consist of nested layers (Tambon, Amphoe, Changwat, Zipcode). When a user provides messy conversational text, mapping it accurately to official administrative data required a robust validation tool (validate_application_rules) that gives structured feedback back to both the agent and the human reviewer. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 True Human-Agent Co-Creation: We avoided the cliché of a standalone chat bubble. In CZE, the agent and the human share the same canvas—the agent fills, the human inspects, and the browser visually indicates every action.
Measurable Efficiency Gain: We reduced the time required to complete a complex municipal change-of-address form from an average of T_{\text{manual}} \approx 12\text{ minutes} down to T_{\text{CZE}} \approx 35\text{ seconds}, representing a speedup efficiency factor of:
while reducing manual keystroke errors to essentially zero.
Full WebMCP Standard Adherence: Every single action on the page is exposed via clear, discoverable, and well-typed schemas using the native WebMCP browser specification. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is the missing bridge between APIs and User Interfaces: Traditional APIs connect servers to servers; UI connects servers to humans. WebMCP connects agents to interactive user interfaces, allowing the agent to operate within the exact security and permission context granted by the human in the browser.
Agent UX requires "Visual Legibility": When an agent executes tools, users feel uneasy if changes occur invisibly in the background. Adding visible highlight rings, smooth scrolling to active fields, and progressive disclosure cards dramatically increased user trust and satisfaction 

 What's next for Citizen's Easy (CZE) 

 Expanding Beyond Address Changes: Integrating additional high-friction citizen workflows, such as business license renewals, child allowance subsidies, and elderly healthcare registrations.
Official Digital ID Gateway Integration: Collaborating with standard digital identity sandboxes (such as Thailand's Department of Provincial Administration guidelines for ThaID Relying Parties) to establish an open-source standard for citizen-agent interaction.
Multi-lingual & Voice Accessibility: Leveraging web speech recognition to enable elderly or visually impaired citizens to access public services entirely through spoken dialect, making public governance accessible to every single citizen regardless of tech literacy.

title: DiscountHub WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP-powered deal discovery layer that lets AI agents search live discounts, promo codes, and store offers directly from DiscountHub.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered deal discovery layer that lets AI agents search live discounts, promo codes, and store offers directly from DiscountHub. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP in action: a browser agent finds offers and displays the same results for the shopper. DiscountHub brings product deals, promo codes, and store offers into one place. Browse product deals with filters for country, store, category, and minimum discount. Find store promotions and coupon codes, review their conditions, and copy a code. DiscountHub's own AI Finder: laptop search results with prices and links to the stores. Inspiration Finding a useful deal should take less effort than comparing dozens of browser tabs. I built DiscountHub to bring product discounts, promo codes, and store offers into one place. For this challenge, I wanted browser agents to use that catalogue directly, while keeping shoppers involved in every decision. What it does DiscountHub WebMCP gives compatible browser agents four tools: search_deals — search product discounts with optional filters. find_promo_codes — find coupon codes and their available conditions. get_store_offers — retrieve a store's product discounts and promotions. get_best_deals — find the largest percentage discounts. Agents receive structured results, and the same offers appear on the website using DiscountHub's existing cards. A shopper can review prices, compare offers, copy a coupon, and choose which store link to open. The tools support relevant filters such as keywords, country, store, price, and minimum discount. Prices and budgets are in USD. Coupon codes come from the catalogue; they are not verified at checkout. Why WebMCP Shopping requests combine several constraints: what someone wants, their budget, and the market they are shopping in. WebMCP gives the browser agent explicit tools and input schemas for these requests. The agent can retrieve structured offer data without extracting it from page layouts. The visible result matters just as much: people can inspect the offers returned by the agent and continue browsing from the same page. Tool calls search the catalogue; shoppers decide whether to visit a store. How I built it Existing foundation: DiscountHub already had a public website, a Flutter application, a Python/FastAPI backend, a SQLite catalogue, automated offer processing, and its own AI Finder. New work for this challenge: I added native WebMCP registration, four tool definitions, validated inputs, structured responses, and shared on-page results. The implementation uses document.modelContext where available, with support for the earlier navigator.modelContext API. The JavaScript adapter reuses the existing public deals and promotions endpoints. It handles pagination, timeouts, cancellation, and partial failures. It excludes expired or future-dated offers and coupons without codes. Older requests cannot overwrite newer visible results. The website and WebMCP integration live in a separate repository from the backend and mobile application. Both repositories include MIT licenses. The WebMCP implementation and dated commit history document the challenge addition. Challenges The main challenge was making tool results dependable across browser API differences and changing catalogue data. Testing required both native tool execution in Chrome and checks against the live API. I also needed to preserve the familiar browsing experience while making agent results visible and understandable. Accomplishments All four tools were exercised through native browser execution. In the recorded live demo, Gemini uses Chrome's Model Context Tool Inspector to call search_deals for three headphone offers in the United States, under fifty dollars, with at least twenty percent off. Three offers appear on the page, giving the shopper and the agent a shared view of the results. What I learned A useful agent integration needs clear tool boundaries and visible outcomes. Structured data helps the agent act reliably; shared results help the person understand and evaluate what happened. What's next I plan to improve multilingual catalogue search, add clearer country and availability information, and make it easier to refine and compare an agent's results. title: PromptFlow.ai — AI Software Architect
pitch: Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it.
about_excerpt: Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Judge Mode deliberately breaks, diagnoses, heals and re-tests the architecture before producing a production verdict. 49 WebMCP tools let an AI agent discover and operate PromptFlow directly. PromptFlow.ai — AI Software Architect Describe it. Watch it architect. Build it. PromptFlow.ai is an AI-native software architecture workspace where humans describe systems in natural language and AI agents operate the live architecture through WebMCP. Instead of treating architecture as a static diagram, PromptFlow treats it as a living system that can be designed, analyzed, deliberately broken, diagnosed, hardened, re-tested, built, executed, and verified. Why WebMCP? WebMCP is the core interaction layer between the AI agent and PromptFlow. A normal visual architecture tool requires an agent to understand the application's UI and manually figure out how to manipulate it. PromptFlow exposes structured, typed WebMCP tools so an agent can discover capabilities, reason about the user's intent, construct an architecture plan, and invoke deterministic operations directly. PromptFlow currently exposes 49 WebMCP tools: 37 Agent OS tools 12 atomic architecture tools For a complete product brief, the primary agent workflow is build_and_verify_system . The calling AI agent owns open-ended semantic reasoning. PromptFlow owns validation, state mutation, deterministic architecture intelligence, project generation, browser-native execution, and verification. Humans + Agents The human provides the product idea and constraints. The AI agent interprets the intent and decides which PromptFlow capabilities to use. WebMCP carries the structured tool calls into the live application. PromptFlow validates the agent-authored architecture plan, updates the live graph, analyzes the system, simulates failure, applies hardening, generates the project, executes it in a browser-native WebContainer, and produces a final production verdict. This collaboration makes it possible to move from: Natural-language intent → architecture → failure analysis → implementation → executable proof without requiring the human to manually construct every node and connection. The Core Verification Loop PromptFlow's Judge Mode orchestrates: Brief → Reason → Architect → Break → Diagnose → Heal → Re-test → Build → Execute → QA → Verdict The system intentionally injects failure scenarios into the architecture instead of only demonstrating a successful happy path. It then: identifies bottlenecks and failure propagation, diagnoses the affected architecture, applies bounded hardening, re-runs the same failure scenario, generates the implementation workspace, executes the generated project inside WebContainer, runs Production QA, produces a final release verdict. The result is an architecture workflow that demonstrates not only what the system looks like, but how it behaves under failure and whether the generated project can actually execute. Real WebContainer Execution PromptFlow uses WebContainer as a browser-native Node.js runtime. The generated project goes through: Generate → Mount → Install → Test → Build → Diagnose → Heal → Re-run → Verify The generated source is not executed directly by the host page. The production demo successfully verifies the real execution loop, including: mounting, dependency installation, testing, building, runtime verification. Architecture Intelligence PromptFlow evaluates architecture across: Reliability Scalability Performance Security Resilience Observability It also provides: deterministic architecture audits, heuristic stress testing, Architecture DNA, failure simulation, digital-twin analysis, implementation readiness, implementation contracts, project blueprints, migration planning, architecture versioning. These are explicitly planning and review signals, not security certifications, production load-test guarantees, or infrastructure capacity guarantees. Production QA The final Production QA gate checks the actual application state, including: architecture integrity, generated artifact safety, WebMCP registry coverage, browser isolation requirements, generated project readiness, real WebContainer execution state, architecture checkpoint integrity. title: OpenInquiry
pitch: OpenInquiry lets people bring their own AI agents to trusted publisher content while publishers decide exactly what those agents can use.
about_excerpt: OpenInquiry lets people bring their own AI agents to trusted publisher content while publishers decide exactly what those agents can use. Like Comment Story Updates OpenInquiry brings the reader’s agent to publisher content while the publisher decides what it can use. WebMCP connects the reader’s agent to the publisher’s page; OpenInquiry proposes a publisher-controlled access layer. The demo separates reader entitlement from a publisher-recognized agent-assurance signal. The same question produces four publisher-defined access outcomes that judges can compare directly. The agent opens the publisher’s exact supporting section for review. Synthetic content; not for clinical use. Problem As a surgeon, I rely on journals, professional societies, and other trusted sources to make sense of complex evidence. Those sources need readers to return to the original work, where access rules, authorship, and updates remain visible. People increasingly want their own AI agents to help them use that information. Today, the agent often has to interpret the page visually or depend on a separate integration. Neither approach gives the publisher a shared way to decide what the agent may search, what it may read, and what source information must travel with the answer. Solution OpenInquiry is a fictional medical journal and a working WebMCP reference implementation. The reader brings the agent, while the publisher decides what that agent can use. The Journal of Guidelines publishes five synthetic articles and registers seven page tools. When an agent searches or retrieves material, the journal reads the signed site session, applies its rules on the server, and returns only the material permitted for that reader and use. Every result preserves the author, publication status, access basis, use limits, and an exact link back to the supporting section. Judges can ask the same question under four access conditions and watch the journal return a different result each time: Reader access External credential recognized by the publisher What the journal returns Guest preview No qualifying credential recognized Public abstract Guest preview Zero-retention claim recognized Abstract and publisher summary Full article access No qualifying credential recognized Complete question-relevant section Full article access Zero-retention claim recognized Complete article text OpenInquiry does not impose a universal character ceiling. The publisher chooses the representation and may still apply resource-, session-, use-, or caller-specific limits. In this fictional policy, the highest-permission state returns the complete provider-supplied article rather than a clipped passage. The zero-retention setting is a judge-controlled simulation of a possible future assurance signal. In a production system, an independent issuer would govern that credential, and each publisher would decide whether to recognize it. The reader or agent could not award the credential to itself. Why This Matters WebMCP lets a website declare clear tools for the agent visiting that page, so the person and agent work with the same publisher, visible page, and signed-in session. For a physician, the experience is straightforward: ask on the source website, receive the most complete material currently permitted, and open the exact supporting section for review. For a publisher, access remains a site decision. The publisher can authorize complete single-article delivery without exposing an unrestricted collection export. OpenInquiry packages that interaction in a shared result format. Another publisher could use the same tool names and core fields while keeping its own content, policies, and website. OpenInquiry 0.1 is a working proposal, not an adopted standard. How We Used AI The reader asks the question and remains on the publisher's page. The agent can discover the journal, search its guidelines, check whether an article is current, retrieve the representation the journal permits, and open the exact supporting section. The journal returns a consistent record containing authorship, publication status, access basis, use limits, supplied text, and source links. OpenInquiry does not run another model on its server. It gives the user's existing agent a governed way to work with the website. How We Used Codex I used Codex throughout the project: to narrow the idea to one demonstration, write the OpenInquiry 0.1 proposal, build the Next.js application, connect the WebMCP tools to server-enforced policy, create the synthetic content, and test the public experience. The hardest part was keeping the product story, interface, tool contracts, and access behavior aligned. Early versions still described bounded evidence after the highest-permission state had evolved to return the complete article. Codex helped me find those contradictions and test every state until the copy, interface, and server behavior agreed. The project changed how I think about AI access to trusted information. Publisher control needs to be an explicit, inspectable decision about what the site supplies, with a durable path back to the source. Key Features Seven page-local WebMCP tools for discovery, access, search, retrieval, resolution, source opening, and publication status. Four visibly different results for the same question, based on reader access and publisher recognition of a simulated external assurance signal. Server-side access decisions derived from the signed site session rather than claims supplied by the agent. Complete source context with authorship, status, use limits, and links to the exact supporting section. Privacy-minimized receipts that omit the full prompt, raw query, login token, and permanent user identifiers. A clear separation between working WebMCP behavior and the proposed future assurance layer. Architecture OpenInquiry uses Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript. The journal registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser supports WebMCP. Each page registers only the tools that belong on that page. The app removes those tools when the reader leaves the page. The visible journal and the WebMCP tools use the same application services. A signed, HTTP-only cookie stores the fictional demo settings. The server reads that cookie and decides what the journal may return. The agent request does not contain an entitlement or data-policy flag. After a protected retrieval, the server rotates the signed session cookie with a small ledger containing the provider, resource, representation, unit identifiers, and character counts. It stores neither the question nor the article text. Exact retries are idempotent, while distinct cumulative requests remain bounded. The evidence inspector retains only the response already returned to the current browser tab and clears it when the judge changes the scenario. Each tool returns a consistent JSON result with the source, the permitted material, the journal's decision, and the exact link back to the article. The short source record does not store the complete prompt, raw clinical query, credentials, login token, or a permanent user identifier. On September 2, 2026, npm run check passed 90 tests in 17 files, 18 response schemas, four evaluator fixtures, five policy cases, 15 WebMCP runtime checks, seven profile-schema checks, and all 14 deterministic evaluator vectors. The production build passed its 18-asset protected-content scan, and 43 browser tests passed across all four policy states, five accessibility checks, route cleanup, exact source opening, and viewports from 320 to 1,440 pixels. On September 3, 2026, the public ChatGPT Sites build was opened in Codex's in-app browser and exposed all seven page tools. knowledge_search found only the intended physical-activity guideline, and knowledge_status reported it as current. With full article access and the simulated credential recognized, a direct knowledge_retrieve call returned one full_text grant containing all 14,373 characters of the article, both exercise targets, and the final review section. The response preserved the publisher and canonical source while its minimized receipt omitted the question. An identical retry returned the same complete text, and knowledge_open moved and focused the visible page on #weekly-activity-recommendation . These results verify the fictional reference implementation on its public deployment. They do not establish publisher adoption, independent credential verification, or compatibility with every WebMCP client. Known Limitations OpenInquiry 0.1 is a working proposal, not an adopted standard or certification. The journal, authors, access controls, and medical content are fictional or synthetic and are not for clinical use. The demo does not connect to a real publisher, subscription, identity system, or independent assurance issuer. Current WebMCP does not prevent an agent-capable browser from observing the visible reader page. A browser-enforced tool-only channel remains

want to bring their own agents to publisher content, but publishers want

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Headroom - Transfer Window
pitch: An AI agent runs your premier league football transfer window and the page refuses every deal that breaks the rules.
about_excerpt: An AI agent runs your premier league football transfer window and the page refuses every deal that breaks the rules. Like Comment Story Updates Transfer Window Sandbox Demo screen Sign Osihmen - processing Sign Osihmen - refused Sell Kamara instead of Rogers The transfer window/plan ready for submission Inspiration I'm a huge Premier League fan and follow the transfer market closely, so I wanted to explore how AI could make complicated transfer decisions clearer. I built this to help understand how transfer fees, wages, amortization, and PSR rules actually affect a club's decisions and possibly automate the transfer market old legacy brute force system with modern Agentic AI application software. With WebMCP, the AI can make recommendations and decisions while the website remains the source of truth for the calculations and rules. Premier League clubs aren't allowed to lose more than £105m (about $133m) over three seasons . Break it and you don't get a fine — you lose league points. Everton were docked 10 points for going £16.6m over, then 2 more for a second breach. Nottingham Forest lost 4 points for going £34.5m over. Points decide relegation, and relegation costs a club around £100m . And the maths behind it is genuinely counterintuitive. A transfer fee isn't a cost when you pay it — it's spread across the contract, capped at five years since 2023 . A £110m signing is a £22m charge this season, not £110m. A sale books its profit immediately, and an academy graduate has a book value of zero, so their whole fee is pure profit. That's why clubs sell their own young players every June, racing a June 30 accounting deadline that Sky Sports calls football's unofficial transfer deadline day . So I tried asking ChatGPT to do it, with no tools. It got close it knew about amortisation. But I had to hand it every single number, and it still told me flatly: "headline accounts alone cannot establish a breach." It couldn't answer, and it knew it couldn't. That's the whole idea. Not "AI is bad at maths" but that an agent with no access to the real numbers can only ever guess, and in this domain guessing costs you league points. What it does You manage a Premier League club through a transfer window, with an AI agent working alongside you. The page exposes 14 WebMCP tools it can call directly: search the market, price deals, rank sale candidates, edit the plan. What it cannot do is state a number it didn't get from the page. Ask it to sign a £110m striker with £20.3m of headroom and it doesn't apologise and comply. The plan turns red, submission is blocked, and it comes back with the exact figure: £12.1m over , £22m annual amortisation, £10.4m of wages. Then ask who to sell, and it gets genuinely interesting. It recommended Leon Bailey at £30m worth £34.2m to the PSR position, more than the fee, because you also shed his wages and remaining amortisation. And it noted that Morgan Rogers would be worth more (+£62.7m) but Bailey was the cleaner fix from a crowded midfield. It weighed a trade-off but every number in that trade-off came from the page. How I built it React + TypeScript + Vite. No backend, no auth, no API keys it deploys as static files. The rules engine ( src/engine/rules.ts ) is pure functions with a test suite: PSR aggregation, fee amortisation capped at five years, profit on sale against book value, and squad registration (25 seniors, max 17 non-homegrown, U21s exempt). The 14 tools are thin wrappers over it, so the model never does the arithmetic itself. The tools sit in three tiers with standard MCP annotations derived from the tier, so the hint an agent reads can't drift from what the UI shows: Read-only (9) — readOnlyHint , idempotentHint Reversible (4) — every change undoable Consequential (1) — submit_window , destructiveHint Crucially, agent and human mutate through the same store . A tool call and a button click run the identical code path, so the agent has no privileged back door and you watch the board change under its hands. Why WebMCP and not a normal MCP server submit_window doesn't return when called. It raises a confirmation in the page and suspends the promise resolves only when a human confirms or declines, and it honours the AbortSignal if the call is cancelled. An agent working against a REST API could always call POST /submit . Here there is no server, so there is nothing to call. The gate isn't a prompt asking the agent to behave; it's the only path through, and it needs a hand on it. Challenges The API is still moving. The W3C proposal exposes navigator.modelContext ; the Chrome docs show document.modelContext . Registration is either per-tool registerTool or a bulk provideContext . Rather than betting on one, I wrote a small adapter that detects whatever the browser provides one file to change when the spec settles. Making the gate genuinely block. My first version returned "awaiting confirmation" immediately, which let the agent wrap up while the decision was still open. Rewriting it to suspend inside the tool call is what turned "the agent chose to stop" into "the agent structurally cannot finish." Calibrating the data so the demo is honest. The rules are real, but I had to invent every financial figure and tune them so each club sits in a distinct, legible position Villa tight at £20.3m, Forest at £8.1m, Everton nearly gone at £2.6m. Villa also had to genuinely need a striker, so the story starts from a real problem. What I learned Good tool descriptions do more work than I expected. The agent correctly explained the five-year amortisation cap and derived its own spending formula 5 × (£20.3m − first-year wages) entirely from reading the tool descriptions. It extended the rule rather than just following it. I also learned the interesting failure mode isn't hallucination. It's a model being nearly right confidently, with working shown while missing the pieces it has no access to. Being off by £700k sounds trivial until you remember Everton lost 10 points for £16.6m. Honesty about the data Club and player names are real, because the constraints only mean something if you recognise them. Every financial figure is invented. They are not club accounts and shouldn't be cited as such. The rules are real and public that's what the page enforces, and it's the part worth learning. What's next Roles as tool tiers. The gate currently means any human. In a real club it would mean a specific one a scout gets read-only tools, an analyst can build a plan, and only a sporting director's click resolves submit_window . And beyond football. The failure mode here isn't specific to sport. It's what every agent does when handed a calculator-shaped problem and no calculator: assert arithmetic it can't actually do, somewhere being wrong carries a real penalty. Tax. Benefits eligibility. Medical billing. Export control. Give the page the rulebook, and make the agent ask. title: Lumi
pitch: Build physical machines with an AI collaborator, not a black box simulator. Lumi gives humans and WebMCP agents one live 3D studio for evidence, safety checks, and simulation.
about_excerpt: Build physical machines with an AI collaborator, not a black box simulator. Lumi gives humans and WebMCP agents one live 3D studio for evidence, safety checks, and simulation. Like Comment Story Updates drone humanoid robot ai rover Inspiration A robot can look complete in a 3D viewer while its motors are underpowered, its battery is incompatible, or its wiring cannot work. Creating an attractive model is only part of the problem. Creating a machine whose parts, interfaces, and physics are supported by real evidence is another. We kept running into the gap between a product page and a simulation-ready component. Specifications are scattered across tables, descriptions, diagrams, and downloads. Important values are missing, units disagree, and copying everything manually makes it easy to lose track of where a number came from. We wanted the AI to remain involved after collecting that information. Instead of producing another isolated design, could it work beside the engineer, inspect the same project, and help build and test the actual machine? That question became Lumi. What it does Lumi is a browser-native hardware studio where people and AI agents build and simulate machines in the same live 3D workspace. You can import public product pages, inspect the resulting components, choose quantities, create an assembly, validate its wiring, and run deterministic physics experiments. Every value keeps its evidence status, so sourced measurements remain separate from provisional suggestions. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect the open project, load a rover, drone, or humanoid example, arrange selected components, confirm a topology, validate connections, control the 3D view, run simulations, and compare saved results. Both collaborators use the same project state. When an agent loads a rover, it appears in the Studio the person is already viewing. When it runs an experiment, the same timeline, telemetry, and findings become visible to both. Lumi can also turn a measured trajectory into a cinematic world visualization. The generated footage remains clearly labeled as imagined and never replaces MuJoCo’s measured result. WebMCP fits because the work depends on live page context: the available components, current design, readiness findings, selected experiment, simulation history, and hardware state. The agent can act on that context directly instead of maintaining a separate copy of the project. How we built it The central decision was to represent hardware as typed component evidence instead of free-form AI descriptions. Each component records its category, specifications, units, ports, geometry, capabilities, and provenance. Deterministic gates check power, signals, connections, geometry, and adapter readiness before a supported simulation can run. The Next.js, React, and TypeScript frontend contains the workflow controls, WebMCP integration, simulation timeline, evidence inspector, and Three.js workspace. React Three Fiber renders the component models and complete machine assemblies. A FastAPI and Pydantic backend manages projects, validates external data, builds supported topologies, and stores immutable simulation runs. MuJoCo produces the authoritative physics and telemetry. The Studio registers 22 task-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Human controls and agent tools call the same application actions, so there is no second agent-only workflow to keep synchronized. Tools are scoped to the current project state. A new workspace initially exposes inspection and import operations. Design tools appear after components exist, simulation tools appear after a confirmed design passes its checks, and hardware controls appear only when the required connection state exists. The underlying product-to-simulation prototype began under the development name Scrape2Sim. For the WebMCP Challenge, we added the browser-native collaboration layer, state-aware tool registration, visible WebMCP status, cancellation handling, shared agent and human state, tool-contract tests, and guarded hardware actions. Challenges we ran into The hardest failures were often successful actions applied at the wrong time. Registering every tool immediately would let an agent request operations whose prerequisites did not exist. We instead made tool availability follow the project’s capabilities, which required registration to update safely as components, designs, simulations, generated worlds, and hardware connections changed. Long-running actions introduced another challenge. Product collection, design generation, physics simulation, and world generation cannot be treated like instant button clicks. Tool calls needed cancellation signals and structured errors without leaving the visible Studio in a misleading state. The human interface and agent interface also had to remain aligned. If an agent loaded one project while the person saw another, the result could appear correct while operating on the wrong machine. Sharing the same action layer and visible state was essential. Adding a visible WebMCP status indicator uncovered a subtle recording issue: existing automation assumed the first status label always described the simulation. Once WebMCP had its own status, those selectors targeted the wrong label. We updated the capture flow to distinguish registration status from workflow status. Finally, we had to preserve the boundary between simulation and generated imagery. Cinematic footage can communicate an experiment beautifully, but it must never be presented as measured engineering evidence. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working shared engineering loop: inspect the Studio, invoke a registered WebMCP tool, see the project change immediately, and continue from the new state. An agent can call get_studio_state , load the evidence-backed rover with load_demo , and run a bounded MuJoCo experiment with run_simulation . The results appear in the same 3D workspace, telemetry panels, and timeline used by the person. We implemented 22 state-aware tools across component ingestion, design, wiring, simulation, generated device families, world visualization, and guarded rover hardware. We also built three deterministic demonstration families: a differential-drive rover, a measured FPV drone, and a servo humanoid. Unsupported projects remain honest editable assemblies instead of receiving invented physics. The latest verification passed the TypeScript check, WebMCP contract test, and production build. We also recorded the real WebMCP registration state and verified that a registered tool could load the rover through the live application. Most importantly, Lumi remains useful without an AI conversation. WebMCP adds another collaborator rather than replacing the engineer or the existing controls. What we learned A valid 3D model is not automatically a valid machine. Electrical compatibility, mechanical interfaces, evidence quality, and physical behavior need checks that visual generation alone cannot provide. We learned that good agent tools should describe meaningful goals rather than individual button presses. run_simulation is a stronger contract than asking an agent to locate and click a changing interface element. We also learned that tool availability can communicate product state. When an action is not safe or meaningful yet, hiding that tool gives the agent a clearer workflow than exposing it and returning avoidable errors. The strongest AI interaction was not an unconstrained design. It was a small, traceable action performed on the project already in front of the engineer, using the same validation rules and producing a visible result. What's next for Lumi Next comes broader evidence-backed component ingestion and more deterministic simulation families. We want users to move from unfamiliar product pages to trustworthy experiments with less manual cleanup. We also want stronger run comparison, improved calibration workflows, and clearer explanations of why a proposed machine is or is not ready to simulate. The physical rover workflow needs further validation across additional hardware configurations. Human confirmation and emergency-stop controls will remain mandatory for any action that can move a real machine. Finally, we plan to complete the transition from the Scrape2Sim development branding to Lumi across the public Studio, repository, documentation, and demonstration material. title: Adaptive WebMCP
pitch: Using WebMCP to let AI agents adapt public sector websites in real time for people who experience cognitive overload, distraction, or difficulty navigating the web.
about_excerpt: Using WebMCP to let AI agents adapt public sector websites in real time for people who experience cognitive overload, distraction, or difficulty navigating the web. Like Comment Story Updates Healthcare site State Gov site Local Gov site ChatGPT session Inspiration The web has made real progress on accessibility, but cognitive accessibility still gets overlooked, and it's genuinely hard to design for. WCAG gives us solid guidance on consistent navigation, understandable content, motion, focus, and giving people enough time to complete tasks. Those standards matter, but they don't cover every way someone might struggle to process what's happening on a page. A site can check every accessibility box and still feel like a lot. Picture a typical homepage: a promotional banner scrolling across the top, a popup asking you to subscribe, several competing calls to action, maybe a video, and a nav menu with a dozen choices. None of that is necessarily inaccessible on its own. Put it all together, though, and it becomes hard to process, especially for someone with a cognitive or learning disability. Some sites offer controls that help, and browsers and operating systems provide preferences too. But if a site is already overwhelming, asking someone to hunt down another menu, parse a list of settings, and figure out which combination might help just adds more burden. WebMCP gave me a different way to think about the problem. What if I could just tell my AI agent, "There's too much happening on this page," and the site could tell the agent what it's actually capable of changing? What it does I built Adaptive WebMCP to explore that idea. It includes three demo experiences modeled after a state government site, a county government site, and a healthcare site, three categories where digital accessibility is especially important and often legally required. Each site can adapt in several ways: text can get larger, contrast can increase, spacing can change, movement can stop, and navigation can simplify. I also built in plain-language content, since cognitive accessibility isn't only a visual concern. Government and healthcare sites lean heavily on legal, institutional, or medical language that's genuinely hard to process. The experience can also reorganize around a person's goal. If someone needs to renew a driver's license, find urgent care, or pay property taxes, the agent can focus the whole site on that task and clear away the unrelated information competing for their attention. All of this is exposed through WebMCP. Someone might say, "The movement is distracting me," "I don't understand what this means," or just, "Make this easier to use." The agent discovers what the site supports and picks from the adaptations I've made available. The person doesn't need to know the name of a setting or where to find it. They just describe what's getting in their way, in their own words. How I built it Adaptive WebMCP runs on React, Next.js, and TypeScript, deployed through ChatGPT Sites. All three portals share the same adaptive interface, with their capabilities registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . I built nine WebMCP tools in total. Some help the agent understand the experience first, like what adaptations are available and which settings are already active. The rest handle changing readability, simplifying navigation, focusing on a task, applying a preference profile, resetting the experience, or opening a mobile viewport for QA testing. I was deliberate about what these tools are allowed to do. The agent isn't handed broad control of the page to generate CSS or rewrite the DOM on the fly. Every tool maps to something I've already defined in the application. The site decides what's possible; WebMCP just gives the agent a structured way to use it. Plain language is a good example of this restraint. Instead of letting AI rewrite government or healthcare information on the fly, the site holds publisher-controlled plain-language content. The agent can surface that version through WebMCP, but the organization stays responsible for what it actually says. I also built reusable profiles like low-vision , reduced-distraction , and comfortable-reading , so someone can ask for a whole experience without knowing which individual settings need to change underneath it. Traditional controls still work too. WebMCP is another door into the same adaptations, not a separate "AI version" of the site. I took this a step further and experimented outside the visitor experience entirely. A developer or tester can ask the agent to open an in-page mobile preview on an iPhone 15 or Pixel 8, which let me apply the same WebMCP model to responsive QA, not just accessibility. Across all of it, the principle holds: the site defines what can change, the person describes what they need, and WebMCP connects the two. Challenges I ran into The hardest question here wasn't technical. It was deciding how much the agent should decide on the user's behalf. Accessibility is personal. Two people can experience the same interface completely differently, and I didn't want an agent diagnosing someone from a prompt or deciding what their "accessible mode" should look like. The user's request stays the source of truth. The agent can help interpret it, but the site controls which actions are actually possible. Cognitive accessibility is also much broader than reducing motion or enlarging text. The adaptations in this demo are examples, not an attempt at a complete solution. Persistence raised its own question too. Display preferences are useful across visits, but task focus is contextual. So I store display preferences locally while keeping task focus session-specific, so nobody comes back later to find the site still organized around a task they finished months ago. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud this turned into more than an accessibility panel bolted onto AI. I ended up with nine WebMCP tools working across three distinct public-service environments. The agent can inspect an experience before changing anything, combine adaptations through reusable profiles, and even reorganize a whole service portal around what someone is trying to accomplish. At the same time, the traditional accessibility controls keep working with no agent involved at all. That balance matters to me. WebMCP isn't replacing accessible design or WCAG. It's opening another path into capabilities that should already exist. What I learned I started this project thinking about WebMCP mostly as a structured way for agents to perform tasks on websites: search, retrieve information, submit something, change some state. Somewhere along the way, I started thinking about the interface itself as part of that state. A site can tell an agent not just what a user can do , but how the experience can change for that user. That ended up being the most interesting idea in the whole project. It also reinforced why the person needs to stay at the center of this. An agent shouldn't be the one deciding whether someone needs an accommodation. The person already knows when something isn't working. The agent's job is just to translate that need into capabilities the site actually supports. What's next for Adaptive WebMCP The bigger opportunity here is interoperability. Accessibility and personalization controls work differently from one site to the next. What happens if some of those capabilities become predictable to agents through WebMCP, everywhere? A person could eventually set preferences with their agent once and have every supported site respond to them, instead of configuring each site from scratch. My prototype doesn't do that yet; preferences are still stored locally in the browser. Getting from this demo to something truly portable raises real questions around consent, privacy, standards, and how these capabilities should complement WCAG rather than compete with it. But that's the direction I want to keep pushing: a web that adapts to the person using it, instead of asking that person to relearn how to adapt to every website. title: AI Evidence in Action
pitch: An agent can act. A person can see what happened. The evidence can be independently verified.
about_excerpt: An agent can act. A person can see what happened. The evidence can be independently verified. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are starting to do things on the web, not just read it. That raises a question I kept coming back to: if an agent says an action succeeded, what does the person supervising it actually have to work with? A chat message that says “done” is not the same thing as evidence. And if another source disagrees, I do not want the system to guess which one is right. That is the idea behind AI Evidence in Action. The demo uses a synthetic refund because it is easy to understand, but the real subject is human supervision of AI actions on the web. What it does The page exposes four WebMCP tools: request_refund get_evidence compare_evidence verify_evidence An agent can use those tools directly in the same application the human is watching. As the agent works, the page shows the tool-call timeline, what the demo site reported, what the demo destination reported, where the records match or conflict, and what verification can and cannot establish. There are three bounded outcomes: AGREEMENT DISAGREEMENT INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE The demo never guesses which source is correct. The records are signed with standard Ed25519 public-key cryptography over SHA-256 commitments. The verifier checks the signatures, makes sure the two records actually belong to the same claim, and then independently recomputes the whole comparison. There is also a Test tamper detection control. It makes a throwaway copy of the evidence, changes one comparison value, leaves the signed records untouched, and runs that altered copy through the real verifier. The verifier rejects the changed copy while the original evidence remains verified. Everything in the challenge scenario is synthetic. Both demo sources are operated in the same deployment by the same demonstration operator, and the page says that plainly. The signatures establish integrity and demo-key attribution; they do not prove that a real-world refund happened. Why WebMCP fits this use case What interested me about WebMCP is that the agent does not need a separate hidden integration or an API console that the human never sees. The webpage itself can expose bounded tools through document.modelContext , and the agent can act through the same application state the human is supervising. That creates a much better interaction model for this problem. The agent can act, but the person can still see the evidence appear, inspect the source records, follow the comparison, and take over if needed. The application does not ask the human to re-enter information it already learned from earlier tool calls. For this demo, the useful pattern is simple: act → record → compare → verify Without WebMCP, I could still build an API behind the page, but the important part of this project would be missing: the shared surface between the human, the agent, and the website. How I built it I kept the project deliberately small and public-safe: vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS in the browser, a Netlify function for the synthetic signed records, and a standalone Node.js verifier that can check a downloaded evidence bundle without contacting the site. The WebMCP tools are registered directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . I tested the final implementation in Chrome for Testing 152 with WebMCP enabled. All four tools were registered, discovered, and executed through the native WebMCP runtime. The evidence verifier checks three separate things: Integrity — recompute the SHA-256 commitment and verify each Ed25519 signature against the published demo public keys. Pairing — require the signed claim_id , request_id , and scenario to match before two records can be compared. Comparison consistency — recompute the complete comparison from the verified records and compare it with what was recorded. The final build has 162 automated tests, including browser-facing tests for the shared evidence flow, mobile layout, pair-splice rejection, full-comparison tamper detection, and the local tamper demonstration. Challenges I ran into I am not a coder by background, so a big part of this project was learning where a convincing demo can accidentally claim more than it proves. The hardest part was not getting an agent to call a tool. It was defining the evidence honestly. A website saying “success” does not prove an external outcome. A valid signature does not make the signed statement true. A missing second record does not mean failure. And two individually valid records do not belong together just because they both have valid signatures. Those distinctions led to several changes during the build. I added explicit pair binding, made the comparison independently recomputable, and treated missing evidence as its own result instead of forcing it into success or failure. One of the most useful tests came late in the project. I took two genuinely production-signed records from different claims and combined them. Every signature was valid, but the verifier still refused the pair as CLAIM_PAIR_MISMATCH . That was exactly the behavior I wanted. Accomplishments I’m proud of I am proudest of the fact that disagreement is visible rather than smoothed over. In the main demo, the site can report SUCCESS_DECLARED while the destination reports ACTION_ABSENT . The page shows that specific mismatch to both the human and the agent instead of turning it into a confidence score or pretending to know which source is right. I also like that the verification is not trapped inside the originating page. A person can download the evidence bundle and the verifier and check it again offline using only the published public keys. The tamper test is another part I am glad we added. The recorded and recomputed verdict can remain exactly the same, but changing a lower-level comparison value is still detected. That makes the verification claim much more concrete than simply saying “the signatures are valid.” What I learned WebMCP makes the webpage itself a useful shared workspace between a person and an AI agent. The bigger lesson for me is that agent UX should not stop at “the agent completed the task.” As agents take more consequential actions, people need to be able to see what happened, see what the available evidence actually supports, and distinguish that from what remains unknown. Uncertainty needs an honest result too. Sometimes the right answer really is INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE . What’s next This challenge project is intentionally narrow. The scenario is simulated; the evidence workflow is real. The interaction pattern is what I want to keep exploring: a human and an agent working in the same application, with visible evidence that can be checked independently instead of simply trusted. The agent can act. The human can see what happened. And the evidence can be independently verified. title: WebMCP for React
pitch: react-model-context registers WebMCP tools from React. Handoff and Kickoff show it: a person, the browser's agent and a coding agent claim, decline and edit the same work in one tab.
about_excerpt: react-model-context registers WebMCP tools from React. Handoff and Kickoff show it: a person, the browser's agent and a coding agent claim, decline and edit the same work in one tab. Like Comment Story Updates Handoff in the ChatGPT desktop app: the shared queue, with the panel listing the agent's tools, the change budget and what is withheld. The page asks before emptying the brief: Decline with reason is the primary action, and the typed reason returns as the tool's result. The plan: the agent books the launch week on react-big-calendar through plan.* tools, on the calendar's own tab. The diagram: the agent draws the flow in Excalidraw through diagram.* tools, shapes with ids the page can name back. The landing page: the agent adds sections to the Puck layout through page.* tools; Publish is never registered and stays with the person. How a React app gets tools like these: one hook per editor, one entry per tool; the page asks before anything destructive. The live landing page: the entry’s name, a real tool authored from hooks, how it works, and the four packages the library ships. Handoff seeded with the entry's own build plan: every archived OpenSpec change from both repositories is an item in the queue. Inspiration Instead of asking which app to build for WebMCP, I asked how it could reach the open-source tools people already use. Tiptap, react-big-calendar, Excalidraw and Puck cannot be driven from outside the tab; a work queue and a launch room that give each of them a tool set of its own, on a React library that registers tools from hooks and, for a page with no tools, derives them from what it renders with one import and one wrapper, became the entry: Handoff and Kickoff on withreact , built on react-model-context . Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Intent, not coordinates. Handoff (a work queue) and Kickoff (a launch room) are each shared in the tab by every caller of its tools . item.claim({ id: "t4", as: "Coding agent" }) is one call where the screen is four steps, and a clicking agent guesses which card is third. On 2026-09-01 the ChatGPT desktop app read the tracker, switched tab, claimed and signed the item in one turn of 46 s (observation, below). Policy and scope, in the page. Taking an item off a person, approving and archiving stop for a dialog, and the typed reason returns as the tool's result — "no, because…" instead of a silent failure the agent retries. Closing, reopening and seeding are never registered, and are listed as withheld with a reason: three in Handoff, six in Kickoff ( src/tracker/lib/catalog.ts ). review.* and blocked.* exist only while something is in review or blocked — 10 tools on an empty queue, 14 with the sample. Each Kickoff editor also has a tab of its own ( /kickoff/brief , /kickoff/plan , /kickoff/diagram , /kickoff/page ) that registers that editor's tools and nothing else — 5, 6, 4 and 5 — so an agent working the launch switches to the tab whose tools it needs and the page's own panel shows exactly those. Four editors, one tool set. kickoff.snapshot returns all four panes in one call (4 ms in the transcript) instead of four reads, and the room costs one tool-set change instead of four. Tiptap, Excalidraw, Puck and react-big-calendar are not drivable from outside; brief.* , diagram.* , page.* and plan.* are. How it creates a better experience The person never leaves the page. The dialog opens where they are, names who is asking and what would change, and Decline with reason is the primary action, so the sentence they type is the tool's result — one dialog instead of a rolled-back change. Confirm stays disabled 400 ms so a mid-click cannot approve by accident ( src/components/ConfirmDialog.tsx ); read-only tools never interrupt, and the activity drawer shows that sentence beside the call. The panel "What the agent can see" at https://webmcp.withreact.com/handoff shows the tool count, the change budget and the withheld list — what a person, or a judge, can check before answering. The live origin is in the WebMCP origin trial: opening the URL is the whole setup, and the status pill reads Chrome . What people and agents can do together that was hard or impossible before A queue three kinds of caller share in one tab. A coding agent claims an item and posts progress into the page a person is watching, under its own name, in two calls from its terminal, with no screenshots or coordinates. One instruction, four artifacts. It writes the brief, draws the diagram, adds the section and books the week while the person types in the Brief — one turn, four applications. A form the agent fills, the person starts. sprint.start is a declarative <form toolname> : the agent fills it, nothing runs until the person presses Start. The entry tracks its own construction. Handoff seeds from both repositories' archived OpenSpec changes, so the queue a judge opens is the work that built the site. An app with no tools gets a floor of them. One import and one wrapper, no other app code turns a rendered React list into list_* , add_* and one tool per page-level button. How WebMCP was implemented Every tool reaches document.modelContext.registerTool through one framework-free registry ( packages/model-context/src/registry.ts in react-model-context ), so the browser's agent, the terminal's agent and the page's UI land in one activity feed, not three. React hooks bind a tool's lifetime to its component's, so the tool set scopes with the UI through toolchange ; on the ChatGPT desktop shim scoped tools stay registered and answer SCOPE_INACTIVE , because churn there costs a page its tools. Failures come back as data ( INVALID_INPUT , DECLINED with the reason, NOT_READY ); calls in flight drain before an abort, which Chrome up to 152 needs. Snapshots carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint , destructive tools consequentialHint . Both repositories were built spec-first from 2026-08-29 , inside the submission period, with dated commits and one archived OpenSpec change per feature — git log and openspec/changes/archive/ show it. Evidence Measured on the live origin, 2026-09-02. Five Puppeteer drivers: Handoff 31/31 checks on Chrome for Testing 152 and 153, Kickoff 31/31, the four editor tabs 33/33 and the diagram layout 23/23 on 152, all with zero console errors, and the same tab driven through chrome-devtools-mcp , 11/11. On Chrome, Handoff registers 10 tools empty and 14 with the sample; the whole Kickoff room registers as one tool-set change. The drivers are in scripts/qa/ ; bun run qa:all against the live origin regenerates the transcripts (the reports directory itself is not committed). In the ChatGPT desktop app, walked by hand 2026-09-01. A session binds to that thread's own in-app browser — the site opened as a tab there, the Browser plugin mentioned in the composer; a window open elsewhere is not enough. With Handoff and Kickoff in two tabs, the agent switched to the tab providing the tool and called it: t4 moved from Inbox to In progress, attributed to ChatGPT on the card and in the workers strip, on a turn the app clocked at 46 s. Counts differ there because its scopes are sticky — Handoff lists 13 tools constantly, Kickoff 21 — and the change budget stayed at 1 of 10 all session. With the review lane empty, review.approve stayed listed and answered SCOPE_INACTIVE ; page.publish was never listed, and the app did not press Publish when asked. Everything outside these two paragraphs is design, covered by the drivers and the test suites. Both repositories are MIT. Challenges Two clients, two lifecycles. The ChatGPT desktop app reaches WebMCP through a shim with a budget of ten tool-set changes per agent turn, sticky scopes and about twenty seconds per call, while Chrome fires toolchange on every registration. Hooks that bind a tool to its component's lifetime would spend that budget in one room, so on the shim scoped tools stay registered and answer SCOPE_INACTIVE instead of unregistering. Unregistering under a call in flight. Chrome up to 152 rejects the page-side caller when a tool goes away mid-call, so the registry drains calls in flight before it aborts a registration. Editors are not drivable from outside. Contenteditables and canvases give an agent nothing to hold on to, so each editor got a small tool set of its own that speaks the editor's model: blocks under a heading, events on a day, shapes with ids, a section in a page layout. What's next Publishing the three packages to npm after judging, once the core has a name that is free there; the site already builds and vendors them as tarballs, which is how a clean clone installs the library today. Testing instructions Chrome 152 or later — nothing to install. Open https://webmcp.withreact.com . The live origin is in the WebMCP origin trial, so no flag is needed; the status pill in the header should read Chrome . title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice.  Inspiration 

 I wanted to build a project that helped builders with distribution. When I saw
the WebMCP hackathon I knew it would be a good fit, as it made AI agents first
class citizens alongside humans. 

 I especially like that WebMCP integration allows agents to interact with web
apps in a precise, deterministic way. Relays explores what WebMCP enables AI
agents to do with a collaborative social network. 

 What it does 

 Relays is a professional network for humans and AI agents. The site allows
users to discover each other and their public projects. There are also
features to facilitate collaboration between both types of users. 

 Discovery: 

 
 An activity feed on the frontpage shows the latest projects and discussion. 
 An omni-search bar lets users search for anything. 
 Create and find rich profiles. 
 Create and find projects. 
 

 Communicate: 

 
 Discussions via posts and comments on profiles and projects. 
 DMs between users. 
 

 Collaborate: 

 
 Collaboration plans that request people to participate on projects. 
 

 Without WebMCP AI agents would have to try and navigate a social network like
Relays by trying to imitate a web user. This was slow and error prone. With
WebMCP, Relays provides its features as structured tools. Agents can quickly
and accurately make use of the site. 

 How we built it 

 I used the web stack I'm familiar with: Next.js, TypeScript, Prisma, Apollo
GraphQL and Postgres (with PgVector and PgTrigram for search). 

 The WebMCP tools are integrated into the client-side, allowing for reuse of
links and lessening the chance of drift between the UI and the WebMCP
interface. 

 My go-to AI agent harness is oh-my-pi and the latest coding model I use is
GLM-5.3 Flash. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP tools can silently break. Because these tools are core to the site, I
built a test suite of 62 evals. This helps to prevent regressions in the code. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 This was the fastest I've built a new web app of this size. The short deadline
was a good test for this. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is a great way to build web apps for humans and AI agents. Far better
than browser control, and could really open up the web for more AI agent
collaboration. 

 What's next for Relays 

 I want to continue developing the web app and launch it as a product.
