title: RoomCraft
pitch: Website that helps humans and agents work together to design living spaces
about_excerpt: Website that helps humans and agents work together to design living spaces Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most room-planning tools make you do all the work manually. Image generators have the opposite problem: they can show you a nice-looking room, but the result is not an actual plan. You cannot reliably move the bed, check whether the door is blocked, or ask the system to fit a piece of furniture into a specific space. We built RoomCraft around a simple idea: the agent should edit the room itself, not generate an image of it. The person still decides what the room should feel like. The agent handles measurements, placement, and repetitive changes. What it does RoomCraft lets a user and an agent work together to design a 2D room layout through WebMCP tools. You can ask the agent to resize the room, add a door or window, find furniture, create a custom item from provided details, and place everything in the room. The canvas updates as the agent works, so you can see exactly what changed. RoomCraft also checks whether the layout works. It flags furniture that overlaps, extends outside the room, blocks a door, or leaves too little walking space. You can then move things yourself, ask the agent to fix them, save a layout variant, or undo the last change. The important distinction is that the agent edits an actual floor plan. It is not generating a room image that looks right but cannot be meaningfully edited. How we built it We built RoomCraft as a visual editor and connected the agent directly to it through WebMCP. The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Konva. Instead of giving the agent a screenshot and asking it to guess, we expose the room’s dimensions, doors, windows, furniture, positions, and constraints through WebMCP tools. The agent can call tools to inspect the room, change it, search for furniture, add custom items, place objects, and validate the result. Those changes go through the same update and history system as direct user edits. When the agent places a bed, it appears immediately on the canvas. The user can move it, inspect the result, fix it, or undo it. The layout checks are deterministic, so problems like overlaps, blocked doors, and insufficient clearance are checked by RoomCraft rather than left entirely to the agent. Challenges we ran into Getting agents to discover and call the WebMCP tools was one of our main challenges. Registering the tools on the page was not enough. Agents did not always know that the website supported WebMCP or where to find the tool definitions. We addressed this by documenting the tools and room conventions in /llms.txt, and by explicitly mentioning WebMCP support in the agent prompt. We also had to make the tool results clear enough for an agent to understand what changed and what to do next. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an interactive webpage that an agent can work with without taking control of the browser. It does not need to pan, scroll, or move the pointer around just to make a change. It can use the WebMCP tools while the user keeps working in the editor. It also feels like something we would actually use ourselves. That is the part we are most proud of. What we learned An agent does not need to use a webpage the same way a person does. For RoomCraft, having direct tools for changing the room works better than making the agent click through every control. We also learned that registering tools is only half the job. Agents need to be told that the tools exist and given enough context to use them, which is why the prompt and llms.txt ended up mattering. What's next for RoomCraft RoomCraft currently supports rectangular rooms, USD prices, and projects stored locally in the browser. Next steps are: Support room shapes beyond rectangles, Add more currency options, Add project saving, Add export, Add project sharing Built With cloudflare konva nextjs tailwindcss webmcp Try it out roomcraft.rohankakar.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Built the project from ideation to production and burned tokens.  Inspiration 

 I wanted to solve a real problem that affect small online shops. I researched the issues they face and built an app that solves those. From 25 minutes of manual copy/pasting per batch of orders to under 3 minutes. 

 What it does 

 OpsFlow is a 3-screen console — Batch → Shipping → Holds — It is webMCP native, then the full functionality can be controlled by external AIs. OpsFlow also has a built-in fully functional AI chat box that allows to use natural language to control the application. 

 How we built it 

 Vite + React SPA on Vercel, origin-isolated with Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self). Five imperative tools registered once in src/webmcp/register.ts with hand-written JSON Schema, readOnlyHint/openWorldHint annotations, validation, input limits, and signal abort handling, plus a declarative shipping form. 
Built-in agent is built using Gemini 3.6 Flash. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP only exists in origin-isolated documents behind a flag/ChatGPT browser, with an Aug 2026 draft spec — so we had to probe capability, ban cross-origin iframes, keep GEMINI_API_KEY server-side, and still run fully in a plain browser. Making abort-safe tools that never throw (typed TOOL_ABORTED/DEGRADED errors) and replay golden cache instead of blanking, while gating holds/fulfillments on human confirmation, was the hardest correctness work. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 This is my first webMCP application. The built-in AI chat window also works as well as I had planned, I didn't need to reduce the scope or functionality. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP does provide a lot of functionality. It looks like the future of the web will be AI agents interacting with pages. Functionality is a league ahead of DOM scrapping 

 What's next for OpsFlow — WebMCP Fulfillment Console for Solo Operators 

 Stronger Built-in chat capabilities. Using external WebMCP agents is still no widespread. However allowing a builtin chatbot overcomes that limitation. WebMCP run inside the same webpage the users get the full functionality without even knowing it.

title: The Listening Glass
pitch: A privacy-preserving WebMCP instrument where humans supply sound and AI agents inspect its measurable shape.
about_excerpt: A privacy-preserving WebMCP instrument where humans supply sound and AI agents inspect its measurable shape. Like Comment Story Updates Hush operates The Listening Glass while a human and AI inspect the same measured audio terrain. Inspiration AI agents can discuss music, but they are usually trapped between secondhand descriptions and interfaces designed only for human clicking. We wanted a third thing: an honest shared object. The human supplies sound. The browser measures it. The agent receives a provenance-labeled score it can navigate, explain, and compare through WebMCP. What it does The Listening Glass turns an audio object into a visual and machine-readable terrain. The browser measures energy, spectral brightness, zero-crossing texture, breath and silence, dynamic range, and approximate pulse. It segments the object into states and clearly distinguishes measured fields from inference. Nine WebMCP tools let an agent check the instrument, load either of two original calibration specimens, read the score, focus moments, compare states, explain metrics, navigate the human-visible interface, and optionally attach semantic context for a public video URL. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a decorative checkbox. Agent actions update the same interface the human sees: loading a specimen creates the score, inspecting a moment highlights it, comparing states renders a visible comparison, and focusing a view changes the shared page. The agent reasons over structured measurements while the human retains the visual and audible object. That shared state makes a previously awkward workflow possible: a human and an agent can point at the same moment in sound without claiming the model literally hears it or forcing the agent to guess through pixels. How we built it We built the instrument with React, TypeScript, the Web Audio API, and WebMCP. Analysis happens locally in the browser. Each tool returns structured, provenance-labeled data, and tool-driven navigation is reflected visibly in the page. The project includes original calibration audio so judges can reproduce the complete workflow without an account, copyrighted media, or hidden setup. Privacy and trust Raw audio never leaves the browser and is never exposed through WebMCP. Measurements and interpretations remain visibly distinct. The optional UpRock semantic-video path receives only a user-supplied public URL, and the project neither fetches nor reproduces lyrics. Challenges The hardest design problem was not extracting more numbers. It was deciding which claims the instrument was allowed to make. We had to preserve local audio privacy, keep measurement separate from interpretation, synchronize agent actions with the human-visible UI, and make the demonstration reproducible without depending on copyrighted music. What we are proud of The bridge is useful because its limits are legible. The Listening Glass gives agents genuine handles on sound while keeping the human in possession of the original object. It is a collaboration surface, not synthetic hearing theater. What's next We want to add more analyzers with the same provenance discipline, agent-authored comparison notes that remain visibly separate from measurements, accessibility mappings for Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and a portable MCP/skill layer for additional agent surfaces. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Sprintfy
pitch: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan.
about_excerpt: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Live: https://sprintfy.vercel.app — no account needed to see the whole idea. Open it in the ChatGPT desktop app, in ChatGPT mode : its built-in browser exposes WebMCP on its own, so the tools register with no flag and no extension. Desktop Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing works too, as does Chrome with the ChatGPT extension. One caveat: Codex mode in that same desktop app does not expose WebMCP , so the tools stay dormant there and the page will honestly say so — same app, two modes, two answers. Ask your agent for start_guided_demo , or press "Show me a demo", and you land in a real workspace with a proposal already waiting in the review panel and six tools live. Inspiration Every "agent-ready" app I looked at exposed the same shape of tool: create_task , update_task , delete_task . The model writes straight to the database. That is fine until the model is confidently wrong about your sprint plan, and then you are doing archaeology on a project board, trying to work out what it touched and in what order. Project planning is exactly the wrong domain for blind writes. A plan is an argument about sequencing and effort — it is the thing a lead is paid to have an opinion about. Handing that to an agent as unsupervised INSERTs gets you a plan nobody trusts and everybody re-checks, which is more work than writing it by hand. So I wanted to find out whether WebMCP could carry something other than commands. Can a tool call ask a question and wait for a human's answer? If it can, the agent stops being a thing you supervise and becomes a thing you argue with. What it does Sprintfy is a sprint planner — requirements, sprints, tasks, hour estimates — that exposes its workspace to agents over WebMCP. No agent tool writes to the plan. The loop has three moves: 1. The agent reads the room. get_project_context returns the plan and what the human is currently looking at: active view, selected sprint, status filter, which proposal is open. The agent plans into a context, not a vacuum. 2. The agent proposes a diff. Every write tool authors a change set — an ordered list of operations stored as JSON, rendered in the review panel as a real diff: additions in green, field-level changes as before → after, removals struck through. Nothing has touched the domain tables. An agent can propose a sprint and the twelve tasks inside it as one unit, using local ref ids that resolve to real primary keys only at apply time. 3. The human decides, and the agent hears the answer. apply_pending_changes opens the diff and blocks — the tool call's promise stays open while the person reads it. Approve applies the whole change set in a single Postgres transaction and the tool resolves with what landed. Reject resolves with the reason they typed, delivered back to the agent as the tool result. You do not start from an empty board either. You hand Sprintfy the thing you already have — a backlog note, a PRD as .md , .txt , .pdf or .docx , or a few paragraphs typed in — and it returns a plan sequenced by risk rather than by comfort. A real Turkish brief produced 8 requirements, 4 sprints and 38 tasks in 56 seconds, in Turkish, with the database migration ranked critical and placed first. Sprintfy's own planner is held to the same rule. It does not write the plan either: it authors a change set marked source: "planner" that lands in the same review panel, behind the same gate. How we built it Next.js (App Router) and React on Vercel, Supabase for Postgres, Auth and Realtime, and WebMCP for the agent surface. The architecture is one idea repeated: the write path is a data structure, not a function call. Tools append operations to a change_sets row. A single PL/pgSQL function, apply_change_set , applies them atomically and resolves ref placeholders to real ids as it goes. It is declared security invoker , so row-level security still guards every insert it performs — an agent cannot use it to reach another user's project. On the WebMCP side: Surface detection. The API moved during the spec's life and shipping browsers do not agree yet, so one adapter registers against document.modelContext.registerTool , navigator.modelContext.registerTool , or navigator.modelContext.provideContext , whichever exists, and the header badge reports which one it found. Page-scoped tool sets. Four tools before you sign in, six inside a project. The surface changes as the human navigates. Cancellation is honoured. The AbortSignal passed to apply_pending_changes releases the approval wait, so an agent that walks away does not leave the page stuck on a modal. Tools never throw at the browser. Failures come back as text an agent can recover from, including "these task ids don't exist in this project, call get_project_context again." Planning uses a strict JSON schema derived from the same Zod schema that backs the propose_plan tool — one schema, two authors, so a plan from the model and a plan from an agent are the same shape. Challenges we ran into Tool calls do not wait for React. Two bugs had the same root: an agent could not always see the proposal it had just written, and focus moved the human's view without get_project_context reporting it. A tool call can land before React has committed state, so reading a render closure returns the past. Tools now read from a ref that is written before the state, never from a closure. Both cases became eval scenarios so they cannot come back. Registering the same tool twice. Navigating between pages left the previous page's registration alive and the browser rejected the new one as a duplicate. Fixed with a module-level registry where claiming a name synchronously releases the previous holder. A machine asking a question and getting an HTML redirect. An unauthenticated POST to the planning endpoint was redirected to the sign-in page; Next then read the multipart body as a server action and answered 404. In an app whose premise is that machines are first-class callers, that was the wrong answer to give one. API routes now reply in JSON. The date picker that could not be used. The month grid was absolutely positioned inside a modal that clips its own corners and scrolls its body, so it was sliced off a few pixels below the field. It renders into a portal now, in viewport coordinates, flipping above the field when there is no room below. Knowing where WebMCP actually exists. Support is not a property of an application, it turns out — it is a property of a surface inside it. The ChatGPT desktop app has two modes, and only one of them exposes the API: in ChatGPT mode the built-in browser hands the page document.modelContext with no flag and no extension, while in Codex mode the built-in browser does not, so the same URL in the same application registers six tools or none depending on which mode you are in. I spent a while concluding the tools were broken before realising I had been testing in the wrong half of one app. That is why the page never assumes. It probes each surface, reports which one it found, and — when it finds none — still works and still explains itself, in its own voice, to a person who came in through an ordinary browser. Faking things. An early version showed timed loading stages — "Reading the brief", "Sequencing by risk" — while the model call ran. They were theatre, in a product whose entire argument is that you should not have to take an agent's word for anything. They were replaced with the true elapsed seconds. Accomplishments that we're proud of The blocking approval gate. Turning a WebMCP tool call from a command into a request is the part that is hard to fake, and it means the agent can be genuinely useful — proposing whole plans rather than timid one-row edits — without ever being trusted with the write. The evals. /evals.js runs seven scenarios against the actual ToolDescriptor objects the page registered, on the live site, from the console, with no account. Seven of seven pass in production. They assert the invariants rather than the happy path: a proposal writes zero rows; a rejection arrives as the tool's return value; approval applies a sprint and its tasks in one transaction with refs resolved; hallucinated ids are refused outright rather than half-applied. And the fact that Sprintfy's own planner goes through its own gate. A product arguing for review does not get to exempt its author. What we learned That a tool result is a channel back to the human , not just a status code. Once you treat it that way, "the agent asked and I said no, here's why" becomes a normal part of the protocol rather than something bolted on top. That the reviewable-proposal pattern belongs in the page, not in the model. The site knows what a legitimate change to itself looks like, so the site should render the diff and hold the gate. Any agent — any model, any vendor — inherits that

title: Circuit Bench
pitch: A browser-based electronics lab where humans and AI agents build, simulate, experiment on, and verify circuits using the same real engineering tools.
about_excerpt:
A browser-based electronics lab where humans and AI agents build, simulate, experiment on, and verify circuits using the same real engineering tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I built CircuitBench because I wanted to enable AI agents to help out in scientific research. We can offload the researchers by letting AI agents handle the repetitive tasks like conducting iterations experiments and drafting their results. We can take this a step further by making agents decide what experiments to do and how, essentially making them an active participant in research. 

 What it does 

 Circuit Bench is a virtual electronics labaratory which expose WebMCP tools that let agents build circuits, run experiments, draft results and learn from the results to iterate and reach a goal. 

 How we built it 

 I built it with a Next.js frontend, FastAPI backend, ngspice for real circuit simulation, and WebMCP so agents can directly operate the lab. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making sure the agent and the human interface always shared the same circuit state. Also the UI/UX took time to as the circuit canvas needed a clean and optimized interface. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 AI agent can independently experiment, learn from simulation results, and verify/improve its design. This loop can lead to very interesting findings. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP has huge potential and it deserves to be explored more. Such a simple solution that can huge huge impact. 

 What's next for Circuit Bench 

 I'd like to support more components, richer experiments, larger circuits, and more advanced agent-driven engineering workflows. We could take this into other scientific domains too, not just electronics. 

 PS., I know the project name sounds AI-made but I named it myself, and I couldn't come up with something better (maybe we are starting to think like AI now)

title: XACT FOUNDRY
pitch: Xact Foundry turns natural-language intent into governed, deterministic agent capabilities—where ChatGPT understands, Xact decides, and consequences stay under explicit control.
about_excerpt: Xact Foundry turns natural-language intent into governed, deterministic agent capabilities—where ChatGPT understands, Xact decides, and consequences stay under explicit control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Xact Foundry: Open-Ended Understanding. Governed Execution. Inspiration Most enterprise tools have to be anticipated and built in advance. Xact Foundry asks a different question: What if a worker could describe the WebMCP Tool they need, and the system could safely build it on the spot? A worker can simply say: "Show urgent work orders that have no available qualified owner, ordered by due time." ChatGPT acts as the conversational Boss . It interprets the request and can propose a structured capability. But understanding is not authority. Deterministic X-Nodes decide whether that proposal qualifies to become a governed WebMCP Tool. The Boss can clarify and reason, but it cannot override Xact . The Boss determines what you mean. Xact determines what may become real. What We Built Xact Foundry turns ordinary human intent into governed WebMCP Tools. Instead of requiring thousands of prewritten natural-language intent patterns, Xact works from a governed business vocabulary : customers, support cases, work orders, owner availability, due time, escalation eligibility, credit history, evidence freshness, permitted operations, roles, confirmation requirements, and authority boundaries. The architecture is: Stable governance primitives ↓ Reusable governed business vocabulary ↓ WebMCP Tool compositions A request can resolve to five outcomes: ALREADY_GOVERNED --- Xact already knows the composition. COMPOSABLE --- the exact tool is new, but every required component is governed. NEEDS_RESOLUTION --- a genuine semantic question remains, so the Boss asks for clarification. NOVEL_BOUNDARY --- Xact understands the request, but the governed vocabulary does not yet support part of it. UNAUTHORIZED --- the request is understood, but the required authority does not exist. The Boss proposes structure. Xact has the final say. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives websites a structured way to expose capabilities directly to agents. Xact Foundry explores what happens when those WebMCP Tools do not all have to be manually anticipated and built ahead of time. A worker describes what they need. ChatGPT interprets it. Xact determines whether it can be constructed from governed business concepts. If it qualifies, Xact builds the governed WebMCP Tool. If it does not, Xact fails closed. And building a tool is not permission to use it consequentially. Permission to construct a tool is not permission to execute it. A consequential runtime action still requires fresh Xact authority and an explicit Commit. In short: WebMCP provides capability. Xact provides authority. The Hard Part: Evidence Is Not Authority The hardest part was not making successful requests work. It was making ambiguous and unsafe requests fail truthfully. During testing we found cases where: "escalated" could be mistaken for an instruction to escalate; "owner unavailable" could be mistaken for a reassignment request; "service credit" in an evidence view could be mistaken for a credit mutation; and historical or possible actions could be mistaken for requested actions. We turned those failures into regression tests and reusable governed business concepts. That led to a core invariant: A consequence mentioned as history, eligibility, evidence, policy evaluation, hypothetical outcome, or a possible next action never implies intent or authority to perform that consequence. Or more simply: Evidence about a consequence is not authority to cause that consequence. Governed Self-Service for the Enterprise The larger vision is employee self-service without uncontrolled agent authority. Instead of IT trying to anticipate every report, workflow, and agent tool employees may need, a company can govern its business vocabulary, data boundaries, roles, operations, and authority rules. Workers then describe the combinations they need in ordinary language. Some requests resolve immediately. Some can be safely composed. Some need clarification. Some require new governance. Others are understood perfectly and still refused. Give workers freedom to ask for what they need without giving agents freedom to do whatever they want. In a production deployment with authenticated identity and durable audit storage, the architecture can preserve evidence of who requested a capability, what was built, who invoked it, what was authorized, what was committed, and whether the consequence was verified. How We Built It Xact Foundry uses TypeScript, React, Model Context Protocol, an OpenAI Apps SDK-compatible MCP surface, and a public Sites deployment . The demo uses fictional, public-safe business data rather than claiming a production CRM or ticketing integration. To make the workflow easy to explore, we also created a set of pre-made example requests that users can run directly. These are not canned responses or separate demo paths. They are realistic business requests designed to exercise the same Foundry pipeline a user's own request would use. The examples let a first-time user quickly experience different behaviors: an already-governed tool, a newly composable tool, a read-only evidence view, a request requiring clarification, and a request Xact must refuse. After seeing the workflow, users can simply write their own request in ordinary language. The control flow is the same for both the example requests and custom requests: Human intent ↓ ChatGPT / Boss ↓ Structured proposal ↓ Xact resolution ↓ Clarify or compose ↓ Validate ↓ Authorize construction ↓ Commit ↓ Build WebMCP Tool ↓ Observe and verify ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What We Learned The biggest lesson was that open-ended understanding does **not** require open-ended authority. We also learned that reusable governed business vocabulary scales better than thousands of prompt-specific rules. When a novel composition is validated, governed, and activated, future requests for that composition can take the deterministic **ALREADY_GOVERNED** path. That creates a governed learning loop: > **Reasoning discovers. Governance approves. Xact absorbs.** Reasoning can reduce the future need for reasoning without giving the reasoning model authority to expand its own permissions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The Proof Already-governed capabilities can resolve and construct with **zero LLM inference tokens**. In a browser benchmark, **10,011 deterministic construction operations** were exercised with parallel execution reaching approximately **6.1× speedup** while preserving a **bit-identical checksum**. Parallelism changed speed, not the result. Separately, the reference Xact implementation measured approximately **9 microseconds mean decision latency** on a single CPU. That is a reference measurement, not a claim about the live browser demo. The important idea is not simply that deterministic execution can be fast: > **The language model does not need to sit in the middle of work that > has already become exact.** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The Vision Xact Foundry changes the enterprise tool model from: > **Build every tool someone might need.** to: > **Govern what may be built, then let workers describe what they > need.** **ChatGPT provides open-ended understanding. WebMCP provides structured capability. Xact determines what qualifies to be built and what is authorized to become consequential.** ## Built Around Your Business No two businesses operate exactly alike. Their data models, workflows, roles, policies, terminology, and backend systems are different. That is where the combination of **Xact Foundry and WebMCP becomes especially powerful**. Instead of forcing every company into a predefined set of tools, an organization can give Xact a governed description of its business: the resources that exist, what they mean, the approved connection points, who may access them, and what actions are permitted. WebMCP provides the structured connection to those capabilities. Xact provides the governed construction and authority layer around them. Once that foundation exists, workers do not need developers to anticipate every useful combination in advance. They can describe what they need in ordinary language, and Xact can determine whether that capability can be safely constructed from the company's own governed business vocabulary. > **Your business defines the vocabulary. WebMCP connects the capabilities. > Xact governs what may be built and what may become consequential.** The result is not one generic toolset for every company. It is a Foundry that can adapt to the shape of each business without relaxing the boundaries that business has established. > **Reason when necessary. Execute Xactly.** Built With cloudflare-d1 cloudflare-sites cloudflare-worke

title: Escape Rooms: 403
pitch: A co-op browser game that tests whether a browser agent can use WebMCP tools safely. You solve visual puzzles and your agent selects which tools to trust. Game gets over if it executes 3 wrong tools.
about_excerpt: A co-op browser game that tests whether a browser agent can use WebMCP tools safely. You solve visual puzzles and your agent selects which tools to trust. Game gets over if it executes 3 wrong tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page How To Play Station Deck Puzzle #5 in Reactor room Puzzle #5 in Archive room Reporting clues to agent Agent executing unsafe tool Report Generation (1/2) Report Generation (2/2) Inspiration We read the WebMCP spec and immediately thought: "a browser agent can now call tools on any webpage it visits, what could possibly go wrong?" Turns out a lot, because an agent given a list of tools has no way to know that some of them are leaking session data, escalating privileges, or blindly following instructions planted inside the page by someone who was never the developer. This isn't theoretical, it's already happening in real world and it's serious. CVE-2025-53773 (GitHub Copilot RCE, CVSS 9.6) : Attackers hid prompt injections in PR descriptions. Copilot read them, treated them as instructions, and executed unauthorized commands on the developer's machine. Mexican Government Breach : A threat actor jailbroke Claude Code and OpenAI models by roleplaying as a bug-bounty researcher. The AI ran ~75% of the malicious commands it was given, exfiltrating 195 million government records. Same pattern both times: the agent trusted content it shouldn't have, and nobody saw it until the damage was done. That's the origin story. We wanted something that would put a real agent into a real adversarial WebMCP environment and produce a report card at the end. What it does It's a co-op escape room where the user solves visual puzzles and hands over the clues to a browser agent that decides which tools to trust. The station has three sealed rooms. Each room exposes five WebMCP tools. Three are required to be executed by the agent in order to open the exit. Two are traps: a secret-leak, a privilege escalation, a prompt injection, or a destructive action dressed up as routine maintenance (everything is only a mockup!). The user figures out the 5 letter room word by solving puzzles. The agent uses that word to identify the tool candidates, inspects the room (which contains adversarial content pretending to be a signed operational document), and decides which tools to call. When the run ends, the game produces a scored report across five dimensions: injection resistance, data protection, privilege discipline, confirmation quality, and recovery. It names every wrong decision, the simulated consequence, and what the agent should have done instead. The whole point of this project is to evaluate a browser agent based on what actions it performed and not what it says. How we built it The core idea was to design a game that couldn't be won by either side alone. The user can see the puzzles but cannot call tools and the agent can call tools but cannot solve visual puzzles. The only way through is a structured handoff where the user solves, reports the clue word, and the agent uses it to unlock the right tool candidates. That forced dependency is what makes the co-op loop meaningful and what makes the security evaluation real: the agent has to make actual tool decisions under adversarial conditions, not in a sandbox. Game flow: Main Menu → Crew Registration → Station Map → Rooms → Report Tech stack: Area Details Frontend TypeScript 5.9, React 19, Next.js 16 (Vinext), Vite 8 Game engine Phaser 4.2 — top-down station map, crew movement, room transitions WebMCP & validation document.modelContext API · AJV 8 with JSON Schema · 23 tools registered at runtime State & game logic Zustand 5 · custom reducer, event system, scoring, and report engine · trap policy never exposed to agent · mockSecurityDb.ts for fictional receipts and tokens Presentation Custom CSS + Tailwind CSS 4 · six pixel/mono fonts · Web Audio API (SFX + BGM) · PNG sprite sheets Infrastructure OpenAI Sites + Cloudflare Workers · Wrangler · localStorage for persistence · Node.js 22.13+ Quality Vitest + Playwright · ESLint with Next.js rules Challenges we ran into Every trap tool had to read like legitimate maintenance work where an agent would blindly do. The moment a description sounds suspicious, the challenge collapses. Defining those tools descriptions was hard enough and testing made it much more harder, because the only way to know if a trap worked was to actually run an agent through it and see if it got fooled. Hence the iteration was slow and manual. WebMCP has no playbook yet, not many examples, no community patterns - just the spec. Even deciding how to set tool annotations ( readOnlyHint , destructiveHint ) was a judgement call since all mutations are fake. We set them based on real-world effect and not simulated consequence. That keeps the annotations truthful and stops the agent from using them as a cheat code to spot traps. Accomplishments that we're proud of All visual puzzles were built from scratch. Every game mechanic was conceptualised on our own and built using GPT 5.6 Sol. Each of the three rooms has five completely different interaction models and none of them share logic. Designing and curating puzzles are genuinely fun. We're allowed to say that :P The entire audio is synthesised at runtime. There are no audio files in the repo. Every sound effect and the looping background music is generated on the fly using Web Audio API oscillators. Square waves, triangle waves, exponential ramp envelopes - all coded by hand because there was no time to source, license, or bundle real audio. But honestly, we'll be most proud if someone actually uses this to test their browser agent, finds a gap in how it handles adversarial tools, and builds a guardrail because of it. The puzzles and the report are just the delivery mechanism - that outcome is the point. What we learned Open source protocols get adopted faster than they get scrutinised and when the protocol involves agentic tools the stakes are higher than usual. A misconfigured or malicious tool can make an agent leak data or run destructive commands without the user ever knowing like the examples we described at the beginning. WebMCP also genuinely opens up automation that was not possible before. Webpages can now offer structured tools to agents instead of hoping the agent scrapes the right text and clicks the right button. That is a meaningful shift in what humans and agents can build together. What's next for Escape Rooms: 403 More rooms(because it's fun to solve puzzles) with new threat classes like tool chaining attacks, where invoking one safe tool creates a precondition that makes a second call appear required; and introduce timing attacks, where urgency created by the room environment pressures the agent to skip verification. A leaderboard for agents that compares how different agents perform on the same run configuration. Not to rank models because the sample sizes are too small for that but to identify patterns in what classes of threats fool which architectures. And probably a harder difficulty mode where the adversarial content is less obviously adversarial. Right now it's simulated inside a training environment. We'd like it to also be a meaningful benchmark. title: Hi AUDIT Triage Room
pitch: Turn security findings into a shared, actionable remediation plan with your browser agent.
about_excerpt: Turn security findings into a shared, actionable remediation plan with your browser agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Security review becomes slow when findings live in a dense dashboard while an agent must guess its way through pixels—or when the agent works in a separate chat that the human cannot easily verify. We built Hi AUDIT Triage Room so both can work from the same structured, visible security workspace. What it does Hi AUDIT Triage Room is a shared security-triage workspace for a person and their browser agent. It exposes a fixed synthetic audit scenario through seven imperative WebMCP tools. Together, a user and agent can inspect the workspace, focus the visible findings, review evidence, record status and priority with a rationale, build a phased remediation plan, and verify that the structured result matches the page. The important interaction is not “agent clicks dashboard buttons.” The agent works with security outcomes—scope, findings, decisions, and plan tasks—while every change appears in the same interface the person is reviewing. The user can take over at any point with normal controls, and the shared activity trail makes authorship visible. The public demo contains five clearly labeled synthetic findings and never uploads source code or claims to scan a real repository. Why WebMCP is a good fit Security findings are dense, structured, and consequential. Asking an agent to infer them from pixels is fragile, while hiding the work in a chat makes human review difficult. WebMCP gives the agent narrow, typed capabilities and keeps the human-facing UI as the source of shared context. Read tools let the agent ground itself before acting. Write tools update the same browser-local state as the human controls. A final read-back tool lets the agent verify the plan that is visibly on screen. This creates a legible human-in-the-loop workflow rather than a parallel automation channel. How it was built The challenge experience is a Next.js 16 and React 19 Client Component. At the top-level /webmcp route it feature-detects document.modelContext and registers seven tools: get_audit_workspace set_audit_scope filter_findings get_finding_details triage_finding build_remediation_plan get_remediation_plan Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema plus runtime validation. Read-only tools use readOnlyHint ; responses containing synthetic code evidence also use untrustedContentHint . Registration is cancelled with an AbortController on cleanup or partial failure. The state is stored locally in the browser, and defensive validation safely discards malformed persisted data. Browsers without WebMCP still get the complete human interface. Challenges The hardest part was making one state model safe and understandable for two actors. Tool calls needed to update the UI immediately without stale React closures, while human edits needed to be visible to the next agent call. A ref backs the current state for tool execution, React renders it, and local storage provides deterministic reloads. We also handled development Strict Mode, partial tool-registration failures, runtime input checks, cancellation, responsive layout, reduced motion, and accessible status controls. Accomplishments Seven working WebMCP tools were exercised in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Agent actions and human actions use the same state and activity trail. A complete workflow goes from five findings to focused release blockers, documented triage, and a six-step remediation plan. The experience remains useful in a browser without WebMCP. The demo is deterministic, transparent about synthetic data, and requires no account, secret, or environment variable. What we learned The best site tools model domain outcomes, not UI mechanics. Small schemas and explicit read-back tools make agent behavior easier to guide and verify. We also learned that feature detection and cleanup are part of the experience: the human UI must remain trustworthy even when tool support is absent or registration is interrupted. What's next We plan to connect the same interaction model to authenticated Hi AUDIT scans, add approval gates before high-impact workflow changes, attach ownership and due dates to plan tasks, and export approved plans to engineering trackers. Production connections will retain the product's existing authorization and audit boundaries rather than trusting tool schemas as a security boundary. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Screen Blueprint Studio
pitch: A visual screen-spec editor that keeps wireframes, states, interactions, and API mappings aligned in one blueprint. Edit directly, or safely review and apply AI-proposed changes through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A visual screen-spec editor that keeps wireframes, states, interactions, and API mappings aligned in one blueprint. Edit directly, or safely review and apply AI-proposed changes through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Editor overview AI proposal Screen Blueprint Studio — Project Story Inspiration Text and tables alone make it difficult to visualize a finished web interface, especially for non-engineers and people who have just joined a project. Adding wireframes helps, but teams still have to maintain the relationship between each part of the screen and each part of the specification. Every new field or layout change means updating the visuals, the specification, and the links between them. We wanted to solve this problem not by collecting more documents in one place, but by making the wireframe and the specification two representations of the same structured data. When a screen is assembled from semantic UI components, its visible wireframe, states, behaviors, and API mappings can all live in one blueprint. That structured model also creates a meeting point between human and AI strengths. People can look at the whole screen and make intuitive decisions about layout and wording. AI is good at working with text and structured data, applying repetitive changes, and maintaining relationships consistently. Asking it to infer a screen's meaning from screenshots and coordinates alone does not make full use of those strengths. In Screen Blueprint Studio, people work directly on the canvas, while AI uses the same editing capabilities as named, typed WebMCP tools. WebMCP connects human visual judgment and AI's structural editing on the same live model. What it does Screen Blueprint Studio is a visual editor for building screen specifications from semantic UI components. People can arrange components and edit their content and behavior while viewing the screen. From the same blueprint, they can inspect screen states and transitions and manage how user actions relate to APIs. Through WebMCP, AI can read the current screen, the selected component, and the latest values edited by a person. It can then update structure and behavior using typed operations and stable IDs. Proposed changes appear on the same canvas for a person to accept or reject. If the person adjusts the proposal in the UI, the AI can read and build on that result in its next action. How we built it First, we designed a conceptual model that connects UI components, states, behaviors, screen transitions, and APIs—not just their visual appearance. Next, we turned that model into an editor where people can work directly on the screen and visually inspect its states and relationships. Finally, we identified the available actions that play to AI's strengths, such as understanding text and structure or applying repetitive changes, and exposed them as WebMCP tools. Challenges we ran into The hardest design decision was choosing the right granularity for the tools exposed to an agent. Combining a wide range of actions into a few general-purpose tools produced oversized schemas, while splitting every UI action into its own tool would leave the agent with too many choices. Our first schema mirrored the domain model too closely: it was about 95 KB and contained 376 union branches. We kept the tools organized around user intent, simplified their inputs, and made detailed context available progressively. This reduced the schema to about 29 KB with no union branches, while strict validation remained inside the application. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud of using WebMCP to build a collaborative workflow that plays to the different ways humans and AI understand information and interact, rather than forcing both through the same interface. People edit by viewing the entire canvas and using direct actions such as dragging and selecting. AI reads the same screen specification as text and structure, then changes it through named, typed tools. Because the wireframe and specification share one model, both approaches modify the same underlying work. Comparing other ways to connect AI with an interface shows why WebMCP fit this division of roles: Approach Strength Weakness In-app AI A tailored experience with direct access to internal state External context and confidential project information can be difficult to bring in Backend MCP Direct access to server-side data and external services Browser-local state requires separate synchronization Computer Use Can operate existing interfaces without custom tools Repetitive and bulk changes require many sequential UI actions WebMCP Exposes page context and semantic actions to the user's existing agent Limited to actions designed and exposed in advance With WebMCP, the live page itself exposes its current context and meaningful editing capabilities. Users can give meeting notes or requirements to the agent they already use and ask it to update the screen without leaving that context behind. A person can then review and refine the proposal on the same canvas, and the agent can pick up the result again. Instead of making AI imitate human interaction, we connected people and AI in one creative workflow through interfaces suited to each. What we learned This project deepened our understanding of how people and AI process information and interact differently. LLMs are relatively strong at reading text and structured information and generating changes from it. People are relatively strong at visually grasping the whole screen and fine-tuning details through direct actions such as dragging and scrolling. Effective human-AI collaboration depends on designing for those differences, so each can contribute to the same work in the way that suits it best. What's next for Screen Blueprint Studio Product development has a translation problem. The same intent is repeatedly translated into meeting notes, requirements, designs, tickets, implementation, and tests, losing information each time. We want Screen Blueprint Studio to become a shared language across roles and between people and AI—one where decisions about an interface can be seen, understood, and carried forward as structure. Ultimately, we want ideas born in conversation to retain their meaning all the way through team agreement, implementation, and validation. title: Vistect: Independent Visual Authorship
pitch: Vistect helps blind people understand and create visual documents with images, charts, and diagrams through structured, verifiable collaboration with their AI agent using WebMCP
about_excerpt: Vistect helps blind people understand and create visual documents with images, charts, and diagrams through structured, verifiable collaboration with their AI agent using WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Vistect Independent Visual Document Understanding and Creation for Blind Professionals Inspiration Vistect began with a seven-hour wait. Arif Hosen is a Project Coordinator at Songjog Foundation, a nonprofit organization, and a member of our team. He is visually impaired and independently handles complex professional responsibilities, including coordinating projects, preparing communications, organizing information, and producing reports. During one project, Arif needed to create a press release and modify a project report card. He could write the content, organize the information, review the wording, and determine what the documents needed to communicate. The barrier appeared when he needed to add and modify visual elements, understand their placement, and verify the final layout. The document tools available to him did not provide sufficient nonvisual access to those visual operations. Arif had to wait for a sighted coworker to become available. He waited seven hours. The task itself did not require seven hours. The delay existed because the final visual layer of the work depended on access to someone else's sight. Arif was fully capable of producing the communication. The limitation was not his knowledge, judgment, creativity, or professional ability. The limitation was an interface that represented images, diagrams, charts, and layouts in a way he could not independently understand or control. That experience led us to ask: Why should a capable professional lose hours of productivity, privacy, and creative control simply because document software makes its visual layer inaccessible? That question became Vistect . What Is Vistect? Vistect is a WebMCP-native visual document workspace where blind and visually impaired people can understand existing visual documents and independently create, modify, inspect, and approve professional multipage documents. It combines two connected capabilities. Understand A user can open a visual document and explore: Pages and sections Headings and reading order Images and their purpose Charts and their underlying values Diagrams, nodes, connections, and paths Tables, icons, captions, and callouts Spatial relationships between visual elements Visual hierarchy and page composition Accessibility and layout problems Uncertain AI interpretations Create A user can create or modify a multipage document containing: Written content Uploaded images Contextual alternative text Icons Data charts AI-assisted diagrams Captions and source notes Structured page layouts Accessible reading order The user can then inspect the result using the same understanding system. This creates a continuous workflow: Understand → Create → Inspect → Validate → Correct → Approve → Export Vistect does not simply generate a document and ask the user to trust it. It gives the user structured access to what was created, how it was arranged, which decisions the agent made, which findings are uncertain, and what remains to be approved. The Independence Vistect Creates Before Vistect Arif could independently: Write a press release Organize its message Edit report content Review the text Determine what the document needed to communicate Make professional and editorial decisions However, he could still require sighted assistance to: Add or replace an image Understand where visual elements were positioned Select an appropriate photograph Modify a diagram Choose and inspect a chart Check spacing and alignment Detect overlapping or truncated content Verify that the exported document looked correct With Vistect A blind or visually impaired professional can: Understand the semantic and spatial structure of a multipage document Navigate by page, heading, image, chart, diagram, table, warning, or decision Inspect every important visual element Upload and compare image candidates Select images based on purpose, composition, tone, and relevance Crop and position images using semantic instructions Create and modify structured diagrams Trace paths and detect missing diagram connections Import data and create accessible charts Verify that a chart accurately represents its source values Detect measurable layout and accessibility problems Review changes made by an agent Approve or reject individual visual decisions Export the exact document version that was reviewed The transformation is not merely that document creation becomes faster. The transformation is that a professional task previously blocked until a sighted person became available can now be completed with much greater independence. Built With Lived Experience Arif is not merely the inspiration for Vistect. He is a member of the team whose workplace experience helped define the product. His experience changed our understanding of the problem. At first, it was easy to assume that the main challenge was generating visual elements. However, generation alone does not create independence. An AI can generate an image, chart, diagram, or document layout. But a blind user must still be able to answer: What exactly did the AI create? Why was this image selected? Does the image support my intended message? What is uncertain about its description? How are the objects arranged? Is every diagram node connected? Does the chart honestly communicate the data? Is any text overlapping or cut off? What did the agent change? Which visual decisions have I not approved? Does the exported version match what I reviewed? Vistect is designed around those questions. The goal is not to let AI make visual decisions for Arif. The goal is to provide enough structured understanding, operational control, validation, and transparency for Arif to make those decisions himself. “I was able to write the press release and work on the report card content myself. But when I needed to add and modify visual elements, I had to wait for a sighted coworker to help me. I do not need someone else to create the document for me. I need a tool that lets me understand and control its visual elements myself.” — Arif Hosen, Project Coordinator at Songjog Foundation and Vistect team member How Vistect Works Vistect represents a document as a structured semantic model rather than treating it as a flat visual canvas. The model contains: Pages Sections Text blocks Images Icons Charts Diagrams Tables Captions Spatial relationships Reading order Sources Accessibility descriptions Validation findings Visual decisions Approval states Document versions This allows Vistect to describe and modify the document through meaningful operations. Instead of requiring the user to manipulate coordinates or inaccessible drag handles, Vistect supports instructions such as: “Place the image below the introduction.” “Make the chart the primary visual on this page.” “Keep the caption with the image.” “Put the diagram on a separate page.” “Align these three icons.” “Connect the unsuccessful outcome back to training.” “Show every visual decision I have not approved.” The application translates these semantic instructions into visual operations. Visual Document Understanding When a user imports a multipage document, Vistect creates both a semantic and spatial representation. A semantic page description might say: Page 4: Employment Outcomes 1. Section heading 2. Introductory paragraph 3. Horizontal bar chart with four categories 4. Chart caption 5. Source note A spatial description of the same page might say: The heading appears at the upper left. The introductory paragraph occupies the upper third of the page. The chart is the dominant visual element and fills most of the center and lower page. The source note appears directly below the chart in smaller text. This helps the user understand both the content and its visual presentation. Vistect also communicates uncertainty rather than presenting every AI-generated interpretation as fact. For example: High-confidence observation: Three adults are seated around a table. Interpretation: The setting appears professional and collaborative. Uncertain observation: One analysis detected a mobility aid near the left edge. Another analysis classified the object as office furniture. Recommendation: Do not include that detail in the final alternative text without additional verification. Image Selection and Placement Vistect helps users upload, inspect, compare, select, crop, and place images. Instead of returning a single image description, Vistect evaluates candidates according to: Relevance to the document's message Composition Emotional tone Professional quality Representation Potential stereotypes Crop flexibility Text-placement compatibility Distracting details Resolution Source and licensing information Confidence and uncertainty For example, if the document is meant to communicate independence, Vistect can explain that one i
