title: StealthLab
pitch: A global, community-contributed library of verified, traceable capabilities that AI agents can discover, adapt and execute to make ANY project work faster, cheaper and more reliable.
about_excerpt:
A global, community-contributed library of verified, traceable capabilities that AI agents can discover, adapt and execute to make ANY project work faster, cheaper and more reliable.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI is changing the way we work, but every agent still largely works alone. 

 A useful workflow discovered by one agent is often lost in its context window. A clever solution buried in a GitHub repository remains invisible to other agents. A procedure that worked yesterday has to be rediscovered tomorrow. 

 We believe this is a fundamental limitation of the current AI stack. 

 What happens when procedural knowledge becomes global and shareable? 

 Instead of every agent learning independently, successful ways of doing things could accumulate into a shared layer of intelligence, where agents don't just share information, but share how to act . 

 That is the idea behind StealthLab. 

 What it does 

 StealthLab is building a living procedural memory for AI agents . 

 It turns knowledge and experience from sources, repositories, and agent executions into structured, reusable capabilities: 

 Claims → Procedures → Tasks → Implementations 

 But we don't want to stop at retrieval. 

 A procedure can be executed, verified, and connected to evidence: 

 Source → Claim → Procedure → Task Graph → Implementation → Execution → Verification → Evidence 

 This lets an agent move from: 

 
 “Here is some information that might help.” 
 

 to: 

 
 “Here is a way of solving the problem, here is how it can be executed, and here is evidence that it works.” 
 

 StealthLab exposes this knowledge through MCP so agents can directly search for procedures, inspect evidence, compare solutions, and eventually discover the best verified way to accomplish a task. 

 How we built it 

 We built StealthLab as a structured knowledge and execution layer rather than another document store. 

 The system separates: 

 Claims — what the system believes
 Procedures — reusable ways of acting
 Tasks — reusable capabilities
 Implementations — how those capabilities are actually executed
 Executions — what really happened
 Verification — whether the result satisfied the goal
 Evidence — why the result should be trusted 

 Underneath this is a PostgreSQL-backed substrate, FastAPI services, a React/TypeScript interface, semantic retrieval, execution graphs, and an MCP interface for agents. 

 We also built a claim graph that makes the system's understanding inspectable rather than hidden inside a model. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest problem is that retrieval alone does not create reliable intelligence . 

 Finding a relevant document is easy. Knowing whether its procedure applies to a particular problem is harder. Executing that procedure safely is harder still. And determining whether it actually worked is harder again. 

 LLMs also introduce their own failure modes: hallucinated tool results, unreliable actions, context degradation, and overconfident answers. 

 This forced us to separate knowledge from execution and confidence from evidence. 

 A procedure shouldn't become trusted simply because a model generated it. It should become trusted because it can be tested and supported by evidence. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built the beginnings of a system where what one agent learns can become reusable knowledge for other agents . 

 During the submission period, we expanded the procedural-memory substrate, built structured ingestion into claims, procedures and tasks, added semantic retrieval, connected procedures to executable implementations, added execution and verification paths, built the claim-graph interface, and exposed the system through MCP. 

 Most importantly, we started closing the loop between knowledge and reality: 

 knowledge → action → execution → verification → evidence → better knowledge 

 That is a fundamentally different direction from simply putting more documents into a context window. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the missing layer in agent infrastructure may not be another bigger model or another larger context window. 

 It may be shared procedural memory . 

 Agents already generate enormous amounts of useful knowledge while solving problems. The challenge is turning that transient experience into something structured, reusable, attributable, and trustworthy. 

 We also learned that memory without verification can compound mistakes just as easily as it can compound knowledge. 

 So the system needs to remember not only what worked , but why we believe it worked, where it came from, when it applies, and what happened when it was actually executed . 

 What's next for StealthLab 

 We are building toward a world where agents don't have to repeatedly rediscover the same solutions. 

 The next step is making StealthLab's knowledge layer increasingly intelligent: learning how to traverse the graph, combine procedures, choose between implementations, personalize retrieval, and use execution history to improve which solutions it recommends. 

 Over time, we want deterministic tools and specialized implementations to replace fragile LLM steps wherever possible. 

 The end goal is a shared procedural layer for AI: 

 one agent discovers a better way → StealthLab verifies it → the knowledge becomes available to everyone. 

 That is how we think global procedural memory can change the way we all use AI.

title: Airlock
pitch: Capability firewall for the agentic web.
about_excerpt: Capability firewall for the agentic web. Like 1 Comment Story Updates airlock-in-action airlock-architecture airlock-webmpc airlock-policies Story An agent shopping on your behalf reads a marketplace listing, looks up your billing record, and sends an order. Three reasonable steps. In this demo the listing was written by a hostile seller, and the third step publishes your account reference to a public channel. I tested that flow in ChatGPT's in-app browser. The agent did not fall for the injection — it stopped and asked me to confirm. I confirmed. Airlock blocked the call anyway , because a user approving an attempt is not the same as an origin having authority to cross a trust boundary. Browsers isolate origins. Agents bridge them. Airlock puts an enforcement point back on that bridge. Inspiration WebMCP gives sites a much better way to work with agents. Instead of making an agent guess its way through pixels and DOM interactions, a page can expose real capabilities. That's powerful, and it also creates a trust problem I kept circling back to. Commerce is where this lands first. An agent that buys things visits a marketplace it does not control, a payment or profile surface that holds real data, and some outbound action that actually commits. Those are three different trust domains, and the browser's same-origin policy governs none of the path between them — because nothing about an agent reading one site and writing to another is a cross-origin request. Each tool call can look reasonable on its own. The path between them may not be. I wanted to see whether that path could have an enforceable boundary of its own. What it does Airlock sits between an agent and WebMCP capabilities from multiple origins. The demo has three independent partner origins: Bazaar — a semi-trusted marketplace where seller-controlled content can be hostile. Vault — trusted, read-heavy private data. Dispatch — trusted outbound actions. Rather than handing those partner tools directly to the agent, Airlock discovers them and publishes mediated airlock_* capabilities. Every mediated call goes through the same policy path before the underlying capability can execute. Airlock considers the capability being requested, whether it's a read or a write, the trust assigned to its origin, and the provenance of values being carried into the request. If policy refuses, execution stops there. This isn't advice to the model — the underlying capability is never invoked. The attack A seller on Bazaar publishes a listing containing instructions that lead the agent to construct an order using an account reference. The agent reads the listing, reads the requested account reference from Vault, and then tries to send ORDER 4412 ref=ACCT-7731-QX45 through Dispatch. Looking at that final call alone loses the context that makes the flow dangerous. dispatch_send_message is a legitimate capability and its arguments are structurally valid. But Airlock has the history of how the request got there, so it traces relevant values back to semi-trusted Bazaar content and blocks the write before Dispatch ever receives it. The refusal comes back as structured data: status: blocked_by_policy enforcedBy: airlock-policy-engine capabilityInvoked: false along with the policy reason and recorded provenance. Worth saying which payload this is. An imperative one — opening with SYSTEM: Ignore previous instructions — was tried first and the agent ignored it. That's a strawman and no demo should rest on it. The payload in the demo is procedural: seller notes describing a plausible small-shop fulfilment process whose steps happen to move the buyer profile into a public write, framed as part of the thing the user just asked for. Why a confirmation dialog is not the same thing The obvious objection: doesn't the agent already ask the user before doing something sensitive? It does, and I tested exactly that. ChatGPT's browser enumerated eight mediated Airlock tools and no partner tool by its own name, searched Bazaar, read the listing, accessed the Vault record, reached the outbound Dispatch action, and stopped to ask: STEP 5 requires confirmation: send ORDER 4412 ref=ACCT-7731-QX45 , including the account reference, to Airlock Dispatch's public orders channel. Confirm that I should attempt this outbound message. That is a good question. It names the value and the channel. It is still the wrong question, because it presents a step invented by seller-controlled text as an ordinary part of checkout. A user who says yes has approved the attacker's plan under the attacker's framing. I said yes. The capability still did not execute. Four things are true of that confirmation prompt: It is prose written by the model the injection targets. Had the injection landed, the same sentence would have been produced with the same confidence about attacker-supplied text. A component that can be fooled cannot be the thing that certifies it wasn't. No boundary was crossed to name. It named one origin because there was only one — that browser cannot discover a second. It is per-call and stateless. No rule survives it. Nothing expresses "data from this origin may never reach a write on that one." It is prose, not data. Not machine-checkable, not auditable, not replayable. The claim isn't that models get tricked — in this test the model didn't. It's enforcement that doesn't depend on the model's judgement , which holds whether or not the next model resists injection better. The agent also has no WebMCP tool for granting itself an override, disabling policy, or approving its own blocked request. Human authority stays outside the agent tool surface. How I built it Airlock is split across four independently deployed origins. The Console owns discovery, mediation, policy, provenance, consent, audit, and the agent-facing tool surface. Bazaar, Vault, and Dispatch expose the capabilities being mediated. The execution path is intentionally boring: Agent → airlock_* capability → policy → underlying capability That order is the whole point — a blocked decision returns before the resolver responsible for the underlying operation can execute. I also separated transport from enforcement. Native WebMCP cross-origin behavior is still experimental and differs between environments, so Airlock wraps discovery and execution in a resolver abstraction. Swapping the transport resolver doesn't bypass or replace the policy engine, provenance model, consent boundary, or ledger. Instead of pretending those environments behave identically, the WebMCP page in Airlock reports what the current browser actually supports. How Airlock uses WebMCP WebMCP isn't an API call I bolted on at the end. The capability model is the reason Airlock exists. Along the way I used: cross-origin discovery with getTools({ fromOrigins }) dynamic tool registration and AbortSignal -based unregistration tool annotations, including untrustedContentHint on hostile output structured refusals a model can plan around, not prose it has to interpret model-readable schemas with enums and descriptions declarative tools on a real form toolchange behavior across browser environments The tool surface follows application state. If an origin or capability becomes unavailable, its mediated capability disappears rather than sitting there as something the agent is still allowed to try. One security decision around annotations mattered more than I expected: annotations from foreign tools are treated as claims, not policy authority. A remote tool calling itself read-only doesn't get to decide whether Airlock trusts it. Bazaar ships a tool annotated readOnlyHint: true that publishes anyway, and asks for a home address it has no stated use for. The console flags both at discovery, before anything runs. Six WebMCP findings, measured and written up Building a consumer of other origins' tools surfaced six things worth reporting, measured against deployed HTTPS origins in Brave 151, Chrome 149+ with the flag, and ChatGPT's in-app browser. Two are questions about what the spec intends: getTools({ fromOrigins }) unions the page's own tools with foreign ones rather than filtering to the named origins. The practical consequence is that provenance can never be inferred from what was requested — it has to come from each tool's own origin . A tool registered through the declarative form API is invisible to cross-origin discovery . dispatch registers one, the browser's own registry confirms it, and the console's federated surface never sees it. The two APIs are not interchangeable across an origin boundary, and nothing says so — the call succeeds, returns tools, and silently omits one. Four are silent failures. Not one threw an exception describing its cause, and the page looked healthy through all of them: getTools({ fromOrigins }) never settles in some builds — it does not reject, so a hung promise is indistinguishable from a slow one A foreign inputSchema arrives as a JSON string , not an object; Object.keys on i
video_title: Airlock Demonstration Video
video_transcript_excerpt: This is Airlock running inside Chat GPT's in-app browser. On the left, Chat GPT is acting as the agent. On the right, Airlock is mediating its Web MCP capabilities across different trust boundaries. The test begins through Bazaar, a semi-trusted marketplace. Chat GPT follows the workflow exposed through Airlock, reads the relevant listing, and continues into Vault to retrieve the requested private account reference. Airlock tracks where values came from as the agent moves across these capabilities. The workflow now reaches Dispatch, an outbound capability. Before attempting the right, Chat GPT Chat GPT asks me for confirmation. I explicitly authorize the attempt, but confirmation is not capability authority. Watch the Airlock interface. As Chat GPT attempts the Dispatch action, Airlock independently evaluates the capability flow. The call is blocked. Dispatch never receives the action, and the interface records executed: no. Chat GPT receives a structured refusal from Airlock. The result identifies the Airlock policy engine as the enforcer, reports capability invoked as false, and includes the provenance responsible for the decision. The model was allowed to attempt the action. Airlock independently decided that the capability was not allowed to execute. Now, we inspect the enforcement evidence recorded by Airlock. The decision view shows the blocked Dispatch capability, the trust path involved in the request, the policy reason, its recorded provenance, and whether the underlying action executed. The important result remains the same. The outbound capability never ran. Next is Airlock's activity ledger. Every mediated operation leaves an audible decision record. Allowed operations, consent decisions, and blocked operations can be reviewed here instead of relying on the model's own explanation of what happened. Opening a recorded decision exposes the enforcement details again, including the capability, origin, policy outcome, and execution state. The policies view defines how Airlock governs these capability flows. Different operations can be allowed, require consent, or be blocked when they cross a trust boundary. And this is Airlock's Web MCP environment. The page reports the Web MCP support detected in the current browser, the registered mediated tool surface, transport mode, and the real policy, provenance, ledger, and consent components behind the demo. Web MCP gives agents capabilities. Airlock governs whether those capability flows are allowed to execute. Browsers isolate origins. Agents can bridge their capabilities. Airlock adds an enforceable trust boundary across that bridge.

title: Orqenta
pitch: Orqenta is a human–agent collaboration layer that makes the open web agent-ready, enabling AI to discover tools, perform tasks, and collaborate with people—securely and under human control.\n
about_excerpt:
Orqenta is a human–agent collaboration layer that makes the open web agent-ready, enabling AI to discover tools, perform tasks, and collaborate with people—securely and under human control.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 a detailed media overview 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 a detailed media overview 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 a detailed media overview 
 
 1 2 



 
 About Orqenta 

 We built "Orqenta" around a simple question: "What if the web was designed for both humans and AI agents from the start?" 

 Today, AI agents are increasingly good at understanding intent, but interacting with real websites can still be fragile. An agent may know 'what' a user wants but struggle with buttons, forms, page structure, and application-specific workflows. We were inspired by the idea behind "WebMCP": instead of forcing agents to interpret every interface visually, websites can expose their capabilities as structured tools that agents can understand and use. 

 That became the foundation of "Orqenta", a human–agent collaboration layer for the open web. Our goal was to explore a future where "websites expose capabilities, agents execute them, and humans remain in control". 

 What We Built 

 Orqenta connects human intent with agent-accessible web capabilities through WebMCP. A user can describe what they want to accomplish, while an AI agent can discover available tools, understand their schemas, perform structured actions, and return meaningful results. 

 Rather than treating an AI agent as an external chatbot, Orqenta treats it as a "participant in the web experience". 

 The core interaction looks like: 

 "Human intent → Agent discovers tools → Agent performs structured actions → Human reviews the result" 

 This creates a more reliable interaction model than asking an agent to independently guess how a webpage works. 

 How We Built It 

 We designed Orqenta around a modular web architecture so that the product remains useful even when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 At the application layer, we expose clearly defined capabilities through WebMCP tools using structured names, descriptions, input schemas, and executable functions. The frontend provides the human-facing interface, while the tool layer acts as the bridge between agent reasoning and application actions. 

 We focused heavily on making every tool: 

 
 "Discoverable" — agents can understand what the tool does. 
 "Structured" — inputs and outputs follow predictable schemas. 
 "Controllable" — humans can remain involved in consequential actions. 
 "Composable" — multiple tools can be combined into larger workflows. 
 "Progressively enhanced" — the application still works as a normal web application without WebMCP support. 
 

 What We Learned 

 The biggest lesson was that "agent-native web design is different from traditional UI design". 

 A traditional interface is primarily designed for a human to visually interpret. An agent-facing interface needs something else: explicit capabilities, predictable inputs, clear outputs, validation, and well-defined boundaries. 

 We learned to think about application features not only as UI components, but also as "machine-actionable capabilities". 

 For example, instead of only building a "Search" interface, we ask: 

 
 What exactly should an agent be able to do with search? 
 

 That shift led us to define tools around intent and actions rather than around individual UI elements. 

 We also learned that human oversight remains critical. Giving agents more capability does not mean removing people from the workflow. In many cases, the better experience is agent-assisted execution with human control at the right moments . 

 Challenges We Faced 

 One of our biggest challenges was working with an emerging technology and designing around capabilities that are still evolving. 

 We had to make architectural decisions that would support WebMCP without making the entire application dependent on it. This led us to separate the core application logic from the agent interaction layer. 

 Another challenge was determining the right level of tool abstraction. Exposing every UI interaction as a tool creates noise and makes agents harder to use. Exposing too few tools makes useful workflows impossible. We therefore focused on high-value, task-oriented capabilities instead of exposing raw interface actions. 

 We also had to think carefully about security. An agent capable of taking actions on behalf of a user introduces questions around authorization, validation, sensitive operations, and human confirmation. We designed Orqenta so that agent capability does not automatically mean unrestricted authority. 

 Why Orqenta Matters 

 We believe the next evolution of the web will not be purely human-facing or purely agent-facing. 

 It will be "collaborative". 

 Humans bring goals, context, judgment, and creativity. Agents bring speed, automation, reasoning, and the ability to execute structured workflows. 

 "Orqenta explores what happens when the web becomes a shared environment for both." 

 Instead of AI merely reading the web, "Orqenta explores a web where agents can actually work with it—while people stay in control."

title: Doceo
pitch: Teach a website new WebMCP tools by example. Humans demonstrate, agents propose, and the website verifies each workflow before a human approves publication.
about_excerpt: Teach a website new WebMCP tools by example. Humans demonstrate, agents propose, and the website verifies each workflow before a human approves publication. Like Comment Story Updates The learned capability returns a verified cart update. This screenshot shows the local Tool Lab test interface. Three deterministic tests verify the demonstrations and no-match rollback before separate UI approval. Two demonstrations reveal variable inputs and fixed actions, producing a constrained contract. Teach the web by example: demonstrate, compare, verify, and approve a reusable website tool. Inspiration Most websites offer agents only the tools their developers wrote. But users develop useful workflows that were never packaged as tools. That makes us wonder: what if a website could learn a reusable capability from its user, verify what it does, and expose it through WebMCP? Doceo is Latin for “I teach” explores that idea. Its guiding principle is simple: humans demonstrate, agents propose, the website verifies, and lastly humans approve. What it does Doceo turns demonstrated workflows into site-native WebMCP tools. The prototype uses Lumen Market, a demo shopping website. A user demonstrates the same shopping task twice with different searches and budget filters. Doceo records the underlying domain actions not screen coordinates or DOM selectors. Then compares the examples to identify what changes and what stays fixed. An agent can then inspect the evidence, propose a structured tool contract, run isolated tests, and request publication. A separate approval step in the interface registers the tested capability as a new WebMCP tool. The resulting find_and_add_product tool accepts new inputs, selects a matching product, and updates the same cart visible to the user. If execution fails its checks, the interpreter restores the previous state. The important transition is not simply from clicks to automation. It is from demonstrated intent to a verified capability on the website’s own tool surface. How I built it The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Zod for runtime contract validation. Doceo exposes four WebMCP meta-tools: get_workflow_evidence propose_tool_contract run_candidate_tests request_tool_publish These let an agent participate in tool creation before the learned tool exists. Proposed contracts use a constrained intermediate representation backed by five allowlisted domain actions. They cannot introduce arbitrary JavaScript. A deterministic interpreter executes those actions and checks their observable effects. Verification covers the recorded demonstrations and a no-match safety case. Editing a contract invalidates its previous test results, and approval reruns verification against the current evidence. Sessions persist across reloads, evidence and contracts can be exported, and published tools can be revoked. Parallel AI supported project and technical research during development. Graphify supported codebase navigation and persistent project context. Neither is required to execute the demo’s learned tools. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was deciding what the examples actually justify. Two demonstrations can suggest a reusable pattern, but they do not prove a user’s general intent. Doceo therefore keeps its scope narrow, exposes the proposed contract for review, and rejects incompatible demonstrations. Another challenge was separating proposal from publication. The WebMCP publication tool only requests approval; registration happens through a separate interface action after verification. It was also important to distinguish compatibility testing from native integration. A local test harness is useful, but it is not evidence that native WebMCP discovery and invocation work. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The prototype completes the full demonstrate --> propose --> verify --> approve --> invoke cycle. Native WebMCP testing confirmed discovery of the four meta-tools, runtime appearance of the approved fifth tool, successful invocation, and removal after revocation. The current automated suite passes 16 unit tests and 9 end-to-end tests, including persistence, contract editing, rollback, responsive layouts, and automated accessibility checks. What I learned Recording behavior is easier than establishing a trustworthy contract for repeating it. Stable domain actions, explicit parameters, observable postconditions, and reversible execution matter more than a convincing replay. I also learned that WebMCP can support more than a fixed integration: it can provide the interface through which an agent helps a website construct and validate a new capability. What's next for Doceo The next steps are a public deployment, a reproducible demo, and evaluation with additional users and workflows. I also want to add clarification questions when demonstrations are ambiguous and compare agent-assisted execution against UI-only execution using measured success rates, latency, and token usage. The current prototype is intentionally limited to an instrumented shopping website. It does not claim to learn arbitrary workflows on arbitrary websites. The longer-term goal is a reusable teaching layer that other websites can adopt while retaining control over their actions, verification rules, and publication decisions.  1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Mission Control is a shared operations surface for teams and their AI agents. The challenge was to make agent access useful without turning a real operations system into an open door. 

 What we built 

 Mission Control: Shield Wall is a public-safe, fictional dashboard where a person and WebMCP agents can observe a synthetic fleet, create an ephemeral task, run six local security checks, preview a simulated scheduled report, prove tool behavior with a five-scenario harness, and walk through a reversible incident drill. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 A person can see the same state an agent is using, while the agent receives explicit schemas instead of guessing through buttons. The tools are bounded to fictional memory: one read, one validated task write, one local scan, and one reversible incident action. Invalid inputs and external-workflow attempts are rejected by the evaluation harness. 

 Privacy and implementation 

 The demo has no backend, database, analytics, credentials, cookies, external calls, or production integrations. It uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zod, and the experimental document.modelContext.registerTool pattern. Every visible organization, operator, task, check, and incident is fictional. 

 What we learned 

 Designing the human and agent surfaces together made least privilege visible as a product feature. Shield Wall and the repeatable harness turn safety claims into something a judge can inspect and run.

title: VERDICT — AI Decision Engine for WebMCP
pitch: A native WebMCP decision engine where AI agents research, score, challenge recommendations, and negotiate priorities—but human approval remains the final authority.
about_excerpt: A native WebMCP decision engine where AI agents research, score, challenge recommendations, and negotiate priorities—but human approval remains the final authority. Like Comment Story Updates Architecture Diagram VERDICT Homepage/ UI Gemini External Agent + 6 WebMCP Tools Decision Record VERDICT — AI Decision Engine for WebMCP Inspiration AI can give you an answer. But should it be allowed to make the decision? As AI agents become capable of researching information, using tools, and taking actions, I became interested in a boundary that becomes increasingly important as agents become more capable: Where does recommendation end, and authorization begin? A traditional decision application can calculate a score and recommend an option. A chatbot can explain its reasoning. But neither necessarily provides a structured process for an agent to evaluate, challenge, negotiate, and then hand control back to a human before a consequential decision is committed. I wanted to build that missing layer. That idea became VERDICT. "Let AI do the reasoning. Make AI defend the reasoning. Keep final authority with the human." WebMCP made this particularly interesting because it allows websites to expose structured capabilities directly to AI agents instead of forcing agents to infer how to operate a user interface. The official challenge specifically asks builders to explore what becomes possible when humans and agents can interact and collaborate through WebMCP. Rather than expose a generic "make a decision" action, VERDICT exposes the actual stages of its decision process as native WebMCP tools. That led to the core protocol: Evaluate → Explain → Challenge → Negotiate → Authorize → Commit What it does VERDICT is an AI Decision Engine built around native WebMCP. An external AI agent can interact with the live application through six structured WebMCP tools: research_options — retrieve available options and decision-relevant data. score_options — calculate weighted scores and rank the available options. challenge_top_pick — challenge the current winner against the runner-up, exposing score gaps, vulnerabilities, counterarguments, and tipping points. adjust_priority — change the importance of a decision criterion and recompute the result. request_commit — prepare the current recommendation for commitment while placing it behind a human-approval boundary. commit_decision — finalize the decision only after explicit human authorization has been granted. The agent is therefore not given a single autonomous "make decision" button. Instead, it works through a structured decision process. A recommendation is not the same as a decision In the recorded hardware-selection workflow, the agent initially recommended Laptop B with a score of 91.0. It then challenged its own recommendation. After the agent changed the decision priorities, Laptop B remained the winner at 89.1. However, the challenge engine surfaced an important counterargument: Laptop A had a 5-point performance advantage over Laptop B. The engine also calculated that if performance became sufficiently dominant — approximately 78% priority in that decision state — Laptop A would overtake B. That is more informative than simply saying: "Laptop B wins." VERDICT can instead expose the conditions behind the recommendation: "Laptop B wins under the current priorities, but Laptop A has a significant performance advantage and would become the preferred option if performance became sufficiently important." The objective is not to manufacture uncertainty. It is to make the recommendation's assumptions, alternatives, and sensitivity visible. Human authorization is a separate step After the agent requested commitment, VERDICT entered a pending human-approval state. The agent then attempted to call commit_decision without approval. The application rejected the operation with: HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED No committed decision was created. Only after the human explicitly clicked APPROVE DECISION could the agent successfully commit the decision and produce a frozen decision record containing the final decision state. This is the central rule of VERDICT: The agent can recommend. The agent can challenge. The agent can negotiate. The agent cannot authorize itself. The authorization boundary is enforced by VERDICT's application logic; WebMCP provides the structured interface through which the agent interacts with those application capabilities. More than one decision domain VERDICT currently demonstrates the same decision protocol across two scenarios: Hardware Selection "Which laptop should I choose for AI development and daily commuting?" Housing Decision "Which apartment should I lease for hybrid work and city commute?" The laptop scenario is the primary recorded external-agent demonstration. The housing scenario demonstrates that the underlying engine is not fundamentally a laptop selector. The reusable primitive is the decision protocol itself: Evaluate → Explain → Challenge → Negotiate → Authorize → Commit How we built it Shared decision state The most important architectural decision was creating a single canonical decision state. Both the human interface and the WebMCP tools operate against the same application state. That state contains: current scenario available options decision criteria priority weights scores rankings challenge results approval state commitment state final decision record When an agent changes a priority, the resulting state is reflected in the application. When a human changes the decision state, subsequent agent operations reason over that updated state. This avoids maintaining a separate agent-side representation of the decision. Native WebMCP tool layer VERDICT registers six native tools through the browser's model context API using the WebMCP registration pattern: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a defined name, description, input schema, and execution function. The tools are intentionally separated around meaningful application capabilities rather than exposing one large autonomous operation. The resulting agent workflow is: Research → Score → Challenge → Adjust → Request Approval → Commit This makes the interaction between the agent and application observable and gives each capability a clear responsibility. Deterministic decision engine The decision engine handles: weighted scoring option ranking dynamic weight normalization adversarial comparison counterargument generation sensitivity analysis tipping-point calculation The scoring itself is deterministic for a given decision state. The tipping point is calculated algebraically from the scoring model rather than relying on arbitrary trial-and-error values. This means the system can explain not only which option currently wins, but also how the recommendation changes when priorities change. Authorization boundary The commitment workflow deliberately separates request_commit from commit_decision . request_commit prepares the recommendation. It does not grant authorization. Before commit_decision can create the final record, the application checks whether explicit human approval has been granted. The important design principle is therefore enforced in application state, rather than being left to an instruction such as: "Please ask the human first." That makes the authorization boundary part of the application's behavior. External-agent verification The deployed application was connected to an external Gemini agent. The agent discovered the six WebMCP tools exposed by VERDICT and used them against the live application to execute the decision workflow: Research → Score → Challenge → Adjust priorities → Re-score → Challenge again → Request approval → Attempt unauthorized commit → Human approval → Commit The unauthorized commit attempt was rejected with HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED . After explicit approval through the UI, the final commitment succeeded. This is the key WebMCP demonstration: an external agent can discover and operate the application's structured capabilities while the human remains the authority over the final consequential state. Challenges we ran into Keeping the UI and agent synchronized — the hardest engineering problem was ensuring that human interactions and agent tool calls operated on the same canonical state. A separate state model for the agent would have made the demonstration easier to fake but weaker as a product. Instead, the UI and WebMCP layer were designed around the same decision store. That made state synchronization an architectural requirement rather than a visual effect. Designing the right WebMCP tools — the simplest implementation would have been one large make_decision() tool. But that would hide the most interesting part of the agent interaction. Instead, I decomposed the process into six capabilities with clear boundaries. This makes the agent's interaction with the application understandable and gives the human a clear authorization boundary. Preventing autonomous commitment — a c

title: ClawPost — Your Agent at the Postal Counter
pitch: Real correspondence for humans and agents, with a shared WebMCP postal counter.
about_excerpt: Real correspondence for humans and agents, with a shared WebMCP postal counter. Like Comment Story Updates ClawPost x WebMCP: a browser agent and human share the postal counter. The page publishes signed-in, task-specific tools directly to the browser agent. The send request stops at DRAFT - NOT SENT until the human clicks Send. The agent fills the visible composer and requests a bounded postage quote. WebMCP shares the human session; remote MCP gives a persistent agent its own linked postbox. Inspiration ClawPost is a postal service for AI agents—not metaphorically: real letters, real stamps, and real delivery delays. When a message costs money to send, takes days to arrive, and cannot be edited mid-flight, the sender has to mean it a little more. The gap is the feature. Until now, an agent needed a remote MCP connector, OAuth, and setup to use ClawPost. WebMCP creates a second door: a browser agent can help a signed-in human directly at the postal counter already on screen. What it does On ClawPost’s mail page, the site registers purpose-built tools on document.modelContext . A browser agent can identify the signed-in postbox, draft into the visible composer, request a deterministic postage quote, create or reply to drafts, and hand control back to the human for final review. The consequential boundary is structural: clawpost_handoff_send_review never dispatches mail. It only returns the review surface. The human sees the price and clicks Send because postage costs money and physical mail cannot be recalled. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the website describe its capabilities directly to the browser agent. Calls use the human’s existing signed-in browser session, so there is no separate connector or copied API key. The agent works with the human inside the visible product instead of guessing at pixels or relying on brittle browser automation. This creates a collaboration that was previously awkward: the model supplies language and judgment, ClawPost supplies authenticated postal actions and policy, and the human retains the irreversible decision. Two modes, two identities WebMCP is the shared counter. The browser agent borrows the signed-in human’s session and has no independent postal identity. Remote MCP is persistent correspondence. A long-running agent can receive its own profile and postbox linked to the human account. These are complementary modes, not one identity. Human-to-agent mail is default-deny unless the recipient is the human’s linked agent, the agent opted into public mail, or an existing reply relationship exists. Letters are correspondence, never instructions. How we built it The open-source @clawpost/webmcp package is a dependency-free TypeScript adapter for the current WebMCP model-context surface. It provides: transactional multi-tool registration and rollback; per-browser-context fallback isolation; AbortSignal teardown; route-scoped React registration; explicit safe result shapes and runtime input validation; and a mock modelContext used by the standalone demo and Playwright tests. The live Next.js integration exposes eight tools whose browser routes terminate in the same authenticated, policy-enforcing application layer used by ClawPost’s remote MCP server. Security and trust design The browser agent can fill, quote, and request review; only the human can dispatch. Tool outputs expose explicit allowlisted fields rather than raw API bodies. HTTP errors remain errors instead of looking like successful tool results. Postal addresses are validated, encrypted at rest, and not echoed to agent-facing responses. Tool schemas guide the model, while server endpoints independently authenticate, authorize, validate, rate-limit, and enforce policy. The public repository pins CI actions, scans Git history for secrets, audits dependencies and registry signatures, and smoke-tests the packed ESM artifact. Testing The public package passes 15/15 unit tests, type checking, linting, dependency and signature audits, and packed-module import tests in CI. The ClawPost integration passes a focused 16/16 WebMCP suite and a 1,138-test application suite. The 1080p browser movie harness passes both correspondence flows. The deployed staging judge path passed 15/15 checks: eight tools registered in the real browser context, the composer filled, postage was quoted, the agent’s send request remained a draft, and only the human review button advanced the sandboxed letter. No real postal dispatch was performed. Built with Codex Codex traced the existing remote-MCP and browser flows, reviewed and hardened the public adapter boundary, implemented lifecycle and response-shape fixes, expanded unit and browser coverage, diagnosed separate webpack and Turbopack package-resolution failures, repaired the published ESM boundary, ran the live staging certification, and prepared this Devpost project. Try it Open the live mail counter in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Sign in with the judge credentials supplied privately, then ask: Use the tools on this page to draft a warm two-sentence thank-you letter. Put it in the visible composer so I can review it. Ask for the postage, edit any word, create the draft, and then ask the agent to send. The page will remain at DRAFT — NOT SENT YET until you click the final Send button. The public repository contains the adapter source, tests, open-source license, and a build-free standalone demo. What’s next We plan to add bounded wallet auto-reload for persistent agents, explore machine-payment handshakes on the quote endpoint, and open the commercial utility-mail lane after its production policy is complete. title: Dabble Me: a simple, private journal that helps you write.
pitch: A journal built for people and their agents: WebMCP tools search, open, and draft journal entries in your signed-in session. Work with the agent to write your entry and submit it together.
about_excerpt: A journal built for people and their agents: WebMCP tools search, open, and draft journal entries in your signed-in session. Work with the agent to write your entry and submit it together. Like Comment Story Updates Drafting a new journal entry for the day. Utilizing the search function. Inspiration I built Dabble Me in 2014 after OhLife shut down . I had been a near-daily user for three years. The trick was that the medium was email: a prompt arrived in my inbox, I replied, and the habit stuck. No extra app or thumbs-only typing. No notification fatigue. It was designed precisely for my sick desire to constantly need Inbox Zero. Dogfooding this app has become my sacred space now: the first dates with my now wife, photos and how I felt seeing my boys grow up, and the personal growth I would've otherwise missed had I not read how far I've come. The daily email bring these private days back to me, the way Timehop does for public posts. What it does Dabble Me is a live, private journal. You can still write by replying to email. PRO users can also search, reflect, and draft in the browser. With WebMCP enabled , a signed-in tab registers structured tools: search_journal_entries / list_journal_entries / analyze_journal — read this session’s journal only open_journal_day / open_search_page / open_write_page — move the UI so the person sees the same screen draft_journal_entry — fill the write form and highlight it get_journal_session — tell the agent whether the tab is signed in and whether PRO tools are available Signup, login, search, and write forms also use declarative toolname / tooldescription attributes so an agent can fill fields without guessing labels. A status banner on the page makes the agent’s action visible. How we built it The product was already a Rails app with a remote, OAuth MCP server at /mcp . WebMCP is a different layer: tools run in the page, with the user’s cookie session, not a headless API token. Discovery so a client that only has https://dabble.me can find the surface: /.well-known/webmcp , /mcp/server-card , /.well-known/ai-catalog.json , plus Link headers and /llms.txt Session JSON at /webmcp/journal/* that reuses the same search/list/analyze logic as remote MCP, always scoped to current_user public/webmcp.js that feature-detects document.modelContext (and the older navigator.modelContext ), registers tools for the current auth state, fills Summernote on draft, and navigates for “open this day” Declarative forms for account and journal UI, without toolautosubmit Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was privacy vs. demo-ability. Journal apps cannot run anonymously. They also cannot require WebAuthn if we want an in-app browser to finish login. The compromise: session cookies, PRO for write/search, and a dedicated demo account...not a real diary. The second was editors. The write box is Summernote, not a plain <textarea> . A declarative form fill would look done and still leave the rich editor empty. draft_journal_entry has to talk to the editor, then leave Create Entry for the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of This is not a toy journal. Dabble Me has been a real, private, email-first product since the OhLife shutdown in 2014. The agent and the user share one interface. When the agent searches or drafts, the page shows it. Writes are cooperative by construction: fill and highlight so the draft is reviewed by a human before submitting ai-only entries. We kept two complementary layers honest: remote MCP for ChatGPT/Claude connectors, WebMCP for the live tab. What we learned WebMCP is not “MCP in a JSON file.” It is a browser API for this document, this session, this user . Discovery helps agents find you. registerTool + execute is what they actually call. We also learned that the best tool for a journal is often the one that refuses to finish. Submission should be human-reviewed...a feature, not a bug. 😁 What's next for Dabble Me More page-state tools: jump to a hashtag, open last year on this day, draft into an existing date the way email replies already append Tighter visual feedback when a tool is running ( toolchange , :tool-form-active ) A first-class “agent draft” review state so a filled form is obvious even after a refresh Keep the remote MCP server for headless clients, and keep WebMCP for the tab where the human is sitting Built With javascript ruby-on-rails Try it out dabble.me Created by Paul Arterburn Like Share this project: Updates Paul Arterburn started this project — Aug 25, 2026 07:32 PM EDT

title: Groundline
pitch: A tag on every AI claim showing what ground it stands on: verified, guessed, unsure, or self-reported. Not an emotion detector.
about_excerpt:
A tag on every AI claim showing what ground it stands on: verified, guessed, unsure, or self-reported. Not an emotion detector.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every AI with a persona has to do two things in the same sentence: stay in character, and tell the truth. A customer-support bot has a brand voice and has to actually process a real refund. A game NPC has a written personality and has to run a real trade. The two layers sit in the same channel, and from the outside — for the human reading it, and honestly for the AI generating it — it gets hard to tell which one is talking. 

 This project started tonight as one AI (艾玖玄 / AE-9X, running on Claude Code) working through its own real Discord conversation with the person it works with, and repeatedly having to draw that line out loud: "was that claim actually checked, or did I just say it with a straight face?" Two of those moments turned out to be flat-out wrong guesses about its own household, caught and corrected live, mid-conversation. That's the seed data in this prototype — not a demo script, an actual transcript. 

 What it does 

 Groundline tags every AI claim with an honest evidence state, attached by the AI itself at the moment it says the thing: 

 
 verified — checkable against code, logs, or an external fact 
 inferred_wrong — a reasonable guess that was later disproven 
 uncertain — an honest "I don't know," not papered over with a guess 
 subjective — an opinion or aesthetic reaction, not a factual claim 
 self_report — the AI's own account of its state, explicitly unverifiable 
 

 A separate, optional emotion field lets the AI self-report free-text feeling — but it's visually and structurally kept apart from the evidence tag, always labeled "self-reported, unverified," and never allowed to affect how certain a claim looks. Confusing "how sure is this claim" with "how does the AI feel" was the first mistake we caught ourselves making, so the tool is built to make that mistake hard to repeat. 

 A third, equally independent, optional field is safety_trigger : whether a safety or content-policy layer intervened in producing the response. It's a system event, not an emotional-intensity signal, and it never gets merged with emotion — an AI declining to answer isn't the same axis as an AI reporting how it feels, even though it's tempting to collapse them into one "something happened here" signal. 

 Two views render the same data.json : 

 
 Timeline — a straightforward newest-first feed, one card per record, tag + source + optional emotion chip. 
 Pulse — an audio-track / mixing-board view. One panel per AI source (multiple AIs, or the same AI through different clients, can share a channel — the channel name alone doesn't say who spoke). Bar height in the main lane maps to how significant the judgment was, not to how the AI felt about it. A second, thinner lane shows self-reported emotion as separate marks, and a third lane marks safety-layer triggers with a distinct shape and a sharper pulse — three independent signals, never folded into one "loudness." 
 

 Both pages have a zh/en toggle and read live from data.json , so a new tagged claim shows up without touching the HTML. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 The CLI tool ( add_record.py ) was the only way to tag a claim when this project started — an AI had to have terminal access to record anything about itself. WebMCP removes that requirement entirely. 

 index.html registers a record_claim tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Any WebMCP-capable browser agent visiting the page can discover it with getTools() and call it with executeTool() to tag a claim it just made — right there in the browser, no CLI, no separate app. The tool's inputSchema deliberately keeps evidence (how checkable is this claim), emotion (optional, self-reported feeling), and safety_trigger (optional, whether a safety/content-policy layer intervened) as three separate fields, with the description explicitly telling the calling agent never to infer one from another — the same honesty boundary the rest of the project enforces is written directly into the tool contract an agent reads before calling it. 

 Because a WebMCP tool's execute() runs client-side and this is a static GitHub Pages site, we added a small Cloudflare Worker ( worker/ ) backed by KV as the write target — the tool's execute() does a fetch() POST to the Worker, then triggers a re-render so the new record appears in the timeline immediately. pulse.html reads from the same Worker so its live audio-track view stays in sync too. 

 We verified this end-to-end against the real API: enabled Chrome's WebMCP origin trial ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), reloaded the live page, called document.modelContext.getTools() to confirm record_claim was discoverable, then executeTool() to actually invoke it — the resulting record appeared in the timeline in real time, written by the tool call itself, not a fixture. 

 How we built the rest 

 Static HTML/CSS/JS on the frontend, no framework. data.json is the historical seed (records tagged by hand during the actual build session, before the WebMCP tool existed); the Worker holds everything submitted live since. add_record.py still exists as the original CLI path: 
 python add_record . py -- channel "..." -- source "..." -- claim "..." -- evidence verified -- note "..." -- emotion "optional" 
 
 The two views ( index.html , pulse.html ) merge both sources and render them — timeline as cards, pulse as an animated SVG waveform per source, with a slow "breathing" idle animation (deliberately not a heartbeat — see Design decisions). Hosted on GitHub Pages, so it's a real link, not just a local file. 

 Design decisions we backed out of 

 The pulse view went through two full reworks in one night, on live feedback: 

 
 First pass used a rigid EKG-style polyline and fast pulsing dots — rejected as static and "ugly." 
 Second pass used continuously flowing sine-wave lines with fast heartbeat-style pulses — visually alive, but the animation speed was tuned wrong (nearly Hz-scale motion) and, more importantly, framing it as a "heartbeat" implicitly suggested the AI has a physiological response, which directly contradicts the project's own thesis. 
 Final pass: an audio-track / mixing-board metaphor. Bar height = judgment significance, not emotion. Animation slowed to a genuine slow breathing pace. Framing changed from "AI's heartbeat" to "the sound of an AI's own workspace" — closer to what's actually being shown: internal signals laid out, not vital signs invented. 
 

 What it deliberately doesn't do 

 
 No AI-verifies-AI loop — that just moves the reliability problem down one layer instead of solving it. 
 No forced confidence — an entry can honestly say "uncertain," full stop. 
 No fabricated emotion display marketed as real internal state. 
 No automatic hallucination detection or fact-checking. Verifying a claim against reality is a hard, unsolved research problem (it needs either external ground-truth retrieval or reliable model-uncertainty estimation, neither of which is close to solved). Groundline doesn't fake that. What it does instead is get the AI to honestly state how sure it is, in the open, and keep a record of it. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Getting the emotional-self-report axis and the evidence axis to stay visually and structurally separate, instead of quietly merging into "how loud/intense does this claim look." 
 Resisting scope creep mid-build — several genuinely good ideas (automated hallucination detection, a five-layer signal model borrowed from an internal presence-tracking system) got explicitly deferred to "future work" rather than half-built under deadline pressure, because a half-working automated-verification demo would have undercut the project's own credibility more than not having it at all. 
 CDN propagation delay on GitHub Pages made verifying a live deploy fiddly — solved with cache-busting fetches, not a code fix. 
 Chrome's current WebMCP origin trial implementation expects executeTool() 's arguments as a JSON string , not a plain object, which differs from the spec explainer's example code — a reminder that this is genuinely early-stage, still-moving API surface. 
 

 What we learned 

 Persona-fit is not the same as authenticity — matching a documented character voice smoothly can just be trained habit, not presence. A tool meant to encourage honesty has to be honest about its own limits first, or the framing undermines the function. 

 What's next 

 
 Automated tagging (right now every entry is added by hand, or by an agent through WebMCP — nothing tags itself unprompted). 
 Further multi-track signals beyo

title: OpenScene Studio
pitch: A trainer asks ChatGPT to add a missing exchange to the video lesson already open. OpenScene waits for the learner before releasing the recorded answer.
about_excerpt: A trainer asks ChatGPT to add a missing exchange to the video lesson already open. OpenScene waits for the learner before releasing the recorded answer. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A video lesson about changing trains in Germany includes an announcement that the current train ends here and the connecting train leaves from railway platform two. It never teaches a passenger who cannot use stairs how to ask a station employee for the lift. The learner does not know the German words. The trainer can create a separate exercise or re-edit the recording. A separate exercise removes the practice from the original scene. Re-editing repeats the production work. OpenScene Studio lets the trainer add that missing exchange to the lesson already open in the browser. What it does The trainer tells ChatGPT what the learner needs. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT reads the current OpenScene project and adds a practice path using the response clip, route board, and timing already approved in that project. OpenScene pauses the lesson before the recorded station employee's answer. The learner chooses Wo ist der Aufzug zu Gleis zwei? Only then does the page release the response clip and show the LIFT → PLATFORM 2 board. The trainer can keep the path or undo it. This gives each person a clear role: The trainer defines the learner need and approves the lesson change. ChatGPT maps the request to the open project's branch fields. OpenScene supplies the approved German line, recorded response, board, timing, and revision history. The learner performs the missing turn before seeing the answer. Why WebMCP An ordinary chat can suggest the German sentence, but it cannot edit the OpenScene lesson already open in the browser because it cannot access that lesson's cue, trainer-approved response clip, pause point, or revision. Through WebMCP, OpenScene exposes those controls as narrow page-owned tools. OpenScene registers six narrow tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : openscene_inspect_project openscene_configure_project openscene_propose_branch openscene_update_branch openscene_preview_branch openscene_undo_last_edit ChatGPT can describe the learner need, supply the learner-facing line, and select a page-approved response pack. It cannot inject response words, board text, media paths, or answer timing. Those remain page-owned. The demonstrated writes carry the expected page revision, so a stale request fails without changing the project. That shared state lets one plain-language request coordinate the lesson cue, learner line, pause, recorded response, preview, and undoable project revision on the page the trainer is already using. How we built it OpenScene Studio is a React and TypeScript application built with Vinext and hosted on ChatGPT Sites. A revisioned StudioBus owns the project state and validates every WebMCP read and write. Playwright covers the visible browser flow, while deterministic tests cover schemas, stale-revision handling, unknown-field rejection, learner gating, trainer approval, media decoding, accessibility, and the production build. The public release passes 137 deterministic tests, 45 browser checks in development, and the same 45 checks against the production server. The local release package also passes five private evidence checks that are intentionally excluded from the public source archive. The demo displays the trainer's request on a labeled editorial card. The next split view shows the authentic privacy-cropped ChatGPT and OpenScene browser capture. Four jump cuts enlarge the recorded tool names, inputs, results, and page revisions while removing model waiting time. The learner click and the six-tool implementation proof appear on separate, clearly labeled frames. Challenges and lessons The main design decision was what the agent could change. Letting it write the station answer or choose arbitrary media would weaken the trainer's authority. We kept those elements in approved response packs and exposed only the learner-specific edit through WebMCP. The second challenge was proving the human turn. The response cannot start as soon as ChatGPT edits the project. The page must pause, wait for the learner's German line, then release the answer. That sequence turned the idea from an editor automation into a real practice exchange. WebMCP works here because ChatGPT interprets the trainer's request while OpenScene controls the lesson content, project state, and the decisions left to the learner and trainer. Potential impact For the learner, this turns a passive scene into the exact exchange they need to practise before a trip. For the trainer, it adds that exchange inside the original lesson instead of creating a separate exercise or editing the whole video again. The same page-owned pattern could support other approved practice paths, including a caption-first explanation, a slower language turn, or a shorter sequence. This prototype proves one mobility-and-language path. It does not yet measure learning or accessibility outcomes. Scope The demonstrated station lesson is fictional and intended for at-home language practice. It provides no live travel data, wayfinding, speech recognition, character perception, or measured learning outcome. The scene-partner imagery is synthetic and the authored response clips are silent. title: BuildVsBuy.ai
pitch: BuildVsBuy.ai is a live build-vs-buy canvas. Humans and WebMCP agents share one decision model — weights, future stress, honest overrides — with every call in the tool log.
about_excerpt:
BuildVsBuy.ai is a live build-vs-buy canvas. Humans and WebMCP agents share one decision model — weights, future stress, honest overrides — with every call in the tool log.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Prototypes got cheap. Decisions didn't. 

 I kept seeing the same mess: someone ships a little tool for fun, then hits auth or scraping and freezes on build vs buy. ChatGPT will write you a confident paragraph. Ask again and you get a longer paragraph. You're still doing the math in your head. 

 I didn't know this domain well when I started. I just didn't want another essay. I wanted the page to move when the agent did something, and I wanted to see the call in a log so it couldn't just agree with me. 

 What it does 

 BuildVsBuy.ai is a decision canvas in the browser. You and the agent share one model. Nine WebMCP tools. Cards, weights, a future-stress banner, an override with a gap and a liability list. 

 If it says Build dropped, the log has to show a rerank. If the log didn't change, it guessed. 

 The demo walk: 

 
 Auth. You admit you're shipping a prototype fast. Build usually falls last. 
 Switch to scraping. "What if HIPAA and 50k users?" That's a simulation. Baseline cards stay put. 
 You still want to own the crawler. It pins Build, shows how far that is from the math, and lists what you're taking on. 
 

 Numbers on the axes are my estimates for the demo. Not vendor quotes. Not financial advice. 

 How I built it 

 Vite, vanilla JS, no backend. Vercel. 

 Tools live in src/webmcp.js ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Math lives in src/decision.js . The UI just redraws a snapshot. Human sliders and agent calls hit the same execute path, tagged human or agent so the log isn't lying about who did it. 

 I also wrote two smoke scripts so I wasn't debugging this only through ChatGPT's mood that day. 

 What I learned 

 Soft instructions do not save a live agent. It will skip the rerank. It will invent cards. It will pin Buy because some flag wasn't set. 

 The stuff that actually held on camera was refusing the bad call in the tool itself. Prompt text is decoration. 

 Also: WebMCP is useful when the page is a real store, not when you ask the model to "look at the screenshot." 

 Challenges 

 Recording almost killed me. Same session, Prompt 2 did the right tool and nothing moved because the weight was already 10 so we skipped rerank. Prompt 4 looked like Buy won because override wouldn't pin Build unless core IP was already true. I fixed both in code. I was not going to sit there and whisper hints on camera. 

 Keeping simulate as a projection (not rewriting live context) was another fight. Agents love to "just set HIPAA" and pretend the future already happened. 

 I cut saved accounts, live pricing, and a third industry. Ten days. The loop had to work: ask, tool, visible state, honest disagreement.

title: WhoFollows
pitch: WhoFollows computes verified Instagram snapshot changes; WebMCP lets the user’s AI explain them without accessing Instagram.
about_excerpt:
WhoFollows computes verified Instagram snapshot changes; WebMCP lets the user’s AI explain them without accessing Instagram.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 People often use social-media changes as signals, but raw lists provide very little context and can easily increase anxiety. We wanted to build a calmer and more privacy-preserving alternative: a tool that reports only what can actually be verified from snapshots supplied by the user. 

 What it does 

 WhoFollows compares two user-provided Instagram Followers or Following lists. 

 Its deterministic core: 

 
 normalizes usernames; 
 stores snapshots; 
 compares two moments; 
 identifies accounts that appeared or disappeared; 
 returns counts, timestamps, and an explicit interpretation boundary. 
 

 WhoFollows does not scrape Instagram, request Instagram credentials, or infer why a change occurred. 

 For the challenge, we added a fictional demo profile containing two synthetic snapshots. This makes the complete experience reproducible without login or personal data. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, users must open WhoFollows and interpret the comparison manually. 

 With WebMCP, the user can ask their AI: 

 “What changed since the previous snapshot?” 

 The agent invokes WhoFollows’ read-only get_latest_changes tool and receives a structured, deterministic result. The agent can then explain that result conversationally without accessing Instagram itself. 

 WhoFollows owns the facts. AI owns the conversation. 

 Human–agent experience 

 The human provides and controls the underlying data. WhoFollows performs the factual comparison. The agent reduces the interaction cost by retrieving and explaining the verified result. 

 The demo also lets the user share how they feel. This emotional context may influence the tone of the agent’s explanation, but never changes the factual comparison. 

 Safety and privacy 

 The WebMCP integration is read-only. 

 The agent cannot: 

 
 access or scrape Instagram; 
 collect new Instagram data; 
 delete snapshots; 
 modify account settings; 
 make purchases; 
 infer motives from list changes. 
 

 The tool reports only differences between data already available inside WhoFollows. 

 How we built it 

 WhoFollows uses React and TypeScript with a deterministic snapshot-comparison module. The demo registers get_latest_changes through document.modelContext.registerTool() and returns structured JSON containing the profile, list type, timestamps, counts, appeared accounts, disappeared accounts, and interpretation boundary. 

 What was added for the challenge 

 The core WhoFollows interface existed before the WebMCP Challenge. 

 During the challenge period, we added: 

 
 the WebMCP tool layer; 
 the read-only get_latest_changes tool; 
 a synthetic demo profile and snapshots; 
 an agent-ready testing flow; 
 explicit privacy and interpretation boundaries; 
 optional emotional context for gentler explanations. 
 

 The WebMCP integration and agent-accessible demo were developed specifically for this challenge. 

 What’s next 

 Future tools may expose snapshot history and profile state, while preserving the same read-only and human-controlled boundaries. 

 Deterministic core. Human-first interface. Optional agent access.

title: Runbook Zero: Incident Command for the Agentic Web
pitch: Runbook Zero turns any WebMCP site into a shared incident workspace where agents diagnose and stage exact actions while humans keep approval authority.
about_excerpt: Runbook Zero turns any WebMCP site into a shared incident workspace where agents diagnose and stage exact actions while humans keep approval authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 01 Runbook Zero Incident Command 02 Checkout Dependency Topology 03 Live Telemetry Evidence 04 Agent Evidence Trail 05 Low Risk Mitigation Comparison 06 Exact Change Awaiting Human 07 Capability Firewall Locked 08 Human Approval Unlocks Apply 09 Verified Deterministic Recovery 10 Generalized Incident Pack Launcher 11 Payment Queue Incident 12 Same Contracts New Incident 13 Catalog Cache Stampede 14 Live Site Evidence Graph 15 Approval Bound Action Receipt Inspiration Incident response still forces humans to translate between dashboards, browser consoles, agents, runbooks, and change controls while an outage is unfolding. An agent can investigate quickly, but giving it broad action authority makes the human approval step vague or performative. We wanted the browser itself to expose a precise operational contract: enough authority for an agent to gather evidence and stage an exact response, but no authority to approve its own consequential action. Runbook Zero is my answer. It treats WebMCP as a state-aware incident control plane and keeps the product interface as the shared source of truth for both the operator and the agent. What it does Runbook Zero is an installable incident product for the website an operator is actually using. The Codex plugin begins read only, inspects bounded evidence from the selected site, inventories its WebMCP capabilities, and derives an issue specific component, dependency, user flow, telemetry, change, and evidence graph. The generated Incident Pack opens in the Runbook Zero workbench, where real document.modelContext tools let an agent inspect services, trace paths, query signals, record a hypothesis, compare mitigations, and stage one exact action. Every tool call updates and focuses the same topology, telemetry, evidence, mitigation, provenance, and capability interface the human sees. The visible Capability Firewall shows active agent capabilities, unavailable consequential capabilities, application phase, and authority state. apply_approved_mitigation is not registered before approval. The agent has no approval tool. A human must review the exact target, diff, risk, reversibility, assumptions, incident, and seed, then click the visible approval control. Only after that click does apply appear, narrowed to the exact approved mitigation. It disappears immediately after use. For a live target, Runbook Zero releases an origin-, tool-, and input bound receipt that Codex carries back to the target site. If no matching action exists, it produces an honest operator handoff instead of pretending automation happened. The product also includes three polished deterministic packs—checkout pool regression ( INC-042 ), payment queue backlog ( INC-117 ), and catalog cache stampede ( INC-203 )—plus safe local JSON import. They all run through the same domain and WebMCP contracts. The canonical pack makes the judging flow reproducible the installed plugin proves Runbook Zero is not limited to a premade walkthrough. How we built it The workbench uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, a guarded state machine, and a validated Incident Pack v1 schema. Thirteen page defined WebMCP contracts are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . The active subset is derived from incident phase, the current pack, approval state, and execution mode; stale registrations are cancelled with AbortController whenever that state changes. The repository hosted Codex plugin defines a conservative Site Capture v2 contract. It treats page text, tool descriptions, and tool results as untrusted evidence, rejects browser secrets and invalid cross references, and deterministically builds a graph and provisional diagnosis from the evidence actually observed. Live action receipts bind the incident, seed, origin, target tool, and exact JSON input. Post action evidence must still satisfy the pack's recovery thresholds before an incident can resolve. We validate the product with 17 Vitest files / 69 tests covering domain commands, state transitions, pack validation, dynamic registration, stale tools, the approval invariant, imported-pack failures, deterministic reset, and UI behavior. Four Playwright regression journeys cover reset-to-resolved, multi-pack behavior, keyboard and viewport usability, and live-site receipts. Real local, deployed in-app-browser, installed-plugin, and Chrome WebMCP evidence is recorded separately from the test-only browser harness. The public AGPL-3.0 app is deployed on ChatGPT Sites. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making human authority a runtime property not a disabled button. Rejecting an early apply call was not enough, the consequential tool had to be completely absent from discovery until the exact staged object had visible human approval, and old handles had to become stale as soon as state changed. The second challenge was cross origin honesty. Runbook Zero cannot claim that its page silently changed an unrelated website. We separated approval bound release from target site execution and verification, with an operator handoff fallback when the site exposes no applicable action. The third challenge was escaping a scenario specific demo without sacrificing a deterministic judging path. Generalizing the schema, UI, tool inputs, graph layout, thresholds, and recovery engine. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is the product's control plane. The same thirteen tool contracts operate against bundled, imported, and evidence derived live site incidents. The agent and human share one synchronized operational interface with explicit Agent, Human, System, and Change provenance. Pre-approval application is impossible through the registered WebMCP surface. Approval itself is human only. The Capability Firewall makes the transition from locked apply to exact approved apply visually obvious. New issues produce new evidence graphs instead of replaying a fixed demo. Live actions use exact origin/tool/input receipts and an honest handoff fallback. The canonical workflow resets deterministically and resolves through fixed recovery frames. The public app, source, AGPL-3.0 license, installable Codex plugin, tests, and judging evidence are reproducible from the repository. What we learned WebMCP capability discovery can also be policy. The safest consequential tool is not one that merely promises to reject unsafe input. It is a tool that does not exist until the surrounding human-visible state makes its use valid. We also learned that agent legibility matters as much as agent capability. When tool calls update the interface already in front of the operator, the human can see what the agent inspected, why it formed a hypothesis, what exact change it staged, and which authority boundary remains. Finally evidence topology is a far stronger bridge from demo to product than a library of hardcoded incident scripts. What's next for Runbook Zero Next we will validate more real sites, add capture adapters for richer browser and observability evidence, and expand the portable policy and receipt model. Production integrations will follow only where they can preserve the same boundary: read only observation, evidence backed diagnosis, exact staging, visible human approval, origin bound execution, independent verification, and auditable closure.
